<webpage_content>
![Home](/themes/custom/rndsystems/images/RnD-Systems_primary-logo_color.svg)

# Immunology News: Researchers Identify NR4A and TOX Transcription Factors As Mediators of CD8+ T Cell Exhaustion – Implications for Cancer Immunotherapy

CD8+ T cell exhaustion or dysfunction is frequently observed in chronic viral infections and cancer due to persistent antigen exposure and chronic T cell receptor (TCR) signaling. The exhausted T cell state is associated with a decrease in proliferative capacity, reduced effector functions, changes in gene expression and metabolism, and elevated and sustained expression of multiple inhibitory receptors, including [PD-1](/target/pd-1), [CTLA-4](/target/ctla-4), [TIM-3](/target/tim-3), [LAG-3](/target/lag-3), [TIGIT](/target/tigit), and [2B4/CD244](/target/2b4-cd244-slamf4). Under steady state conditions, these inhibitory receptors, also known as [immune checkpoint](https://www.rndsystems.com/products/immune-checkpoint) proteins, are transiently expressed on activated T cells and play a key role in maintaining immune homeostasis by regulating the duration and magnitude of T cell responses. In the exhausted T cell state, the expression of these receptors remains high and T cell activity is reduced, thereby preventing effective elimination of pathogens and tumors.

### **CTLA-4 and PD-1 Have Been Targeted to try to Reverse T Cell Exhaustion**

Exhausted T cells were initially characterized in mice infected with chronic lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV), but a similar T cell phenotype was also later reported in humans with hepatitis C virus (HCV) or [human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)](/research-area/immunology/infectious-diseases) infections, and in human cancer. Subsequent studies showed that the severity of T cell exhaustion typically correlated with the number of inhibitory receptors that were co-expressed. As a result, researchers and clinicians have tried to improve anti-viral and anti-tumor immune responses by targeting one or more of these inhibitory receptors using antibodies that block their interactions with their respective ligands to try to reverse the exhausted phenotype and restore T cell functions. Some of these studies have shown remarkable promise. For example, monoclonal antibodies directed against the T cell co-inhibitory receptors, CTLA-4 or PD-1 have resulted in increased patient survival in a number of different cancer types including melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and non-small cell lung cancer. Unfortunately, however, clinicians have found that blocking CTLA-4 or PD-1 is only effective in a minority of patients and many of the patients that initially respond to treatment later become resistant or relapse likely due to an upregulation of other inhibitory receptors. Similarly, [CAR T-cell therapy](/resources/webinars/cell-and-gene-therapies-cancer-future-promises-and-challenges), which has been successful in the treatment of leukemias and lymphomas, has not been successfully used to treat solid tumors at least in part because the CAR T cells become exhausted. Consequently, researchers started searching for the specific factors that drive the development of the exhausted T cell phenotype with the hope of understanding how this phenotype is being generated and identifying additional potential targets for cancer immunotherapy.

### **The Transcription Factor NR4A1 is Involved in the Development of T Cell Exhaustion**

In April 2019, two papers published in *Nature* reported that the nuclear receptor transcription factor (NR4A) family plays a key role in regulating the induction of T cell exhaustion.1,2 In the first paper by Liu, *et al*., the authors used an *in vitro* T cell tolerance induction system to analyze the gene expression and epigenetic features of mouse tolerant T (Ttol) cells. This analysis demonstrated that anergy-related genes and transcriptional repressors were up-regulated in Ttol cells, while effector genes and mitochondria-, ribosome-, and proteasome-related genes were suppressed.1 Additionally, the authors showed that both the gene loci for anergy-associated genes and exhaustion-related genes, including the genes encoding the inhibitory receptors, LAG-3, PD-1, and TIGIT, displayed histone H3 trimethylation on lysine 4 (H3K4me3), indicating that these genes were actively transcribed in Ttol cells, while those encoding transcription factors and effector cytokines associated with different T cell subsets had low levels of H3K4me3 and were not actively transcribed. Significantly, one particular transcription factor that was up-regulated in Ttol cells was [Nr4a1](/target/NGFI-B-alpha-Nur77-NR4A1), which the authors investigated further to try to understand the role that this factor was playing in these cells. Subsequent experiments demonstrated that overexpression of Nr4a1 in CD4+ T cells led to an up-regulation of anergy-related genes and a down-regulation of [IL-2](/target/il-2) and [IFN-gamma](/target/ifn-gamma) expression, while deletion of Nr4a1 in either CD4+ or CD8+ T cells led to an increase in IL-2 and/or IFN-gamma expression, suggesting that Nr4a1 was involved in mediating the Ttol phenotype. Using either an oral tolerance or peptide-induced tolerance model in wild-type and *Nr4a1-/-* mice, the authors showed that Nr4a1 is required for the *in vivo* induction of T cell tolerance as development of the Ttol phenotype was blocked in the absence of Nr4a1. Having previously observed that Nr4a1 was up-regulated in chronic virus-associated T cell exhaustion, the authors next investigated the role of Nr4a1 in a mouse model of lymphoma and found that *Nr4a1-/-* CD8+ T cells adoptively transferred into tumor-bearing mice expressed lower levels of PD-1 and TIM-3, showed better tumor infiltration, and were significantly more efficient at eliminating tumors than wild-type CD8+ T cells. Using chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing to identify Nr4a1 binding sites, they found that a significant number of Nr4a1 binding sites overlapped with [c-Jun](/target/c-jun) binding sites and the top Nr4a1-binding sites were AP-1 consensus sequences, suggesting that Nr4a1 induces T cell tolerance by antagonizing AP-1-mediated gene expression.

### **Deletion of the NR4A Transcription Factors Improves CAR T Cell Functions**

In the second paper, Chen, *et al*. found that two NR4A family members, *NR4A1* and *NR4A2*, were up-regulated in CD8+ tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) in human melanoma.2 They also showed that the expression of these proteins strongly correlated with the expression of PD-1 and TIM-3 and that the accessible chromatin regions in CD8+PD-1high TILs from human melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer were enriched for NR4A binding motifs, suggesting that the NR4A transcription factor family was involved in mediating T cell exhaustion. The authors further investigated the activities of the NR4A transcription factors by looking at the functions of wild-type CD8+ CAR T cells compared to *Nr4a* triple knockout (*Nr4a1-/-Nr4a2-/-Nr4a3-/-*) CD8+ CAR T cells in two mouse solid tumor models. This analysis demonstrated that tumor-bearing mice adoptively transferred with *Nr4a* triple knockout CD8+ CAR T cells displayed pronounced tumor regression and enhanced survival relative to those that received either wild-type CD8+ CAR T cells or CD8+ CAR T cells with a single knockout of [*Nr4a1*](/target/NGFI-B-alpha-Nur77-NR4A1), [*Nr4a2*](/target/nurr1-ngfi-b-beta-nr4a2), or [*Nr4a3*](/target/NR4A3-NOR1). Subsequent examination of the gene expression and chromatin accessibility profiles in *Nr4a* triple knockout CD8+ CAR TILs compared to wild-type CD8+ CAR TILs, revealed that the *Nr4a* triple knockout TILs showed reduced expression of inhibitory receptors, including PD-1, TIM-3, TIGIT, 2B4/CD244, and CD38, increased expression of effector genes, and a strong enrichment in open chromatin containing binding motifs for transcription factors involved in effector functions. As a result, this group concluded that the NR4A transcription factor family regulates the T cell exhaustion phenotype and may be potential next generation targets for cancer immunotherapy.

### **TOX and TOX2 Transcription Factors are also Involved in the Induction of CD8+ T Cell Exhaustion**

These two papers were followed by a series of papers published in June and July of 2019 that suggested that the (HMG)-box transcription factors [TOX](/target/thymocyte%20selection-associated%20high%20mobility%20group%20box) and [TOX2](/target/TOX2) are also involved in the induction of the exhausted T cell phenotype.3-8 Using mouse models of acute or chronic infection, Yao, *et al*., Khan, *et al*., Alfei, *et al*., and Scott, *et al*., all demonstrated that *Tox* expression was up-regulated in exhausted CD8+ T cells that developed in response to chronic viral infection.5-8 Additionally, Wang, *et al*., Khan, *et al*., and Scott, *et al*. showed that TOX is also highly expressed in tumor-infiltrating PD-1high CD8+ T cells in a number of different types of human cancers and that this expression correlates with high expression of CTLA-4, TIM-3, TIGIT, and PD-1.3, 6, 8 Furthermore, using a CAR T cell model, Seo, *et al*. found that like the NR4A transcription factors, *Tox* and *Tox2* were highly induced in exhausted PD-1highTIM-3high CD8+ CAR T cells. The authors went on to show that tumor-bearing mice adoptively transferred with CD8+ T cells from *Tox2-/-* mice that also expressed a CAR retrovirus and four shRNAs targeting *Tox* displayed pronounced tumor regression and enhanced survival relative to those that received either wild-type CD8+ CAR T cells or CD8+ CAR T cells deficient in either *Tox* or *Tox2* alone. Like some of the other groups, they also demonstrated the involvement of the NFAT transcription factor family in the induction of *Tox*, *Tox2*, *Nr4a2*, and *Nr4a3* expression in exhausted CD8+ T cells in the absence of AP-1 binding. As a result, they suggested a model in which NFAT induces both the Tox and Nr4a family transcription factors, which together mediate the induction of the CD8+ T cell exhaustion program. Collectively, these observations demonstrate that inhibition of the NR4A and/or TOX family transcription factors may represent powerful new strategies for cancer immunotherapy.

args.summary:
This article from R&D Systems covers recent immunology research identifying NR4A and TOX transcription factors as key mediators of CD8+ T cell exhaustion, with important implications for cancer immunotherapy. CD8+ T cell exhaustion occurs in chronic viral infections and cancer due to persistent antigen exposure and chronic TCR signaling, characterized by reduced proliferative capacity, decreased effector functions, and sustained expression of multiple inhibitory receptors including PD-1, CTLA-4, TIM-3, LAG-3, TIGIT, and 2B4/CD244. Blocking CTLA-4 or PD-1 has shown promise in treating melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and non-small cell lung cancer, but is only effective in a minority of patients, with many eventually developing resistance or relapse. CAR T-cell therapy has also struggled with solid tumors partly due to T cell exhaustion.

Two papers published in Nature in April 2019 identified the NR4A nuclear receptor transcription factor family as key regulators of T cell exhaustion. Liu et al. showed that Nr4a1 overexpression in CD4+ T cells upregulated anergy-related genes and downregulated IL-2 and IFN-gamma, while Nr4a1 deletion increased IL-2/IFN-gamma expression. Nr4a1-/- CD8+ T cells in a lymphoma model expressed lower PD-1 and TIM-3, showed better tumor infiltration, and eliminated tumors more efficiently than wild-type cells. The mechanism involves Nr4a1 antagonizing AP-1-mediated gene expression. Chen et al. found NR4A1 and NR4A2 upregulated in CD8+ tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in human melanoma, with expression correlating with PD-1 and TIM-3. Nr4a triple knockout (Nr4a1, Nr4a2, Nr4a3) CD8+ CAR T cells showed pronounced tumor regression and enhanced survival in two mouse solid tumor models compared to wild-type or single-knockout CAR T cells.

A series of papers from June-July 2019 demonstrated that the HMG-box transcription factors TOX and TOX2 are also involved in inducing T cell exhaustion. Multiple groups (Yao, Khan, Alfei, Scott, Wang, and Seo) showed TOX is upregulated in exhausted CD8+ T cells during chronic viral infection and highly expressed in PD-1high tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells across several human cancers, correlating with CTLA-4, TIM-3, TIGIT, and PD-1 expression. Seo et al. showed that CD8+ T cells deficient in both Tox and Tox2 displayed pronounced tumor regression and enhanced survival in CAR T cell models. The NFAT transcription factor family induces Tox, Tox2, Nr4a2, and Nr4a3 expression in exhausted CD8+ T cells in the absence of AP-1 binding. A proposed model suggests NFAT induces both the Tox and Nr4a families, which together mediate CD8+ T cell exhaustion. Collectively, inhibition of NR4A and/or TOX family transcription factors may represent powerful new strategies for cancer immunotherapy.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850)Abstract

N 6-methyladenosine (m 6 A) RNA methylation, primarily mediated by methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3), has emerged as a redox-sensitive epitranscriptomic switch in atherosclerosis (AS). Oxidative stress (OS) remodels the vascular transcriptome via m 6 A reprogramming, driving endothelial dysfunction, vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) phenotypic transition, and macrophage inflammatory activation. Reactive oxygen species directly influence METTL3 expression and activity, while METTL3 reciprocally modulates oxidative stress by regulating antioxidant defenses, ROS-scavenging enzymes, and redox homeostasis. Mechanistically, METTL3 promotes mitochondrial fission by enhancing Drp1 translation and suppresses mitochondrial biogenesis via destabilizing PGC-1α transcripts, converging to impair redox resilience and amplify inflammation. Inhibition of METTL3 alleviates intimal hyperplasia, restores contractile phenotypes, and may synergize with antioxidant therapy, mitochondrial quality control reinforcement, or pyroptosis suppression. Beyond METTL3, METTL4-mediated mitochondrial DNA 6 mA methylation also contributes to AS, with selective antagonists providing vascular protection. Natural products such as tanshinone and quercetin modulate m 6 A pathways, offering molecularly defined yet culturally rooted interventions. Deciphering the bidirectional crosstalk between ROS and epitranscriptomic regulation will guide precision therapeutics that bridge oxidative biology, RNA regulation, and translational cardiovascular medicine.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850)Abstract

**Keywords:**METTL3, m 6 A RNA methylation, Atherosclerosis, Reactive oxygen species, Pyroptosis, Mitochondrial quality control

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850)Introduction

1
Atherosclerosis (AS), characterized by lipid accumulation, immune cell infiltration, and vascular remodeling, is a chronic inflammatory disease that underlies major cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke. It remains one of the leading causes of mortality and disability worldwide. Extensive research has established oxidative stress—defined as an imbalance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and antioxidant defenses—as a key driver in the development and progression of AS. Oxidative stress contributes directly to endothelial dysfunction, inflammatory activation, and plaque instability [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib1)]. Beyond causing molecular damage to proteins, DNA, and lipids, ROS also function as signaling molecules that influence cellular fate at the levels of transcription, translation, and post-translational modification.

Among various stress-responsive regulatory mechanisms, epitranscriptomic modifications—particularly N6-methyladenosine (m 6 A) methylation of mRNA—have gained considerable attention. This reversible RNA modification plays pivotal roles under various pathological stress conditions. In cardiovascular disease, METTL3, a core m 6 A methyltransferase, has been implicated in regulating vascular inflammation, immune cell activation, and phenotypic switching of endothelial and smooth muscle cells [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib2)]. However, its upstream regulation and downstream effectors under oxidative stress remain incompletely defined. Recent evidence indicates that oxidative stress modulates METTL3 expression and enzymatic activity via multiple redox-sensitive pathways [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib3)]. Conversely, METTL3 affects the expression of antioxidant enzymes, inflammasome components, and mitochondrial function-related proteins [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib4)]. This reciprocal regulation suggests a potential feedback loop between oxidative stress and m 6 A-dependent post-transcriptional control, which may play a critical role in vascular pathophysiology.

Notably, two redox-sensitive mechanisms—pyroptosis and mitochondrial quality control (MQC)—have recently emerged as key processes contributing to vascular dysfunction under oxidative stress [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib5)]. Pyroptosis, a form of programmed inflammatory cell death mediated by the NLRP3 inflammasome and gasdermin D (GSDMD), is closely associated with endothelial injury and plaque progression. MQC, a complex system that maintains mitochondrial homeostasis—including mitophagy, fusion/fission dynamics, mitochondrial biogenesis, and mitochondrial-derived vesicles (MDVs)—plays a decisive role in determining cell fate under stress.

Taken together, these findings raise a fundamental scientific question: How does METTL3 integrate redox signaling to modulate downstream pyroptosis and mitochondrial quality control processes, thereby influencing endothelial homeostasis and the progression of atherosclerosis? To address this question, this review will focus on three major themes ([Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#fig1)): (1) The regulation of METTL3 by oxidative stress in AS-related models; (2) The role of METTL3-mediated m 6 A modification in the control of pyroptosis and MQC pathways; (3) The therapeutic potential and challenges of targeting the "oxidative stress–METTL3–pyroptosis/MQC axis" in the treatment of atherosclerosis.Fig. 1**The Process of Atherosclerosis Development.** The development of atherosclerosis involves multiple pathological processes, including pyroptosis, mitochondrial quality control, and oxidative stress.Fig. 1

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850)METTL3: A central epigenetic regulator in atherosclerosis

2
m 6 A is the most prevalent internal modification of eukaryotic mRNA. As a rapid, reversible, and stress-sensitive mechanism of gene regulation, m 6 A has garnered considerable attention in cardiovascular research in recent years. Within the m 6 A “writer” complex, METTL3 functions as the core catalytic subunit, forming a complex with METTL14 and WTAP to mediate methylation deposition [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib6)]. Through recognition by “reader” proteins such as YTHDF1/2/3, m 6 A-modified transcripts undergo dynamic regulation of stability, translational efficiency, and decay, thereby precisely influencing cellular function [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib7)]. Increasing evidence indicates that METTL3 plays a critical role in the pathogenesis and progression of AS, exhibiting context- and cell type-specific functions during different stages of the disease. ### METTL3 in endothelial cells

2.1
Endothelial dysfunction represents an early and pivotal event in the initiation of atherosclerosis. Various pathological stimuli—such as oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL), hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, and oscillatory shear stress—have been shown to significantly upregulate METTL3 expression in vascular endothelial cells [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib10),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib8),[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib9)]. This upregulation is not incidental but reflects a fundamental molecular adaptation of endothelial cells to injurious signals. Upon induction, METTL3 acts as a key m 6 A methyltransferase, targeting transcripts involved in inflammatory and apoptotic signaling. By enhancing m 6 A modification on these mRNAs, METTL3 stabilizes their expression and promotes translation, thereby shifting endothelial cells toward a pro-inflammatory and pro-death phenotype, exacerbating vascular injury.

Mechanistically, in human aortic endothelial cells stimulated with oxLDL, METTL3 is activated and increases m 6 A methylation on NLRP3 (NOD-like receptor family, pyrin domain containing 3) mRNA, enhancing its stability and preventing degradation [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib9)]. Sustained NLRP3 expression leads to inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation, which promotes the maturation and secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18. Activated caspase-1 also cleaves GSDMD, triggering pyroptosis, thereby amplifying the inflammatory microenvironment in a feed-forward manner [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib11),[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib12)]. In addition, METTL3 mediates endothelial responses to atheroprone flow by upregulating NLRP1, downregulating KLF4, and activating the NF-κB signaling cascade [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib10)].

Beyond inflammation, METTL3 has also been implicated in the regulation of mitochondrial quality control. It represses the expression of key mitophagy-related genes, including FUNDC1 and PINK1 [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib13),[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib14)]. FUNDC1 is a hypoxia-responsive receptor mediating receptor-dependent mitophagy, whereas PINK1/Parkin represents the canonical pathway for eliminating damaged mitochondria. Suppression of these genes impairs the clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria in endothelial cells [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib14),[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib15)], resulting in mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS accumulation. Excessive ROS not only damages cellular components (e.g., lipids, proteins, DNA) but also serves as a potent amplifier of injury signaling. ROS can further activate the NLRP3 inflammasome [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib16),[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib17)] and may feed back to enhance METTL3 expression or activity. This creates a deleterious loop, thereby perpetuating endothelial dysfunction.

These mechanistic insights are strongly supported by in vivo studies. METTL3 knockout reduces neointima formation in a partial carotid ligation model in mice [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib10)]. Under oscillatory shear stress, METTL3 expression is increased, which promotes m 6 A modification of metabolic regulators HK1, PFKFB3, and GCKR. This results in enhanced glycolysis, elevated endothelial dysfunction, and suppressed GCKR expression [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib18)]. In ApoE−/− mice with endothelial-specific deletion of METTL3, mitochondrial integrity is preserved, mitochondrial membrane potential is restored, and oxidative and ER stress markers (CHOP, PERK, and ATF5) are attenuated [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib19)]. Concurrently, ROS production is significantly reduced, leading to the preservation of microvascular endothelial function.

Taken together, METTL3 serves as a pivotal regulatory hub in endothelial cells during the early stages of atherosclerosis. It is upregulated in response to pathological stimuli and orchestrates m 6 A-dependent modulation of key cellular processes—including NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis and mitochondrial homeostasis. These interconnected mechanisms converge to drive endothelial dysfunction and promote disease progression.

### METTL3 in macrophages

2.2
Macrophages are central regulators in the development and progression of AS. Their dysfunction manifests primarily through excessive lipid uptake, sustained pro-inflammatory cytokine release, and foam cell formation—the latter being a predominant component of the atherosclerotic lipid core. Studies have demonstrated that in response to atherosclerosis-relevant stimuli such as oxLDL and lipopolysaccharide (LPS), the expression of METTL3 is significantly upregulated in macrophages [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib20),[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib21)]. As a pivotal m6A methyltransferase, METTL3 dynamically regulates the stability and translational efficiency of mRNAs associated with inflammation and lipid homeostasis, thus contributing to immune dysregulation and metabolic imbalance in macrophages.

Once activated, METTL3 enhances m6A methylation on transcripts encoding key inflammatory mediators, including interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and NLRP3 inflammasome [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib20),[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib22)]. These modifications stabilize the mRNAs and promote their translation, sustaining a pro-inflammatory state. NLRP3 inflammasome activation leads to caspase-1 cleavage of GSDMD, initiating pyroptosis in macrophages and releasing large amounts of inflammatory contents (e.g., IL-1β, IL-18), further amplifying the inflammatory cascade. Moreover, METTL3-mediated m6A enrichment on SLC7A11 accelerates its mRNA degradation via YTHDF2, promoting ferroptosis in macrophages [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib23)]. In addition, METTL3 enhances the YTHDF1-dependent translation of inflammatory mediators by activating the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK signaling pathway, further augmenting IL-6 and TNF-α expression and contributing to plaque development [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib24)]. In vivo evidence supports this mechanism: myeloid-specific METTL3 deletion in atherosclerotic models reduces BRAF expression and ERK phosphorylation, thereby decreasing pro-inflammatory cytokine levels and slowing lesion progression [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib24)].

Beyond inflammation, METTL3 also modulates lipid metabolism in macrophages. METTL3 has been shown to increase HDGF expression via m 6 A modification in M1-polarized macrophages. HDGF upregulation promotes glycolysis, inflammation, and lipid accumulation, collectively exacerbating atherosclerotic plaque progression [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib25)]. While FTO, another m6A-related enzyme, has been extensively studied in the context of adipogenesis and obesity [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib26)], METTL3, together with METTL14 and WTAP, facilitates mitotic clonal expansion (MCE) during adipocyte differentiation by regulating cell cycle transitions [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib27)]. Furthermore, inhibition of METTL3 has been shown to restore autophagy via AKT1S1 mRNA stabilization, leading to reduced lipid accumulation [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib28)]. Similar regulatory patterns have been observed in nonvascular disease models. For example, high-fat diet exposure enhances METTL3-mediated m 6 A modification of CPT1A, promoting M2 macrophage polarization and immune evasion in hepatocellular carcinoma [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib29)]. In addition, METTL3 modulates the expression of CD36—a key scavenger receptor for modified lipoproteins—thereby contributing to mediate foam cell formation and insulin resistance in polycystic ovary syndrome [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib30),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib31)]. These findings suggest that METTL3 not only participates in inflammation but also plays an important role in shaping macrophage lipid fate and energy metabolism under pathological stimuli.

Recent studies have also linked METTL3 to mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in macrophages. METTL3, in concert with YTHDF2, represses the expression of PGC-1α, cytochrome _c_ (CYCS), and NDUFC2 (NADH: Ubiquinone Oxidoreductase Subunit C2), leading to decreased ATP production and oxygen consumption rate (OCR) [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib32)]. These defects increase both cytosolic and mitochondrial ROS, further elevating pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. Impaired PGC-1α signaling disrupts mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle function, and fatty acid oxidation, all of which exacerbate cellular stress [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib33),[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib34)]. Moreover, the accumulation of damaged mitochondria that are not properly cleared through mitophagy results in excessive ROS leakage—particularly superoxide (O 2−)—from the electron transport chain (ETC). ROS act as direct inducers of DNA, protein, and lipid damage, and importantly, promote NLRP3 inflammasome activation and GSDMD cleavage, thus further facilitating pyroptosis [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib35)]. This underscores a vicious cycle wherein METTL3-induced mitochondrial dysfunction aggravates oxidative stress and cell death, reinforcing inflammation in atherosclerotic plaques.

### METTL3 in vascular smooth muscle cells

2.3
Under physiological conditions, vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) in the medial layer of blood vessels exhibit a contractile phenotype characterized by the expression of contractile proteins such as smooth muscle α-actin (SM α-actin) and SM22α, which are essential for maintaining vascular tone. Upon exposure to pathological stimuli—including ox-LDL, hyperglycemia, and pro-inflammatory cytokines—VSMCs undergo a phenotypic switch. This transformation involves downregulation of contractile proteins and acquisition of proliferative, migratory, and synthetic capabilities [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib36)]. This phenotypic transition exerts dual effects on AS progression: in the early stages, VSMC migration into the intima and excessive proliferation accelerate plaque development; in later stages, collagen synthesis by synthetic VSMCs contributes to fibrous cap stability, although aberrant differentiation may promote plaque calcification and necrotic core expansion.

ROS directly drives this phenotypic modulation by activating pro-inflammatory pathways and inducing DNA damage. ROS also stimulates the secretion of monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) by VSMCs, enhancing leukocyte recruitment and local inflammation [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib37)]. Notably, aging further exacerbates this vulnerability. In aged individuals, VSMCs exhibit heightened sensitivity to oxidative insults, with significantly increased MCP-1 expression, compromised Nrf2-mediated antioxidant defense, and exaggerated responses to hydrogen peroxide [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib38),[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib39)]. METTL3 plays a pivotal role in these processes by regulating m6A RNA methylation in VSMCs under stress conditions. Suppression of METTL3 has been shown to attenuate neointimal hyperplasia, restore contractile phenotype markers such as α-SMA and SM22α, and concurrently reduce synthetic phenotype indicators including OPN and PCNA [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib40)]. Several m6A-modified downstream effectors of METTL3 have been implicated in VSMC phenotypic regulation.(1)PFN1/p-ANXA2/STAT3 axis: METTL3, in conjunction with YTHDF3, enhances translation of PFN1 in an m6A-dependent manner. PFN1 recruits Src kinase to promote STAT3 phosphorylation, which interacts with phosphorylated ANXA2—an essential step for STAT3 activation and subsequent VSMC phenotypic switching [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib41)].(2)ATG5/ATG7-mediated autophagy: METTL3 promotes autophagosome formation by upregulating ATG5 and ATG7. Knockdown of either autophagy gene abrogates the METTL3-induced phenotypic switch in human aortic smooth muscle cells (HASMCs) [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib42)].(3)miR-375–3p/PDK1 axis: METTL3 represses miR-375–3p maturation through m6A methylation, thereby relieving its inhibitory effect on PDK1 mRNA. Since PDK1 is an upstream kinase of Akt, this pathway enhances VSMC proliferation and migration [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib43)]. In vivo experiments have shown that METTL3 silencing enhances collagen content in plaques and reduces necrotic core areas [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib43)].(4)PI3K/AKT signaling: METTL3 knockdown destabilizes Pi3k mRNA, leading to inactivation of the PI3K/AKT pathway and suppression of the phenotypic switch in VSMCs [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib40)].

Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction converge as central drivers of VSMC malfunction, with METTL3 acting as a critical integrator. Overexpression of METTL3 has been shown to impair mitophagy via reduced m6A methylation of genes in the PINK1/Parkin pathway, resulting in mitochondrial accumulation and dysfunction [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib14)]. This leads to compromised ETC function, increased ROS leakage (notably superoxide anions, O 2•-), and reduced mitochondrial antioxidant defense (elevated MDA, decreased SOD) in ox-LDL-stimulated VSMCs [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib44)]. Importantly, METTL3 also regulates ferroptosis-related antioxidant pathways. METTL3 facilitates m6A methylation of the long noncoding RNA NORAD in a YTHDF2-dependent manner, enhancing its interaction with RNA-binding protein HuR [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib45)]. The NORAD-HuR complex stabilizes GPX4 mRNA, upregulating GPX4 protein levels [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib45)]. As a core ferroptosis suppressor, GPX4 reduces lipid ROS and iron accumulation while maintaining GSH levels, thus protecting VSMCs from oxidative injury and slowing aortic dissection progression [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib45)].

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850)Oxidative stress and redox regulation of METTL3 in atherosclerosis

3
Oxidative stress is a central driver of atherosclerosis, primarily through the overproduction of ROS, which causes oxidative damage and activates a broad spectrum of stress-responsive signaling pathways (e.g., MAPK, NF-κB, Nrf2) that reshape cellular transcriptional programs [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib1)]. Beyond its role as an upstream inducer of the m 6 A regulatory network, oxidative stress can directly modulate both the expression and enzymatic activity of METTL3. This modulation influences the epitranscriptomic landscape of RNA, while METTL3-mediated m 6 A modifications, in turn, feed back to regulate redox homeostasis—together forming a dynamic, bidirectional regulatory loop [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib46)].

### How oxidative stress regulates the expression and activity of METTL3

3.1
Under conditions that elevate ROS—such as exposure to oxLDL, H 2 O 2, high glucose, or high lipid levels—METTL3 mRNA abundance is markedly increased. This upregulation appears to occur via multiple, non-mutually exclusive mechanisms.

#### Transcriptional regulation

3.1.1
Oxidative stress has been shown to enhance the interaction between PCAF and METTL3, increasing METTL3 acetylation. This modification disrupts the association between METTL3 and EIF3H, thereby impairing ribosomal translational efficiency and suppressing cell proliferation [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib3)]. In an age-related hearing loss model, oxidative stress reduced the m 6 A methylation of SIRT1 mRNA, which was accompanied by a corresponding decrease in METTL3 expression [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib3)]. In pancreatic β-cells, METTL3 expression is influenced by both ER stress and ROS levels, suggesting that oxidative stress may modulate METTL3 to alter immune-related functions [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib3)].

#### Translational control and protein stability

3.1.2
Oxidative stress may also modulate METTL3 protein abundance and activity through post-translational mechanisms:

**Ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation:** E3 ubiquitin ligases play a pivotal role in protein ubiquitination and turnover. Members of the NEDD4 family (e.g., ITCH, WWP1, Smurf1, Smurf2) have been implicated in regulating LDL receptor expression and cholesterol metabolism, thereby influencing atherosclerotic progression. Pharmacological inhibition or activation of these ligases can ameliorate cardiovascular dysfunction [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib47)]. TRIM21, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, interacts directly with METTL3 to promote K48-linked polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib48)]. TRIM21 overexpression has been shown to suppress LPS-induced neutrophil infiltration, cytokine release, and NF-κB pathway activation [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib49)]. Similarly, RNF113A interacts with circ_0001187 to facilitate METTL3 degradation [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib50)]. Excessive ROS may perturb the activity of E3 ligases, altering substrate recognition and ubiquitination efficiency [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib51)]. Collectively, these findings suggest that oxidative stress–induced ROS can indirectly regulate METTL3 expression by modulating E3 ligase activity.

**Post-translational modifications:** METTL3 undergoes multiple covalent modifications, including phosphorylation, acetylation, and SUMOylation. For example, extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs) phosphorylate METTL3 at three conserved serine residues (S43, S50, S525), reducing its ubiquitination and degradation, thereby enhancing its stability and enzymatic activity [[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib52)]. METTL3 can also be SUMOylated at lysine residues K177, K211, K212, and K215, which significantly suppresses its methyltransferase activity without affecting stability, localization, or interactions with METTL14 and WTAP [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib53)]. ROS have been reported to influence acetylation [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib54)], phosphorylation, and ubiquitination [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib55)]. Although direct evidence for ROS-mediated regulation of METTL3 modifications remains lacking, indirect findings strongly support this possibility.

#### Epigenetic and RNA-based regulation

3.1.3
Oxidative stress can induce specific microRNAs or lncRNAs that interact with METTL3 mRNA or protein, thereby modulating its expression. For instance, miR-33a targets the 3′UTR of METTL3 to suppress its expression in non-small cell lung cancer, attenuating cell proliferation and invasion [[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib56)]. The lncRNA MALAT1 interacts with METTL3 to modulate site-specific m 6 A deposition [[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib56)]. In gastric cancer, miR-1269b, miR-4429, and miR-181–5p downregulate METTL3, thereby inhibiting malignant behaviors (He, Wu, Sun, & [[[57]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib57), [[58]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib58), [[59]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib59)]. Additionally, circRPMS1 forms a complex with Sam68 and p53 that accumulates at the METTL3 promoter to promote its transcription, influencing EBV-associated gastric carcinoma aggressiveness [[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib60),[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib61)]. These findings underscore that METTL3 expression is also subject to fine-tuned epigenetic and RNA-based control.

### How METTL3 modulates oxidative stress responses

3.2
As an m6A “writer,” METTL3 orchestrates redox homeostasis by methylating transcripts of oxidative stress–related genes, thereby influencing their stability and translation efficiency. Through these epitranscriptomic modifications, METTL3 can fine-tune intracellular ROS levels both by modulating ROS production and by affecting antioxidant capacity. One well-characterized mechanism involves the regulation of antioxidant signaling via non-coding RNA processing. METTL3 promotes miR-873–5p maturation through DROSHA and DGCR8, which in turn upregulates Nrf2, leading to enhanced expression of downstream antioxidant genes and suppression of ROS accumulation [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib62)]. In endothelial cells, OS upregulates METTL3 expression, increases global m6A methylation, augments NF-κB p65 Ser536 phosphorylation, and promotes monocyte adhesion [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib10)]. Knockdown of METTL3 abolishes OS-induced hypermethylation and inflammatory activation, whereas METTL3 overexpression phenocopies the OS effects [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib10)].

Beyond antioxidant pathways, METTL3 has been shown to repress mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. Coordinated with YTHDF2, METTL3 downregulates PGC-1α, CYCS, and NDUFC2, thereby reducing ATP production and OCR. This metabolic suppression leads to intracellular and mitochondrial ROS accumulation, accompanied by increased pro-inflammatory cytokine release in activated monocytes [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib63)]. In contrast, in macrophages challenged with LPS, METTL3 knockdown markedly enhances IL-6, TNF-α, and NADPH oxidase (Nox1, Nox2, Ncf1, Ncf2) expression, ROS generation, and phosphorylation of MAPKs and AKT [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib64)]. This apparent context-dependent discrepancy suggests that METTL3 may target distinct gene sets in different cell types or activation states, thereby exerting either pro-oxidant or antioxidant effects.

METTL3 also modulates ROS levels by regulating antioxidant enzyme expression. In several models, METTL3 targets mRNAs encoding key antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2, GPX4, and catalase, promoting their degradation or suppressing their translation, thereby diminishing antioxidant defense capacity. Conversely, METTL3-mediated m6A methylation of Hmox1 mRNA in an IGF2BP3-dependent manner can stabilize the transcript, leading to tubular epithelial cell iron overload and ferroptotic death [[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib65)]. In another axis, METTL3 enhances pri-miR-34a maturation via DGCR8, and miR-34a overexpression markedly suppresses SIRT1 expression, further weakening cellular antioxidant defense [[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib66)].

Collectively, oxidative stress modulates METTL3 expression and activity through multiple signaling pathways, while METTL3 reciprocally shapes oxidative stress intensity and persistence via m6A-dependent gene regulation. This bidirectional network not only governs the functional state of endothelial cells, macrophages, and other atherosclerosis-associated cell types but also likely intersects with downstream processes such as pyroptosis and mitochondrial quality control, influencing cell fate decisions in the atherosclerotic microenvironment.

### METTL3-mediated m6A modification in the regulation of pyroptosis

3.3
During the progression of atherosclerosis, pyroptosis occurs extensively in vascular endothelial cells, macrophages, and vascular smooth muscle cells. This process promotes local inflammatory amplification, membrane rupture, and atherosclerotic plaque destabilization. Pyroptosis is initiated by inflammasome activation and depends on caspase-1–mediated cleavage of GSDMD, which forms membrane pores and enables the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β. Recent studies have revealed that m6A RNA modification regulates the fate of key pyroptotic transcripts, with METTL3 serving as a central catalytic component. Clinical evidence supports this notion: in macrophages derived from peripheral blood mononuclear cells of patients with acute coronary syndrome, circ_0029589 expression is reduced. IRF-1 represses circ_0029589 via METTL3-dependent m6A modification, thereby facilitating macrophage pyroptosis and inflammatory cytokine release [[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib67)].

NLRP3 has emerged as a critical m6A-regulated target. In oxLDL-stimulated HUVECs, METTL3 expression is markedly upregulated and deposits m6A marks on target transcripts, increasing the stability and translation efficiency of pyroptosis-related mRNAs, including NLRP3, cleaved caspase-1, IL-1β, IL-18, and GSDMD-N [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib68)]. This modification promotes inflammasome assembly and activation. METTL3 cooperates with the m6A “reader” YTHDF1 to enhance NLRP3 protein translation [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib69)], thereby augmenting GSDMD cleavage and driving pyroptotic execution [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib68)]. YTHDF2 also contributes by regulating the stability of IL-1β and IL-18 transcripts [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib68)], positioning it as another key METTL3 cofactor in inflammatory amplification. Furthermore, as discussed earlier, METTL3 responds to pro-atherogenic hemodynamic forces in endothelial cells by promoting pro-inflammatory signaling—manifested as NLRP1 upregulation, KLF4 suppression, and NF-κB pathway activation (Chien et al., 2021)—all of which may create a cellular environment primed for pyroptotic initiation. This suggests that METTL3 not only modulates inflammasome components directly via m6A but also shapes the upstream inflammatory milieu that sensitizes cells to pyroptotic triggers.

### METTL3 and the regulation of mitochondrial quality control

3.4
The MQC system is a central mechanism for maintaining cellular homeostasis by eliminating dysfunctional mitochondria, sustaining energy metabolism, and limiting ROS release. MQC encompasses mitophagy, mitochondrial fusion and fission, mitochondrial biogenesis, and the generation of MDVs. Oxidative stress is a primary activating signal for MQC. Recent evidence indicates that m6A RNA modification acts as a novel upstream regulatory layer in MQC, with METTL3 emerging as a pivotal modulator ([Fig. 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#fig2)).Fig. 2**Mitochondria-driven crosstalk between oxidative stress and pyroptosis underlies atherosclerotic progression.** Excessive ROS, triggered by pro-atherogenic stimuli (e.g., oxLDL, high glucose/lipid levels, LPS, ischemia), drive mitochondrial quality control imbalance, characterized by impaired mitophagy, enhanced mitochondrial fission, and disrupted energy metabolism. These events lead to mitochondrial fragmentation and reduced redox resilience. In parallel, the accumulation of mitochondrial ROS and damaged organelles amplifies inflammasome activation, pro-inflammatory cytokine release, and gasdermin D–mediated plasma membrane pore formation, culminating in pyroptotic cell death. The vicious cycle between oxidative damage and inflammatory cell death contributes to vascular endothelial dysfunction, foam cell formation, and plaque destabilization in AS. Therapeutic targeting of these pathways—by restoring MQC and reducing ROS-driven pyroptosis—may offer promising strategies to mitigate atherosclerotic burden.Fig. 2

#### METTL3 and the mitophagy pathway

3.4.1
Mitophagy is a protective process that selectively removes damaged mitochondria, thereby reducing ROS production and preventing cell death. Multiple studies have shown that METTL3 modulates the expression of key mitophagy regulators via m∧6A modification, thereby controlling autophagy flux (Pu et al., 2025). Two canonical mitophagy pathways have been the primary focus.(i)The FUNDC1 pathway:

FUNDC1 is a hypoxia-inducible receptor located on the outer mitochondrial membrane that binds to the autophagy marker LC3, mediating receptor-dependent mitophagy [[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib70)]. Under hypoxic conditions, FUNDC1 interacts with the ER membrane protein calnexin, recruiting the mitochondrial fission protein DRP1 to mitochondria-associated ER membranes (MAMs). This facilitates mitochondrial fission and autophagosome formation, ultimately leading to mitochondrial degradation [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib71)]. Moreover, as an anchoring protein at MAMs, FUNDC1 regulates ER-mitochondrial Ca2+ signaling and mitochondrial dynamics. In vascular endothelial cells, FUNDC1 modulates cytosol–mitochondria Ca2+ flux, influencing the phosphorylation status of serum response factor and enhancing its binding to the VEGFR2 promoter, thereby activating angiogenesis-related gene expression [[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib72)]. In cardiomyocytes, FUNDC1 knockdown improves mitochondrial function, lowers mitochondrial Ca2+ concentration, reduces pyroptosis, and promotes ubiquitination-dependent degradation of IP3R2 [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib13)]. Silencing METTL3 suppresses FUNDC1 mRNA stability via m∧6A reader IGF2BP2, attenuating cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory responses, and pyroptosis [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib13)]. The stability of FUNDC1 transcripts has also been confirmed to be directly regulated by METTL3-mediated m∧6A modification [[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib73)]. This evidence collectively suggests that METTL3–FUNDC1 signaling integrates mitochondrial clearance, Ca2+ homeostasis, and inflammation control, thereby linking MQC to vascular and cardiac pathophysiology.(ii)The PINK1/Parkin pathway:

The PINK1/Parkin axis is the most extensively studied mitophagy pathway, activated primarily in response to loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) and mitochondrial injury. In the context of AS, this pathway not only mediates the clearance of damaged mitochondria but also influences macrophage polarization, endothelial cell function, and VSMC migration and proliferation—key processes affecting plaque formation and stability [[[74]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib74), [[75]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib75), [[76]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib76)]. oxLDL stimulation induces ΔΨm depolarization, increases mtROS production, and upregulates Drp1 phosphorylation, thereby promoting mitochondrial fission and damage. Subsequently, PINK1 accumulates on the outer mitochondrial membrane, recruiting Parkin from the cytosol to mitochondria, and enhancing MAP-LC3 colocalization with mitochondria, thus activating mitophagy flux [[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib77)]. This is accompanied by reduced expression of mitochondrial membrane proteins such as TOMM40, TOMM20, and COX IV-1, and by suppression of the pro-apoptotic protein Bax, establishing a crosstalk between autophagy and apoptosis that lowers VSMC death and promotes plaque stability [[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib77)]. Given that m∧6A modifications have been implicated in the regulation of mitochondrial fission and autophagy-related transcripts, it is plausible that METTL3 also modulates PINK1/Parkin-driven mitophagy in vascular cells, although direct mechanistic evidence in AS models remains to be established.

Although the direct role of METTL3 in regulating the PINK1/Parkin pathway in AS remains to be fully elucidated, studies from other disease models offer valuable mechanistic insights. For instance, in lung cancer, METTL3 promotes m6A modification of DCP2 mRNA, leading to its degradation, which indirectly upregulates PINK1 expression. This activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway enhances mitophagy and contributes to chemoresistance [[78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib78)]. Conversely, in a renal injury model, silencing METTL3 in human proximal tubular epithelial cells reduces the m6A modification level of PINK1 transcripts, thereby increasing their stability in a manner dependent on the m6A reader protein YTHDF2 [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12663850#bib14)]. args.summary:
This scientific review article, published in Redox Biology (2025, doi:10.1016/j.redox.2025.103918; PMID: 41240787; PMCID: PMC12663850), examines the role of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA methylation in atherosclerosis (AS), with a focus on methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3) as a redox-sensitive epitranscriptomic switch. The article is authored by researchers from Guang'anmen Hospital, China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences, Beijing.

KEY FINDINGS:
- METTL3 links redox imbalance to atherosclerosis via m6A RNA methylation; reactive oxygen species (ROS) promote METTL3 expression and m6A-mediated regulation of mitochondrial dynamics.
- METTL3 modulates mitochondrial quality control (MQC) and triggers pyroptosis in vascular cells through a bidirectional regulatory loop with oxidative stress.

CELL-SPECIFIC ROLES OF METTL3:
1. Endothelial cells: METTL3 is upregulated by oxLDL, hyperglycemia, and oscillatory shear stress. It increases m6A methylation on NLRP3 mRNA (enhancing stability), leads to inflammasome assembly and pyroptosis, represses mitophagy genes (FUNDC1, PINK1), and induces NLRP1/KLF4/NF-κB signaling. Endothelial-specific METTL3 deletion preserves mitochondrial integrity and reduces ROS in ApoE-/- mice.
2. Macrophages: METTL3 stabilizes inflammatory transcripts (IL-6, TNF-α, NLRP3), promotes ferroptosis via SLC7A11 degradation, enhances HDGF expression, and represses PGC-1α, CYCS, and NDUFC2—reducing ATP and oxygen consumption rate while increasing ROS.
3. VSMCs: METTL3 drives phenotypic transition from contractile to synthetic via the PFN1/p-ANXA2/STAT3 axis, ATG5/ATG7-mediated autophagy, miR-375-3p/PDK1 axis, and PI3K/AKT signaling. It also impairs PINK1/Parkin mitophagy and regulates ferroptosis via the NORAD-HuR-GPX4 pathway.

REGULATION OF METTL3 BY OXIDATIVE STRESS (multiple mechanisms):
- Transcriptional (PCAF-mediated acetylation)
- Post-translational (ubiquitination via TRIM21 and RNF113A; ERK phosphorylation at S43, S50, S525 enhances stability; SUMOylation at K177, K211, K212, K215 suppresses activity)
- Epigenetic/RNA-based (miR-33a, MALAT1, miR-1269b, miR-4429, circRPMS1)

PYROPTOSIS MECHANISMS:
- METTL3 enhances NLRP3 translation via YTHDF1, promotes GSDMD cleavage, and cooperates with YTHDF2 to regulate IL-1β and IL-18 transcript stability.

MITOCHONDRIAL QUALITY CONTROL:
- METTL3 suppresses FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy (via IGF2BP2 reader) and modulates PINK1/Parkin pathway, impairing clearance of damaged mitochondria and amplifying ROS-driven pyroptosis.

THERAPEUTIC IMPLICATIONS:
- METTL3 inhibition alleviates intimal hyperplasia, restores contractile VSMC phenotypes (α-SMA, SM22α), and may synergize with antioxidant therapy, mitochondrial quality control reinforcement, or pyroptosis suppression.
- METTL4-mediated mitochondrial DNA 6mA methylation also contributes to AS.
- Natural products (tanshinone, quercetin) modulate m6A pathways as potential interventions.

The review highlights three major themes: (1) regulation of METTL3 by oxidative stress in AS models, (2) role of METTL3-mediated m6A modification in pyroptosis and MQC pathway control, and (3) therapeutic potential of targeting the "oxidative stress–METTL3–pyroptosis/MQC axis" in atherosclerosis treatment.

1 Department of Microbiology and Molecular Genetics, University of California Irvine School of Medicine, Irvine, CA 92697, USA; juhwan828@gmail.com 2 Department of Microbiology and Molecular Genetics, Chao Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of California Irvine School of Medicine, Irvine, CA 92697, USA * Correspondence: ginalee@uci.edu Abstract: Nutrients and metabolic pathways regulate cell growth and cell fate decisions via epigenetic modiﬁcation of DNA and histones. Another key genetic material, RNA, also contains diverse chemical modiﬁcations. Among these, N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most prevalent and evolutionarily conserved RNA modiﬁcation. It functions in various aspects of developmental and disease states, by controlling RNA metabolism, such as stability and translation. Similar to other epigenetic processes, m6A modiﬁcation is regulated by speciﬁc enzymes, including writers (methyltransferases), erasers (demethylases), and readers (m6A-binding proteins). As this is a reversible enzymatic process, metabolites can directly inﬂuence the ﬂux of this reaction by serving as substrates and/or allosteric regulators. In this review, we will discuss recent understanding of the regulation of m6A RNA modiﬁcation by metabolites, nutrients, and cellular metabolic pathways.
Keywords: N6-methyladenosine; m6A; RNA methylation; RNA chemical modiﬁcation; RNA epi-transcriptome; metabolites; nutrient signaling; metabolic pathways 1. Introduction RNA plays an essential role in gene expression control. In addition to transferring genetic information from DNA to protein, RNA controls protein expression by providing messenger RNA (mRNA) for translation. mRNA is generated by the processing of nascent RNA, which involves the splicing of introns, 5′cap addition, and 3′ polyadenylation. In addition to these well-known RNA maturation processes, RNA also undergoes chemical modiﬁcation at its bases and ribose rings [1,2]. The N6-adenosine methylation (m6A or N6-methyladenosine) is the most abundant mRNA internal modiﬁcation. It was discovered in the 1970s [3,4] when other RNA processes were discovered, although follow up studies have lagged. Nearly three decades later, the identiﬁcation of methyltransferases [5–7] and demethylases [8,9] proved that m6A modiﬁcation is not a random event, but rather an enzyme-mediated selective process. In addition, transcriptome-wide sequencing of m6A-modiﬁed mRNAs revealed that m6A is enriched around the stop codon and deposited at a consensus motif [10,11]. These seminal studies reignited m6A research, which is now extended to various RNA species including long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) [12,13], riboso-mal RNA (rRNA) [14,15], and small nuclear RNA (snRNA) [16,17], opening a new ﬁeld of RNA epitranscriptomics. m6A modiﬁcation alters RNA structure and RNA–protein inter-actions, which control RNA fates such as splicing [18], stability [19–21], localization [22], and translation efﬁciency [23,24], ultimately affecting protein expression. m6A-dependent gene expression plays crucial roles in normal development including embryogenesis, stem cell maintenance [25,26], and neurogenesis [27,28] and its dysregulation causes diseases such as cancer [29–31] and diabetes [32,33]. There are several comprehensive reviews about molecular biological and pathophysiological functions of m6A [34–37]. In this review, we discuss m6A RNA modiﬁcation from a metabolic perspective.

Enzymes Involved in m6A RNA Modiﬁcation The primary m6A writer complex is composed of methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3), METTL14, and an adaptor protein, Wilms’ tumor 1-associating protein (WTAP) [7] (Figure 1A).
Additional components of this complex are VIRMA/KIAA1429 [38], zinc ﬁnger CCCH-type containing 13 (ZC3H13) [39], and RNA binding motif protein 15 (RBM15) [13]. The writer complex methylates speciﬁc adenosine residues on mRNA and non-coding RNAs in RRA*CH consensus motif (R represents A or G; H represents A, C or U; A* is the methylated adenosine) [10,11]. ZCCHC4 contains an autoinhibitory loop in the RNA binding surface, which is opened upon 28S rRNA binding [43]. This sort of mechanism may determine substrate RNA spec-ificity among various m6A methyltransferases. Once adenosine is methylated, a variety of m6A binding proteins (readers) are re-cruited (Figure 1A). These include YT521-B homology domain family proteins (YTHDF and YTHDC) [44], heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (HNRNP) [45], and insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein (IGF2BP) families [20]. These proteins control the fate of target RNAs, such as folding into secondary structures [45], splicing [18], nu-clear export [22], liquid–liquid phase separation [46], stability [20,21], and translation [23,24]. On the other hand, demethylase enzymes (erasers) are responsible for removing m6A (Figure 1A). Potential m6A erasers are alkB homolog 5 (ALKBH5) and fat mass and obe-sity-associated (FTO, also known as ALKBH9) proteins, which belong to ALKB family of dioxygenases [8,9]. The discovery of these specific m6A processing proteins (i.e., writers, erasers and readers), provided evidence that m6A modification is a highly regulated, re-versible cellular process. Figure 1. N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methylation process and its biological functions. (A) m6A writers (methyltransferase) methylate RNA in the adenine nucleobase of amino group at N6 position. The consensus motif of methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3) is RRA*CH (R = A/G; A* = methylated A; H = A/C/U). Once m6A is deposited on RNA, m6A reader proteins are recruited and determine RNA fates, such as splicing, stability, and translation efﬁciency, which ultimately affect gene expression. m6A is removed from RNA through demethylation by eraser proteins. (B) METTL16 methylates stem-loop structure in 3’ untranslated region (UTR) of S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) synthase, methionine adenosyltransferase 2A (MAT2A). In SAM-repleted conditions, MAT2A is methylated and degraded. Oppositely, in SAM-depleted conditions, METTL16 induces splicing and expression of MAT2A. (C) Methylation of A4220 in 28S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) by zinc ﬁnger CCHC domain-containing protein 4 (ZCCHC4) promotes ribosome assembly and translation. (D) Domain composition of m6A enzymes. (Top, writers) m6A writers contain methyltransferase (MTase) domains. METTL3 contains Cys-Cys-Cys-His (CCCH) zinc ﬁnger motifs. METTL16 has two vertebrate conserved region (VCR) domains in C-terminus. ZCCHC4 possesses several zinc ﬁnger motifs, including Gly-Arg-Phe (GRF), Cys2-His2 (C2H2), and Cys-Cys-His-Cys (CCHC) domains. (Bottom, erasers) Fat mass and obesity-associated protein (FTO) and alkb homolog 5 (ALKBH5) contain αKG-Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenase domains conserved in dioxygenase family enzymes. WTAP, Wilms’ tumor 1-associated protein; eIF3, eukaryotic initiation factor 3; YTHDF, YTH domain family; YTHDC, YTH domain-containing protein; IGF2BP, insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein; HNRNP, heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins; FTO-CTD, FTO C-terminal domain.
In addition to the METTL3–METTL14 complex, there are several other classes of m6A RNA methyltransferases. METTL16 is primarily responsible for the methylation of snRNA and some mRNAs [40]. METTL16 targets a distinct consensus motif, UACA*GAGAA, in the RNA stem-loop structure [41,42] (Figure 1B). Different from the METTL3–METTL14 heterodimer complex, METTL16 functions as a homodimer [42].
18S and 28S rRNA methylations are catalyzed by METTL5-tRNA methyltransferase 112 (TRMT112) complex [14] and zinc ﬁnger CCHC domain-containing protein 4 (ZC-Metabolites 2021, 11, 80 3 of 11 CHC4) [15], respectively (Figure 1C). These proteins localize in the nucleolus where ribo-some synthesis and maturation occur. In contrast to other methyltransferases, ZCCHC4 contains an autoinhibitory loop in the RNA-binding surface, which is opened upon 28S rRNA binding [43]. This sort of mechanism may determine substrate RNA speciﬁcity among various m6A methyltransferases.
Once adenosine is methylated, a variety of m6A binding proteins (readers) are re-cruited (Figure 1A). These include YT521-B homology domain family proteins (YTHDF and YTHDC) [44], heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (HNRNP) [45], and insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein (IGF2BP) families [20]. These proteins control the fate of target RNAs, such as folding into secondary structures [45], splicing [18], nuclear export [22], liquid–liquid phase separation [46], stability [20,21], and translation [23,24].
On the other hand, demethylase enzymes (erasers) are responsible for removing m6A (Figure 1A). Potential m6A erasers are alkB homolog 5 (ALKBH5) and fat mass and obesity-associated (FTO, also known as ALKBH9) proteins, which belong to ALKB family of dioxygenases [8,9]. The discovery of these speciﬁc m6A processing proteins (i.e., writers, erasers and readers), provided evidence that m6A modiﬁcation is a highly regulated, reversible cellular process.
3. Regulation of m6A Writers by SAM and SAH Similar to other typical enzymatic reactions, m6A writer-mediated methylation is dynamically regulated by substrates and products. S-adenosyl methionine (SAM/AdoMet) is a universal methyl donor for the cellular methylation processes (Figure 2A). Indeed, METTL3 was originally identiﬁed as a SAM-binding protein [5]. In cells, METTL3 forms a stable heterodimeric complex with METTL14. Even though both METTL3 and METTL14 contain methyltransferase domains (Figure 1D), the catalytic site of METTL14 lacks the SAM binding motif and only METTL3 contains enzymatic activity. Rather, METTL14 maintains METTL3–METTL14 complex stability and recruits RNA substrates for efﬁcient m6A writing [47–49].
One-carbon metabolism, composed of folate and methionine cycles, is the metabolic pathway responsible for SAM production (Figure 2B). Two amino acids, serine and methio-nine, play key roles in providing carbons to this pathway. Serine provides a one-carbon unit to the tetrahydrofolate (THF) cofactor, generating methyl-THF. Then, another car-bon acceptor, homocysteine, receives one-carbon from methyl-THF. On the other hand, methionine adenosyl transferase (MAT) produces SAM using methionine and adenosine 5′-triphosphate (ATP) as substrates. Finally, SAM provides a methyl group to adenosine on RNAs and becomes S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH/AdoHcy). As is often the case with metabolic enzymes, the product of this methylation reaction, SAH, is a strong allosteric inhibitor of METTL3 methyltransferase activity [50] (Figure 2A).
It has been shown that the perturbation of cellular SAM levels affects DNA and histone methylation [51]. Interestingly, the Km (substrate concentration at half maximum reaction rate) of SAM for METTL3 is much lower (~100 nM) than cellular SAM levels (>10 µM) [50,52], suggesting that METTL3 is constitutively active regardless of ﬂuctuations in cellular SAM levels. Ironically, intracellular SAH levels (~5 µM) are higher than the IC50 (half maximal inhibitory concentration) of SAH for METTL3 (~1 µM) [50,52,53], suggesting that METTL3 can also be constitutively inhibited by high SAH levels. However, it is possible that the subcellular, local concentrations of SAM and SAH are likely different from their concentrations in total cell lysates. In addition, other binding proteins of SAM or SAH can change the levels of free SAM and SAH available for METTL3. The metabolic balance of SAM and SAH in local subcellular environments and their control of METTL3 activity merits further investigation.
