## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356)Abstract

Activated effector T (T E) cells augment anabolic pathways of metabolism, such as aerobic glycolysis, while memory T (T M) cells engage catabolic pathways, like fatty acid oxidation (FAO). However, signals that drive these differences remain unclear. Mitochondria are metabolic organelles that actively transform their ultrastructure. Therefore, we questioned whether mitochondrial dynamics controls T cell metabolism. We show that T E cells have punctate mitochondria, while T M cells maintain fused networks. The fusion protein Opa1 is required for T M, but not T E cells after infection and enforcing fusion in T E cells imposes T M cell characteristics and enhances antitumor function. Our data suggest that, by altering cristae morphology, fusion in T M cells configures electron transport chain (ETC) complex associations favoring oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and FAO, while fission in T E cells leads to cristae expansion, reducing ETC efficiency and promoting aerobic glycolysis. Thus, mitochondrial remodeling is a signaling mechanism that instructs T cell metabolic programming.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356)Abstract

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356)INTRODUCTION

T cells mediate protective immunity against pathogens and cancer and posses the unique ability to proliferate at an unparalleled rate in an adult organism. In this regard, one naïve T (T N) cell can clonally expand into millions of ‘armed’ T E cells in just a few days ([Williams and Bevan, 2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R60)). Concomitant with T cell activation is the engagement of aerobic glycolysis and elevated OXPHOS ([Chang et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R10), [Sena et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R48)), the former of which is characteristic of the Warburg effect shared by tumor cells and unicellular organisms ([Vander Heiden et al., 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R55)). Once antigen is cleared, most T E cells die, but a subset of long-lived T M cells persists with enhanced mitochondrial capacity marked by a reliance on FAO to fuel OXPHOS, which equips them to rapidly respond should infection or cancer recur ([Pearce et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R38)). These extensive changes in phenotype and function of T cells go along with a dynamic metabolic range ([MacIver et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R28), [Buck et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R4)). Failure to engage specific metabolic programs impairs the function and differentiation of T cells. As such, T cells represent an amenable system to study changes in cell metabolism that occur as part of normal development, and not as a result of transformation. Establishing the precise reasons why and how, these and other cells emphasize one particular metabolic pathway over another remains a challenge.

Mitochondria are essential hubs of metabolic activity, antiviral responses, and cell death that constantly remodel their structure via nuclear encoded GTPases ([Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R34)). Mitochondrial fission generates discrete and fragmented mitochondria that can increase ROS production ([Yu et al., 2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R62)), facilitate mitophagy ([Frank et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R19), [Toyama et al., 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R52)), accelerate cell proliferation ([Taguchi et al., 2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R51)), and mediate apoptosis ([Youle and Karbowski, 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R61)). Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) is a cytosolic protein that translocates to the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) upon phosphorylation to scission mitochondria. Fusion of mitochondria into linear or tubular networks limits deleterious mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) ([Santel et al., 2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R45)), induces supercomplexes of the ETC maximizing OXPHOS activity ([Cogliati et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R14), [Mishra et al., 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R31)), and enhances endoplasmic reticulum (ER) interactions important for Ca 2+ flux ([de Brito and Scorrano, 2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R17)). In addition, mitochondria elongate as a survival mechanism in response to nutrient starvation and stress, linking fusion to cell longevity ([Gomes et al., 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R22), [Rambold et al., 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R41), [Friedman and Nunnari, 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R21)). OMM fusion is mediated by mitofusin 1 and 2 (Mfn1, Mfn2), while inner membrane fusion is controlled by optic atrophy 1 (Opa1). Total deletion in any of these proteins is embryonically lethal and mutations in the genes that encode them underlie the cause of several human diseases ([Chan, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R9), [Archer, 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R1)).

Mitochondrial membrane remodeling is acutely responsive to changes in cell metabolism ([Mishra and Chan, 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R32), [Wai and Langer, 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R56)), but whether it instructs metabolic pathway utilization has been inferred but not extensively studied. In general, deletion of any of the dynamics machinery perturbs OXPHOS and glycolytic rates at baseline ([Liesa and Shirihai, 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R27)). Tissue-specific deletion of Mfn2 in muscles of mice disrupts glucose homeostasis ([Sebastian et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R47)) and Drp1 ablation in the liver results in reduced adiposity and elevated whole-body energy expenditure, protecting mice from diet-induced obesity ([Wang et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R58)). A recent study has also suggested a link between Drp1 mediated fission and its affect on glycolysis during cell transformation ([Serasinghe et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R49)). The central question of whether fission/fusion and associated changes in cristae morphology actively control the adoption of distinct metabolic programs and therefore regulates T cell responses however, remains unanswered.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356)RESULTS

### Unlike T E cells, T M cells maintain a fused mitochondrial network

We reported that T M cells have more mitochondrial mass than T E or T N cells and suggested that mitochondria in these T cell subsets are morphologically distinct ([van der Windt et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R53), [van der Windt et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R54)). These observations prompted us to assess mitochondrial structure in T cells. We infected mice with _Listeria monocytogenes_ expressing ovalbumin (OVA) (LmOVA) and isolated T E and T M cells for ultrastructure analysis by electron microscopy (EM). We found that T E cells had small, distinct mitochondria dispersed in the cytoplasm, while T M cells had densely packed, somewhat tubular, mitochondria ([Figure 1A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F1)). To investigate these morphological differences, we differentially cultured activated OVA-specific T cell receptor (TCR) transgenic OT-I cells in interleukin-2 (IL-2) and IL-15 to generate IL-2 T E and IL-15 T M cells ([Figure S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD1)) ([Carrio et al., 2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R6)). These culture conditions approximate T cell responses _in vivo_ and allow us to generate large numbers of cells amenable to further experimentation _in vitro_ ([O’Sullivan et al., 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R36)). We found that IL-2 T E and IL-15 T M cells possessed similar mitochondrial ultrastructure as their _ex vivo_ isolated counterparts ([Figure 1B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F1)). Using confocal microscopy we observed that while a day after activation the mitochondria appeared fused, from days 2–6 the IL-2 T E cells exhibited predominantly punctate mitochondria ([Figure 1C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F1)). In contrast, once cells were exposed to IL-15, a cytokine that supports T M cell formation ([Schluns et al., 2002](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R46)), the mitochondria formed elongated tubules. Magnified images from these experiments emphasized the marked differences in mitochondrial morphology between IL-2 T E and IL-15 T M cells ([Figure 1D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F1)). We also examined the protein expression of several critical regulators of mitochondrial dynamics. We found that by day 6, fusion mediators Mfn2 and Opa1 were lower in T E cells compared to T M cells, while fission factor Drp1 was phosphorylated at its activating site Ser616 in T E cells ([Figure 1E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F1)) ([Marsboom et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R29)). Together these data suggest that mitochondria in T E cells are actively undergoing fission while in T M cells, these organelles exist in a fused state.

### Mitochondrial inner membrane fusion protein Opa1 is necessary for T M cell generation

To test whether mitochondrial fusion was important for T M cell development we crossed Mfn1, Mfn2, and Opa1 floxed mice to OT-I CD4 Cre transgenic mice to conditionally delete these proteins in T cells. Peripheral T cell frequencies in these mice were grossly normal (**data not shown**). We differentially cultured Mfn1−/−, Mfn2−/−, and Opa1−/− OT-I T cells in IL-2 and IL-15 and found that only Opa1−/− T cells had a survival defect when cultured in IL-15 ([Figure 2A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F2)), but not in IL-2. We measured the efficiency of gene deletion by mRNA and/or protein analyses ([Figure S2A–C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD2)). While Mfn1 and 2 were efficiently deleted, we found residual expression of Opa1 particularly in IL-15 T M cells, suggesting that cells that retained some expression of Opa1 in IL-15 cultures had a survival advantage ([Figure 2A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F2)). Assessment of mitochondrial ultrastructure revealed that the cristae were altered and disorganized in the absence of Opa1 in agreement with published results for other cells ([Figure 2B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F2)) ([Zhang et al., 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R63), [Cogliati et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R14)). Consistent with their survival defect, Opa1−/− IL-15 T M cells had decreased OXPHOS activity, as measured by O 2 consumption rate (OCR, an indicator of OXPHOS) to extracellular acidification rate (ECAR, an indicator of aerobic glycolysis) ratio, and spare respiratory capacity (SRC), compared to normal cells ([Figure 2C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F2)). SRC is the extra mitochondrial capacity available in a cell to produce energy under conditions of increased work or stress and is thought to be important for long-term cell survival and function (measured as OXPHOS activity above basal after uncoupling with FCCP) ([Nicholls, 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R33), [van der Windt et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R53)). To determine whether Opa1 is required for T M cell development _in vivo_, we adoptively transferred Opa1−/− OT-I T N cells into congenic recipients, infected these mice with LmOVA, and assessed T M cell formation in the weeks after infection. Control and Opa1−/− OT-I T cells mounted normal T E cell responses (day 7) to infection, while Opa1−/− OT-I T M cell formation (days 14–21) was drastically impaired ([Figure 2D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F2)). Consistent with diminished T M cell development, a significantly higher proportion of short-lived effector to memory precursor effector cells were present within the Opa1−/− OT-I donor cell population 7 days after infection ([Figure S2D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD2)) ([Kaech et al., 2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R25)). In addition, at day 10 post infection, a time point when T E cells contract while T M cells emerge, Opa1−/− T cells isolated _ex vivo_ had decreased SRC compared to control cells ([Figure S2E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD2)), correlating with their decreased survival. To assess whether Opa1−/− T M cells existed in too low an abundance to be discerned by flow cytometry, we challenged these mice with a second infection. We observed no recall response (day 3 and 6 p.c.) from Opa1−/− T cells when assessing frequency ([Figure 2E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F2)) or absolute numbers ([Figure 2F](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F2)), while there was considerable expansion of control donor cells. These data illustrate that Opa1 is required for T M, but not T E cell generation.

### Mitochondrial fusion imposes a T M cell phenotype, even in the presence of activating signals

Genetic loss of function of Opa1 revealed that this protein is critical for T M cell formation. Given the fused phenotype of mitochondria in T M cells, we hypothesized that Opa1-mediated mitochondrial fusion supports the metabolism needed for T M cell development. We used a gain of function approach to enhance mitochondrial fusion. Culturing T cells with the ‘fusion promoter’ M1 ([Wang et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R57)), and the ‘fission inhibitor’ Mdivi-1 ([Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R7)) ([Figure 3A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F3)) induced mitochondrial fusion in IL-2 T E cells, rendering them morphologically similar to IL-15 T M cells ([Figure 3B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F3)). Treatment with these drugs enhanced other T M cell properties in activated IL-2 T E cells, including increased mitochondrial mass ([Figure 3C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F3)), OXPHOS and SRC ([Figure 3D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F3)), CD62L expression ([Figure 3E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F3)) and robust metabolic activity, as indicated by bioenergetic profiling in response to secondary stimulation with PMA+ionomycin, followed by addition of oligomycin (ATP synthase inhibitor), FCCP, and rotenone with antimycin A (ETC complex I and III inhibitors), all drugs that stress the mitochondria ([Figure 3F](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F3) and [S3A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD3)). However, we did not observe increased mtDNA in these cells ([Figure S3B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD3)). We found that ECAR and the OCR/ECAR ratio increased after drug treatment ([Figure S3C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD3)), indicating elevated metabolic activity overall, with a predominant increase in OXPHOS over glycolysis. While we observed these changes in mitochondrial activity, we did not measure any significant differences in mitochondrial membrane potential or ROS after drug treatment ([Figure S3D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD3)). The expression of other activation markers were also not substantially affected, although a small decrease in KLRG1 and increase in CD25 was measured ([Figure S3E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD3)). Additionally, we performed a genetic gain of function experiment and transduced activated IL-2 T E cells with retrovirus expressing Mfn1, Mfn2, or Opa1. Similar to enforcement of fusion pharmacologically, we found that cells transduced with Opa1 had more mitochondria ([Figure 3G](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F3)) and OXPHOS ([Figure 3H](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F3)), than empty vector control or Mfn-transduced T cells, as well as increased overall metabolic activity, with a predominant increase in OXPHOS over glycolysis ([Figure S3F](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD3)). T M cell associated markers such as CCR7 and CD127 were increased on transduced cells, as well as T E cell proteins, such as PD-1 ([Figure S3G](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD3)). Overexpression of each target gene over the control was confirmed by mRNA expression ([Figure S3H](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD3)). Together our results show that mitochondrial fusion confers T M cell phenotypes on activated T E cells even in culture conditions that program T E cell differentiation.

### T cell mitochondrial fusion improves adoptive cellular immunotherapy against tumors

A consideration when designing adoptive cellular immunotherapy (ACI) is to improve T cell fitness during _ex vivo_ culture so that when T cells are re-introduced into a patient they are able to function efficiently and persist over time ([Restifo et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R42), [Maus et al., 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R30), [O’Sullivan and Pearce, 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R35)). Our data showed that fusion-promoting drugs created metabolically fit T cells. We predicted that enforcing fusion would also enhance the longevity of IL-2 T E cells _in vivo_. To test this, we adoptively transferred control and M1+Mdivi-1 treated OT-I T cells into congenic mice and tracked donor cell survival. We found significantly more drug treated T cells in the spleen ([Figure 3I](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F3)) and lymph nodes ([Figure 3J](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F3)) 2 days after transfer. To determine if the persistence of these cells would be maintained better long term than controls, we infected mice with LmOVA >3 weeks later and measured T cell responses against the bacteria. We found that drug-treated cells selectively expanded in response to infection ([Figure 3K](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F3)) and could be recovered in significantly greater numbers in the spleen 6 days post challenge ([Figure 3L](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F3)).

Next, we assessed whether these drugs could be used to promote T cell function in an ACI model. We injected EL4-OVA tumor cells into mice. Then either 5 or 12 days later we adoptively transferred IL-2 T E cells that had been treated with DMSO or M1+Mdivi-1. In both settings, mice that received ‘fusion-promoted’ T cells were able to control tumor growth significantly better than mice that received control treated cells ([Figure 4A and B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F4)). The cytolytic ability ([Figure S4A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD4)) and proliferation ([Figure S4B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD4)) of the fusion enforced IL-2 T E cells were similar to controls, however, they expressed significantly higher levels of IFN-γ and TNF-α when restimulated with PMA+ionomycin _in vitro_ ([Figure S4C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD4)). We also exposed activated human T cells to M1+Mdivi-1 treatment _in vitro_ and found that they had visibly more fused mitochondria ([Figure 4C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F4)), and exhibited the bioenergetic profile ([Figure 4D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F4)) and surface marker expression ([Figure 4E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F4)) characteristic of T M cells, compared to control treated cells. Parameters such as mitochondrial mass ([Figure 4E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F4)) and other surface markers ([Figure S4D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD4)) were not significantly altered. These data suggest that promoting fusion in T cells may be a translatable treatment for enhancing human therapy.

### Mitochondrial fusion promotes T M cell metabolism, but Opa1 is not required for FAO

Our data showed that Opa1 was necessary for T M cell formation, but the question of how Opa1 acted to support T M cells remained. We hypothesized that mitochondrial fusion, via Opa1 function, was needed for FAO, as the engagement of this pathway is required for T M cell development and survival ([Pearce et al., 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R39), [van der Windt et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R53), [van der Windt et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R54)). This hypothesis was based on our observations that these two processes seemed to be linked in T M cells and also on a recent report that mitochondrial fusion is important for efficient FAO via lipid droplet trafficking under starvation conditions ([Rambold et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R40)). We treated IL-2 T E and IL-15 T M cells with M1+Mdivi-1 or vehicle and then measured OCR in response to etomoxir, a specific inhibitor of mitochondrial long chain FAO ([Deberardinis et al., 2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R18)), and mitochondrial inhibitors. We found that the increased OCR and SRC evident in these cells after M1+Mdivi-1 treatment was due to enhanced FAO ([Figure 5A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F5) and [S5A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD5)). IL-2 T E cells transduced with Opa1 also exhibited elevated OCR that decreased in the presence of etomoxir compared to controls ([Figure 5B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F5)). Bone marrow derived macrophages (BM-Macs) cultured with M1+Mdivi-1 increased OCR and SRC to levels similar to M2 polarized macrophages, which engage FAO much like T M cells do ([Figure S5B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD5)) ([Huang et al., 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R24)). Importantly, M1+Mdivi-1 treatment did not increase OCR ([Figure 5C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F5)) or affect ECAR ([Figure S5C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD5)) in Opa1−/− IL-2 T E cells compared to controls, suggesting a requirement for Opa1 in augmenting OCR and FAO. However, in contrast to what we expected, when we assessed bioenergetics of Opa1+/+ and Opa1−/− IL-2 T E ([Figure 5D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F5)) and _ex vivo_ isolated T E cells ([Figure 5E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F5)), we found that both are equally responsive to etomoxir. Our results show that while Opa1 can promote FAO in T cells, it is not compulsory for engagement of this metabolic pathway.

### Mitochondrial cristae remodeling signals metabolic adaptations in T M and T E cells

Although Opa1+/+ and Opa1−/− IL-2 T E cells could equally engage FAO ([Figure 5D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F5)), we observed that ECAR was significantly increased in Opa1−/− cells both _in vitro_ and _ex vivo_ ([Figure 6A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)). Furthermore, unlike controls, we observed no additional drop of OCR in Opa1−/− IL-2 T E cells after the addition of oligomycin ([Figure 6B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)), suggesting that in the absence of Opa1, only FAO supports OXPHOS, and that substrates, such as glucose-derived pyruvate, are not used for mitochondrial ATP production in this setting. We cultured Opa1+/+ and Opa1−/− IL-2 T E cells with 13 C-labeled glucose and traced 13 C into TCA cycle metabolites. While the percent of 13 C-labeled pyruvate was higher in Opa1−/− T cells, the frequency of 13 C-labeled TCA cycle intermediates was significantly reduced in Opa1−/− T cells compared to controls ([Figure 6C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6) and [S6A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD6)), a result that is supported by their higher ECAR ([Figure 6A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)). These data suggested that without mitochondrial fusion, pyruvate is preferentially secreted as lactate, rather than oxidized in the mitochondria. Therefore, we questioned whether FAO is a ‘default’ pathway for mitochondria in a resting, or fused state (i.e. Opa1 sufficiency), and that the induction of aerobic glycolysis is a major downstream effect of fission (i.e. Opa1 deficiency). If this were the case, then a balance between fission and fusion, modulated by proteins such as Opa1, could act as a primary signal to dictate the metabolic phenotype of T cells. In support of this idea, T cells from polyclonal T cell-conditional deleted Opa1 mice had higher ECAR and an increased proportion of CD8 T cells with an activated effector phenotype in the basal state based on surface marker expression ([Figure S6B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD6)).

Opa1 is critical for inner mitochondrial membrane fusion, but also for other processes like cristae remodeling ([Frezza et al., 2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R20), [Cogliati et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R14)). We observed major changes in cristae morphology in Opa1−/− T cells ([Figure 2B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F2)). Given the importance of Opa1 in T M cell development ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F2)), we further assessed cristae morphology in T E and T M cells isolated _ex vivo_ after LmOVA infection ([Figure 6D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)), as well as IL-2 T E and IL-15 T M cells ([Figure 6E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)), and found that T E cells had many cristae with slightly wider and loosely organized intermembrane space, than T M cells. Opa1 overexpression induces cristae tightening and close association of ETC complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane ([Cogliati et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R14), [Civiletto et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R13)). Therefore, we surmised that in the absence of Opa1, cristae disorganization leads to dissociation of ETC complexes and subsequently less efficient ETC activity in T cells ([Figure 2C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F2)). We assessed OCR after oligomycin in relation to OCR after rotenone and antimycin A treatment (i.e. proton leak), which indicates the coupling efficiency of OXPHOS to mitochondrial ATP production. Consistent with decreased OXPHOS efficiency, we observed elevated proton leak in Opa1−/− T cells compared to controls ([Figure 6F](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)). This was also true for _ex vivo_ isolated T E cells compared to T M cells ([Figure 6G](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)), as well as IL-2 T E and IL-15 T M cells ([Figure 6H](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)). Together these data suggest that there are cristae differences between T E and T M cells, which may contribute to their distinct metabolic phenotypes.

We reasoned that fusion renders tightly configured cristae, which results in closely associated ETC complexes and efficient OXPHOS ([Patten et al., 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R37)), producing conditions that favor the entrance of pyruvate into the TCA cycle. NADH generated from the TCA cycle is able to easily donate electrons to complex I, which are passed efficiently along the ETC. Our data suggest that this predominantly occurs in T M cells. However, if electron transport across the ETC became less efficient, caused by physical separation of the individual complexes due to cristae remodeling via mitochondrial fission, then electrons could linger in the complexes and imbalance redox reactions. NADH levels would build, slowing forward momentum of the TCA cycle. To restore redox balance, cells could augment glycolysis and shunt pyruvate as excreted lactate (i.e. aerobic glycolysis), regenerating NAD+ from cytosolic NADH. We speculate that this occurs in T E cells. Correlating with this idea, we previously reported that T E and T M cells have different ratios of NAD+/NADH (i.e. redox balance) with T M cells maintaining higher NAD+/NADH than T E cells. We also showed that NADH levels dramatically rise in T M cells compared to T E cells when exposed to rotenone and antimycin A, indicating that T M cells consume more NADH for the purpose of donating electrons to the ETC ([van der Windt et al., 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R53)). Together our data suggest that fission and fusion regulate cristae remodeling, which alter ETC efficiency and redox balance, ultimately controlling metabolic adaptations in T cells.

To examine this idea further, we assessed cristae morphology in T E and T M cells by EM after TCR stimulation. We hypothesized that if cristae remodeling induces aerobic glycolysis, changes in cristae structure could be visualized after T cell activation. T M cells rapidly augment aerobic glycolysis when restimulated ([van der Windt et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R54)). We activated IL-15 T M cells with αCD3/CD28 beads ([Figure 6I](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)), or with PMA+ionomycin ([Figure S6C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD6)), in the presence or absence of Mdivi-1 to modulate activity of mitochondrial fission protein Drp1 ([Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R7)). We observed dramatic changes to cristae morphology by EM, with the intermembrane space widening over time in controls compared to drug treated cells. These data are consistent with the hypothesis that fission-induced mitochondrial cristae remodeling supports metabolic reprogramming in T cells.

### T M cells maintain tight cristae with closely associated ETC complexes

Our data suggested that unlike T E cells, T M cells have tight cristae with closely associated ETC complexes. To investigate this biochemically, we treated native lysates of IL-2 T E and IL-15 T M cells with increasing concentrations of digitonin to disrupt cell membranes (including mitochondrial). The crude membrane-bound fraction was separated from solubilized proteins by centrifugation. Both pellet and soluble supernatants were loaded on a denaturing reducing gel and then probed for various mitochondrial proteins by western blot. We found that mitochondria in IL-2 T E cells were susceptible to digitonin disruption, indicated by the fact that ETC complex proteins became less detectable in the pellet, and enriched in the soluble fraction in 0.5% detergent ([Figure 6J](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6) and [S6D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#SD6)). This was in contrast to IL-15 T M cells, where ETC proteins did not solubilize to the same extent as those in IL-2 T E cells into the supernatant, even when 2% digitonin was used. To investigate whether this phenomenon was unique to the mitochondrial compartment, we also probed for the ER integral protein calnexin and found that it solubilized similarly in 0.5% digitonin in both cell types. Overall these data suggest that there is more exposed mitochondrial membrane between proteins in IL-2 T E than IL-15 T M cells, and is consistent with the idea that T M cells have tight cristae which yield efficient ETC activity, while T E cells have looser cristae with less efficient ETC activity, ultimately supporting their distinct metabolic phenotypes.

### Mitochondrial fission in activated immune cells facilitates aerobic glycolysis

Our data supports a model wherein cristae remodeling, through fission and fusion events, is a mechanism to regulate efficient OXPHOS and FAO in T M cells, as well as the induction of aerobic glycolysis in T E cells. To more directly test this idea, we assessed ECAR of IL-15 T M cells stimulated with αCD3/28 beads in the presence or absence of Mdivi-1. We found that when mitochondrial fission protein Drp1 was inhibited with Mdivi-1, T cell activation did not robustly increase aerobic glycolysis when compared to controls ([Figure 6K](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)), which correlated with our EM data ([Figure 6I](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)). Since fission is associated with cell division ([Taguchi et al., 2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R51)), we tested our idea in a non-proliferating cell that substantially augments aerobic glycolysis upon stimulation ([Krawczyk et al., 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R26)). We stimulated bone marrow derived dendritic cells (BM-DCs) and macrophages (BM-Macs) with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) with or without interferon (IFN)-γ in the presence or absence of Mdivi-1 and measured ECAR. Aerobic glycolysis was curtailed in BM-DCs and BM-Macs after stimulation when Drp1 was inhibited ([Figure 6L](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)). The blunted ECAR in Mdivi-1 treated cells correlated with decreased nitric oxide synthase 2 (Nos2) protein expression in the BM-Macs ([Figure 6M](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#F6)), indicating that their activation was also repressed. These data show that cristae remodeling and/or fission acts as a signal to drive the induction of aerobic glycolysis, and subsequent cell activation via Drp1.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356)DISCUSSION

Although T M cells rely on FAO for development and survival, precisely why T M cells utilize FAO and the signals that drive the induction of aerobic glycolysis in T E cells remain unclear. Our data suggest that manipulating the structure of a single organelle can have profound consequences that impact metabolism and ultimately cell differentiation. We found that Opa1 regulated tight cristae organization in T M cells, which facilitated efficient ETC activity and favorable redox balance, allowing continued entrance of pyruvate into mitochondria. We originally hypothesized that Opa1 would be required for FAO. However, we found that Opa1−/− IL-2 T E and _ex vivo_ T E cells generated during infection utilized FAO to the same level as controls. While this was true for T E cells, this may not be the case for T M cells, whose survival is severely impaired _in vitro_ and _in vivo_ when Opa1 deficient. It is possible that Opa1−/− T cells are unable to form T M cells because they cannot efficiently engage FAO under the metabolic constraints imposed during T M cell development. Previous studies point to the existence of a ‘futile’ cycle of fatty acid synthesis (FAS) and FAO in T M cells ([O’Sullivan et al., 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R36), [Cui et al., 2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R15)) whereby carbon derived from glucose is used to build fat that is subsequently burned by mitochondria. T M cells have a lower overall metabolic rate than T E cells, and tightly configured cristae may be important to ensure that any pyruvate generated will efficiently feed into the TCA cycle not only for reducing equivalents, but also for deriving citrate for FAS. Without tight cristae and efficient ETC activity, electrons may loiter in the complexes causing more ROS which could be damaging, but also provide signals that drive cell activation ([Sena et al., 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R48)).

We did not observe a defect in T M cell survival in Mfn1−/− or Mfn2−/− T cells, but this does not exclude the possibility that OMM fusion or additional activities ascribed to each protein are not important. Mfn1 and Mfn2 form homotypic and heterotypic interactions, suggesting that in the absence of one, the other can compensate ([Chen et al., 2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4974356#R12)). Our results show that unlike Opa1−/− T cells, _in vitro_ cultured Mfn1−/− or Mfn2−/− T cells do not have a survival defect when differentiated in IL-15, even though, like Opa1−/− T cells, they are more glycolytic and OXPHOS-impaired compared to controls (**data not shown**). Our imaging data showed that T M cells maintained fused mitochondrial networks, suggesting that OMM fusion also has a compulsory role in T M cell development. However, unlike Opa1, retroviral expression of Mfn1 and Mfn2 did not confer a T M cell phenotype in T E cells. In this setting, an increase in OMM fusion without a concomitant increase in inner membrane fusion may still yield loose cristae morphology and a redox state that by default results in sustained excretion of lactate.

## Abstract

* * *

Activated effector T (TE) cells augment anabolic pathways of metabolism, such as aerobic glycolysis, while memory T (TM) cells engage catabolic pathways, like fatty acid oxidation (FAO). However, signals that drive these differences remain unclear. Mitochondria are metabolic organelles that actively transform their ultrastructure. Therefore, we questioned whether mitochondrial dynamics controls T cell metabolism. We show that TE cells have punctate mitochondria, while TM cells maintain fused networks. The fusion protein Opa1 is required for TM, but not TE cells after infection, and enforcing fusion in TE cells imposes TM cell characteristics and enhances antitumor function. Our data suggest that, by altering cristae morphology, fusion in TM cells configures electron transport chain (ETC) complex associations favoring oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and FAO, while fission in TE cells leads to cristae expansion, reducing ETC efficiency and promoting aerobic glycolysis. Thus, mitochondrial remodeling is a signaling mechanism that instructs T cell metabolic programming.

args.summary:
This is a Europe PMC article page for the scientific paper "Mitochondrial Dynamics Controls T Cell Fate through Metabolic Programming" published in Cell (09 Jun 2016, 166(1):63-76). DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2016.05.035; PMID: 27293185; PMCID: PMC4974356. The article has free full text available in Europe PMC.

The paper is authored by 19 researchers (including Buck MD, O'Sullivan D, Pearce EL) from institutions including the Max Planck Institute of Immunobiology and Epigenetics (Freiburg, Germany), Washington University School of Medicine (St. Louis, MO), University of California Los Angeles, and the University of Freiburg.

Key findings from the abstract:
- Activated effector T (TE) cells augment anabolic pathways such as aerobic glycolysis, while memory T (TM) cells engage catabolic pathways like fatty acid oxidation (FAO).
- TE cells have punctate mitochondria, while TM cells maintain fused networks.
- The fusion protein Opa1 is required for TM, but not TE cells, after infection.
- Enforcing fusion in TE cells imposes TM cell characteristics and enhances antitumor function.
- Fusion in TM cells configures electron transport chain (ETC) complex associations favoring oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and FAO by altering cristae morphology, while fission in TE cells leads to cristae expansion, reducing ETC efficiency and promoting aerobic glycolysis.
- Conclusion: Mitochondrial remodeling is a signaling mechanism that instructs T cell metabolic programming.

The page lists five similar articles, including papers on AMPKα1 and T-cell memory, BCL11B and OPA1-mediated mitochondrial fusion, and memory CD8(+) T cells using cell-intrinsic lipolysis. Funding sources include Bundesministerium für Bildung und Forschung, Burroughs Wellcome Fund, Max-Planck-Gesellschaft, NCI NIH HHS, NIAID NIH HHS, National Institutes of Health, and National Science Foundation. Three commentary articles on this work also appear in Cell Research, Cell, and Nature Reviews Immunology.

Effect of T cell mitochondrial quality control on immunometabolism. The differentiation and function of immune cells largely depend on specific metabolic programs determined by mitochondria. Mitochondrial metabolism is closely linked to mitochondrial morphology, which is influenced by mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics, mitophagy, and mitochondrial transfer. Furthermore, mitochondrial biogenesis favors the metabolic reprogramming in T cells, with the crucial regulatory molecule being PGC-1α. PD-1 signaling promotes these metabolic alterations by driving Blimp1-mediated inhibition of PGC-1α. Mitochondrial dynamics, which include fusion and fission, determine T-cell differentiation and fate. Effector T cells possess fissed mitochondria with loosened cristae, whereas memory T cells have fused mitochondria with tighter cristae and expanded space. PD-1 signaling reduces the activity of mitochondrial fission protein Drp1; forcing mitochondrial fusion drives memory T cell differentiation. Mitochondrial autophagy (mitophagy) maintains T cell homeostasis. However, T cells gradually become exhausted under chronic antigenic stimulation, and this exhaustion is closely related to mitochondrial dysfunction in T cells. Mitochondria play a crucial role in the metabolic reprogramming of T cells to achieve the desired immune response. Here, we compiled the latest research on how mitochondrial metabolism determines T cell function and differentiation, with the mechanisms mainly including mitochondrial biogenesis, fission, fusion, mitophagy, and mitochondrial transfer. In addition, the alterations in mitochondrial metabolism in T-cell exhaustion were also reviewed. Furthermore, we discussed intervention strategies targeting mitochondrial metabolism to reverse T cell exhaustion in detail, including inducing PGC-1α expression, alleviating reactive oxygen species (ROS) production or hypoxia, enhancing ATP production, and utilizing mitochondrial transfer. Targeting mitochondrial metabolism in exhausted T cells may achieve the goal of reversing and preventing T cell exhaustion. Keywords: [T-cell exhaustion](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=T-cell+exhaustion); [mitochondria](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=mitochondria); [metabolism](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=metabolism); [metabolic reprogramming](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=metabolic+reprogramming); [mitochondrial dynamics](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=mitochondrial+dynamics) ## 1. Introduction During many chronic infections, such as lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis), and cancer, persistent antigen exposure can lead to dysfunction or even exhaustion of antigen-specific T cells [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B1-ijms-26-07400)]. Exhausted T cells exhibit overexpression of multiple inhibitory receptors, such as PD-1 and T cell immunoglobulin mucin 3 (TIM-3), and lymphocyte activation gene 3 (LAG-3), along with a gradual reduction in effector function and proliferative capacity, and a progressive loss of memory T cell potential, including the antigen-independent self-renewal ability and the capacity to generate strong recall responses [[2](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B2-ijms-26-07400)]. Additionally, exhausted T cells exhibit altered transcription factor expression, including upregulated expression of B lymphocyte-induced maturation protein-1 (Blimp-1) and thymocyte selection-associated HMG box (TOX) [[3](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B3-ijms-26-07400),[4](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B4-ijms-26-07400)]. Persistent antigen stimulation, high levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and hypoxia are key drivers of T-cell exhaustion [[5](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B5-ijms-26-07400),[6](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B6-ijms-26-07400)]. Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy, such as nivolumab, can rejuvenate exhausted T cells; however, it still has many limitations [[7](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B7-ijms-26-07400),[8](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B8-ijms-26-07400)]. Therefore, it is necessary to explore new mechanisms of T cell exhaustion, particularly the role of mitochondrial metabolism in its regulation, to identify new therapeutic targets for treating T cell exhaustion. The immune status of T cells is determined by their metabolic fitness, leading to different functional abilities and disease outcomes [[9](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B9-ijms-26-07400)]. During acute infection, naïve T cells undergo metabolic reprogramming from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) towards aerobic glycolysis to provide a quick energy source and meet the increased bioenergetic requirements of effector T cells [[10](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B10-ijms-26-07400),[11](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B11-ijms-26-07400)]. After effector T cells undergo a contraction stage, a small number of memory T cells persist, and these transformed memory T cells are characterized by their utilization of mitochondrial OXPHOS and fatty acid oxidation (FAO) for energy to sustain a recall response during reinfection [[12](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B12-ijms-26-07400)]. During chronic infection, continuous antigenic stimulation drives T cell dysfunction and even exhaustion. Exhausted T cells can be divided into two subsets: progenitor exhausted T cells and terminally exhausted T cells [[13](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B13-ijms-26-07400)]. Progenitor exhausted T cells are a type of “stem-like” T cell population with self-renewal capacity that responds to PD-1 pathway blockade therapy, while terminally exhausted T cells exhibit impaired proliferative ability and do not respond to PD-1 blockade [[14](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B14-ijms-26-07400),[15](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B15-ijms-26-07400),[16](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B16-ijms-26-07400)]. Progenitor exhausted CD8+ T cells exhibit intermediate expression of PD-1, high expression of CD127, chemokine receptor CXCR5, and T-cell factor 1 (TCF-1), whereas terminally exhausted T cells show high expression of PD-1 and TIM-3, with a loss of expression of TCF-1 and CXCR5 [[17](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B17-ijms-26-07400)]. CXCR5+ CD8+ T cells also express several genes related to the self-renewal and maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells in the Wnt signaling pathway [[18](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B18-ijms-26-07400)]. Metabolically, progenitor exhausted T cells use mitochondrial FAO and OXPHOS for energy [[19](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B19-ijms-26-07400)], whereas terminally exhausted T cells primarily rely on glycolytic metabolism, with impaired glycolysis and OXPHOS [[20](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B20-ijms-26-07400),[21](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B21-ijms-26-07400),[22](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B22-ijms-26-07400)]. The exhausted T cells mentioned in this review mainly refer to terminally exhausted T cells. Mitochondria are the energy factories of cells, and mitochondrial activity plays a critical role in the activation and maintenance of antigen-specific responses, particularly during memory responses and T-cell exhaustion [[23](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B23-ijms-26-07400)]. Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of T-cell exhaustion. The mitochondrial metabolic capacity can be an important factor to consider when designing immunotherapies to rescue exhausted T cells in cancer or chronic infections [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B24-ijms-26-07400)]. Therefore, studying the changes in mitochondrial metabolism during exhaustion can help identify new targets for therapeutic intervention. ## 2. Mitochondrial Metabolism Determines T Cell Function and Fate Mitochondria are widely recognized as the powerhouse of cells, producing adenosine triphosphate (ATP) through OXPHOS to provide energy for cellular functions. They serve as the primary metabolic regulators of T cells [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B24-ijms-26-07400)]. Mitochondrial function and energy metabolism influence T cell function, activation, proliferation, differentiation, memory, and exhaustion [[25](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B25-ijms-26-07400)]. Furthermore, mitochondrial metabolism determines T-cell fate and function through metabolic reprogramming [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B24-ijms-26-07400),[26](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B26-ijms-26-07400),[27](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B27-ijms-26-07400)]. It is closely linked to mitochondrial morphology, which is affected by mitochondrial biogenesis, fission, fusion, mitochondrial autophagy (mitophagy), and mitochondrial transfer [[28](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B28-ijms-26-07400),[29](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B29-ijms-26-07400)] ([Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#fig_body_display_ijms-26-07400-f001)). ![Image 11: Ijms 26 07400 g001](https://www.mdpi.com/ijms/ijms-26-07400/article_deploy/html/images/ijms-26-07400-g001-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#fig_body_display_ijms-26-07400-f001) **Figure 1.** Effect of T cell mitochondrial quality control on immunometabolism. The differentiation and function of immune cells largely depend on specific metabolic programs determined by mitochondria. Mitochondrial metabolism is closely linked to mitochondrial morphology, which is influenced by mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics, mitophagy, and mitochondrial transfer. Furthermore, mitochondrial biogenesis favors the metabolic reprogramming in T cells, with the crucial regulatory molecule being PGC-1α. PD-1 signaling promotes these metabolic alterations by driving Blimp1-mediated inhibition of PGC-1α. Mitochondrial dynamics, which include fusion and fission, determine T-cell differentiation and fate. Effector T cells possess fissed mitochondria with loosened cristae, whereas memory T cells have fused mitochondria with tighter cristae and expanded space. PD-1 signaling reduces the activity of mitochondrial fission protein Drp1; forcing mitochondrial fusion drives memory T cell differentiation. Mitochondrial autophagy (mitophagy) maintains T cell homeostasis. Mitochondrial transfer can alter the metabolic status of both donor and recipient by affecting mitochondrial mass, thus becoming a target for immunotherapy. ### 2.1. Mitochondrial Biogenesis Facilitates T Cell Metabolic Reprogramming Mitochondrial biogenesis is an important part of mitochondrial quality control [[30](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B30-ijms-26-07400)]. Mitochondrial biogenesis occurs rapidly in nascent activated CD8+ T cells and is crucial for supporting cytokine generation by T cells in early immune responses [[31](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B31-ijms-26-07400)]. Proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1 α (PGC-1α) is a critical regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and mitochondrial plasticity [[32](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B32-ijms-26-07400)]. PGC-1a is located upstream of the mitochondrial biogenesis system and serves as a junction between mitochondrial external stimulus signals and internal regulation. PGC-1α activates peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α (PPAR-α) and acts as a coactivator of PPAR-α in the transcriptional regulation of mitochondrial FAO capacity [[33](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B33-ijms-26-07400)]. Overexpression of PGC-1α enhances mitochondrial biogenesis, restores T cell function, and improves anti-tumor immunity [[21](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B21-ijms-26-07400)]. ### 2.2. Mitochondria Dynamics Control T Cell Fate Mitochondrial cristae morphology reflects metabolic states [[34](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B34-ijms-26-07400)]. Mitochondria are highly dynamic organelles that maintain normal counts, shape, and function through constant fusion and division, a process commonly referred to as mitochondrial dynamics [[35](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B35-ijms-26-07400)]. Fusion relieves stress by mixing the contents of partially damaged mitochondria, while fission helps to remove damaged mitochondria, promotes apoptosis under high cellular stress, and is necessary for generating new mitochondria [[36](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B36-ijms-26-07400)]. Mitochondrial fusion is associated with increased OXPHOS and ATP generation [[37](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B37-ijms-26-07400)]. Furthermore, the dynamics of mitochondrial fusion and fission are controlled by proteins that regulate mitochondrial form. For example, fission is governed by the mitochondrial fission factor (Mff) and dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), whereas optic atrophy 1 (OPA1), mitofusin 1 (MFN1), and mitofusin 2 (MFN2) favor mitochondrial fusion and promote cellular ATP generation [[30](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B30-ijms-26-07400),[38](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B38-ijms-26-07400),[39](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B39-ijms-26-07400)]. Mitochondrial dynamics determine T cell fate through metabolic programming [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B26-ijms-26-07400)]. Effector T cells possess fissed mitochondria with loosened cristae, whereas memory T cells have fused mitochondria with tighter cristae and expanded space. Altering mitochondrial fission/fusion drives changes in cristae morphology, further inducing metabolic programming and ultimately controlling T cell differentiation. Memory T cells are characterized by enhanced mitochondrial function [[40](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B40-ijms-26-07400)]. Forcing mitochondrial fusion drives memory T cell differentiation by promoting OXPHOS and FAO, while mitochondria fission facilitates aerobic glycolysis within effector T cells [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B26-ijms-26-07400),[41](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B41-ijms-26-07400)]. Furthermore, mitochondrial fission produces discrete and fragmented mitochondria, which contribute to elevated ROS production and promote mitochondrial polarization [[42](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B42-ijms-26-07400),[43](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B43-ijms-26-07400)]. Under normal circumstances, the small amount of ROS generated by mitochondria is crucial for promoting T cell activation and proliferation to acquire effective functions. Excessive mitochondrial ROS can activate continuous nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) signaling [[23](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B23-ijms-26-07400)], leading to terminal exhaustion [[5](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B5-ijms-26-07400)]. Since Drp1-mediated fission promotes mitophagy, decreased Drp1 activity or DRP1 deletion may lead to T cell exhaustion by inhibiting mitophagy [[44](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B44-ijms-26-07400)]. Interestingly, there are also opposing views on the role of Drp1. Specifically, Drp1 deficiency leads to mitochondrial fusion, while Drp1 knockout drives the conversion from effector T cells to a memory phenotype [[45](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B45-ijms-26-07400)]. For instance, the treatment of T cells with ‘mitochondrial fission inhibitor’ mdivi-1 [[46](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B46-ijms-26-07400)] and the ‘fusion promoter’ M1 [[47](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B47-ijms-26-07400)] induces mitochondrial fusion, thereby conferring a memory T cell phenotype and promoting the generation of memory-like T cells [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B26-ijms-26-07400)]. Therefore, inhibiting fission may prevent ROS production and favor the formation of memory T cells [[43](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B43-ijms-26-07400),[48](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B48-ijms-26-07400)]. The role of Drp1 in exhaustion and memory formation remains to be explored. ### 2.3. Mitochondrial Autophagy (Mitophagy) Maintains Cellular Homeostasis Mitophagy, the process of selectively eliminating dysfunctional mitochondria, is essential for mitochondrial quality control [[49](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B49-ijms-26-07400)]. Damaged mitochondria are often accompanied by a reduction in electron transport chain (ETC) efficiency, which then leads to a decrease in ATP generation [[50](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B50-ijms-26-07400)]. Dysfunctional mitochondria or elevated depolarized mitochondria are the main source of ROS that cause oxidative damage and lead to cell necrosis [[51](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B51-ijms-26-07400),[52](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B52-ijms-26-07400)]. However, mitophagy removes ROS to maintain mitochondrial integrity [[53](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B53-ijms-26-07400)]. Repressing mitophagy results in excessive ROS accumulation and causes apoptosis in cells [[54](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B54-ijms-26-07400)]. Mitophagy is mediated by the PTEN-induced putative protein kinase 1 (PINK1)/Parkin-directed pathway [[55](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B55-ijms-26-07400),[56](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B56-ijms-26-07400)]. Park2 is an E3 ligase that also mediates mitophagy, which can destroy mitophagy activity after removal and further promote the acquisition of T cell mitochondrial depolarization phenotype. Consistently, the blockade of mitophagy by oligomycin plus the mitophagy inhibitor mdivi-1 also favors the formation of depolarized mitochondria, which reinforces T-cell exhaustion [[57](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B57-ijms-26-07400)]. In addition, mitophagy is vital for memory formation, primarily by eliminating dysfunctional mitochondria and maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis [[58](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B58-ijms-26-07400),[59](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B59-ijms-26-07400)]. ### 2.4. Mitochondrial Transfer Modulates Intercellular Communication Mitochondrial transfer/transplantation is the process of transporting healthy/functional mitochondria from donor cells into surrounding cells with damaged mitochondria, thereby increasing mitochondrial mass and improving functionality [[60](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B60-ijms-26-07400),[61](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B61-ijms-26-07400),[62](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B62-ijms-26-07400)]. Currently, there are four main modes of mitochondrial transfer, including extracellular vehicles (EVs), endocytosis, gap junctions, and tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) [[29](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B29-ijms-26-07400),[63](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B63-ijms-26-07400),[64](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B64-ijms-26-07400)]. On one hand, cancer cells could deprive mitochondria of T cells through intercellular nanotubes-TNTs to evade the immune system and enhance cancer aggressiveness [[65](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B65-ijms-26-07400)]. In this regard, mitochondrial transfer seems to be a detrimental phenomenon for tumors. On the other hand, T cells also acquire mitochondria from other cells, promoting cell proliferation and differentiation, suggesting that mitochondrial transfer may be a novel strategy for treating chronic infections [[66](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B66-ijms-26-07400)]. Altogether, mitochondrial transfer functions as a double-edged sword for T cells. However, a major limitation currently hindering the translation of mitochondrial transfer into clinical practice is its low efficiency (about 10%, up to 28%) and the lack of a simple method for tracking transferred mitochondria [[67](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B67-ijms-26-07400)]. ## 3. Changes in Mitochondrial Metabolism in T-Cell Exhaustion The metabolic characteristics of exhausted T cells include disrupted mitochondrial energy and respiration, increased depolarized mitochondria, and accumulation of ROS, leading to reduced glucose uptake, defective glycolysis, and OXPHOS [[6](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B6-ijms-26-07400)]. PD-1 signaling promotes these metabolic alterations by driving Blimp1-mediated inhibition of PGC-1α, a major regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. The repression of PGC-1α is particularly prominent in viraemic HIV-1-infected exhausted CD8 T cells [[68](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B68-ijms-26-07400)]. Inhibition of PGC-1α leads to elevated mitochondrial ROS, which acts as a phosphatase inhibitor, activates phosphotyrosine signaling, and induces NFAT localization, thereby promoting the activation of exhaustion-associated genes, such as TOX and Blimp1. Enforcing the expression of PGC-1α can reverse PD-1-induced bioenergetic deficiency and rescue exhausted T cells [[6](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B6-ijms-26-07400)]. Exhausted T cells display a reduction in abnormal mitochondrial morphology and mass, an increase in mitochondrial size, a decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential, and a loss of mitochondrial fitness [[69](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B69-ijms-26-07400)], indicating mitochondrial dysfunction. This contributes to the inability of exhausted T cells to effectively utilize OXPHOS for energy [[22](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B22-ijms-26-07400)]. Compared to memory T cells, exhausted T cells maintain a slightly larger mitochondrial mass and significantly increased amounts of depolarized mitochondria [[70](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B70-ijms-26-07400)]. Mechanically, oxidative stress caused by mitochondrial dysfunction antagonizes the proteasomal degradation of hypoxia-inducing factor 1α (HIF-1α), which mediates the glycolytic reprogramming of progenitor exhausted T cells towards terminally exhausted T cells [[71](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B71-ijms-26-07400)]. Additionally, PD-1 signaling induces alterations in cristae morphology, such as reducing the number and length of mitochondrial cristae, and decreasing the expression of CHCHD3 and CHCHD10, which are involved in cristae structure and organization, ultimately leading to apparent mitochondrial dysfunction [[72](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B72-ijms-26-07400)]. PD-1 signaling directly decreases mitochondrial fission by downregulating Drp1 phosphorylation [[73](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B73-ijms-26-07400)]. Additionally, ATP is not only necessary for the functions of activated T cells, such as cell proliferation and cytokine production, but also for the homeostasis of mitochondria [[74](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B74-ijms-26-07400)]. Continuous antigen stimulation disrupts T cell OXPHOS, driving exhaustion through impaired ATP generation and limited self-renewal gene expression [[75](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B75-ijms-26-07400)]. During chronic infection, ATP is reduced and insufficient, thereby unable to maintain mitochondrial function and mass, leading to T cell dysfunction. CD39, also known as external nucleoside triphosphate diphosphate hydrolase-1 (ENTPD1), is the prototype of the ENTPDase family and catabolizes extracellular pro-inflammatory ATP and ADP into AMP. AMP is further degraded by the ecto-5′-nucleotidase CD73 into anti-inflammatory adenosine, which is subsequently converted to inosine by adenosine deaminase [[76](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B76-ijms-26-07400),[77](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B77-ijms-26-07400)]. CD39 is highly expressed on exhausted T cells and is defined as a new marker of T cell exhaustion [[78](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B78-ijms-26-07400),[79](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B79-ijms-26-07400)]. CD73 has also emerged as a promising therapeutic target. Furthermore, the exhausted T cells also exhibit significant downregulation of mitochondrial genes encoding specific mitochondrial proteins [[80](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B80-ijms-26-07400)]. These genes encode proteins, including mitochondrial fusion protein OPA1 and carnitine palmitoyl transferase 1α (CPT-1α), which is involved in controlling mitochondrial FAO and driving memory T cell formation [[81](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B81-ijms-26-07400)]. Exhausted CD8+ T cells display various structural or functional mitochondrial changes, which are caused by impaired mitochondrial mitophagy capacity [[57](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B57-ijms-26-07400)]. In addition, the mitochondrial dysfunction in exhausted T cells is associated with the depletion of mitochondrial transcriptional factor A (Tfam), which leads to dysfunction. Tfam deficiency in T cells can result in severe mitochondrial DNA loss, disrupting T cell receptor (TCR)-driven cell proliferation and effector function [[82](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B82-ijms-26-07400),[83](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B83-ijms-26-07400)]. Moreover, mitochondrial phosphatase PTPMT1-mediated metabolism is necessary to maintain the differentiation and expansion of effector T cells. Loss of PTPMT1 impairs T cell anti-tumor immunity and accelerates T cell exhaustion [[84](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B84-ijms-26-07400)]. ## 4. Potential Therapeutic Strategies for Mitochondrial Metabolic Regulation in Reversing T-Cell Exhaustion Exhausted T cells exhibit a repressed mitochondrial metabolism and decreased mitochondrial mass. Correcting mitochondrial dysfunction and restoring mitochondrial function has been shown to reinvigorate exhausted T cell function [[80](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B80-ijms-26-07400),[85](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B85-ijms-26-07400)]. Restoring mitochondrial mass can improve cell function. Furthermore, enhancing mitochondrial function might represent a therapeutic strategy for reversing exhausted T cells [[21](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B21-ijms-26-07400)]. Several strategies, such as inducing PGC-1α expression, alleviating ROS production or hypoxia, inducing ATP production, and utilizing mitochondrial transfer, may be effective ([Table 1](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#table_body_display_ijms-26-07400-t001)). ### 4.1. Inducing PGC-1α Expression Enforcing mitochondrial biogenesis is beneficial for boosting T cell immune response, and promoting the biogenesis and function of mitochondria can prevent T cell exhaustion [[86](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B86-ijms-26-07400)]. In combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors, enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis may enhance the efficacy of immunotherapy and combat immune exhaustion [[80](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B80-ijms-26-07400)]. PGC-1α enhances mitochondrial biogenesis [[87](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B87-ijms-26-07400)]. Bezafibrate, a mitochondrial activator and PGC-1α agonist, improves the antitumor response to PD-1 blockade nivolumab [[88](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B88-ijms-26-07400)]. Another mitochondrial regulator, complement C1q binding protein (C1QBP), contributes to mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1α. Insufficient C1QBP can result in compromised mitochondrial fitness in T cells, exacerbating T cell exhaustion, while the overexpression of C1QBP may modify the state of exhaustion [[89](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B89-ijms-26-07400)]. Overexpression of PGC-1α promotes memory formation [[90](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B90-ijms-26-07400)] and restores mitochondrial function and exhausted CD8 T cell function by reversing metabolic dysregulation [[6](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B6-ijms-26-07400),[21](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B21-ijms-26-07400)]. Furthermore, the costimulatory molecule 4-1BB promotes PGC-1α-dependent mitochondrial fusion and biogenesis by activating p38-MAPK and enhancing metabolism [[91](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B91-ijms-26-07400)]. 4-1BB costimulation can enhance mitochondrial fusion and biogenesis [[92](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B92-ijms-26-07400)]. Overexpression of 4-1BB increased mitochondrial mass and transmembrane potential, thereby enhancing mitochondrial respiratory capacity [[93](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B93-ijms-26-07400)]. Moreover, 4-1BB agonists enhance T cell activity in a PGC-1α-dependent manner, induce a memory-like state, and metabolically facilitate the anti-PD-1 response [[92](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B92-ijms-26-07400)]. Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) transfers electrons from complexes I and II to complex III, a crucial step in ATP production. The concentration of CoQ10 is regarded as an indicator of mitochondrial function. Additionally, hydrogen gas, a PGC-1α activator, activates CoQ10 to rejuvenate exhausted CD8+ T cells, thereby enhancing the clinical efficacy of nivolumab [[94](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B94-ijms-26-07400)]. Moreover, AMPK has been proven to drive mitochondrial biogenesis by promoting the activation of PGC-1α [[95](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B95-ijms-26-07400)]. Metformin, an activator of AMPK, increases PGC-1α expression and restores mitochondrial FAO to promote mitochondrial function, thus reinvigorating CD8+ T cell exhaustion [[96](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B96-ijms-26-07400),[97](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B97-ijms-26-07400),[98](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B98-ijms-26-07400)]. IL-15 can also induce PGC-1α expression and promote mitochondrial biogenesis [[99](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B99-ijms-26-07400)]. ### 4.2. Alleviating ROS Production Neutralizing intracellular ROS can restore T cell self-renewal and reverse metabolic defects, as ROS accumulation limits cell proliferation and self-renewal gene expression in chronically infected T cells. Utilizing antioxidants (ROS scavengers) to restore T cell function offers a promising approach for rescuing exhausted T cell immunity. Antioxidants mitigate ROS production and reduce the effects of oxidative damage [[100](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B100-ijms-26-07400)]. Treatment with N-Ac alone or in conjunction with anti-PD-L1 therapy enhances anti-tumor immunity [[101](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400#B101-ijms-26-07400)]. However, T cells gradually become exhausted under chronic antigenic stimulation, and this exhaustion is closely related to mitochondrial dysfunction in T cells., Exhausted T cells exhibit overexpression of multiple inhibitory receptors, such as PD-1 and T cell immunoglobulin mucin 3 (TIM-3), and lymphocyte activation gene 3 (LAG-3), along with a gradual reduction in effector function and proliferative capacity., Forcing mitochondrial fusion drives memory T cell differentiation by promoting OXPHOS and FAO, while mitochondria fission facilitates aerobic glycolysis within effector T cells., The metabolic characteristics of exhausted T cells include disrupted mitochondrial energy and respiration, increased depolarized mitochondria, and accumulation of ROS, leading to reduced glucose uptake, defective glycolysis, and OXPHOS., Targeting mitochondrial metabolism in exhausted T cells may achieve the goal of reversing and preventing T cell exhaustion.
args.summary:
This is a scientific review article published in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences (IJMS) on July 31, 2025, titled "Mitochondrial Metabolism in T-Cell Exhaustion" by Fei Li, Yu Feng, Zesheng Yin, and Yahong Wang from Lanzhou University, China. The article reviews the role of mitochondrial metabolism in T-cell exhaustion, which occurs under chronic antigen stimulation from infections (e.g., HIV, HBV, HCV, tuberculosis) and cancer.

Key points:
1. Exhausted T cells overexpress inhibitory receptors (PD-1, TIM-3, LAG-3), have reduced effector function and proliferative capacity, and exhibit altered transcription factor expression (Blimp-1, TOX).

2. Mitochondrial metabolism determines T cell function and fate through biogenesis, dynamics (fusion/fission), mitophagy, and mitochondrial transfer. PGC-1α is a critical regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. Effector T cells have fragmented mitochondria with loosened cristae, while memory T cells have fused mitochondria with tighter cristae.

3. Exhausted T cells show disrupted mitochondrial energy metabolism, increased depolarized mitochondria, ROS accumulation, reduced glucose uptake, and defective glycolysis and OXPHOS. PD-1 signaling promotes these changes by inhibiting PGC-1α via Blimp1.

4. Progenitor exhausted T cells (stem-like, self-renewing) use FAO and OXPHOS, while terminally exhausted T cells rely on glycolytic metabolism. Terminally exhausted T cells express high PD-1 and TIM-3, lose TCF-1 and CXCR5 expression.

5. Potential therapeutic strategies include: inducing PGC-1α expression (using bezafibrate, 4-1BB costimulation, CoQ10, hydrogen gas, metformin, IL-15), alleviating ROS production (using antioxidants like N-acetylcysteine and MitoQ), enhancing ATP production, and utilizing mitochondrial transfer.
