## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353)Introduction

Immune resolution of an initial encounter with a pathogen or vaccination usually results in populations of memory T cells that are specific for the introduced antigens and can prevent or reduce the severity of a subsequent infection. The majority of effector T cells that initially expand from infection or immunization will undergo cell death during a contraction phase, while a small fraction will differentiate into a lasting memory T cell population[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R1)–[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R3)]. These memory T cells exist in larger numbers and respond more rapidly than naïve T cells[[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R4)]. Therefore, the efficacy of vaccines could be improved by supporting the development of memory T cells.

T cells utilize mitochondrial dynamics to respond to their metabolic needs. The size and shape of mitochondria are altered through a balance of fission and fusion[[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R5)]. In response to T cell receptor (TCR) engagement, quiescent T cells can rapidly increase metabolism to support expansion and differentiation. Effector T cells engage both aerobic glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) metabolism to support the energetic and biosynthetic demands of an activated, proliferative cell[[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R6)–[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R8)]. Furthermore, memory T cells favor fatty acid oxidation (FAO) and OXPHOS, which are supported by increased mitochondrial mass and an elongated mitochondrial network in memory T cells [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R9), [10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R10)]. The elongated mitochondrial morphology and increased mitochondrial mass of memory T cells create a metabolic spare respiratory capacity (SRC) which allows memory cells to rapidly respond to a secondary antigen encounter[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R11)]. As the mitochondrial fission process primarily relies on the scission activity of the GTPase, Dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1)[[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R12), [13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R13)], targeting DRP1 may provide an avenue to augment memory T cell development, survival, or responsiveness.

Supporting the idea that the manipulation of mitochondrial morphology may provide an opportunity to augment immunological memory, the pharmacological treatment of effector T cells with the mitochondrial fusion enforcer, M1, and mitochondrial division inhibitor, M-divi, endow effector T cells with increased SRC and mitochondrial mass comparable to that of in vitro memory-like T cells[[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R10)]. At the time of this discovery, M-divi was widely used as a specific inhibitor of the mitochondrial fission protein, DRP1, but this has since come into question when it was shown to not affect mitochondrial morphology and to inhibit complex I of the electron transport chain in mammalian cells[[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R14)]. Thus, it cannot be concluded from this study that inhibition of mitochondrial fission is directly responsible for promoting memory cell differentiation.

The notion that targeting DRP1 can be leveraged to support memory T cell development and function is potentially countered by several roles for DRP1 in T cell biology. First, deletion of DRP1 in T cells is likely to be detrimental to activation and proliferation. During the process of T cell activation, DRP1 assists in positioning mitochondria near the immune synapse, without which T cell receptor (TCR) signal strength is reduced[[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R15)]. Diminished TCR signaling could limit T cell expansion, but also limit differentiation into effector populations. Additionally, interfering with mitochondrial dynamics can hinder cell division[[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R16), [17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R17)]. Pertaining to this, Simula et al. previously demonstrated that LckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice have reduced numbers of thymocytes and mature T cells in the blood and spleen, and only produce about half as many antigen specific T cells compared to controls 4d after exposure to tumor antigen[[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R18)]. Thus, constraining DRP1 may limit the pool of memory precursor cells. Second, DRP1 is also implicated in maintaining the health of mitochondria, as damaged mitochondria are removed through the process of mitophagy[[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R19)]. T cells with unhealthy mitochondria might not be expected to efficiently populate the memory pool or might be compromised in their capacity to respond to a secondary exposure to antigen. However, T cells become less susceptible to programmed cell death when DRP1 is inhibited[[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R20)]. DRP1-dependent fission also occurs following TCR signaling and ultimately results in activation induced cell death[[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R21)]. Thus, DRP1 has complex roles in contributing to T cell survival and memory T cell development that need further clarification before being effectively leveraged for the purposes of improved vaccination.

Based on these considerations, we sought to generate further insights into the relationship between mitochondrial fission and T cell differentiation, particularly how DRP1 affects the development of in vivo effector T cells, memory T cells, or the capacity for those memory cells to mount a secondary response to antigen challenge. We therefore utilized mouse models of T cell specific DRP1 deletion to address these unknowns.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353)Materials and Methods

### Animals

All mice were treated in accordance with policies established by the University of Virginia Animal Care and Use Committee protocol 3292. _Drp1_ _f_ lfl mice were developed by Dr Hiromi Sesaki and generously provided by Dr David Kashatus at the University of Virginia[[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R22)]. E8iCreERT2 mice were generously provided by Dr Dario Vignali at the University of Pittsburgh[[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R23)]. C57BL/6NCr (027) and B6-Ly5.2/Cr (564) mice were purchased from the National Cancer Institute. dLckCre (012837) and Thy1.1 (000406) mice were purchased from Jackson[[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R24), [25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R25)].

### In vitro T cell stimulation

Mouse T cells were labeled with Cell Trace Violet (CTV; 5 μM; Invitrogen) according to the manufacturers protocol. CTV labeled mouse T cells were then cultured _in vitro_ for 2–3 days with anti-CD3 (5 μg/mL plate bound; eBioscience, clone 17A2), anti-CD28 (2 μg/mL soluble; eBioscience, clone 37.51), and IL-2 (10 IU/mL; Chiron). Cell culture media is RPMI with 10% FBS (Corning), HEPES, Non-essential amino acids, essential amino acids, gentamicin, sodium pyruvate, L-glutamine, and β-Mercaptoethanol (all from Gibco).

### T cell stimulation for cytokine assessment

Murine T cells were stimulated in vitro with OVA 257–264 peptide pulsed (10 μg/mL; Genscript) LB15.13 antigen presenting cells (ATCC) or with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA; 0.2 μg/mL; Thermo Fisher) and Ionomycin (0.14 μg/mL; Sigma) in the presence of Brefeldin A (3 μg/mL; Thermo Fisher) for 4–6 hours. Cell culture media is RPMI with 10% FBS (Corning), HEPES, Non-essential amino acids, essential amino acids, gentamicin, sodium pyruvate, L-glutamine, and β-Mercaptoethanol (all from Gibco).

### Flow Cytometry Staining

Single cell suspensions were prepared via mechanical homogenization, 70 μm filtration (Genesee), and red blood cell lysis (Sigma). Cell viability was assessed with fixable aqua or far-red LIVE/DEAD Fixable Dead Cell Stains (Life Technologies) in PBS. H-2K b/SIINFEKL dextramer (Immudex) was used to identify ovalbumin 257–264 (OVA) specific T cells followed by a panel of all other surface antibodies. Surface staining was performed in FACS buffer (PBS containing 2% BSA, 0.08% sodium azide). For cytokine staining, Cytofix/Cytoperm Fixation and Permeabilization Solution (BD Biosciences) and Perm/Wash Buffer (BD Biosciences) were used. For nuclear staining, Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer Set (eBioscience) was used. At the end of staining, samples were preserved using FACS lysis (BD Biosciences) and stored in FACS buffer. Live cell staining was performed entirely in PBS and immediately acquired. 123 count eBeads (Invitrogen) were used to calculate cell counts and UltraComp eBeads (Invitrogen) for single stain preparations.

### MitoTracker Green (MTG) and Tetramethylrhodamine ethyl ester (TMRE) staining

For MTG and TMRE staining, samples were stained with Aqua Live/Dead dye and antibodies specific to surface proteins as above and then incubated at 37°C for 20 minutes with 50 nM MTG (M-7514, ThermoFisher) or 100 nM TMRE (ab113852, Abcam) diluted in serum-free RPMI with HEPES, Non-essential amino acids, essential amino acids, gentamicin, sodium pyruvate, L-glutamine, and β-Mercaptoethanol (all from Gibco). All samples were washed with 1xPBS twice and immediately analyzed by flow cytometry while keeping them on ice in 0.2% FBS in 1xPBS.

### Flow cytometry acquisition and analysis

Samples stained for flow cytometry were collected and compensation algorithm applied on an AttuneNxT cytometer (ThermoFisher). The resulting FCS files were analyzed, and plots generated using FlowJo 10 (BD). All flow cytometry data is pre-gated on single cells, lymphocyte scatter, viable cells, and CD45 expression.

### In vivo priming

Mice were injected intraperitoneally (IP) with 100 μg αCD40 (FGK45; BioXcell), 75 μg polyI:C (Invivogen), and 500 μg ovalbumin (Sigma) in 200 μL of PBS, ph 7.4 (Gibco).

Secondary responses were initiated in OVA primed mice by IP challenge with 2×10 8 p.f.u. recombinant AdenoOVA, originally provided by Dr Young Hahn, University of Virginia.

### Seahorse Mitochondrial Stress Test

CD8+ T cells were magnetically enriched (ThermoFisher) washed with 1xPBS and seeded in XFe96 cell culture miniplate in XF minimal media (Agilent) supplemented with 10 mM glucose (Sigma), 2 mM glutamine (Invitrogen), and 2 mM sodium pyruvate (ThermoFisher). Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was measured by extracellular flux analysis using a Seahorse XFe96 analyzer (Agilent) in response to 1 μM oligomycin, 1 μM fluoro-carbonyl cyanide phenylhydrazone (FCCP), and 0.5 μM rotenone/antimycin (all from Sigma except antimycin, MP Biochemical).

### Mixed bone marrow chimera mouse generation

Donor mouse femurs and tibia were collected from Thy1.1+CD45.2+ wild type and Thy1.2+CD45.2+ dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice then centrifuged at ≥10,000g to collect bone marrow. Thy1.2+CD45.1+ recipient mice were irradiated over two sessions for a total of 1300 rads then 500,000 donor cells were transferred into recipient mice intravenously. Mice were kept on sulfa water for 8 weeks prior to experimental use.

### Adoptive T cell transfer

T cells were isolated using magnetic enrichment for CD8+ T cells (Invitrogen) followed by magnetic enrichment for CD44 PE-stained cells (Miltenyi) in MACS buffer (PBS containing BSA and EDTA). 10,000 resulting cells were intravenously injected into recipient mice in 100 uL of PBS. Mice were challenged as described above 24 hours post cell transfer.

### Mitochondrial Confocal Imaging

Naïve or in vitro stimulated CD8+ T cells were incubated with 300 nM MitoTracker Deep Red (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 30 minutes, mounted with Wescor Cytopro cytocentrifuge, and then fixed with 4% PFA (Electron Microscopy Sciences) in cytoskeleton buffer. Cells were permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich), stained for CD8 (Biolegend, catalog 344702, clone SK1) and DAPI (300 nM, Thermo Fisher Scientific), and mounted with Prolong Gold Antifade reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Secondary donkey anti–mouse IgG AlexaFluor488 antibodies (Life Technologies, polyclonal) were used. Images were acquired on a Zeiss LSM880 confocal microscope with Airyscan for super-resolution imaging using a 63×/1.40NA Plan-Apochromat oil objective and 405-, 488-, 561-, and 633-nm lasers and default settings for pinhole and filters. Images were processed using ZEN software and FIJI. To process mitochondrial images in FIJI, 50-pixel rolling ball background subtraction was used. Temporal color code function in FIJI was used for z-series color coding. Images of mitotracker Deep Red staining of CD8+ T cells were manually scored in a blinded-manner for fissed or fused mitochondria to quantify the mitochondrial morphology of CD8+ T cells.

### Statistical Analysis

All data are presented as individual values with mean ± SEM or ± SD as indicated in figure legends. All statistics were calculated by performing unpaired or paired two-tailed t-tests or one-way ANOVA for 95% confidence limits in GraphPad Prism 9.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353)Results

### dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice produce functional effector T cells but not to the extent of _Drp1_ flfl mice

While previous studies have indicated that the primary effector CD8+ T cell response may be reduced in LckCre x Drp1 flfl mice (where DRP1 is removed prior to maturation of single positive T cells), these studies were performed either in vitro or by interrogating very early (d4) responses to tumor lysate immunization[[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R18)]. Thus, it is unknown whether the magnitude of the primary CD8+ T cells response is compromised in the absence of DRP1 in vivo, nor whether restricting DRP1 expression impacts effector functions or the generation of a secondary response to antigen. Further, the diminution of primary CD8+ T cell responses observed in the prior study could have been a consequence of the loss of DRP1 during T cell development. Therefore, we generated a mouse model of DRP1 restriction in late-development T cells by crossing mice with Cre transgene expression controlled by the distal Lck promoter and _Drp1_ floxed mice, where DRP1 is only deleted in the mature CD4+ and CD8+ T cells[[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R22), [24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R24)]. We characterized the naïve populations of T cells from the thymi and spleens of naïve dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice ([Figure S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD5)). While the subpopulations of thymic T cells are slightly shifted towards single positive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells ([Figure S1A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD5)–[J](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD5)), ultimately neither the percentage nor the number of mature CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, B cells, and NK cells were altered in the spleens of naive dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl animals compared to controls ([Figure S1K](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD5)–[S1V](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD5)). Furthermore, the mitochondrial mass and mitochondrial membrane potential of naïve CD8+ T cells were not altered in the absence of DRP1 ([Figure S1W](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD5)–[S1Z](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD5)). Therefore, naïve dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice have apparently comparable T cell populations to control animals, providing an equivalent baseline population to further investigate the impact of DRP1-loss on T cell activation and differentiation. Given the equivalent mitochondrial membrane potential, we confirmed that loss of DRP1 impacted the fission of mitochondria by stimulating CD8+ T cells in vitro to encourage mitochondrial fission[[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R10)]. We visualized mitochondrial morphology by super-resolution confocal microscopy and generated stacked images of individual CD8+ T cells to observe mitochondrial morphology across multiple planes. Following 2d stimulation with αCD3 and αCD28, more than 75% of DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells are dominated by elongated mitochondria compared to 25% of DRP1-replete CD8+ T cells, confirming the impact of the loss of DRP1 on mitochondrial fission ([Figure S2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD2)). We further assessed these stimulated cells to determine if mitochondrial elongation, due to DRP1 deficiency, enhances the SRC of CD8+ T cells. Surprisingly, DRP1-deficient activated CD8+ T cells did not have significantly altered SRC and perform comparable OXPHOS to DRP1-replete CD8+ T cells as measured by Seahorse analyzer ([Figure S3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD3)).

We next assayed whether CD8+ T cells become activated, proliferate, and perform effector functions in the absence of DRP1 in vivo. After immunizing dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice or controls with agonistic αCD40, polyI:C, and OVA protein, we found that dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice can generate an OVA 257–264 specific CD8+ T cell response 7d later (the peak of the primary response) ([Figure 1A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)–[1C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)) but that the magnitude of this response ([Figure 1D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)) is more than 2.5-fold lower than that found in _Drp1_ flfl controls immunized in the same manner. Effector functions were initially assessed after stimulating splenocytes with the mitogens PMA and Ionomycin. We found a significant but modest reduction in the proportion of OVA 257–264 specific DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells that express CD107a, a marker of degranulation, ([Figure 1E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)–[1F](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)) but equivalent per cell expression ([Figure 1G](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)). No differences were found in IFNγ expression ([Figure 1H](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)–[1J](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)), while a modest reduction was seen in the proportion of DRP1-deficient OVA 257–264 specific CD8+ T cells to produce the cytokine TNFα ([Figure 1K](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)–[1L](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)) but again with equivalent per cell expression ([Figure 1M](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)).

However, since DRP1 deletion could compromise T cell receptor signaling and activation, [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R15)] we further questioned if these primary CD8+ T cells were capable of full effector function when stimulated via the TCR[[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R15)]. Therefore, we re-stimulated primary effector CD8+ T cells with antigen presenting cells pulsed with SIINFEKL OVA 257–264 peptide. Equivalent percentages of DRP1-deficient and DRP1-replete CD8+ T cells were able to degranulate, as marked by CD107a ([Figure 1N](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)–[O](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)), however, there was a notable absence of CD107a-high expressors in the DRP1-deficient population ([Figure 1P](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)). As with mitogen stimulation, neither the percentage of cells producing IFNγ ([Figure 1Q](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)–[R](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)) nor the amount of IFNγ produced are compromised in the absence of DRP1 ([Figure 1S](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)). We additionally assessed the impacts of DRP1 loss on mitochondrial content. While loss of DRP1 increased elongation of mitochondria, loss of DRP1 does not alter the mitochondrial mass as measured by MTG nor the mitochondrial membrane potential as measured by TMRE ([Figure S4A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD4)–[D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD4)), which is consistent with the comparable SRC observed in stimulated CD8+ T cells ([Figure S3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD3)). Thus, despite the expected impact of loss of DRP1 on CD8+ T cell expansion, a significant primary response develops, and those cells differentiate into effector cells capable of cytokine production.

### DRP1’s influence on T cell effector responses is CD8+ T cell intrinsic

Since dLckCre also affects the expression of DRP1 in CD4+ T cells, which are known to support CD8+ T cell responses[[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R26)], we determined if the effects of loss of DRP1 on the primary response were due to intrinsic activity of DRP1 within CD8+ T cells. Therefore, we generated E8iERT2Cre x _Drp1_ flfl mice, which have an inducible CD8+ T cell-specific deletion of DRP1 in response to tamoxifen treatment or sham treated controls. Mice were injected intraperitoneally with 75 mg/kg of tamoxifen in corn oil for three consecutive days prior to priming. The deletion of DRP1 after tamoxifen treatment was confirmed by western blot ([Figure S5A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD6)). We observed a 3-fold decrease in the magnitude of the primary OVA 257–264-specific CD8+ T cell response in tamoxifen treated mice compared to controls, indicating that the effects of losing DRP1 on the magnitude of the CD8+ T cell response are intrinsic to CD8+ T cells ([Figure 2A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F2)–[D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F2)). We further determined if these CD8+ T cells, which were activated in the presence of DRP1-replete CD4+ T cells, produce cytokines. We find complete functional responses after stimulating splenocytes with the mitogens PMA and Ionomycin ([Figure 2E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F2)–[2J](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F2)). However, this method of stimulation for cytokine production does not engage the TCR, therefore, we alternatively re-stimulated with antigen presenting cells pulsed with SIINFEKL OVA 257–264 peptide to assess cytokine production. 1.5-fold fewer E8iERT2Cre x _Drp1_ flfl OVA 257–264 specific CD8+ T cells have CD107a expression ([Figure 2K](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F2)–[L](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F2)) and about 3-fold fewer produce IFNγ ([Figure 2N](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F2)–[O](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F2)) while the expression per CD107a+ cell ([Figure 2M](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F2)) or the amount of IFNγ per cell ([Figure 2P](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F2)) is not compromised. These results confirm the effect of DRP1 loss on primary CD8+ T cell expansion found in dLckCre x Drp1 flfl CD8+ T cells, indicating that the effects of DRP1 are CD8+ intrinsic and that T cells lacking DRP1 may have a defect in T cell receptor signaling that leads to diminished cytokine production.

### In vitro stimulated dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl cells demonstrate delayed proliferation as well as decreased T cell receptor signaling and expression

To help understand the reduced primary effector CD8+ T cell response found in vivo ([Figure 1D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)), we questioned whether DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells failed to become activated, were delayed in proliferation, or were dying. Cell Trace Violet (CTV) labelled DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells, stimulated in vitro with αCD3 and αCD28, demonstrated delayed proliferation compared to controls. After 2 days of stimulation, DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells have one less division than control CD8+ T cells ([Figure 3A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F3)–[B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F3)). This is consistent with findings from Simula _et al_. where isolated DRP1-deficient T cells stimulated for 5 days in vitro had delayed late-stage proliferation within hours of synchronous release[[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R18)]. While dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl CD8+ T cells are capable of a surprising amount of division, a greater portion remain in early stages of division while DRP1-replete T cells progress to higher rounds of division ([Figure 3C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F3)). Surprisingly, T cell viability was not compromised during any stage of division within 2 days of stimulation ([Figure 3D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F3)). Comparable amounts of CD8+ cells upregulated CD25 ([Figure 3E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F3)) and CD44 ([Figure 3F](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F3)) demonstrating that the expression of activation markers post TCR-engagement is not compromised by deletion of DRP1. A possible explanation for the production of functional effector T cells in the absence of mitochondrial fission would be the upregulation of mitochondrial biogenesis. However, based on PGC1α staining, biogenesis is equivalent in DRP1-deficient and DRP1-replete CD8+ T cells ([Figure 3G](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F3)). 4 days after stimulation, the majority of CD8+ T cells have extensively divided based on CTV dilution, but a small portion of dLckCre x _Drp1_ _f_ lfl CD8+ T cells remained undivided ([Figure 3H](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F3)–[3I](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F3)). Thus, we conclude that DRP1 is not required for CD8+ T cells to become activated and divide, but the kinetics of division are delayed without DRP1.

Taken together with the reduction in the production of some cytokines ex vivo after TCR stimulation, but not after PMA/ionomycin which bypasses the TCR, we questioned if TCR signaling in DRP1-deficient cells is compromised. Therefore, we stimulated CD8+ T cells with αCD3 over a time course from 1 to 20 minutes and assessed phospho-tyrosine kinase signaling via flow cytometry. All time points assessed demonstrate a drastic decrease in the phosphorylation of CD3ζ of DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells starting at a 1.8-fold decrease and becoming more separated over time ([Figure 3J](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F3)). DRP1 has previously been shown to participate in the structural formation of the immune synapse of Jurkat T cells[[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R15)], therefore, aberrations in TCR signaling are likely in the dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl model or any model of DRP1 deficiency. We also questioned if DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells expressed the TCR on the cell surface at levels comparable to DRP1 replete CD8+ T cells. Flow cytometry analysis showed that the expression of the TCRαβ is modestly reduced in DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells from the spleens of naïve mice compared to DRP1-replete CD8+ T cells ([Figure 3K](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F3)), which could contribute to the observed reduction in TCR-based signaling Thus, while the absence of DRP1 does not compromise the ability of the majority of CD8+ T cells to undergo the process of activation and division, TCR signaling is decreased and TCR expression is decreased, potentially reducing the kinetics of T cell activation and division.

### Diminished primary response in dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice does not interfere with secondary response

After confirming that DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells can develop into a pool of primary effectors, we next determined how the absence of DRP1 affects memory CD8+ T cell development and their subsequent ability to mount a response to a secondary exposure to OVA antigen. Due to the compromised primary response, on the one hand we anticipated that a secondary response could have similarly reduced magnitude and function. On the other, sustained mitochondrial elongation may enhance the generation or activity of memory CD8+ T cells. dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice were primed with agonistic αCD40, polyI:C, and OVA protein then challenged 28 days later with recombinant adenovirus expressing OVA (AdenoOVA). We analyzed the secondary response 5 days post challenge. Interestingly, we find found an equivalent percentage ([Figure 4A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F4)–[4C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F4)) and number ([Figure 4D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F4)) of OVA 257–264 specific CD8+ T cells in dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice and controls. To quantify cytokine production of OVA 257–264 specific T cells by flow cytometry, we stimulated splenocytes with OVA 257–264 (SIINFEKL) peptide-pulsed antigen presenting cells in the presence of BFA. In contrast to the primary response, these DRP1-deficient OVA 257–264 specific secondary CD8+ T cells degranulate ([Figure 4E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F4)–[4G](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F4)), produce IFNγ ([Figure 4H](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F4)–[4J](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F4)), and TNFα ([Figure 4K](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F4)–[4M](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F4)) to the same extent as DRP1-replete OVA 257–264 specific secondary CD8+ T cells. Functionally, DRP1 deficient OVA 257–264 specific secondary CD8+ T cells do not exhibit the same defect identified in DRP1-deficient OVA 257–264 specific primary CD8+ T cells.

### CD8+ memory T cells develop independently of DRP1

Effector CD8+ T cells of a secondary response result from the expansion of a small quiescent memory T cell pool[[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R27)]. In order to achieve a comparable secondary response to DRP1-replete CD8+ T cells, we hypothesized that DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells produced memory T cells in greater number or proliferative capacity relative to the magnitude of the primary response. Thus, we enumerated the quiescent memory T cells that developed in the spleen after resting dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl and control animals for 28 days post-priming with agonistic αCD40, polyI:C, and OVA protein. The absence of _Drp1_ in memory CD8+ T cells was confirmed using qPCR ([Figure S5B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD6)). We found an equivalent number of memory OVA 257–264 specific CD8+ T cells in dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl as compared to controls ([Figure 5A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)–[5D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)). This equivalency in the memory CD8+ T cell population develops despite originating from ~2.7 times fewer effector CD8+ T cells at 7 days post-priming ([Figure 1D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)). Memory cells are often found in sites such as lymph nodes and lungs where they are better poised for rapid secondary responses[[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R28)]. As DRP1 has previously been shown to be contribute to primary effector CD8+ T cell trafficking[[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R18)], we also evaluated whether the absence of DRP1 affected the distribution and subtypes of memory CD8+ T cells. Interestingly, we identified equivalent amounts of memory OVA 257–264 specific CD8+ T cells in inguinal lymph nodes ([Figure 5E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)–[5H](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)) and lungs ([Figure 5M](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)–[5P](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)). However, some subtypes of memory CD8+ T cells do shift in the absence of DRP1. Within the inguinal lymph node, OVA 257–264 specific memory CD8+ T cells of dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice are predominately effector memory cells as defined by CD62L lo CCR7 lo while the CD62L hi CCR7 hi central memory cells are significantly reduced ([Figure 5I](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)–[L](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)). Meanwhile, the fraction of OVA 257–264 specific memory CD8+ T cells resident to the lung is equivalent in dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl and control mice ([Figure 5Q](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)–[R](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)). Within the population of CD8+ T cells that are not circulating, tissue resident memory CD8+ T cells of the lung can be further identified by the expression of CD69 and CD103[[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R29)]. In the absence of DRP1, the highly retained CD69+CD103+ double positive tissue resident memory T cells are equivalent between dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl and control mice ([Figure 5S](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)–[U](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)).

We further questioned the functionality of DRP1-deficient memory CD8+ T cells by transferring an equivalent number of quiescent memory cells from dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl into naïve recipient mice or from control _Drp1_ flfl mice into naïve recipient mice. These mice, containing equivalent DRP1-deficient or DRP1-replete memory T cells were then challenged with αCD40, polyI:C, and OVA protein. 5 days after challenge, the secondary OVA 257–264 specific CD8+ T cells resulting from dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl cells were reduced by half compared to littermate controls ([Figure 5V](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F5)). Thus, in contrast to the complete secondary response seen in dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice ([Figure 4D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F4)), the secondary response from adoptively transferred memory cells replicates the magnitude of the defect found in DRP1-deficient primary responses. This data suggests that in the absence of DRP1, secondary CD8+ T cells are impaired when removed from the DRP1-deficient environment. Further, this impairment does not appear to be related to mitochondrial health as DRP1-deficient memory CD8+ T cells do not have altered mitochondrial mass or mitochondrial membrane potential compared to DRP1-replete memory CD8+ T cells ([Figure S4E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD4)–[H](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD4)).

### DRP1-deficient T cells cannot compete with WT T cells during primary, memory, or secondary responses

While the dLckCre x Drp1 flfl model provides an assessment of the role for DRP1 in T cells in general, DRP1 is deleted in both CD8+ and CD4+ T cells. Additionally, we noted a deeper reduction in the CD8+ T cell response in E8iERT2Cre x _DRP1_ flfl CD8+ T cell numbers than observed in dLckCre mice, suggesting a qualitative difference in CD8+ T cell responses when DRP1-deficient and -replete CD8+ T cells are present in the same host. To examine this further, we developed mixed bone marrow chimera mice in order to further address the CD8+ T cell intrinsic role of DRP1, as well as to evaluate whether the absence of DRP1 in CD8+ T cells results in a competitive disadvantage. In mixed bone marrow chimeras, 50% of the CD4+ T cells will be replete with DRP1 and will be able provide classical helper T cell functions to DRP1-deficient and replete CD8+ T cells. Cells resulting from the wild type donor are CD45.2+ Thy1.1+ while the dLckCre x _DRP1_ flfl cells are CD45.2+ Thy1.2+. The resulting mixed bone marrow chimera mice were not exactly a 50/50 ratio of dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl to _Drp1_ flfl ([Figure 6A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F6)), therefore, data from future timepoints were normalized to the reconstituted distribution and raw data is included in [Supplemental Figure 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#SD7). Chimeras were primed as previously, rested to develop memory, and challenged using Adeno-OVA. As seen in dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice ([Figure 1D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)), DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells in mixed bone marrow chimera mice also demonstrate a reduced primary response ([Figure 6B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F6)) compared to their DRP1-replete counterparts, further supporting the notion that the deficit that arises from the absence of DRP1 is CD8+ T cell intrinsic. Interestingly, the control CD8+ T cells make a 6-fold larger primary response than DRP1-deficient T cells ([Figure 6B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F6), [6E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F6)), a more extreme difference than observed in dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice ([Figure 1D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F1)) and more equivalent to the reduction in response observed in E8iERT2CREx _Drp1_ flfl mice ([Figure 2D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F2)). Despite the significant impact to the primary response, mixed bone marrow chimera mice rested to memory ultimately develop equivalent numbers of OVA 257–264 memory CD8+ T cells from WT and dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl donors ([Figure 6C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F6), [6E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F6)), consistent with the relatively superior memory CD8+ T cell development in the absence of DRP1 observed in the dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice. In contrast to the results from dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice, the secondary response of mixed bone marrow chimeras was also dominated by DRP1-replete CD8+ T cells. The control response was approximately 2.5-fold greater than the DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells ([Figure 6D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F6), [6E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F6)). Thus, despite dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice forming strong secondary responses, these cells expand weakly in the presence of wild-type secondary CD8+ T cells ([Figure 6F](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F6)).

### Contracting CD8+ T cells are not less prone to cell death or altered differentiation

The equivalency in the number of memory CD8+ T cells in control and DRP1-deficient mice, in multiple model systems, despite clear disparities in primary responses, suggests a difference in the efficiency of generating memory CD8+ T cells. For dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl memory CD8+ T cells to recover from the impaired primary response, the effector CD8+ T cells likely have improved survival or altered differentiation towards memory development. As elongated mitochondrial phenotypes are utilized to promote survival during stress conditions[[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R30)], we first hypothesized that the deletion of DRP1 allowed CD8+ T cells to better survive the programmed contraction phase. To assess if dLckCre x Drp1 flfl mice have reduced apoptosis, we stained cells for Annexin V 10 days post-priming, once the contraction phase has begun. We found no evidence for decreased phosphatidylserine exposure or apoptosis in live DRP1-deficient OVA 257–264 specific CD8+ T cells ([Figure 7A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F7)–[D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F7)). The poly-caspase FLICA reagent also revealed no decrease in cell death of DRP1-deficient OVA 257–264 specific CD8+ T cells ([Figure 7E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F7)–[G](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F7)). Further, the fraction of OVA 257–264 T cells expressing the anti-apoptotic molecule BCL2 was not increased, nor the amount of BCL2 per cell, ([Figure 7H](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F7)–[J](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F7)). These data indicate that neither a decrease in death nor an increase in survival during contraction 10 days post priming explain the recovery of CD8+ T cells from dLckCre x _Drp1_ flfl mice after the primary response.

Given the absence of evidence of differential survival, we hypothesized that a greater proportion of CD8+ T cells lacking DRP1 were destined to become memory precursors (CD127 hi KLRG1 lo ;MPEC) over short lived effector (CD127 lo KLRG1 hi ;SLEC) T cells. However, we found no significant differential SLEC:MPEC representation in the primary response between dLckCre x Drp1 flfl mice and controls ([Figure 8A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F8)–[B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F8), [D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F8)). This data is further supported by comparable levels of TBET ([Figure 8E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F8)–[G](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F8)) and EOMES ([Figure 8E](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F8)–[F](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F8), [H](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#F8)) at 10 days post-priming, whereas increases would indicate preferential effector or memory differentiation, respectfully[[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R31), [32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980353#R32)]. STUDY TITLE: "The mitochondrial fission protein DRP1 influences memory CD8+ T cell formation and function" — A research article published in the Journal of Leukocyte Biology (2024 Mar 29;115(4):679. doi: 10.1093/jleuko/qiad155), PMCID: PMC10980353, PMID: 38057151.

AUTHORS: Marissa G. Stevens (Department of Pathology, University of Virginia), Frank M. Mason (Department of Medicine, Vanderbilt University Medical Center), and Timothy N.J. Bullock (Department of Pathology, University of Virginia, corresponding author). All authors conceived the project, designed experiments, interpreted data, and wrote the manuscript; Stevens performed experiments/analyzed data; Mason performed all microscopy imaging; Bullock supervised and acquired funding.

RESEARCH BACKGROUND: Memory T cells favor fatty acid oxidation and OXPHOS metabolism supported by elongated mitochondrial networks and increased mitochondrial mass, which create spare respiratory capacity (SRC) for rapid response to secondary antigen encounters. Since mitochondrial fission relies primarily on the GTPase Dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1), targeting DRP1 was hypothesized as a way to promote memory T cell development and improve vaccination protocols. Prior pharmacological studies (using M1 and M-divi) suggested mitochondrial elongation could support memory-like states, but M-divi's specificity for DRP1 has since been questioned (it was shown to inhibit complex I of the electron transport chain rather than affecting mitochondrial morphology).

HYPOTHESIS: Deletion of DRP1 would lead to mitochondrial elongation and generate a large memory T cell population that could be exploited to enhance vaccination.

METHODS: The study used dLckCre x Drp1 fl/fl mice (DRP1 deleted in mature T cells via distal Lck promoter), E8iERT2Cre x Drp1 fl/fl mice (inducible CD8+ T cell-specific DRP1 deletion via tamoxifen), mixed bone marrow chimeras, adoptive T cell transfer, flow cytometry, Seahorse mitochondrial stress tests, super-resolution confocal microscopy (Zeiss LSM880 with Airyscan), CTV proliferation tracking, and TCR signaling analysis via phospho-CD3ζ measurement. Mice were primed intraperitoneally with 100 μg αCD40, 75 μg polyI:C, and 500 μg ovalbumin, with secondary responses initiated via challenge with 2×10^8 pfu recombinant AdenoOVA 28 days later.

KEY RESULTS:
1. Naïve dLckCre x Drp1 fl/fl mice have comparable T cell populations (CD4+, CD8+, B cells, NK cells), mitochondrial mass, and mitochondrial membrane potential to controls. Following in vitro stimulation, >75% of DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells showed elongated mitochondria vs. 25% of controls, but SRC and OXPHOS were not significantly altered.

2. Primary responses: DRP1 deletion compromised primary CD8+ T cell responses (more than 2.5-fold lower magnitude in dLckCre mice; 3-fold decrease in tamoxifen-treated E8iERT2Cre mice). Effects were confirmed CD8+ T cell intrinsic. Some modest reductions in CD107a and TNFα production were noted, but IFNγ production was intact.

3. In vitro findings: DRP1-deficient CD8+ T cells showed delayed proliferation (one less division after 2 days), intact activation marker expression (CD25, CD44) and viability, but drastically decreased CD3ζ phosphorylation (starting at 1.8-fold decrease) and modestly reduced TCRαβ surface expression.

4. Secondary responses: Despite compromised primary responses, dLckCre x Drp1 fl/fl mice mounted secondary responses equivalent to controls in percentage, number, degranulation, IFNγ, and TNFα production. However, adoptively transferred DRP1-deficient memory cells produced a secondary response reduced by half compared to controls when removed from the DRP1-deficient environment.

5. Memory development: Equivalent numbers of memory OVA 257-264 specific CD8+ T cells formed in DRP1-deficient and control mice (spleen, inguinal lymph nodes, lungs), despite originating from ~2.7 times fewer effector cells. This recovery was NOT explained by reduced apoptosis (no change in Annexin V, FLICA, or BCL2), nor by differential differentiation toward memory precursor cells (no changes in SLEC:MPEC representation, TBET, EOMES, BLIMP1, or BCL6).

6. Competitive disadvantage (mixed bone marrow chimeras): In competition with DRP1-replete CD8+ T cells, DRP1-deficient cells showed a 6-fold smaller primary response, equivalent memory cell generation, but a 2.5-fold smaller secondary response — indicating DRP1-deficient T cells cannot compete with wild-type T cells during primary, memory, or secondary responses.

CONCLUSION: While deletion of DRP1 compromises primary effector CD8+ T cell responses (likely due to decreased TCR expression/signaling), a disproportionately large memory CD8+ T cell pool forms, and memory cells mount comparable secondary responses. However, the relative propensity to form memory cells was not associated with differentiation toward memory precursors or decreased cell death. In a competitive environment with DRP1-replete CD8+ T cells, DRP1 deletion compromised all responses, indicating that approaches targeting DRP1 need to be carefully tailored before use in vaccination protocols.

ABSTRACT HIGHLIGHT: "The absence of DRP1 limits primary CD8+ T cell responses, yet memory and secondary responses are intact, unless in competition with DRP1-replete CD8+ T cells."

KEYWORDS: CD8+ T cell, Memory T cell, Metabolism, Mitochondria, Cytokine, T cell receptor, Differentiation, Cell Death.

Dynamin-related protein-1 (Drp1)-dependent mitochondrial ﬁssion plays a crucial role in sustaining T-cell motility, proliferation, survival, and glycolytic engagement. Interest-ingly, such processes are exactly those inhibited by PD-1 in tumor-inﬁltrating T cells. Here, we show that PD-1pos CD8+ T cells inﬁltrating an MC38 (murine adenocarcinoma)-derived murine tumor mass have a down-regulated Drp1 activity and more elongated mitochondria compared with PD-1neg counterparts. Also, PD-1pos lymphocytic elements inﬁltrating a human colon cancer rarely express active Drp1. Mechanistically, PD-1 sig-naling directly prevents mitochondrial fragmentation following T-cell stim-ulation by downregulating Drp1 phosphorylation on Ser616, via regulation of the ERK1/2 and mTOR pathways. In addition, downregulation of Drp1 activity in tumor-inﬁltrating PD-1pos CD8+ T cells seems to be a mecha-nism exploited by PD-1 signaling to reduce motility and proliferation of these cells. Overall, our data indicate that the modulation of Drp1 activity in tumor-inﬁltrating T cells may become a valuable target to ameliorate the anticancer immune response in future immunotherapy approaches.

1. Introduction Programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) is a T-cell surface receptor that downregulates T-cell activation and the immune response [1]. PD-1 signaling is activated by PD-1 interaction with its ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2, expressed on adjacent cells [2], and it dampens signals originating from T-cell receptor (TCR) and CD28, such as the activation of mammalian target of rapamy-cin (mTOR) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways [3,4].
Besides being frequently observed in T cells during chronic infections [5], acti-vation of PD-1 signaling has also been widely reported in tumor-inﬁltrating T cells, contributing to their func-tional exhaustion and poor antitumor response [6].
Consistently, antagonistic PD-1 antibodies efﬁciently reinvigorate tumor-inﬁltrating T cells, thereby amelio-rating antitumor response [7,8].
Mitochondria are central modulators of cellular bioenergetics, and their dynamic morphology is tightly linked to cell functions. Among the mitochondrial-shaping proteins, dynamin-related protein-1 (Drp1) is the main proﬁssion protein and it is recruited from the cytosol to mitochondria thanks to post-translational modiﬁcations and to several receptors, such as Mff and Fis1 [9,10]. Interestingly, mitochondrial morphol-ogy is tightly linked to an optimal T-cell functionality [11]. Particularly, Drp1-dependent mitochondrial frag-mentation sustains T-cell motility and proliferation, and effector T (Teff) cell apoptosis following TCR engagement [12,13]. Also, Drp1-dependent mitochon-drial relocation at the immunological synapse controls the inﬂux of calcium upon T-cell activation [14], sus-taining the cMyc-dependent upregulation of glycolytic enzymes [13,15], thus allowing the metabolic repro-gramming required to cope with the increased bioener-getic demand of an activated T cell [16,17]. All these processes contribute to an optimal antitumor T-cell response, which is indeed defective in T cells lacking Drp1 [13].
Of note, most of these Drp1-dependent processes are also downregulated by PD-1 co-inhibitory signal-ing, especially when considering tumor-inﬁltrating T cells. Indeed, PD-1 signaling reduces T-cell prolifera-tion and motility (both of them requiring Drp1) [4,13,18], and it also promotes a shift from a glycolysis-based metabolism (supported by Drp1) toward an OXPHOS-based metabolism (requiring mitochondrial fusion) [19]. Given this striking inverse correlation, we asked whether PD-1 signaling may modulate Drp1 activity, and to what extent this modu-lation may downregulate several processes in T cells.
This point is of extreme importance, since the molecular mechanisms by which PD-1 regulates the aforementioned processes in T cells are not yet com-pletely understood.
We here show that tumor-derived PD-1pos CD8+ T cells exhibit a signiﬁcant downregulation of Drp1 activity and a more fused mitochondrial network.
Mechanistically, PD-1 signaling prevents Drp1 activa-tion following T-cell stimulation by regulating its phosphorylation on Ser616 through the modulation of extracellular-regulated kinase 1/2 (ERK1/2) and mTOR proteins. Also, we provide evidence that Drp1 downregulation contributes to the reduced prolifera-tion and motility of PD-1pos tumor-inﬁltrating T cells, and, as a consequence, we identify Drp1 as a possible target for future therapeutic approaches aiming at restoring antitumor response in PD-1pos exhausted CD8+ T cells.

By com-paring the expression levels of different mitochondrial-shaping proteins in CD8+ TILs, we observed that PD-1pos CD8+ TILs do not show altered levels of total Drp1 compared with PD-1neg counterparts (Fig. 1A).
However, we observed a speciﬁc downregulation of Drp1 phosphorylation on its activating residue Ser616 (Fig. 1A and Fig. S1D), while the inhibitory phospho-rylation on Ser637 did not vary. Also, we did not observe any differences in the expression of other main profusion (Mfn1, Mfn2, Opa-1) or proﬁssion (Fis1, Mff) proteins (Fig. 1A).

args.summary:
This scientific paper (published in Molecular Oncology, 2022, Vol 16, pp. 188-205) from researchers at University of Rome Tor Vergata and collaborators investigates how PD-1 signaling induces T cell exhaustion through a Drp1-dependent mechanism involving mitochondrial dynamics.

**Key Findings:**
- Tumor-infiltrating PD-1pos CD8+ T cells in MC38 (murine adenocarcinoma) tumors show downregulated Drp1 activity (reduced phosphorylation on Ser616) and more elongated/fused mitochondria compared to PD-1neg counterparts
- PD-1pos CD8+ T cells in human colon cancer also rarely express active (phosphorylated) Drp1
- Mechanistically, PD-1 signaling prevents mitochondrial fragmentation following T-cell stimulation by downregulating Drp1 phosphorylation on Ser616 via inhibition of both ERK1/2 and mTOR pathways downstream of TCR/CD28 signaling
- ERK1/2 inhibitor FR180204 prevents Drp1 phosphorylation and mitochondrial fragmentation; ERK activation via C6-ceramide rescues Drp1 activity in PD-1-engaged cells
- mTOR inhibitor RAD-001 also prevents Drp1 phosphorylation independently of ERK1/2
- Downregulation of Drp1 activity reduces motility and proliferation of PD-1pos tumor-infiltrating T cells

**Therapeutic Implications:**
- Anti-PD-1 therapy effectiveness is significantly impaired in mice with T-cell-restricted Drp1 ablation (Drp1-cKO mice), with reduction in efficacy dropping from ~60% to ~20%
- Anti-PD-1 treatment rescues Drp1 phosphorylation in PD-1pos CD8+ TILs to levels comparable to PD-1neg CD8+ T cells in control mice
- Drp1 ablation does not affect PD-1 expression itself
- Modulation of Drp1 activity in tumor-infiltrating T cells may be a valuable therapeutic target to ameliorate anticancer immune response in future immunotherapy approaches

**Methods Used:** Western blot, immunofluorescence, immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry, Seahorse metabolic analysis, transwell migration assays, MC38 tumor model in WT and Drp1 conditional-KO (Drp1fl/fl Lck:cre+) mice, in vitro T cell stimulation with anti-CD3/28±PD-L1 beads, siRNA silencing, pharmacological inhibitors (RAD-001, FR180204, Akti-1/2, C6-ceramide).

**Conclusions:** PD-1 signaling directly prevents mitochondrial fragmentation following T-cell stimulation by downregulating Drp1 phosphorylation on Ser616 via ERK1/2 and mTOR pathway regulation. Drp1 downregulation in PD-1pos exhausted CD8+ T cells represents a mechanism contributing to reduced T-cell motility, proliferation, and antitumor response, and restoration of Drp1 activity is a key step for effective anti-PD-1 immunotherapy.

<webpage_content>
Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Pharmacological Research journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/yphrs Invited Review Targeting Drp1 and mitochondrial ﬁssion for therapeutic immune modulation Luca Simulaa,b, Michelangelo Campanellac,d, Silvia Campelloa,⁎ a Dept. of Biology, University of Rome Tor Vergata, Rome, Italy b Dept. of Paediatric Haemato-Oncology, IRCCS Bambino Gesù Children Hospital, Rome, Italy c Department of Comparative Biomedical Sciences, The Royal Veterinary College, University of London, Royal College Street NW1 0TU, London, United Kingdom d Consortium for Mitochondrial Research (CfMR), University College London, Gower Street, WC1E 6BT, London, United Kingdom A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Drp1 Mitochondrial dynamics T cells Tumor immune-surveillance Pharmacological approaches A B S T R A C T Mitochondria are dynamic organelles whose processes of fusion and ﬁssion are tightly regulated by specialized proteins, known as mitochondria-shaping proteins. Among them, Drp1 is the main pro-ﬁssion protein and its activity is tightly regulated to ensure a strict control over mitochondria shape according to the cell needs. In the recent years, mitochondrial dynamics emerged as a new player in the regulation of fundamental processes during T cell life. Indeed, the morphology of mitochondria directly regulates T cell diﬀerentiation, this by af-fecting the engagment of alternative metabolic routes upon activation. Further, Drp1-dependent mitochondrial ﬁssion sustains both T cell clonal expansion and T cell migration and invasivness. By this review, we aim at discussing the most recent ﬁndings about the roles played by the Drp1-dependent mitochondrial ﬁssion in T cells, and at highlighting how its pharmacological modulation could open the way to future therapeutic ap-proaches to modulate T cell response.
1. Introduction Mitochondria are eukaryotic organelles ensheated by a double-membrane, the inner one (IMM) characterized by several invaginations called cristae, where the supercomplexes of the electron transport chain (ETC) are located. The network of mitochondria is highly dynamic and the continuos processes of fusion and fragmentation (a.k.a. ﬁssion) are tightly regulated by several mitochondria-shaping proteins. Fusion is mainly regulated by Mitofusin-1 and Mitofusin-2 (which coordinate the fusion of the outer mitochondrial membrane, OMM) and Opa-1 (Optic atrophy-1, which regulates IMM fusion) [1,2]. Opa-1 also controls the organization of mitochondrial cristae and, therefore, directly aﬀect the eﬃciency of the mitochondrial respiration (OXPHOS) [3]. The orga-nelle fragmentation is regulated mainly by the activity of the dynamin-like GTPase Drp1 (Dynamin-Related Protein 1) [4]. In the inactive state, this protein normally localizes in the cytosol and is phosphorylated on serine637 (inhibitory phosphorylation) [5]. Its activation requires both the dephosphorylation of serine637, this directing Drp1 towards the OMM, and the phosphorylation on serine616, which activates Drp1 to execute mitochondria fragmentation [6]. Thus, Drp1 activity can be modulated by several protein kinases and phosphatases as well as other post-translational modiﬁcations, such as SUMOylation [5–7]. Docking of Drp1 to the OMM is regulated by diﬀerent receptors and modulators, such as Mﬀ[8] and hFis1 [9–11]. Further, Dynamin2 (Dyn2) has been recently proposed to work in concert with Drp1 to orchestrate the diﬀerent steps required for mitochondrial fragmentation [12]. Besides regulating mitochondrial fragmentation, Drp1 can also directly control the morphology of the mitochondria cristae in a Opa-1-independent way, although the exact mechanism is not known yet [13]. Besides the general concept that mitochondrial dynamics are crucial for responding to distinct and speciﬁc cellular and physiological needs, mitochondrial fragmentation is very important for cell proliferation [14,15], death [16], migration [17], metabolism [16], ROS production [18] and mi-tophagic mitochondrial clearance [19], among other processes. Inter-estingly, all these processes are essential for a correct function of the adaptive immune system. Indeed, T cells continuosly migrate [20], get activated and expand extensively upon antigen encounter [21,22], dramatically change their metabolism [23] and eventually undergo a programmed form of cell death [24]. Consequently, several works in the recent years have linked mitochondrial fragmentation to the adaptive immune system activity. By this review, we aim at providing an updated and complete view of the diﬀerent roles played by Drp1-dependent mitochondrial ﬁssion in the adaptive immune cells with a critical emphasis at the possibility to develop therapeutic strategies https://doi.org/10.1016/j.phrs.2019.104317 Received 14 May 2019; Received in revised form 15 June 2019; Accepted 16 June 2019 ⁎ Corresponding author.
E-mail address: silvia.campello@uniroma2.it (S. Campello).
