In the past, lactate was regarded as the terminal product of glycolysis and considered a waste byproduct produced when the demand for ATP surpasses the available oxygen supply (Joshua and Sven [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR43 "Joshua DR, Sven E. Lactate: the ugly duckling of energy metabolism. Nat Metab. 2020;2(7):566–71.")). However, lactate is now recognized as not only an energy substrate but also a signaling molecule that participates in the regulation of cellular metabolic activities (Joshua and Sven [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR43 "Joshua DR, Sven E. Lactate: the ugly duckling of energy metabolism. Nat Metab. 2020;2(7):566–71."); Brooks[2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR14 "Brooks G. The Science and Translation of Lactate Shuttle Theory. Cell Metab. 2018;27(4):757–85.")). Lactate accumulation can promote metabolic reprogramming and immune evasion in tumor cells, thereby contributing to tumor resistance (Lihua et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR55 "Lihua C, et al. Lactate-Lactylation hands between metabolic reprogramming and immunosuppression. Int J Mol Sci. 2022;23(19):11943.")). Moreover, elevated lactate levels can induce phenotypic changes in macrophages, subsequently modulating inflammatory processes (Yunda et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR111 "Yunda F, et al. Emerging roles of lactate in acute and chronic inflammation. Cell Commun Signal. 2024;22(1):276.")). Interestingly, recent studies have revealed that lactate can also act as a protein modification substrate, playing a crucial role in regulating the tumor microenvironment and inflammatory responses by mediating histone or non-histone lactylation (Certo et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR18 "Certo M, et al. Understanding lactate sensing and signalling. Trends Endocrinol Metab. 2022;33(10):722–35."); Xiaoning et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR99 "Xiaoning Y, et al. Histone lactylation: from tumor lactate metabolism to epigenetic regulation. Int J Biol Sci. 2024;20:1833.")). N6-Methyladenosine (m 6 A) modification is the most common post-transcriptional modification of mRNA in eukaryotic cells,It plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression, RNA stability, and translation efficiency, and is dynamically controlled by m 6 A-related regulatory enzymes (m 6 A-REE) (Erdem and Yang [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR27 "Erdem S, Yang S. RNA m6A methylation across the transcriptome. Mol Cell. 2023;83(3):428–41.")). However, the upstream regulatory mechanisms governing m 6 A-RRE mediated m 6 A modification remain inadequately understood. Recent studies have suggested that the activation of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) induced by lactate accumulation may serve as a potential upstream regulatory mechanism influencing m 6 A-RRE mediated m 6 A modification in both tumors and sepsis (Jia et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR37 "Jia X, et al. Lactylation-driven METTL3-mediated RNA m(6)A modification promotes immunosuppression of tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells. Mol Cell. 2022;82(9):1660–77."); Dan et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR24 "Dan W, et al. Histone lactylation-regulated METTL3 promotes ferroptosis via m6A-modification on ACSL4 in sepsis-associated lung injury. Redox Biol. 2024;74:103194.")). Notably, some studies have indicated that m 6 A-RRE can also modulate the m 6 A modification of key enzymes involved in glycolysis, further regulating lactate levels (Chen et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR19 "Chen H, et al. RNA N-Methyladenosine Methyltransferase METTL3 facilitates colorectal cancer by activating the mA-GLUT1-mTORC1 Axis and Is a Therapeutic Target. Gastroenterology. 2021;160(4):1284-1300.e16.")), (Kai et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR44 "Kai L, Xiufeng L, Fan L. IGF2BP3 boosts lactate generation to accelerate gastric cancer immune evasion. Apoptosis. 2024;29:2147–60.")). These findings imply that the interplay between lactate and m 6 A modification plays a significant role in the pathogenesis of diseases. This paper primarily aims to summarize the functions of lactate and investigate the reciprocal regulation between lactate and m 6 A modification across different disease contexts.

## Lactate metabolism

The body primarily obtains energy through glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation, with lactate acting as the final product of glycolysis (Joshua and Sven [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR43 "Joshua DR, Sven E. Lactate: the ugly duckling of energy metabolism. Nat Metab. 2020;2(7):566–71.")). The traditional understanding is that lactate in cells primarily originates from anaerobic glycolysis: glucose undergoes a series of catalytic reactions to be converted into pyruvate, which is then directly reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase LDH (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#Fig1)) (Brooks[2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR14 "Brooks G. The Science and Translation of Lactate Shuttle Theory. Cell Metab. 2018;27(4):757–85."); Fantin et al. [2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR30 "Fantin V, St-Pierre J, Leder P. Attenuation of LDH-A expression uncovers a link between glycolysis, mitochondrial physiology, and tumor maintenance. Cancer Cell. 2006;9(6):425–34.")). Currently, it is believed that cells can obtain energy through the glycolytic pathway and produce lactate in aerobic conditions,this phenomenon was first discovered in cancer cells by Warburg (known as the “Warburg effect”) (Warburg [1925](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR94 "Warburg O. Iron, the oxygen-carrier of respiration-ferment. Science. 1925;61(1588):575–82.")). Additionally, increasing evidences suggest that the “Warburg effect” not only exists in cancer cells but has also been observed in immune cells (Zoé et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR121 "Zoé D, et al. Warburg-associated acidification represses lactic fermentation independently of lactate, contribution from real-time NMR on cell-free systems. Sci Rep. 2023;13:17733."); Benjamin et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR9 "Benjamin N, et al. Lactate and Immunosuppression in Sepsis. Shock. 2017;49(2):120–5."); Michelangelo et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR60 "Michelangelo C, et al. Lactate modulation of immune responses in inflammatory versus tumour microenvironments. Nat Rev Immunol. 2020;21(3):151–61."); Eva et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR29 "Eva K, Viktoria P, Tereza G. Revisiting the warburg effect with focus on lactate. Cancers (Basel). 2022;14(24):6028.")). In addition, in cancer cells, glutamine enters the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) cycle via enzymes such as glutaminase, where it is converted into nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate hydrogen and pyruvate,the resulting carbon provides a carbon skeleton for the production of lactate (Ralph et al. [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR75 "Ralph JD, et al. Beyond aerobic glycolysis: transformed cells can engage in glutamine metabolism that exceeds the requirement for protein and nucleotide synthesis. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2007;104(49):19345–50."); Zacharias et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR112 "Zacharias F, et al. Ovarian cancer and glutamine metabolism. Int J Mol Sci. 2023;24(5):5041.")). Lactate is transported across the plasma membrane by monocarboxylate transporters (MCT), with MCT1 primarily responsible for uptake and MCT4 for export (Alpaslan et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR5 "Alpaslan T, et al. Metabolic heterogeneity confers differences in melanoma metastatic potential. Nature. 2019;577(7788):115–20.")). Extracellular lactate can enter target cells through intercellular shuttling via MCT1 (Tomoya et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR89 "Tomoya S, et al. Monocarboxylate transporters 1 and 2 Are responsible for L-Lactate uptake in differentiated human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y Cells. Biol Pharm Bull. 2024;47:764–70."); Valéry et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR90 "Valéry LP, et al. Monocarboxylate transporters in cancer. Mol Metab. 2019;33:48–66.")). The transport direction of lactate is influenced by its concentration gradient (Alpaslan et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR5 "Alpaslan T, et al. Metabolic heterogeneity confers differences in melanoma metastatic potential. Nature. 2019;577(7788):115–20.")). Lactate is primarily eliminated through oxidation to pyruvate (Mithileshkumar et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR61 "Mithileshkumar J, In-Kyu L, Kyoungho S. Metabolic reprogramming by the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase-lactic acid axis: Linking metabolism and diverse neuropathophysiologies. Neurosci Biobehav Rev. 2016;68:1–9.")),Pyruvate subsequently employs pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) to translocate into the mitochondria, where it undergoes metabolism via TCA cycle (Mithileshkumar et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR61 "Mithileshkumar J, In-Kyu L, Kyoungho S. Metabolic reprogramming by the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase-lactic acid axis: Linking metabolism and diverse neuropathophysiologies. Neurosci Biobehav Rev. 2016;68:1–9.")). Furthermore, lactate can be converted into glucose through the gluconeogenesis pathway,it also promotes the production of lactyl-CoA, which plays a role in the lactylation of histone and non-histone protein (Xiaolu et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR98 "Xiaolu L, et al. Lactate metabolism in human health and disease. Signal Transduct Target Ther. 2022;7:305.")), (Chi-An et al. [1985](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR20 "Chi-An WE, et al. Gluconeogenesis and hepatic glycogenolysis during exercise at the lactate threshold. J Appl Physiol. 1985;2012:114.")).

**Fig. 1**

![Image 8: Fig. 1](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs10565-024-09951-9/MediaObjects/10565_2024_9951_Fig1_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9/figures/1)

Extracellular glucose enters the cell through the action of GLUT1, which is regulated by AMPK. Subsequently, a series of enzymes including HK2, PFKM, ALDO, PGM1, and PKM2 work together to produce pyruvate. Pyruvate is then converted into lactate by LDH. Furthermore, pyruvate participates in the TCA cycle with the assistance of PDH and PDK1/2. MCT1 facilitates the transport of extracellular lactate into the cell while MCT4 is responsible for exporting intracellular lactate from the cell. Lactate plays a role in promoting lactyl-CoA production and contributes to histone or non-histone lactylation under the writers, erasers or readers. Additionally, lactate activates the GPR81 receptor, can be involved in immune regulation and serves as a substrate for energy metabolism

## Main functions of lactate

### Mediating lactylation

Lactylation is a recently discovered post-translational modification induced by lactate, which was first identified in histone by Zhang et al. (Zhang et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR115 "Zhang D, et al. Metabolic regulation of gene expression by histone lactylation. Nature. 2019;574(9):575–80.")). Histone is primarily composed of H1, H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 subunits (The 8-mer made of 2 molecules each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 is the core component of the nucleosome), and various acyl groups can be linked to the amino and carboxyl terminal amino acid residues of these subunits. Lactate covalently binds to the lysine (K) residues of histone in a concentration-dependent manner, resulting in their lactylation (Martín et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR58 "Martín V, et al. Rectal and vaginal eradication of streptococcus agalactiae (Gbs) in pregnant women by using lactobacillus salivarius cect 9145, a target-specific probiotic strain. Nutrients. 2019;11(4):810.")). The most common modification site is H3K18, where a lactate group is added at the K18 site of histone H3, thereby altering the function and regulatory processes of this histone in the cells (Jingyu et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR40 "Jingyu L, et al. Lactate regulates major zygotic genome activation by H3K18 lactylation in mammals. Natl Sci Rev. 2024;11:nwad295.")). Interestingly, lactylation also exists on non-histone proteins (Dominique et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR26 "Dominique OG, et al. Non-enzymatic Lysine Lactoylation of Glycolytic Enzymes. Cell Chem Biol. 2019;27(2):206–13.")). For example, a study has found that the abnormal increase in blood lactate levels in sepsis patients can lactacylate the high mobility group protein 1(HMGB1) in macrophages, promoting exosome secretion and release, disrupting endothelial integrity, and leading to endothelial barrier dysfunction (Kun et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR48 "Kun Y, et al. Lactate promotes macrophage HMGB1 lactylation, acetylation, and exosomal release in polymicrobial sepsis. Cell Death Differ. 2021;29:133–46.")).

Lactylation has been shown to be regulated by lactate levels (Erika et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR28 "Erika LV, et al. Quantification of lactoyl-CoA (lactyl-CoA) by liquid chromatography mass spectrometry in mammalian cells and tissues. Open Biol. 2020;10(9):200187.")). And this process necessitates the involvement of specific lactate dehydrogenase “Writers” and lactate dehydrogenase “Erasers” for regulation (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#Tab1)) (Yang et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR105 "Yang K, et al. Lactate promotes macrophage HMGB1 lactylation, acetylation, and exosomal release in polymicrobial sepsis. Cell Death Differ. 2022;29(1):133–46."); Cui et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR23 "Cui H, et al. Lung myofibroblasts promote macrophage profibrotic activity through lactate-induced histone lactylation. Am J Respir Cell Mol Biol. 2021;64(1):115–25.")). A study has demonstrated that knockdown of p300 in mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages significantly impairs lactate-induced histone lactylation (Cui et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR23 "Cui H, et al. Lung myofibroblasts promote macrophage profibrotic activity through lactate-induced histone lactylation. Am J Respir Cell Mol Biol. 2021;64(1):115–25.")). And, overexpression of p300 in HEK293T cells leads to an increase in histone H3K18 lactylation levels (Zhang et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR114 "Zhang D, et al. Metabolic regulation of gene expression by histone lactylation. Nature. 2019;574(7779):575–80.")). Another study indicated that the p300/ CREB binding protein (CBP) inhibitor C646 antagonized lactate-induced lactylation of non-histone protein HMGB1 in RAW 264.7 cells, and knockdown of p300 or CBP also significantly inhibited this phenomenon (Yang et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR105 "Yang K, et al. Lactate promotes macrophage HMGB1 lactylation, acetylation, and exosomal release in polymicrobial sepsis. Cell Death Differ. 2022;29(1):133–46.")). These findings suggest that p300 and CBP play a role as “Writers” in the process of lactylation. Additionally, new evidences confirm that histone acetyltransferase binding to ORC1(HBO1), YiaC, and lysine acetyltransferase 8 (KAT8) can act as “Writers” to catalyze the addition of lactate to lysine, affecting the activity of metabolic enzymes, promoting translational extension, and protein synthesis,HBO1 seems to preferentially promote H3K9 lactylation (Ziping et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR120 "Ziping N, et al. HBO1 catalyzes lysine lactylation and mediates histone H3K9la to regulate gene transcription. Nat Commun. 2024;15(1):3561."); Hanyang et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR34 "Hanyang D, et al. YiaC and CobB regulate lysine lactylation in Escherichia coli. Nat Commun. 2022;13(1):6628."); Bingteng et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR10 "Bingteng X, et al. KAT8-catalyzed lactylation promotes eEF1A2-mediated protein synthesis and colorectal carcinogenesis. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2024;121(8):e2314128121.")). These findings provide new insights into the regulation of protein lactylation by p300, CBP, YiaC, HBO1 and KAT8 in different biological environments,however, further research is needed to determine whether they act independently or synergistically. Class I histone deacetylases (HDAC1-3) and silent information regulator proteins (SIRT1-3) are particularly effective in deacylation modification (Carlos et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR17 "Carlos M-Y, et al. Class I histone deacetylases (HDAC1–3) are histone lysine delactylases. Sci Adv. 2022;8(3):eabi6696.")). Interestingly, in vitro experiments have demonstrated that HDAC1 and HDAC3 function as “Erasers” by reducing the lactylation level of H4K5 in HeLa cells (Carlos et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR17 "Carlos M-Y, et al. Class I histone deacetylases (HDAC1–3) are histone lysine delactylases. Sci Adv. 2022;8(3):eabi6696.")). Zhao et al. further validated the specific delactylation enzyme activity of HDAC1 and HDAC3 through overexpression and knockdown experiments in cells in 2022 (Moreno-Yruela et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR64 "Moreno-Yruela C, et al. Class I histone deacetylases (HDAC1–3) are histone lysine delactylases. Science advances. 2022;8(3):eabi6696.")). Additionally, Zessin et al. discovered potential delactylation enzyme activity for HDAC6 and HDAC8 in the same year (Zessin et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR113 "Zessin M, et al. Uncovering robust delactoylase and depyruvoylase activities of HDAC isoforms. ACS Chem Biol. 2022;17(6):1364–75.")). Subsequently, SIRT2 and SIRT3 were also identified as potential delactylation enzymes, with SIRT3 demonstrating a higher activity towards H4K16 (Zu et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR122 "Zu H, et al. SIRT2 functions as a histone delactylase and inhibits the proliferation and migration of neuroblastoma cells. Cell Discov. 2022;8(1):54."); Jin et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR38 "Jin J, et al. SIRT3-dependent delactylation of cyclin E2 prevents hepatocellular carcinoma growth. EMBO Rep. 2023;24(5):e56052.")). Lactylation requires specific “Readers” for recognition (Xinglin et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR100 "Xinglin H, et al. Dux activates metabolism-lactylation-MET network during early iPSC reprogramming with Brg1 as the histone lactylation reader. Nucleic Acids Res. 2024;52(10):5529–48.")). A study on induced pluripotent stem cell reprogramming conducted a proteomic analysis during an immunoprecipitation experiment targeting H3K18 lactylation in embryonic stem cells, revealing the selective recruitment of Brahma-related gene 1 (Brg1) (Xinglin et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR100 "Xinglin H, et al. Dux activates metabolism-lactylation-MET network during early iPSC reprogramming with Brg1 as the histone lactylation reader. Nucleic Acids Res. 2024;52(10):5529–48.")). Both H3K18 lactylation and Brg1 were enriched at the promoters of genes linked to pluripotency and epithelial connectivity (Xinglin et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR100 "Xinglin H, et al. Dux activates metabolism-lactylation-MET network during early iPSC reprogramming with Brg1 as the histone lactylation reader. Nucleic Acids Res. 2024;52(10):5529–48.")). Thus, Brg1 is proposed as a “Reader” for histone lactylation. In summary, these findings indicate that lactylation can be regulated by both lactylation enzymes and de-lactylation enzymes, functioning under the influence of corresponding recognition enzymes. However, it is important to note that these regulatory enzymes exhibit a lack of specificity.

### Participation in immune regulation

Immune cells can rapidly activate in response to tissue damage, microbial infections, or cellular stress, activating inflammation pathways and eliminating threats (Rathinam and Chan [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR76 "Rathinam VA, Chan FK. Inflammasome, Inflammation, and Tissue Homeostasis. Trends Mol Med. 2018;24(3):304–18.")). Immune evasion plays a crucial role in the development of cancer within the tumor microenvironment (Tay et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR86 "Tay C, Tanaka A, Sakaguchi S. Tumor-infiltrating regulatory T cells as targets of cancer immunotherapy. Cancer Cell. 2023;41(3):450–65.")). Lactate has been identified as an important factor in promoting tumor growth by exerting immunosuppressive effects, including inducing, recruiting, and regulating immune suppressor cells (Tay et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR86 "Tay C, Tanaka A, Sakaguchi S. Tumor-infiltrating regulatory T cells as targets of cancer immunotherapy. Cancer Cell. 2023;41(3):450–65.")). A study has demonstrated that lactate can inhibit the function of T lymphocytes and NK cells, thus facilitating tumor immune evasion (Brand et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR13 "Brand A, et al. LDHA-Associated Lactic Acid Production Blunts Tumor Immunosurveillance by T and NK Cells. Cell Metab. 2016;24(5):657–71.")). Lactate can enter the cytoplasm of CD8 + T lymphocytes, leading to a decrease in intracellular PH and inhibiting the proliferation and cytotoxic function of these cells (Apostolova and Pearce [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR7 "Apostolova P, Pearce EL. Lactic acid and lactate: revisiting the physiological roles in the tumor microenvironment. Trends Immunol. 2022;43(12):969–77.")). A high lactate microenvironment can also impair NK cell stability and effectiveness (Brand et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR13 "Brand A, et al. LDHA-Associated Lactic Acid Production Blunts Tumor Immunosurveillance by T and NK Cells. Cell Metab. 2016;24(5):657–71.")). Concentrations above 20 mM can induce apoptosis in both T lymphocyte and NK cells (Brand et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR13 "Brand A, et al. LDHA-Associated Lactic Acid Production Blunts Tumor Immunosurveillance by T and NK Cells. Cell Metab. 2016;24(5):657–71.")). Additionally, lactate can regulate macrophage metabolic reprogramming, suppressing M1 (pro-inflammatory)50 macrophage activation and M2 (anti-inflammatory) polarization, thereby influencing tumor progression and inflammation development (Bangjun et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR8 "Bangjun X, et al. Lactate and lactylation in macrophage metabolic reprogramming: current progress and outstanding issues. Front Immunol. 2024;15:1395786.")). Additionally, lactate can activate the immune escape mechanism in cancer cells through autocrine signaling by stimulating the G protein-coupled receptor 81 (GPR81) on the cell membrane (Brown and Ganapathy [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR16 "Brown T, Ganapathy V. Lactate/GPR81 signaling and proton motive force in cancer: Role in angiogenesis, immune escape, nutrition, and Warburg phenomenon. Pharmacol Ther. 2020;206:107451.")).

### Involvement in signal transduction

GPR81 is a selective lactate-sensitive receptor expressed in brain, fat, cancer, and retinal cells (Brown and Ganapathy [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR15 "Brown TP, Ganapathy V. Lactate/GPR81 signaling and proton motive force in cancer: Role in angiogenesis, immune escape, nutrition, and Warburg phenomenon. Pharmacol Ther. 2019;206:07451.")). Lactate activates GPR81 to transmit signaling molecules and perform biological functions (Certo et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR18 "Certo M, et al. Understanding lactate sensing and signalling. Trends Endocrinol Metab. 2022;33(10):722–35.")). For instance, it promotes the dephosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) and enhances cell apoptosis in ischemic brain injury (Shen et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR81 "Shen Z, et al. Inhibition of G protein-coupled receptor 81 (GPR81) protects against ischemic brain injury. CNS Neurosci Ther. 2014;21(3):271–9.")). In cancer cells relying on lactate as their primary energy source due to the “Warburg effect”, the absence of GPR81 impairs mitochondrial function and significantly reduces tumor growth (Roland et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR77 "Roland CL, et al. Cell surface lactate receptor GPR81 is crucial for cancer cell survival. Cancer Res. 2014;74(18):5301–10.")).Lactate inhibits Yes-related protein (YAP) and NF-κB activation via GPR81-mediated signaling, reducing macrophage pro-inflammatory responses to LPS stimulation (Yang et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR104 "Yang K, et al. viaLactate Suppresses Macrophage Pro-Inflammatory Response to LPS Stimulation by Inhibition of YAP and NF-κB Activation GPR81-Mediated Signaling. Front Immunol. 2020;11:587913.")). These findings indicate that GPR81 is a key target for lactate-regulated signaling, significantly influencing tumor growth and inflammation regulation.

### As an energy metabolic substrate

Lactate can function as an energy substrate, capable of uncoupling mitochondrial energy production driven by carbohydrates from glycolysis (Joshua and Sven [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR43 "Joshua DR, Sven E. Lactate: the ugly duckling of energy metabolism. Nat Metab. 2020;2(7):566–71.")). When blood glucose levels are low, lactate acts as an energy supplement to meet the excitatory activities of the brain (Brooks [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR14 "Brooks G. The Science and Translation of Lactate Shuttle Theory. Cell Metab. 2018;27(4):757–85."); Dienel [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR25 "Dienel G. Brain Glucose Metabolism: Integration of Energetics with Function. Physiol Rev. 2019;99(1):949–1045.")). A study has shown that in the absence of glucose, lactate also participates in synaptic transmission activities in the brain (Schurr et al. [1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR80 "Schurr A, West C, Rigor B. Lactate-supported synaptic function in the rat hippocampal slice preparation. Science. 1988;240(4857):1326–8.")). Moreover, research has confirmed that when the shuttling of lactate in the hypothalamic ventricular membrane-neuroglial cells is inhibited, the energy balance of the pre-agouti-related peptide neurons is disrupted (Lhomme et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR102 "Lhomme T, Clasadonte J, Imbernon M, Fernandois D, Sauve F, Caron E, da Silva Lima N, Heras V, Martinez-Corral I, Mueller-Fielitz H, Rasika S, Schwaninger M, Nogueiras R, Prevot V. Tanycytic networks mediate energy balance by feeding lactate to glucose-insensitive POMC neurons. J Clin Invest. 2021;131(18):e140521. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI140521
                  
                .")). This indicates that lactate may be a primary energy substrate in specific environments.

## m 6 A modification

Common epigenetic modifications mainly consist of DNA methylation, histone modification, non-coding RNA, RNA methylation modification, and chromatin remodeling (Jonas et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR42 "Jonas C, et al. The rise of epitranscriptomics: recent developments and future directions. Trends Pharmacol Sci. 2023;45(1):24–38.")). In mammals, m 6 A modification is the most prevalent epigenetic alteration in mRNA, which can impact gene transcription, splicing, stability, and translation (Zhigalova et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR118 "Zhigalova NA, et al. The Functions of N(6)-Methyladenosine in Nuclear RNAs. Biochemistry (Mosc). 2024;89(1):159–72."); Meyer et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR59 "Meyer KD, et al. 5’ UTR m(6)A Promotes Cap-Independent Translation. Cell. 2015;163(4):999–1010."); Molinie et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR63 "Molinie B, et al. m(6)A-LAIC-seq reveals the census and complexity of the m(6)A epitranscriptome. Nat Methods. 2016;13(8):692–8.")). The dynamic regulation of m 6 A modification is carried out by methyltransferases (Writers) (Bokar et al. [1994](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR12 "Bokar J, et al. Characterization and partial purification of mRNA N6-adenosine methyltransferase from HeLa cell nuclei. Internal mRNA methylation requires a multisubunit complex. J Biol Chem. 1994;269(26):17697–704."); Śledź and Jinek [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR84 "Śledź P, Jinek M. Structural insights into the molecular mechanism of the m(6)A writer complex. eLife. 2016;5:e18434.")) and demethylases (Erasers) (Karthiya and Khandelia [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR45 "Karthiya R, Khandelia P. m6A RNA methylation: ramifications for gene expression and human health. Mol Biotechnol. 2020;62(10):467–84.")). Under the action of enzymes (Readers) that can recognize the RNA base sites with m 6 A modifications, the fate of the target RNA is regulated (Shi et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR82 "Shi R, et al. Linking the YTH domain to cancer: the importance of YTH family proteins in epigenetics. Cell Death Dis. 2021;12(4):346.")), (Huang et al. [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR36 "Huang H, et al. Recognition of RNA N-methyladenosine by IGF2BP proteins enhances mRNA stability and translation. Nat Cell Biol. 2018;20(3):285–95.")), (Meyer et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR59 "Meyer KD, et al. 5’ UTR m(6)A Promotes Cap-Independent Translation. Cell. 2015;163(4):999–1010.")).

The occurrence of m 6 A depends on the catalytic action of the methyltransferase complex (MTC), which is mainly composed of methyltransferase-like protein 3 (METTL3), methyltransferase-like protein 14 (METTL14), Wilms’ tumor 1-associated protein (WTAP), Vir-like m 6 A methyltransferase-associated (VIRMA/KIAA1429), and RNA binding motif protein 15 (RBM15) (Bokar et al. [1994](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR12 "Bokar J, et al. Characterization and partial purification of mRNA N6-adenosine methyltransferase from HeLa cell nuclei. Internal mRNA methylation requires a multisubunit complex. J Biol Chem. 1994;269(26):17697–704."); Śledź and Jinek [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR84 "Śledź P, Jinek M. Structural insights into the molecular mechanism of the m(6)A writer complex. eLife. 2016;5:e18434.")). METTL3 is the core component of MTC, containing an S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) binding domain that catalyzes the transfer of the methyl group from SAM to the adenine base in RNA (Stephanie et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR85 "Stephanie O, et al. A comprehensive review of m6A/m6Am RNA methyltransferase structures. Nucleic Acids Res. 2021;49(13):7239–55.")). METTL14 and METTL3 form a stable complex in a 1:1 ratio to stabilize the structure of MTC (Wang et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR92 "Wang P, Doxtader K, Nam Y. Structural Basis for Cooperative Function of Mettl3 and Mettl14 Methyltransferases. Mol Cell. 2016;63(2):306–17.")). This complex is recruited and guided to nuclear speckles by the action of WTAP and RBM15 to jointly promote the installation of m6A methylation (Schöller et al. [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR79 "Schöller E, et al. Interactions, localization, and phosphorylation of the mA generating METTL3-METTL14-WTAP complex. RNA (New York, NY). 2018;24(4):499–512."); Patil et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR70 "Patil D, et al. m(6)A RNA methylation promotes XIST-mediated transcriptional repression. Nature. 2016;537(7620):369–73.")). In addition, VIRMA/KIAA1429, zinc finger CCCH-type containing 13 (ZC3H13), and methyltransferase-like protein 16 (METTL16) play a significant role in the complex recruitment and promotion of MTC complex formation in this regulatory process (Yue et al. [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR109 "Yue Y, et al. VIRMA mediates preferential mA mRNA methylation in 3’UTR and near stop codon and associates with alternative polyadenylation. Cell Discov. 2018;4:10.")), (Knuckles et al. [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR47 "Knuckles P, et al. Zc3h13/Flacc is required for adenosine methylation by bridging the mRNA-binding factor Rbm15/Spenito to the mA machinery component Wtap/Fl(2)d. Genes Dev. 2018;32:415–29.")), (Warda et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR95 "Warda A, et al. NHuman METTL16 is a -methyladenosine (mA) methyltransferase that targets pre-mRNAs and various non-coding RNAs. EMBO Rep. 2017;18(11):2004–14.")).

Currently, the identified demethylases mainly include fat mass and obesity-associated gene (FTO), AlkB homolog 5 (ALKBH5), and ALKBH3. FTO is the first identified enzyme capable of catalyzing m6A demethylation, and its dysregulation plays an important role in diseases such as cancer by affecting demethylation modifications (Sarah Kassem et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR78 "Sarah Kassem A, Habiba A, Abdulrahim AS. FTO m6A demethylase in obesity and cancer: implications and underlying molecular mechanisms. Int J Mol Sci. 2022;23(7):3800.")). ALKBH5 catalyzes m6A demethylation in a manner dependent on Fe (II) and α-ketoglutarate (Aik et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR2 "Aik W, et al. Structure of human RNA N⁶-methyladenine demethylase ALKBH5 provides insights into its mechanisms of nucleic acid recognition and demethylation. Nucleic Acids Res. 2014;42(7):4741–54.")). In addition, new research has reported the demethylation function of ALKBH3 (Mohua et al. [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR62 "Mohua D, et al. Multiprotein dynamic combinatorial chemistry: a strategy for the simultaneous discovery of subfamily-selective inhibitors for nucleic acid demethylases FTO and ALKBH3. Chem Asian J. 2018;13(19):2854–67.")). However, there is currently limited research on this topic.

The proteins that recognize “Readers” can be categorized into direct and indirect “Readers”. Direct “Readers” primarily consist of proteins containing the YTH domain, which binds to regions on RNA where m 6 A has occurred. In the mammalian genome, there are three types of YTH domain proteins: YTHDC1, YTHDC2, and the YTHDF protein family (Tingting et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR88 "Tingting Z, et al. Crystal structure of the YTH domain of YTHDF2 reveals mechanism for recognition of N6-methyladenosine. Cell Res. 2014;24(12):1493–6."); Peter et al. [2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR71 "Peter S, Ilona R, Stefan S. YTH: a new domain in nuclear proteins. Trends Biochem Sci. 2002;27(10):495–7.")). YTHDC1 mainly functions in the nucleus, YTHDC2 has roles in both the nucleus and cytoplasm, and the YTHDF family primarily operates in the cytoplasm (Hailing et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR33 "Hailing S, et al. YTHDF3 facilitates translation and decay of N(6)-methyladenosine-modified RNA. Cell Res. 2017;27(3):315–28."); Magdalena Natalia et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR56 "Magdalena Natalia W, et al. Regulation of m(6)A transcripts by the 3’→5’ RNA helicase YTHDC2 Is essential for a successful meiotic program in the mammalian germline. Mol Cell. 2017;68(2):374–87.")). YTHDC1 promotes RNA splicing and export by recruiting mRNA splicing factors (Woodcock et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR97 "Woodcock C, et al. Biochemical and structural basis for YTH domain of human YTHDC1 binding to methylated adenine in DNA. Nucleic Acids Res. 2020;48(18):10329–41.")). YTHDC2 has an RNA helicase domain and interacts with RNA helicases that regulate translation to promote the translation of target RNA (Phillip et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR72 "Phillip JH, et al. Ythdc2 is an N(6)-methyladenosine binding protein that regulates mammalian spermatogenesis. Cell Res. 2017;27(9):1115–27.")). YTHDF1 enhances mRNA translation and protein synthesis by recruiting initiation factors (Wang et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR91 "Wang X, et al. N(6)-methyladenosine Modulates Messenger RNA Translation Efficiency. Cell. 2015;161(6):1388–99.")), YTHDF2 promotes the cleavage of bound mRNA, leading to transcript degradation (Park et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR1 "Park OH, et al. Endoribonucleolytic Cleavage of m(6)A-Containing RNAs by RNase P/MRP Complex. Mol Cell. 2019;74(3):494–507.")), while YHTDF3 enhances the functions of both YHTDF1 and YHTDF2 by binding to them respectively (Lasman et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR50 "Lasman L, et al. Context-dependent functional compensation between Ythdf mA reader proteins. Genes Dev. 2020;34:1373–91.")). Indirect readers such as IGF2BPs, EIF3, and members of heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein (HNRNP) family also play important roles in improving mRNA stability and efficiency of translation initiation complex formation (Alarcón et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR3 "Alarcón C, et al. HNRNPA2B1 Is a Mediator of m(6)A-Dependent Nuclear RNA Processing Events. Cell. 2015;162(6):1299–308."); Müller et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR65 "Müller S, et al. IGF2BP1 promotes SRF-dependent transcription in cancer in a m6A- and miRNA-dependent manner. Nucleic Acids Res. 2019;47(1):375–90."); Lee et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10565-024-09951-9#ref-CR51 "Lee A, et al. eIF3d is an mRNA cap-binding protein that is required for specialized translation initiation. Nature. 2016;536(7614):96–9.")).

args.summary:
This is a review article published on 02 December 2024 in Cell Biology and Toxicology (Volume 40, article 107) examining the roles of lactate and its interplay with N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification in disease pathogenesis. The article is open access, with 16k Accesses and 29 Citations, authored by Fajuan Tang, Dongqiong Xiao, Xihong Li, and Lina Qiao.

**Key findings:**

1. **Lactate functions**: Once considered a waste byproduct of glycolysis, lactate is now recognized as a multifunctional molecule that (a) mediates histone and non-histone lactylation to regulate gene transcription, (b) influences immune suppression by affecting T lymphocytes, NK cells, and macrophages, (c) activates G protein-coupled receptor 81 (GPR81) for signal transduction, and (d) serves as an energy substrate. Lactate accumulation promotes metabolic reprogramming and immune evasion in tumor cells.

2. **Lactylation mechanism**: Lactylation is a recently discovered post-translational modification first identified in histones by Zhang et al. (2019). The most common modification site is H3K18. Lactate covalently binds to lysine residues of histones in a concentration-dependent manner. Non-histone lactylation also occurs (e.g., HMGB1 in sepsis).

3. **Lactylation regulatory enzymes**: "Writers" include p300, CBP, HBO1, YiaC, and KAT8 (with HBO1 preferentially promoting H3K9 lactylation). "Erasers" include HDAC1-3, SIRT1-3 (SIRT3 showing higher activity toward H4K16), HDAC6, HDAC8, and SIRT2. "Readers" include Brg1, identified as a histone lactylation reader in iPSC reprogramming studies.

4. **m6A modification**: The most prevalent post-transcriptional epigenetic alteration in eukaryotic mRNA. Regulated by methyltransferases (Writers: METTL3, METTL14, WTAP, VIRMA/KIAA1429, RBM15, ZC3H13, METTL16), demethylases (Erasers: FTO, ALKBH5, ALKBH3), and recognition proteins (Readers: YTHDC1, YTHDC2, YTHDF1-3, plus indirect readers including IGF2BPs, EIF3, and HNRNP family).

5. **The interplay between lactate and m6A**: Lactate-mediated lactylation at histone H3K18 can modulate downstream target m6A modifications by enhancing transcriptional expression of m6A-related regulatory enzymes. Conversely, m6A-related regulatory enzymes are also subject to lactylation by lactate, and can influence key glycolytic pathway enzymes or MCT4 (lactate transporter) to impact lactate levels. For example, LDH activation induced by lactate accumulation serves as a potential upstream regulator of m6A modifications in tumors and sepsis.

6. **Clinical relevance**: These interactions play crucial roles in cancer, liver and lung fibrosis, myocardial ischemia, cerebral hemorrhage, and sepsis.

## Abstract

Accumulated evidence has implicated the diverse and substantial influence of lactate on cellular differentiation and fate regulation in physiological and pathological settings, particularly in intricate conditions such as cancer. Specifically, lactate has been demonstrated to be pivotal in molding the tumor microenvironment (TME) through its effects on different cell populations. Within tumor cells, lactate impacts cell signaling pathways, augments the lactate shuttle process, boosts resistance to oxidative stress, and contributes to lactylation. In various cellular populations, the interplay between lactate and immune cells governs processes such as cell differentiation, immune response, immune surveillance, and treatment effectiveness. Furthermore, communication between lactate and stromal/endothelial cells supports basal membrane (BM) remodeling, epithelial-mesenchymal transitions (EMT), metabolic reprogramming, angiogenesis, and drug resistance. Focusing on lactate production and transport, specifically through lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and monocarboxylate transporters (MCT), has shown promise in the treatment of cancer. Inhibitors targeting LDH and MCT act as both tumor suppressors and enhancers of immunotherapy, leading to a synergistic therapeutic effect when combined with immunotherapy. The review underscores the importance of lactate in tumor progression and provides valuable perspectives on potential therapeutic approaches that target the vulnerability of lactate metabolism, highlighting *the Heel of Achilles* for cancer treatment.

## Introduction

Lactate secretion is widely recognized as a classic metabolic hallmark of cancer, often referred to as the Warburg effect. This phenomenon describes the preference of cancer cells to favor glycolysis for energy production, even in the presence of oxygen, leading to increased lactate production.[1](#ref-CR1 "Ge, T. et al. Crosstalk between metabolic reprogramming and epigenetics in cancer: updates on mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities. Cancer Commun. 42, 1049–1082 (2022)."),[2](#ref-CR2 "Hanahan, D. & Weinberg, R. A. Hallmarks of cancer: the next generation. Cell 144, 646–674 (2011)."),[3](#ref-CR3 "Hanahan, D. Hallmarks of cancer: new dimensions. Cancer Discov. 12, 31–46 (2022)."),[4](#ref-CR4 "Warburg, O. On the origin of cancer cells. Science 123, 309–314 (1956)."),[5](/articles/s41392-024-02082-x#ref-CR5 "Liberti, M. V. & Locasale, J. W. The Warburg effect: how does it benefit cancer cells? Trends Biochem. Sci. 41, 211–218 (2016).") Recent studies have not only confirmed this understanding but have also delved deeper into the role of lactate in cancer initiation and progression, highlighting its multifaceted contributions beyond merely being a byproduct of cellular metabolism.[6](#ref-CR6 "Thompson, C. B. et al. A century of the Warburg effect. Nat. Metab. 5, 1840–1843 (2023)."),[7](#ref-CR7 "Zhong, X. et al. Warburg effect in colorectal cancer: the emerging roles in tumor microenvironment and therapeutic implications. J. Hematol. Oncol. 15, 160 (2022)."),[8](#ref-CR8 "Lu, J. The Warburg metabolism fuels tumor metastasis. Cancer Metastasis Rev. 38, 157–164 (2019)."),[9](#ref-CR9 "Liao, M. et al. Targeting the Warburg effect: a revisited perspective from molecular mechanisms to traditional and innovative therapeutic strategies in cancer. Acta Pharm. Sin. B 14, 953–1008 (2024)."),[10](/articles/s41392-024-02082-x#ref-CR10 "Siska, P. J. et al. The immunological Warburg effect: can a metabolic-tumor-stroma score (MeTS) guide cancer immunotherapy? Immunol. Rev. 295, 187–202 (2020).")

The traditional view of lactate as a waste product has been challenged by groundbreaking research employing advanced imaging techniques such as 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (FDG-PET). A pivotal study by DeBerardinis et al. demonstrated that lactate serves as a vital nutrient for tumor regions, which fundamentally alters the perception of its role in cancer biology.[11](/articles/s41392-024-02082-x#ref-CR11 "Hensley, C. T. et al. Metabolic heterogeneity in human lung tumors. Cell 164, 681–694 (2016)."),[12](/articles/s41392-024-02082-x#ref-CR12 "Sushentsev, N. et al. Hyperpolarised 13C-MRI identifies the emergence of a glycolytic cell population within intermediate-risk human prostate cancer. Nat. Commun. 13, 466 (2022).") In experiments involving non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) xenografts in mice, researchers injected both 13C-glucose and 13C-lactate. They discovered that metabolites derived from 13C-lactate in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, such as citrate, glutamate, and malate, were found to be twice as abundant compared to those derived from glucose.[13](/articles/s41392-024-02082-x#ref-CR13 "Faubert, B. et al. Lactate metabolism in human lung tumors. Cell 171, 358–371, (2017).") Abnormal lactate-related metabolisms instigate tumor progression. Lactate metabolism and aberrant glucose and fatty acid metabolism induced by lactate map the metabolic evolution in tumor ecosystem, which coordinates tumor progression.

## Research history of lactate metabolism and lactylation

In 1780, the Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele was the first to isolate lactic acid from sour milk. Since then, its metabolic role and significance in tumors have gradually been clarified (Fig. [2](/articles/s41392-024-02082-x#Fig2)). Soon, Jöns Jacob Berzelius discovered that lactic acid is also produced by muscles during exercise in 1808. Its structure was established by Johannes Wislicenus in 1873.[29](/articles/s41392-024-02082-x#ref-CR29 "Brooks, G. A. The tortuous path of lactate shuttle discovery: From cinders and boards to the lab and ICU. J. Sport Health Sci. 9, 446–460 (2020).") Lactic acid is an organic acid with the chemical formula C3H6O3. Lactate is the ionized form of lactic acid. When lactic acid dissolves in water, it can lose a hydrogen ion (proton), resulting in lactate (C3H5O3−).[30](/articles/s41392-024-02082-x#ref-CR30 "Mäki-Arvela, P., Simakova, I. This is a review article published in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy (Volume 10, Article 38, 2025) titled "Lactate and lactylation in cancer," authored by Jie Chen, Ziyue Huang, Renbing Jia, and colleagues. The article has 81k accesses and 489 citations, reflecting its significance.

KEY TOPIC: The review examines the multifaceted roles of lactate in cancer progression, moving beyond its traditional characterization as a metabolic waste product. It integrates the Warburg effect, lactate metabolism, and the newly discovered epigenetic modification called lactylation as therapeutic targets for cancer treatment.

HISTORICAL TIMELINE:
- 1780: Carl Wilhelm Scheele first isolated lactic acid from sour milk
- 1808: Jöns Jacob Berzelius discovered lactic acid produced by muscles during exercise
- 1873: Structure of lactic acid established by Johannes Wislicenus
- 1927: Warburg found glycolysis dominated glucose metabolism under aerobic conditions in tumors
- 1956: Warburg interpreted this as suppressed mitochondrial function (mitochondrial dysfunction theory)
- 1972: Efraim Racker coined the term "Warburg effect"
- 1980: FDG-PET adopted to trace glucose metabolism and indirectly quantify lactate metabolism in vivo
- 1985: Lactate shuttle concept introduced (continuously refined since)
- 2019: Histone lactylation first documented by Zhang et al. — the addition of a lactyl (La) group to lysine residues on histone proteins

KEY FINDINGS AND MECHANISMS:
1. LACTATE AS FUEL: Studies (Faubert, Hui, etc.) using isotope tracing (13C-glucose and 13C-lactate) in NSCLC xenografts showed metabolites derived from lactate in the TCA cycle (citrate, glutamate, malate) were twice as abundant as those from glucose. Lactate serves as a direct carbon source for the TCA cycle.

2. WARBURG EFFECT REVISED: Recent research challenges Warburg's original mechanism. The emerging view is that mitochondrial overload leads to excessive lactate release rather than a simple glycolytic switch. Lactate can be produced in significant amounts without impairing aerobic respiration.

3. LACTATE SHUTTLE: Introduced in 1985, it bridges anaerobic glycolysis and aerobic respiration. Three physiological functions: (1) lactate as a major energy source, (2) lactate as glucose xenobiotic precursor (via Cori cycle), (3) lactate as a signaling molecule.

4. METABOLIC SYMBIOSIS: In TME, anoxic tumor cells use LDHA for lactate production, which exits via MCT4 and is taken up by aerobic tumor cells via MCT1, where LDHB converts it back to pyruvate for ATP generation. This is shown to drive tumor proliferation, invasion, and metastasis.

5. TRANSPORT: Lactate transported via monocarboxylate transporters (MCT1, MCT4). MCT1 is induced by c-Myc; MCT4 is hypoxia-induced and highly expressed in glycolytic tissues and cancer cells. High expression of MCT1/4 in melanoma, glioblastoma, and NSCLC is associated with poor prognosis.

6. LACTYLATION: A post-translational modification connecting metabolism and epigenetics. Extends to both histone and non-histone proteins, influencing cell processes and accelerating tumor onset, proliferation, metastasis, and drug resistance.

7. LACTATE'S MULTIFACETED ROLES in TME: affects cell signaling pathways, augments lactate shuttle, boosts oxidative stress resistance, contributes to lactylation. Regulates immune cells (differentiation, immune response, surveillance, treatment effectiveness) and stromal/endothelial cells (basal membrane remodeling, EMT, metabolic reprogramming, angiogenesis, drug resistance).

THERAPEUTIC IMPLICATIONS:
- Targeting lactate production (LDH) and transport (MCT) shows promise
- LDH and MCT inhibitors act as both tumor suppressors and enhancers of immunotherapy (synergistic effect when combined)
- AZD3965, an MCT1 inhibitor, is the first lactate metabolism-targeting drug in a Phase I/II clinical trial (NCT01791595) for advanced solid tumors and non-Hodgkin lymphoma
- The review frames lactate/lactylation-targeted therapy as "the Heel of Achilles" for cancer treatment

--- SOURCE 2: Frontiers | Mitochondrial dynamics and metabolic regulation control T cell fate in the thymus ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2023.1270268/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**Original Research Article: "Mitochondrial dynamics and metabolic regulation control T cell fate in the thymus"**

Published in Frontiers in Immunology (Sec. T Cell Biology), Vol 14, 15 January 2024. DOI: 10.3389/fimmu.2023.1270268. Authors: Rima Elhage, Mairead Kelly, Nicolas Goudin, Jérôme Megret, Agnès Legrand, Ivan Nemazanyy, Cécilia Patitucci, Véronique Quellec, Timothy Wai, Ahmed Hamaï, and Sophie Ezine (Institut Necker Enfant-Malades, INSERM, Université de Paris; Institut Pasteur, CNRS, Paris, France).

**Objective:** To characterize cellular and mitochondrial metabolism, and mitochondrial dynamics in different thymic T cell populations, and determine if these changes directly affect proliferation and/or differentiation of thymic lymphocytes.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Mitochondrial mass and membrane potential (ΔΨm)** increase from TN2 to TN3 stage (maximum at TN3), then significantly decrease in TN4 and continue to decline in DP and SP mature thymocytes. Mitochondrial mass and membrane potential are higher in CD4+ SP than CD8+ SP cells.

2. **Glucose uptake** (2-NBDG) increases during TN2→TN4 transition, peaks at TN4 stage, then decreases in DP and SP cells (lowest at DP stage).

3. **Metabolic flux (Seahorse analysis):** TN4 progenitors show the highest basal OCR (25 pmol/min/μg protein) vs TN3 (15 pmol/min/μg) and mature cells (~10 pmol/min/μg). TN3 and TN4 show maximal respiratory capacity 4-7 times higher than mature cells. TN4 has significantly higher basal ECAR and glycolysis than TN3. DP cells show drastically reduced ECAR and glycolytic capacity compared to SP cells.

4. **Mitochondrial morphology:** TN progenitors (TN1/TN2) have essentially fused mitochondria (66% fused). TN3/TN4 have 44-46% fused mitochondria. DP and SP mature thymocytes predominantly have fragmented mitochondria (66% in DP, 62% in CD4+, 80% in CD8+). Peripheral splenocytes also show fragmented morphology.

5. **In vitro inhibition of mitochondrial fission (Mdivi-1, Drp1 inhibitor):** Treatment of TN3 cells on OP9-DL4 feeder cells affected TN→DP transition—reduced proportion of DP, increased TN percentage, and decreased total cell numbers. TN3 cells decreased while TN4 slightly increased, suggesting accelerated TN3→TN4 transition. Similar results with M1 (mitochondrial fusion promoter). Total cell numbers declined, indicating effects on proliferation/differentiation.

6. **Metabolomic analysis (LC-MS, ~140 metabolites):** TN4 cells are more glycolytic (higher glucose, pyruvate, lactate) while TN3 relies more on OXPHOS (higher fumarate, malate, FAD, ATP, more oxidized state with higher NADP and GSSG/GSH ratio). TN4 expresses higher HK2 and PKM2; TN3 expresses higher HK1. DP cells show succinate accumulation. Phosphocreatine increases with differentiation (DP, CD4, CD8). Cystathionine characterizes DP cells.

7. **In vivo glycolysis inhibition (2-DG, 750 mg/kg every 2 days for 2 weeks):** Reduced total thymocyte number by half (113.5M control vs 53.8M treated, p<0.01). Increased TN3 frequency and decreased TN4, suggesting developmental arrest at TN3→TN4 transition. Specifically reduced proliferation (Ki67) in TN4, glucose absorption in TN3/TN4/CD4/CD8, and mitochondrial membrane potential in TN2/TN3/TN4.

8. **IL-7R deficient mice:** Total thymocytes reduced ~42-fold (208M vs 4.9M). Increased TN2-TN3 frequency, decreased TN4, blocking TN3→TN4 transition. TN4 progenitors had reduced proliferation. This demonstrates the glucose/IL-7R connection affects β-selection transition.

**Conclusion:** The study identifies mitochondrial dynamics and metabolic regulation (glycolysis, OXPHOS, glucose/IL-7R signaling) as essential components during β-selection transition, playing a major role in thymic development.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our results showed that thymic progenitors (CD3-CD4-CD8- triple negative, TN), in active division, have essentially a fused mitochondrial morphology and rely on high glycolysis and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). As TN cells differentiate to double positive (DP) and single positive (SP) stages, they became more quiescent, their mitochondria fragment and they downregulate glycolysis and OXPHOS.", "In vivo inhibition of glycolysis using 2-deoxyglucose (2-DG) and the absence of IL-7 signaling, led to a decline in glucose metabolism and mitochondrial membrane potential... affecting the TN3 to TN4 transition (also called β-selection transition), by enhancing the percentage of TN3, leading to a decrease in the total number of thymocytes.", "In vitro inhibition of the mitochondrial fission during progenitor differentiation on OP9-DL4 stroma, affected the TN to DP thymocyte transition by enhancing the percentage of TN and reducing that of DP, leading to a decrease in the total number of thymic cells including SP T cells.", "The LC-MS based analysis of their metabolome showed that they are distinct: TN3 rely more on OXPHOS whereas TN4 are more glycolytic.", "In vivo treatment with 2-DG significantly reduced the number of total thymocytes by half (p<0.01) (control group: 113.5 million cells ±10.3 versus 53.8 million ±4 in the 2-DG-treated group)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Mitochondrial Dynamics Controls T Cell Fate through Metabolic Programming - PubMed ---
URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27293185

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PubMed page for the 2016 Cell article "Mitochondrial Dynamics Controls T Cell Fate through Metabolic Programming" by Buck et al. (PMID: 27293185, PMCID: PMC4974356). 

The study investigates how mitochondrial dynamics (fusion/fission) regulates T cell metabolism and fate. Key findings:
- Effector T (TE) cells have punctate/fragmented mitochondria, while memory T (TM) cells maintain fused mitochondrial networks.
- The fusion protein Opa1 is required for memory T cell development and survival, but not for effector T cells after infection.
- Enforcing mitochondrial fusion in effector T cells imposes memory T cell characteristics and enhances antitumor function.
- Mitochondrial fusion in TM cells alters cristae morphology, configuring ETC complex associations to favor oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and fatty acid oxidation (FAO).
- Mitochondrial fission in TE cells leads to cristae expansion, reducing ETC efficiency and promoting aerobic glycolysis.
- Pharmacological promotion of fusion (using M1 + Mdivi-1) improves adoptive cellular immunotherapy against tumors in mouse models.
- Human CD8+ T cells similarly undergo mitochondrial remodeling, suggesting translational relevance.

The article includes 6 main figures showing EM and confocal microscopy, Seahorse metabolic analyses, in vivo infection and tumor models, and human T cell data. It is published in Cell, Vol. 166, Issue 1, pp. 63-76.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Activated effector T (TE) cells augment anabolic pathways of metabolism, such as aerobic glycolysis, while memory T (TM) cells engage catabolic pathways, like fatty acid oxidation (FAO).", "We show that TE cells have punctate mitochondria, while TM cells maintain fused networks.", "The fusion protein Opa1 is required for TM, but not TE cells after infection, and enforcing fusion in TE cells imposes TM cell characteristics and enhances antitumor function.", "Our data suggest that, by altering cristae morphology, fusion in TM cells configures electron transport chain (ETC) complex associations favoring oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and FAO, while fission in TE cells leads to cristae expansion, reducing ETC efficiency and promoting aerobic glycolysis.", "Mitochondrial remodeling is a signaling mechanism that instructs T cell metabolic programming."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Mitochondrial Dynamics Controls T Cell Fate through ... ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Europe PMC article page for the scientific paper "Mitochondrial Dynamics Controls T Cell Fate through Metabolic Programming" published in Cell (09 Jun 2016, 166(1):63-76). DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2016.05.035; PMID: 27293185; PMCID: PMC4974356. The article has free full text available in Europe PMC.

The paper is authored by 19 researchers (including Buck MD, O'Sullivan D, Pearce EL) from institutions including the Max Planck Institute of Immunobiology and Epigenetics (Freiburg, Germany), Washington University School of Medicine (St. Louis, MO), University of California Los Angeles, and the University of Freiburg.

Key findings from the abstract:
- Activated effector T (TE) cells augment anabolic pathways such as aerobic glycolysis, while memory T (TM) cells engage catabolic pathways like fatty acid oxidation (FAO).
- TE cells have punctate mitochondria, while TM cells maintain fused networks.
- The fusion protein Opa1 is required for TM, but not TE cells, after infection.
- Enforcing fusion in TE cells imposes TM cell characteristics and enhances antitumor function.
- Fusion in TM cells configures electron transport chain (ETC) complex associations favoring oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and FAO by altering cristae morphology, while fission in TE cells leads to cristae expansion, reducing ETC efficiency and promoting aerobic glycolysis.
- Conclusion: Mitochondrial remodeling is a signaling mechanism that instructs T cell metabolic programming.

The page lists five similar articles, including papers on AMPKα1 and T-cell memory, BCL11B and OPA1-mediated mitochondrial fusion, and memory CD8(+) T cells using cell-intrinsic lipolysis. Funding sources include Bundesministerium für Bildung und Forschung, Burroughs Wellcome Fund, Max-Planck-Gesellschaft, NCI NIH HHS, NIAID NIH HHS, National Institutes of Health, and National Science Foundation. Three commentary articles on this work also appear in Cell Research, Cell, and Nature Reviews Immunology.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Mitochondrial Metabolism in T-Cell Exhaustion - MDPI ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/15/7400

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences (IJMS) on July 31, 2025, titled "Mitochondrial Metabolism in T-Cell Exhaustion" by Fei Li, Yu Feng, Zesheng Yin, and Yahong Wang from Lanzhou University, China. The article reviews the role of mitochondrial metabolism in T-cell exhaustion, which occurs under chronic antigen stimulation from infections (e.g., HIV, HBV, HCV, tuberculosis) and cancer.

Key points:
1. Exhausted T cells overexpress inhibitory receptors (PD-1, TIM-3, LAG-3), have reduced effector function and proliferative capacity, and exhibit altered transcription factor expression (Blimp-1, TOX).

2. Mitochondrial metabolism determines T cell function and fate through biogenesis, dynamics (fusion/fission), mitophagy, and mitochondrial transfer. PGC-1α is a critical regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. Effector T cells have fragmented mitochondria with loosened cristae, while memory T cells have fused mitochondria with tighter cristae.

3. Exhausted T cells show disrupted mitochondrial energy metabolism, increased depolarized mitochondria, ROS accumulation, reduced glucose uptake, and defective glycolysis and OXPHOS. PD-1 signaling promotes these changes by inhibiting PGC-1α via Blimp1.

4. Progenitor exhausted T cells (stem-like, self-renewing) use FAO and OXPHOS, while terminally exhausted T cells rely on glycolytic metabolism. Terminally exhausted T cells express high PD-1 and TIM-3, lose TCF-1 and CXCR5 expression.

5. Potential therapeutic strategies include: inducing PGC-1α expression (using bezafibrate, 4-1BB costimulation, CoQ10, hydrogen gas, metformin, IL-15), alleviating ROS production (using antioxidants like N-acetylcysteine and MitoQ), enhancing ATP production, and utilizing mitochondrial transfer.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
T cells play a vital role in resisting pathogen invasion and maintaining immune homeostasis. However, T cells gradually become exhausted under chronic antigenic stimulation, and this exhaustion is closely related to mitochondrial dysfunction in T cells., Exhausted T cells exhibit overexpression of multiple inhibitory receptors, such as PD-1 and T cell immunoglobulin mucin 3 (TIM-3), and lymphocyte activation gene 3 (LAG-3), along with a gradual reduction in effector function and proliferative capacity., Forcing mitochondrial fusion drives memory T cell differentiation by promoting OXPHOS and FAO, while mitochondria fission facilitates aerobic glycolysis within effector T cells., The metabolic characteristics of exhausted T cells include disrupted mitochondrial energy and respiration, increased depolarized mitochondria, and accumulation of ROS, leading to reduced glucose uptake, defective glycolysis, and OXPHOS., Targeting mitochondrial metabolism in exhausted T cells may achieve the goal of reversing and preventing T cell exhaustion.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Bioenergetic insufficiencies due to metabolic alterations regulated by PD-1 are an early driver of CD8+ T cell exhaustion ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4988919

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Immunity (August 2, 2016; 45(2):358; PMCID: PMC4988919; PMID: 27496729) by Bertram Bengsch, Andy L. Johnson, Makoto Kurachi, Pamela M Odorizzi, Kristen E. Pauken, John Attanasio, Erietta Stelekati, Laura M. McLane, Michael A. Paley, Greg M. Delgoffe, and E. John Wherry (corresponding author) from the University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine and University of Pittsburgh Cancer Institute.

The study investigates metabolic dysregulation in exhausted CD8+ T (Tex) cells during chronic infection. Using the chronic clone 13 strain of lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) compared to the acutely resolving Armstrong (Arm) strain in mice, the researchers found that within the first week of chronic infection—before severe dysfunction develops—virus-specific CD8+ T cells were already unable to match the bioenergetics of effector T cells from acute infection.

Key findings include:
- Early Tex cells showed suppressed glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), with reduced glucose uptake and use despite persisting mTOR signaling and upregulation of anabolic pathways.
- Transcriptional profiling via GSEA showed enrichment for OXPHOS, citrate cycle, fatty acid metabolism, and amino acid metabolism genes in early clone 13 infection, with Cpt1a identified as a key enriched gene.
- Early Tex cells had higher mitochondrial mass but significantly more depolarized mitochondria, increased mitochondrial ROS, and altered mitochondrial morphology (fused mitochondria with cristae elongation).
- PD-1 was identified as a key upstream regulator of early metabolic dysfunction. Genetic deletion of PD-1 (Pdcd1−/−) increased glucose uptake, reduced mitochondrial depolarization, improved respiration and glycolytic capacity, and enhanced polyfunctionality in early infection.
- PD-1 repressed expression of PGC-1α (PPARγ coactivator 1α), a key transcriptional regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and energy metabolism. Retroviral overexpression of PGC-1α corrected metabolic alterations and improved effector function in developing Tex cells.
- Overexpression of Glut-1 (Slc2a1) enhanced the T cell response during early clone 13 infection but not Arm infection.
- In established chronic infection, PD-L1 blockade (anti-PD-L1 therapy) reprogrammed metabolism specifically in the PD-1 Int T-bet Hi progenitor subset of Tex cells (reduced mitochondrial mass, increased glucose uptake), but not the PD-1 Hi Eomes Hi terminally differentiated subset.
- Short-term rapamycin treatment (mTOR inhibition) reduced mitochondrial mass and depolarization in early Tex cells, but also reduced polyfunctionality, suggesting the metabolic benefit may come at the expense of remaining effector function.

The study concludes that metabolic dysregulation is an early driver (not merely a consequence) of T cell exhaustion, and suggests that manipulating glycolytic and mitochondrial metabolism may enhance checkpoint blockade outcomes in chronic infections and cancer.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We found that during the first week of chronic lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) infection, before severe dysfunction develops, virus-specific CD8+ T cells were already unable to match the bioenergetics of effector T cells generated during acute infection."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: Frontiers | T-Cell Exhaustion in Chronic Infections: Reversing the State of Exhaustion and Reinvigorating Optimal Protective Immune Responses ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2018.02569/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Frontiers in Immunology review article (published November 9, 2018) examines T-cell exhaustion in chronic infections, focusing on mechanisms and potential strategies to reverse exhaustion and reinvigorate immune responses. T-cell exhaustion is a state of dysfunction of antigen-specific T cells reported in HIV, HBV, HCV infections, and cancer, characterized by hierarchical loss of effector functions (starting with IL-2 production), sustained upregulation of co-inhibitory receptors, altered transcriptional/epigenetic signatures, and metabolic dysfunction.

Key mechanisms include:
- **PD-1 pathway**: PD-1 plays a dominant role; it inhibits TCR signaling via SHP2 recruitment, blocks PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, and promotes T-cell motility arrest. PD-1 blockade promotes T-cell function and reduces viral load in chronic infections.
- **Other co-inhibitory receptors**: CTLA-4, TIM-3, LAG-3, CD160, 2B4 are co-expressed on exhausted T cells; concurrent blockade shows synergistic reversal of exhaustion.
- **Cytokines**: IL-10 blockade enhances T-cell function; IL-2, IL-7, IL-12, IL-21, and IFN-I also show therapeutic potential.
- **Transcriptional changes**: Key transcription factors include T-bet, EOMES, FOXO1, Blimp-1, NFAT, BATF, IRF4. T-bet
  regulates non-terminal progenitor exhausted cells, while EOMES regulates terminally differentiated subsets.
- **Epigenetic alterations**: Exhausted T cells have distinct chromatin accessibility patterns; PD-1 promoter remains demethylated even after viral load reduction, indicating a stable epigenetic program.
- **Metabolic programming**: PD-1 signaling shifts metabolism from glycolysis to FAO, reduces mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC1α suppression, and increases ROS production. Mitochondrion-targeted antioxidants improve antiviral function.

The review discusses potential therapeutic strategies including immune checkpoint blockade, cytokine therapy, CAR-T cell engineering, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to reduce PD-1 expression. It emphasizes the need for better understanding of human anti-viral immunity and the discovery of a master lineage-specific transcription factor for exhausted T cells.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
T-cell exhaustion denotes the physical elimination of antigen-specific T cells, also observed in chronic lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) infection of mice.,The state of exhaustion is mainly characterized by sequential loss of T cell effector functions in a hierarchical manner where loss of interleukin (IL)-2 production is the earliest sign.,Exhausted T cells can co-express PD-1 together with cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4), T cell immunoglobulin domain and mucin domain-containing protein 3 (TIM-3), 2B4 (CD244), lymphocyte activation gene 3 protein (LAG-3), CD160, and several others.,PD-1 signaling reduces AKT activation and thus suppress mTOR activity, switching T cell metabolism from glycolysis to FAO.,Targeting metabolic dysfunctions with mitochondrion-targeted antioxidants are reported to remarkably improve the antiviral activity of exhausted HBV-specific CD8+ T cells suggesting the pivotal role for ROS in T-cell exhaustion.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: Take my breath away—mitochondrial dysfunction drives CD8 ---
URL: https://repositorium.meduniwien.ac.at/obvumwoa/content/titleinfo/9639186/full.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Journal Club article published in Genes & Immunity (2024) 25:4–6, authored by Felix Clemens Richter, Mariia Saliutina, Ahmed N. Hegazy, and Andreas Bergthaler. The article critically reviews and discusses a study by Wu et al. (2023, Nature Communications) that establishes a direct causal link between mitochondrial dysfunction and CD8+ T cell exhaustion.

Key content:

1. **Background**: CD8+ T cell exhaustion occurs in chronic diseases like cancer and chronic viral infections, characterized by decreased cytolytic protein/cytokine expression and upregulation of inhibitory receptors (PD-1, TIM-3, LAG-3). Progenitor exhausted T cells (TPEX) give rise to terminally exhausted T cells (TEX). Immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) therapy aims to reinvigorate exhausted T cells, with TPEX being most amenable to this treatment, but not all patients respond.

2. **Previous evidence**: Impaired mitochondrial state with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production is a key feature of T cell exhaustion. TPEX exhibit high mitochondrial respiratory capacity that deteriorates in TEX. Promoting mitophagy improved mitochondrial fitness and reduced exhaustion. However, formal proof of mitochondrial dysfunction as a driver was lacking.

3. **Key findings from Wu et al. study**: 
   - TPEX relied on mitochondrial respiration, while TEX reduced OXPHOS gene expression and shifted to glycolysis
   - TPEX had higher mitochondrial turnover than TEX (dysfunctional mitochondrial quality control in TEX)
   - Genetic deletion of Slc25a3 (mitochondrial inorganic phosphate transporter/mPiC) in T cells abrogated mitochondrial respiration and drove exhaustion marker expression (TIM-3, LAG-3), reduced cytokine production, and increased apoptosis
   - Slc25a3-deficient T cells showed exhaustion phenotype even in acute LCMV Armstrong infection, suggesting mitochondrial impairment drives exhaustion independent of antigen persistence
   - Overexpression of Slc25a3 boosted mitochondrial respiration and shifted cells toward TPEX phenotype
   - Mechanism: reduced pentose phosphate pathway metabolites and NADPH availability → increased mitochondrial ROS → HIF1α stabilization (not NFAT) drove transcriptional control of exhaustion markers
   - Deletion of Hif1a reduced glycolysis and shifted phenotype toward TPEX characteristics
   - Pharmacological treatment with 2-Deoxyglucose (2-DG), a glycolysis inhibitor, improved CD8+ T cell function in chronic viral infection and slightly improved CAR T cell anti-tumor response

4. **Conclusion**: The study provides a causative link between mitochondrial quality/respiration and T cell exhaustion, suggesting mitochondrial dysfunction is a driver (not mere bystander) of CD8+ T cell exhaustion. Targeting T cell metabolism could complement classical ICI therapy and improve therapeutic efficacy. The effects of ICI therapy on rewiring TPEX metabolism remain ill-defined.

5. **Affiliations**: Medical University of Vienna, CeMM Research Center for Molecular Medicine of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, and Deutsches Rheuma-Forschungszentrum. Received 25 October 2023, published online 22 January 2024.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"CD8+ T cell exhaustion is a phenomenon often observed in individuals battling chronic diseases like cancer and chronic viral infections. Prolonged exposure to antigens desensitizes CD8+ T cells, leading to a diminished capacity to mount effector responses."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 11: Disturbed mitochondrial dynamics in CD8+ TILs reinforce T cell exhaustion. - Abstract ---
URL: https://europepmc.org/article/med/33020660

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Europe PMC article page for the scientific paper "Disturbed mitochondrial dynamics in CD8+ TILs reinforce T cell exhaustion," published in Nature Immunology on October 5, 2020 (Volume 21, Issue 12, pages 1540-1551). The article has DOI 10.1038/s41590-020-0793-3 and PMID 33020660.

The paper was authored by 20 researchers including Yu YR, Imrichova H, Wang H, Chao T, Xiao Z, Gao M, Rincon-Restrepo M, Franco F, Genolet R, Cheng WC, Jandus C, Coukos G, Jiang YF, Locasale JW, Zippelius A, Liu PS, Tang L, Bock C, Vannini N, and Ho PC. Affiliations include the Department of Oncology at University of Lausanne (Switzerland), CeMM Research Center for Molecular Medicine of the Austrian Academy of Sciences (Vienna, Austria), Duke University School of Medicine (Durham, NC, USA), Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (Switzerland), and National Taiwan University (Taipei, Taiwan). Funding was provided by the Swiss National Science Foundation.

KEY FINDINGS FROM THE ABSTRACT:
- Tumor-infiltrating T lymphocytes (TILs) accumulate depolarized mitochondria due to decreased mitophagy activity
- These TILs display functional, transcriptomic, and epigenetic characteristics of terminally exhausted T cells
- Reduced mitochondrial fitness is induced by coordination of T cell receptor stimulation, microenvironmental stressors, and PD-1 signaling
- Pharmacologically enforced accumulation of depolarized mitochondria induced epigenetic reprogramming toward terminal exhaustion, demonstrating that mitochondrial deregulation causes T cell exhaustion
- Supplementation with nicotinamide riboside enhanced T cell mitochondrial fitness and improved responsiveness to anti-PD-1 treatment
- The study reveals insights into how mitochondrial dynamics and quality orchestrate T cell antitumor responses and commitment to the exhaustion program

The article cites 70 references and lists several similar articles including related work on mitochondrial stress driving T cell exhaustion under hypoxia (PMID 33398183), endoplasmic reticulum stress contributing to mitochondrial exhaustion of CD8+ T cells (PMID 30659052), and immune checkpoint inhibitor effects on TIL differentiation in glioblastoma (PMID 30659023). A commentary on this article appears in Cell Metabolism (2020;32(6):905-907, DOI 10.1016/j.cmet.2020.11.004).
</summary>
