--- SOURCE 1: Progression of m6A in the tumor microenvironment ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-024-02092-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Cell Death Discovery (Volume 10, Article 331, 2024) examining the role of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modification in the tumor microenvironment (TME). The paper has 7717 accesses and 38 citations.

The article covers three main sections:
1) m6A modification components: writers (methyltransferases including METTL3, METTL5, METTL14, METTL16, WTAP, RBM15/15B, VIRMA/KIAA1429, PCIF1, ZC3H4, ZC3H13), erasers (demethylases FTO, ALKBH5, and ALKBH3), and readers (YTHDF1/2/3, YTHDC1/2, IGF2BPs, and cytoplasmic METTL3).
2) The relationship between m6A methylation and TME characteristics including hypoxia, metabolic reprogramming (glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism), and immunosuppression.
3) Potential therapeutic strategies targeting m6A in the TME.

Key findings include:
- m6A is the most common epigenetic modification in eukaryotic mRNAs, occurring at the N6 position of adenosine, mostly in coding sequences, 3' ends of transcripts, and stop codons.
- TME is characterized by hypoxia (oxygen partial pressure below 10 mmHg), metabolic reprogramming, acid accumulation, and immunosuppression.
- Under hypoxia, HIF-1α promotes YTHDF1/2 expression in HCC and lung squamous cell carcinoma; low FTO expression accelerates CRC malignant progression while high ALKBH5 promotes female malignant tumors.
- m6A regulates the Warburg effect (glycolysis) through YTHDF1/2/3, YTHDC1/2, WTAP, METTL3, and FTO, affecting T cell immune function and immune evasion.
- In lipid metabolism, METTL3 reduces CES2 levels to promote lipid deposition in HCC; YTHDF2 regulates cholesterol metabolism in gliomas.
- In amino acid metabolism, YTHDF1 promotes glutaminase expression affecting tumor metabolism.
- m6A-mediated metabolic dysregulation generates an acidic environment; both hypoxia and acidity promote immunosuppressive TME by inhibiting T cells, B cells, and NK cells while supporting immunosuppressive cells (TA-MSCs, CAFs).

Open questions addressed include how m6A proteins function in each tumor type, the interplay between TME cells, m6A, and tumors regarding treatment efficacy, and whether m6A could be a therapeutic target by affecting metastatic niches.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"m6A is the most common epigenetic modification in eukaryotic mRNAs."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Mettl3-catalyzed m6A methylation determines CD8+ T cell ... ---
URL: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.01.06.697843v1.full-text

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a bioRxiv preprint (DOI: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.01.06.697843) titled "Mettl3-catalyzed m6A methylation determines CD8+ T cell differentiation fate in tumor." It is a new results preprint that has not been peer-reviewed.

**Authors and Affiliations:** Puspendu Ghosh, Debashree Basak, Shaun Mahanti, Soham Chowdhury, Ishita Sarkar, Anwesha Mandal, Anwesha Kar, Snehanshu Chowdhury, and Shilpak Chatterjee (Division of Cancer Biology and Inflammatory Disorder, IICB-Translational Research Unit of Excellence; CSIR-Indian Institute of Chemical Biology, Kolkata, India; Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR), Ghaziabad, India); Anupam Gautam (University of Tübingen and Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen, Germany); Sandip Paul (JIS Institute of Advanced Studies and Research, JIS University, Kolkata, India). Corresponding author: Shilpak Chatterjee (schatterjee@iicb.res.in).

**Summary of Key Findings:**

**Background/Problem:** Heterogeneity in patient responses to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) is dictated by the relative abundance of exhausted CD8+ T cell (Tex) subsets. Progenitor exhausted (pTex) cells remain sensitive to ICB, while terminally exhausted (tTex) cells are refractory. The molecular cues determining these divergent fates were poorly defined.

**Main Finding:** The RNA methyltransferase Mettl3 is identified as a central regulator of Tex fate. Across murine tumor models, human T cells, and adoptive transfer systems, Mettl3 expression is selectively enriched in tTex cells and inversely correlated with TCF1+ pTex populations.

**Mechanism:** Mettl3 drives terminal exhaustion by stabilizing DNMT3B transcripts via m6A modification, which enforces CpG methylation and chromatin compaction at memory-associated loci. This establishes the Mettl3-m6A-Dnmt3b axis as a molecular rheostat coupling epitranscriptomic regulation to epigenetic remodeling.

**Therapeutic Implications:** Inhibition of the Mettl3-Dnmt3b axis reprograms chromatin accessibility toward memory-like states, preserving progenitor potential and effector function. T cells lacking Mettl3-Dnmt3b activity persist longer, mount robust recall responses, and achieve superior tumor control with enhanced responsiveness to PD-1 blockade — revealing a tractable pathway to improve the durability of cancer immunotherapy.

**Key Experimental Results:**

**Result 1 — Mettl3 expression positively correlates with CD8+ T cell exhaustion:** Using MC38 and YUMM1.7 murine tumor models, YUMM1.7 tumors were found to harbor more tTex cells (PD1+Tim3+) and were less responsive to ICB. Mettl3 expression was elevated in YUMM1.7 intratumoral CD8+ T cells and increased with tumor progression, correlating positively with exhaustion markers (PD1, Tim3, CD39, TOX) and inversely with TCF1. scRNA-seq analysis of 9,056 murine CD8+ T cells revealed Mettl3 enriched in exhausted clusters (Tex1, Tex2) and largely absent from the pTex/memory cluster. Analysis of human scRNA-seq data from 4,588 intratumoral CD8+ T cells across five malignancies (breast cancer x2, colorectal cancer, endocervical adenocarcinoma, skin melanoma) confirmed METTL3 was significantly higher in Tex cells than in pTex clusters. Chronically stimulated human CD8+ T cells exhibited markedly higher Mettl3 expression than acutely stimulated cells.

**Result 2 — Mettl3 inhibition alleviates exhaustion while promoting T Mem generation in vitro:** In vitro differentiation experiments with human CD8+ T cells showed Mettl3 expression progressively increased under chronic TCR stimulation (Tex conditions) but declined under IL-15/IL-7 memory-inducing conditions. Mettl3 knockdown (shRNA) impaired Tex differentiation (reduced PD1+Tim3+, PD1+CD39+, PD1+CTLA4+ frequencies, increased TCF1) and improved cytokine production (IFN-γ, TNF-α), while Mettl3 overexpression enhanced exhaustion. Under memory conditions, Mettl3 knockdown promoted stem cell memory (SCM)-like cell formation (CD45RA+CD62L+), elevated memory markers (TCF1, FOXO1, CCR7), and enhanced recall responses. A rescue experiment confirmed that reintroducing Mettl3 into knockdown cells restored the exhausted phenotype.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here, we identify the RNA methyltransferase Mettl3 as a central regulator of Tex fate. Across murine tumor models, human T cells, and adoptive transfer systems, Mettl3 expression is selectively enriched in tTex cells and inversely correlated with TCF1+ pTex populations."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Targeting the RNA m6A modification for cancer immunotherapy ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12943-022-01558-0

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published on March 16, 2022, in Molecular Cancer (Volume 21, article number 76), titled "Targeting the RNA m6A modification for cancer immunotherapy." It is an open-access article by Xinxin Li, Shoubao Ma, Youcai Deng, Ping Yi, Jianhua Yu, and colleagues.

The article provides a comprehensive overview of how N6-methyladenosine (m6A), the most abundant epigenetic modification of RNA, influences cancer immunotherapy. It covers:

1. **Regulation of m6A modification**: m6A is dynamically regulated by three types of enzymes—writers (methyltransferases like METTL3, METTL14, WTAP, RBM15, VIRMA, ZC3H13), erasers (demethylases FTO and ALKBH5), and readers (binding proteins like YTHDC1/2, YTHDF1/2/3, HNRNP family, IGF2BPs, PRRC2A).

2. **Role in immune cells**:
   - **NK cells**: YTHDF2 and METTL3 positively regulate NK cell anti-tumor immunity.
   - **Macrophages**: METTL3 promotes proinflammatory cytokine production and anti-tumor function; METTL14 boosts CD8+ T cell activation; YTHDF2 negatively regulates inflammatory responses.
   - **Dendritic cells**: METTL3 promotes DC activation and maturation; YTHDF1 negatively regulates anti-tumor immune responses by enhancing lysosomal protease translation.
   - **T cells**: METTL3 regulates CD4+ T cell homeostasis, Treg cell function, and Tfh cell differentiation; ALKBH5 positively regulates IFN-γ expression.

3. **Role in remodeling the tumor microenvironment (TME)**: m6A regulators in tumor cells affect immune cell infiltration and ICB efficacy. METTL3 and METTL14 expression levels correlate with immune cell infiltration in various cancers (CRC, HCC, BC, CC, HNSCC, TGCT, ccRCC).

4. **Therapeutic strategies proposed**: Combining m6A regulator inhibitors with immune checkpoint blockers; developing programmable m6A gene-editing systems; enhancing anti-tumor immune responses in T cells/NK cells via m6A modification; using nanoparticles targeting tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) to deliver m6A-related molecules.

The review aims to help understand how m6A modifications intrinsically and extrinsically shape immune responses in the TME to improve cancer immunotherapy design.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant epigenetic modification of RNA, and its dysregulation drives aberrant transcription and translation programs that promote cancer occurrence and progression.,The RNA m6A modification process is dynamically and reversibly regulated by three types of enzymes: m6A methyltransferases (writers), m6A demethylases (erasers), and m6A binding proteins (readers).,The m6A modification modulated immune cell activation and infiltration into the tumor microenvironment (TME) and thus may affect the efficacy of immunotherapy.,Our group first reported the multifaceted roles of YTHDF2-mediated m6A methylation in NK cell immunity.,Alteration of the m6A modification in tumor cells influences the infiltration, activation, and effector functions of infiltrated immune cells in the TME, making targeting m6A—and especially m6A regulators in tumor cells—a promising strategy for improving cancer immunotherapy.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive review article published in the Journal of Translational Medicine (2025) by Chen et al., examining how m6A RNA methylation modification regulates tumor immunity and its potential as a target for cancer immunotherapy. The paper explores the roles of m6A modification—a dynamic, reversible RNA methylation process involving "writers" (methyltransferases like METTL3/METTL14/WTAP), "erasers" (demethylases like FTO and ALKBH5), and "readers" (YTH domain proteins, hnRNPs, IGF2BP family)—in both innate and adaptive immune cells.

**Key findings on innate immunity:**
- **NK cells**: METTL3 expression positively correlates with NK effector functions; YTHDF2 promotes NK cell activity via a STAT5-YTHDF2 feedback loop and regulates NK cell proliferation.
- **Dendritic cells (DCs)**: METTL3-mediated m6A enhances CD40, CD80, and TIRAP translation, stimulating T cell activation; YTHDF1 recognizes m6A-marked lysosomal protease transcripts, increasing their translation and degrading antigens, while YTHDF1 absence enhances DC antigen presentation.
- **Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs)**: METTL3 promotes M1 polarization via STAT1 mRNA stability; METTL3 deficiency reduces YTHDF1-mediated SPRED2 translation, enhancing NF-κB/STAT3 activation and tumor growth; YTHDF2 absence reprograms TAMs to anti-tumor phenotype via IFN-γ-STAT1 signaling.
- **Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs)**: m6A modification affects MDSC expansion and function through YTHDF2, METTL3, and ALKBH5, influencing recruitment via chemokine axes (e.g., CXCL1/CXCR2, Axin2-Wnt-DKK1).
- **Neutrophils**: WTAP-mediated m6A methylation upregulates ENO1, inducing glycolysis in breast cancer; senescent neutrophils secrete exosomal piRNA-17560 enhancing FTO expression.
- **γδ T cells**: ALKBH5 regulates γδ T cell development via Jagged1/Notch2 signaling; METTL3 balances γδ T1 and T17 subpopulations.
- **Mast cells**: METTL3/WTAP expression correlated with mast cell infiltration in esophageal and gastric cancers.

**Key findings on adaptive immunity:**
- m6A modification regulates T cell and B cell development, differentiation, and function in the tumor microenvironment by influencing mRNA stability and translation efficiency of key immune molecules.
- m6A regulates T cell differentiation into effector and regulatory subtypes, affecting anti-tumor immune activity.

The review concludes that m6A modification represents a promising therapeutic target for cancer immunotherapy, including combination strategies with immune checkpoint inhibitors and CAR-T cell therapy.
</summary>

</key_excerpts>

The LCMV (lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus) mouse model was used. LCMV Armstrong causes an acute, cleared infection, while LCMV Clone 13 (which differs by only three amino acids) causes a persistent chronic infection. Zinkernagel and Doherty used this model to discover MHC restriction (Nobel Prize 1996). LCMV has dominant epitopes (Db/NP396, Db/GP33, Kb/GP34) and a subdominant one (Db/GP276). TCR-transgenic P14 cells specific for the gp33 epitope were used.

KEY CONCEPTS: Upon acute infection, CD8+ T-cells differentiate into short-lived effector cells (SLECs: KLRG1high, CD127low) and memory precursor effector cells (MPECs: KLRG1low, CD127high) that form long-lived memory (Tcm and Tem). In chronic infections, persistent antigen stimulation drives CD8+ T-cells into a state of "exhaustion" – dysfunctional cells with impaired cytokine production (IL-2, TNF, IFNγ) and high expression of inhibitory receptors such as PD-1, LAG-3, CD244, CD160, Tim-3, and CTLA-4. Exhaustion is driven by cell-intrinsic factors (inhibitory receptors), cell-extrinsic factors (IL-10, TGF-β negatively; IL-2, IL-7, IL-21 positively), and CD4+ T-cell help. Treg cells suppress virus-specific T-cell responses. Key transcription factors controlling exhaustion include Irf4, T-bet, Blimp-1, Eomes, VHL, and Foxo1.

Transcriptional profiling revealed TOX (Thymocyte selection-associated high mobility group box protein) as one of the most upregulated genes in chronically stimulated T-cells. TOX expression correlates with the chronic phenotype, is induced by high antigen levels, and is maintained after antigen withdrawal. TOX was also found to be expressed in human HCV-specific CD8+ T-cells, correlating with high PD-1 levels (and persisting even after antiviral treatment).

In the absence of TOX, dysfunctional T-cells are forced toward an effector phenotype with decreased PD-1, increased KLRG-1, and greater cytokine production, leading to better viral clearance but increased immunopathology. TOX absence also caused a substantial loss of the critical Tcf-1+ progenitor population, impairing long-term survival of dysfunctional CD8+ T-cells. The Tcf-1+ memory-like progenitor population (identified in both mouse and human chronic infections) maintains the immune response and responds to PD-1 blockade.

CONCLUSION: TOX is a key regulator of the differentiation program that drives chronically stimulated T-cells toward a dysfunctional/exhausted phenotype. --- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Metabolic Control of m6A RNA Modification - eScholarship.org ---
URL: https://escholarship.org/content/qt8z134484/qt8z134484.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article by Joohwan Kim and Gina Lee (University of California Irvine) published in Metabolites (2021, Vol. 11, Issue 2) examining how metabolites, nutrients, and cellular metabolic pathways regulate N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modification. m6A is the most prevalent and evolutionarily conserved internal mRNA modification, controlling RNA metabolism including stability and translation, and plays roles in development and disease states such as cancer and diabetes.

The review describes the key m6A enzymes (writers, erasers, and readers): The main writer complex consists of METTL3/METTL14 and adaptor proteins (WTAP, VIRMA, ZC3H13, RBM15), which methylates adenosine at the RRA*CH consensus motif. Other methyltransferases include METTL16 (targets UACA*GAGAA motif in snRNA/mRNAs, functions as homodimer), METTL5-TRMT112 (18S rRNA), and ZCCHC4 (28S rRNA, which has an autoinhibitory loop that opens upon substrate binding). Readers (YTHDF, YTHDC, HNRNP, IGF2BP) control RNA fate including splicing, stability, export, and translation. Erasers are ALKBH5 and FTO (ALKB family dioxygenases), making m6A a reversible process.

Regulation of m6A by metabolites: S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) is the universal methyl donor produced by one-carbon metabolism (folate and methionine cycles, with serine providing one-carbon units). The product SAH acts as a strong allosteric inhibitor of METTL3. Notably, the Km of SAM for METTL3 (~100 nM) is much lower than cellular SAM levels (>10 µM), while SAH levels (~5 µM) exceed the IC50 (~1 µM), suggesting complex regulatory dynamics. METTL16 provides SAM-dependent feedback regulation: high SAM leads to MAT2A mRNA methylation and degradation, while low SAM causes METTL16 to tightly bind MAT2A mRNA and promote its splicing/translation to synthesize more SAM.

Eraser regulation: FTO and ALKBH5 are αKG (α-ketoglutarate)-Fe(II)-O2-dependent dioxygenases. TCA cycle metabolites succinate and fumarate act as competitive inhibitors of αKG (IC50 ~30 µM for ALKBH5, ~150 µM for FTO; citrate also inhibits with IC50 ~300 µM). The oncometabolite R-2-hydroxyglutarate (R-2HG), produced by mutant IDH enzymes, competitively inhibits FTO (IC50 ~130 µM). Surprisingly, R-2HG exhibited anti-tumor activity by increasing m6A on cMyc and CEBPA mRNAs, destabilizing these growth-promoting transcripts. Iron (Fe(II), Km ~1 µM for ALKBH5) is essential for demethylation, with iron delivery via transferrin complexes released in lysosomes. NADPH and NADH were identified as FTO activators (NADPH strongest, ~90% induction in FTO vs ~30% in ALKBH5); the pentose phosphate pathway is the main NADPH source, and NADK/G6PD knockdown increased cellular m6A levels. FTO-mediated m6A demethylation is linked to adipogenesis, and FTO knockout mice resist high-fat diet-induced obesity.

The review concludes by highlighting future directions: studying whether low methionine diets (which extend lifespan) work via m6A methyltransferase inhibition, tissue-specific m6A differences potentially driven by metabolic activities, connections between nutrient-signaling pathways (mTORC1, PI3K-Akt, AMPK) and m6A regulation, metabolic regulation of m6A readers, and the potential for combined targeting of cancer metabolism and m6A enzymes for therapeutics. The work was funded with no external funding.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The N6-adenosine methylation (m6A or N6-methyladenosine) is the most abundant mRNA internal modification." "As this is a reversible enzymatic process, metabolites can directly influence the flux of this reaction by serving as substrates and/or allosteric regulators." "R-2HG suppressed the growth of tumors expressing high FTO levels. Specifically, the R-2HG-induced m6A modification of cMyc and CEBPA mRNAs destabilized these transcripts. Therefore, by decreasing the growth-promoting cMyc and CEBP signaling activities, R-2HG suppresses tumor progression." "From the screen, NADH and NADPH were identified, along with vitamin C (ascorbate), a previously known cofactor of dioxygenases... NADPH was the strongest binding partner and activator of FTO, followed by NADH." "Fto knockout mice are resistant to high-fat diet-induced obesity, while the overexpression of Fto results in obesity."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: M6A Demethylase ALKBH5 in Human Diseases: From Structure to Mechanisms ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/2/157

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Biomolecules (2025, Vol. 15, Issue 2, Article 157; DOI: 10.3390/biom15020157) by Miaochun Fang, Liwen Ye, Yue Zhu, Linying Huang, and Shun Xu from Guangdong Medical University, China. The review comprehensively examines the m6A demethylase ALKBH5 in human diseases, from structure to mechanisms.

The article covers:
1. **Background**: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant, dynamically reversible internal modification in eukaryotic RNA, enriched in long internal exons, stop codons, or 3' UTRs of mRNA and lncRNAs, occurring in the RRACH consensus motif. It regulates gene expression post-transcriptionally. ALKBH5 is one of two major endogenous m6A demethylases (along with FTO).

2. **Structure**: ALKBH5 belongs to the AlkB subfamily of Fe(II)/αKG dioxygenases (9 members: ALKBH 1-8 and FTO). The human ALKBH5 gene is localized at 17p11.2 and encodes a 395-amino-acid protein (~43 kD). Its core structure consists of a double-stranded β-helix (DSBH) domain containing eight antiparallel β-strands and two nucleotide recognition loops (NRL1 and NRL2). The DSBH scaffolds three Fe(II)-binding residues (His204, Asp206, His266) forming a conserved HXDXnH module. NRL2 contains Lys147 and Arg148 that interact with RNA phosphate backbones for substrate recognition.

3. **Catalytic mechanism**: Demethylation involves dioxygen activation and substrate oxidation. Fe(II) and 2OG activate dioxygen, forming a Fe(IV)-oxo intermediate that oxidizes inert C-H bonds. ALKBH5 demethylates m6A by oxidizing N6-methyl, forming a transient N6-hydroxymethyladenosine (hm6A) intermediate that spontaneously decomposes into adenosine within a few hours, releasing formaldehyde and producing succinate.

4. **Biological functions**: ALKBH5 localizes to Golgi apparatus, cytosol, and nuclear speckles. It regulates RNA metabolism (splicing, translation, mRNA stability - though with both stabilizing and destabilizing effects on different mRNAs), cell proliferation (G0/G1 cell cycle arrest when silenced), apoptosis, development (essential for spermatogenesis, oocyte meiosis, neuronal development), oxidative stress response, mental stress response (hyperactivated in major depressive disorder), and cancer (acts as both oncogene in some cancers and tumor suppressor in others, including lung, glioblastoma, hepatocellular, colorectal, gastric, endometrial, and breast cancers).

5. **Human diseases**:
   - **Metabolic disorders**: Regulates glucose metabolism (glycolysis, aerobic oxidation, pentose phosphate pathway, glycogen synthesis, gluconeogenesis) and lipid metabolism (adipogenesis regulation); role in T2DM remains controversial.
   - **Immune system disorders**: Involved in neutrophil mobilization, bacterial infection defense, viral infection immunity (PEDV, rotavirus, HIV-1), rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, tumor immune microenvironment shaping, and autoimmune diseases (EAE, thyroid disease, primary Sjögren's syndrome).
   - **Reproductive system disorders**: Promotes reproductive system cancers (ovarian, cervical, endometrial), essential for germ cell (sperm and oocyte) development, and impacts miscarriage (both increasing and reducing risk depending on context).

6. **Inhibitors**: The review highlights development of ALKBH5 inhibitors, though the concluding sections on inhibitor development were not fully captured in the available text.

The article has 25 citations, 6,717 article views, and belongs to the Molecular Medicine section of Biomolecules. The review emphasizes that ALKBH5 shows bidirectional roles in multiple diseases and represents a potential therapeutic target but requires further investigation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant, dynamically reversible, and evolutionarily conserved internal chemical modification in eukaryotic RNA."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Frontiers | The role of RNA m6A demethylase ALKBH5 in the mechanisms of fibrosis ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cell-and-developmental-biology/articles/10.3389/fcell.2024.1447135/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology (16 August 2024, Volume 12, DOI: 10.3389/fcell.2024.1447135) titled "The role of RNA m6A demethylase ALKBH5 in the mechanisms of fibrosis" by authors Ziwei Liao, Jing Wang, Mengrou Xu, Xiaoyan Li, and Hongming Xu from the Department of Otorhinolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery, Shanghai Children's Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine.

**Core topic:** ALKBH5 is a demethylase that removes N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications from RNA. Beyond its role in RNA metabolic regulation (stability, translation, post-transcriptional modification), ALKBH5 has recently been found to play important regulatory roles in tissue fibrosis. This review synthesizes research on ALKBH5's mechanisms in fibrosis, acknowledging that reported effects are inconsistent.

**Structure and function of ALKBH5:** ALKBH5 belongs to the iron(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent AlkB oxygenase family. It is found primarily in nuclear speckles and acts as an mRNA-binding protein with newly synthesized RNA as its main substrate. Its catalytic center contains a double-stranded β-helix (DSBH) domain composed of 11 β strands and 5 α helices, which binds Fe2+ and 2OG (2-oxoglutarate). Fe2+ binding stabilizes the enzyme and creates a hydrophobic environment favorable for substrate binding. ALKBH5 can regulate ferroptosis, though whether Fe metabolism affects its function remains unreported.

**Effects on cellular functions in fibrosis:** Fibrosis involves excessive fibroblast activation, extracellular matrix deposition, and transformation into myofibroblasts (via EMT/EndMT and MMT). ALKBH5 regulates multiple cell types:
- **Parenchymal cells:** Protects cardiomyocytes by stabilizing MG53, SIRT1, and STAT3 mRNAs (suppressing apoptosis, oxidative stress, I/R injury). However, in diabetic cardiomyopathy it aggravates high-glucose-induced apoptosis via FOXO3/CDR1/Hippo, and exacerbates doxorubicin-induced apoptosis via ARID2. In hepatocytes, inhibiting ALKBH5 induces autophagy by reducing AXL mRNA stability.
- **Immune cells:** Promotes neutrophil migration and emergency granulopoiesis (via G-CSFR, CXCR2, NLRP12). Promotes IFN-γ and CXCL2 expression in CD4+ T cells; inhibits γδ T cell development via Jagged1/Notch2; regulates Treg cell migration via CCL28.
- **Macrophages:** Promotes macrophage recruitment (via lncRNA NEAT1, MAP3K8, IL-8); affects M1/M2 polarization bidirectionally (M1 in diabetic retinopathy via A20 reduction; M2 in radiation-induced liver fibrosis via CCL5); promotes MMT in cardiac fibrosis via IL-11; reduces Slamf7 to promote macrophage autophagy.
- **Endothelial cells:** Promotes angiogenesis via SPHK1, VEGF-A, CTGF, lncRNA PVT1, and circ-CCT3; opposing findings exist (WNT5A regulation under hypoxia).
- **Fibroblasts:** Promotes myofibroblast transformation via ErbB4 (cardiac) and FOXM1 (lung); inhibits HSC activation via PTCH1/Hedgehog signaling and Drp1.

**Effects on organ fibrosis:**
- **Pulmonary fibrosis:** Dual effects—promotes silica-induced fibrosis via FOXM1/miR-320a-3p axis, but inhibits radiation-induced fibrosis (via Zbtb7b/IL-6), silica-induced inflammation (via Slamf7), and PM2.5-induced fibrosis (via YAP1 signaling).
- **Liver fibrosis:** Generally ameliorates liver fibrosis via Drp1 (mitochondrial fission inhibition) and PTCH1/Hedgehog inactivation in HSCs, but promotes radiation-induced liver fibrosis via TIRAP/NF-κB/JNK-Smad2 pathways.
- **Cardiac fibrosis:** Beneficial for ischemia/reperfusion repair (via SPHK1, EGFR/PI3K/AKT/mTOR, ErbB4, ALKBH5-m6A-YTHDF1-YAP axis promoting cardiomyocyte proliferation), but aggravates diabetic cardiomyopathy (FOXO3/CDR1/Hippo), doxorubicin toxicity (ARID2), and AngII-induced hypertension fibrosis (IL-11/MMT).
- **Renal fibrosis:** Alleviates UUO-induced fibrosis via EMT regulation (E-cadherin, snail), but inhibiting ALKBH5 slows chronic glomerulonephritis (via TRIM13) and I/R-induced kidney injury (via CCL28/Treg axis), showing conflicting results.

**ALKBH5 inhibitors:** Non-selective inhibitors (NOG, PDCA, IOX3, MV1035, Dexmedetomidine) compete with 2OG but lack selectivity. Specific inhibitors include Ena15 (non-competitive), Ena21 (competitive), DDO-2728 (competitive; active against AML), and compound 20m (1-phenyl-1H-pyrazole scaffold). Natural inhibitors include citrate (displaces metal ions and 2OG) and chlorogenic acid (CGA, inhibits ALKBH5 to alleviate hepatic steatosis).

**Conclusion:** ALKBH5 regulates diverse cell types through different pathways, with variable effects on fibrosis depending on cell type, stimulation conditions, and research models. Future research should focus on developing ALKBH5 inhibitors targeting specific cells or specific mechanisms of action. Funding was provided by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Nos. 82272270 and 82171121) and the Science and Technology Commission of Shanghai Municipality Funds (22ZR1451700).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"ALKBH5 is one of the demethylases involved in the regulation of RNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification. Its main function is to remove the m6A modification from RNA... thereby participating in the dynamic regulation of RNA."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: [PDF] Metabolic regulation of mitochondrial dynamics - David Chan ---
URL: https://chanlab.sites.caltech.edu/documents/2777/Mishra_Chan_JCB_2016.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article titled "Metabolic regulation of mitochondrial dynamics" by Prashant Mishra (Children's Medical Center Research Institute, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center) and David C. Chan (Division of Biology and Biological Engineering, California Institute of Technology), published in the Journal of Cell Biology on February 8, 2016.

**Core Topic:** The review examines how cellular metabolism regulates the four key mitochondrial dynamic behaviors—fusion, fission, transport, and mitophagy—and how these dynamics reciprocally influence bioenergetics. Mitochondria play a central role in metabolism (OXPHOS, Krebs cycle, β-oxidation, calcium handling, heme biosynthesis), and dysfunction is linked to metabolic diseases, cancers, neurodegenerative diseases, and aging.

**Metabolic control of fusion:** Fusion is mediated by three dynamin superfamily GTPases—Mfn1, Mfn2 (outer membrane), and Opa1 (inner membrane). High OXPHOS activity correlates with mitochondrial elongation. OXPHOS stimulates the metalloprotease Yme1L to proteolytically process Opa1 (from long to short form), activating inner-membrane fusion, while membrane depolarization activates Oma1 to cleave and inactivate Opa1. Other regulatory mechanisms include oxidative stress-induced disulfide-mediated dimerization of mitofusins, ERK phosphorylation of Mfn1 linking MAPK pathway, and NM23-H4-mediated GTP loading onto Opa1. Human mutations in Mfn2 cause Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A; Opa1 mutations cause dominant optic atrophy.

**Metabolic control of fission:** Fission is mediated by Drp1 (Dynamin-related Protein 1), recruited to mitochondria via receptors Mff, Fis1, MiD49, and MiD50. Key regulation occurs through Drp1 phosphorylation: PKA phosphorylation at Ser637 inhibits fission (promoting elongation under exercise, β-adrenergic stimulation, nitrogen starvation), while calcineurin dephosphorylation at Ser637 activates fission. Phosphorylation at Ser616 (by PKA in brown adipose tissue thermogenesis, or by Erk1/2 in oncogenic Ras-driven tumorigenesis) activates fission. AMPK phosphorylates Mff to activate fission during energy deficiency, and MiD51 binds ADP/GDP as a nucleotide sensor. Drp1 mutations are linked to microcephaly, neonatal lethality, and refractory epilepsy.

**Metabolic control of transport:** Mitochondrial transport along microtubules is mediated by kinesin (anterograde) and dynein (retrograde), connected to mitochondria via Miro proteins (Miro1/Miro2) and Milton (Trak1/Trak2) adaptors. High calcium causes pausing/mitochondrial stalling at active synapses (via Miro EF-hand calcium sensing and syntaphilin anchoring). ATP depletion/hypoxia promotes anterograde movement via AMPK or HIF-1α pathways. High glucose causes O-GlcNAc transferase-mediated glycosylation of Milton, immobilizing mitochondria at nutrient-rich locations.

**Metabolic control of mitophagy:** The best-studied pathway involves Pink1 and Parkin (linked to familial Parkinson's disease). Depolarization causes Pink1 accumulation on the outer membrane, which recruits and activates Parkin (an E3 ligase), leading to widespread ubiquitination of outer-membrane proteins and targeting to autophagic membranes. Mitophagy is also activated by energy stress (via AMPK phosphorylating ULK1/ULK2), hypoxia (via PGAM5 dephosphorylating FUNDC1 to recruit LC3), and oxidative conditions (via Rheb relocalization to Nix). The authors note in vivo evidence for mitophagy importance remains sparse.

**Future directions:** The review concludes that mitochondrial functions and behaviors do not operate independently but influence each other (e.g., depolarization triggers fission, inhibits fusion, and promotes mitophagy). Understanding how to regulate mitochondrial behavior may provide therapeutic approaches for disease, and new areas like organelle interactions (with lipid droplets and ER) remain to be explored.

The work was supported by NIH grant GM110039 and the Muscular Dystrophy Association. Submitted November 9, 2015; accepted January 6, 2016.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"As the site for numerous biochemical processes—including oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), the Krebs cycle, β-oxidation of fatty acids, calcium handling, and heme biosynthesis—the mitochondrion plays a central role in cellular metabolism."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Mitochondrial metabolism and cellular function | BMG LABTECH ---
URL: https://www.bmglabtech.com/en/blog/mitochondrial-metabolism-and-cellular-function

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post by Dr. Barry Whyte, an Application Scientist and Science Writer at BMG LABTECH US, explores mitochondrial metabolism and cellular function. It argues that mitochondria are more than just the cell's "powerhouses"—their metabolism extends beyond ATP production to include essential anabolic and catabolic processes, generation of reactive oxygen species, and regulation of apoptosis and immune function.

The article details the structure and function of mitochondria, describing their double membrane structure, cristae (inner membrane folds), the mitochondrial matrix where the citric acid cycle and beta-oxidation occur, and the intermembrane space that regulates apoptosis and cellular signaling. It outlines the three core metabolic pathways: (1) the citric acid cycle (TCA/Krebs cycle), which generates one GTP, three NADH, and one FADH2 per acetyl unit oxidized; (2) oxidative phosphorylation, which produces 36 ATP molecules per glucose molecule through the electron transport chain and ATP synthase; and (3) beta-oxidation for fatty acid degradation. The article also covers lipid and amino acid metabolism, and the NAD/NADH ratio as a real-time proxy for mitochondrial respiration.

The post discusses mitochondrial dysfunction and its links to cancer, diabetes, neurodegenerative conditions, aging, and ischemic injuries. It highlights the dual role of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species in tumors—promoting proliferation while excessive production can induce cell death or senescence.

The core of the article focuses on applications for measuring mitochondrial metabolism on microplate readers, including:
- Oxygen measurement (using MitoXpress-Intra, roGFP2 probes, and the Atmospheric Control Unit for hypoxia/ischemia-reperfusion studies)
- ATP measurement (using luminescence-based assays like CellTiter-Glo and ENLITEN)
- NAD/NADH ratio measurement (via absorbance at 340 nm using the ultrafast spectrometer)
- Lactate measurement (using Lactate-Glo assay) as a downstream product

Key instrument features highlighted include the Atmospheric Control Unit (oxygen control as low as 0.1%), ultrafast spectrometer (full absorbance data from 220-1000 nm in <1 second), LVF Monochromator, Enhanced Dynamic Range, incubation and shaking (up to 700-1100 rpm), well scanning, high sampling rates (100 data points/second), and reagent injectors.

The article concludes that microplate readers offer quantitative, high-throughput, scalable analysis of multiple mitochondrial parameters and support research into therapies targeting mitochondrial function for diseases like Parkinson's, diabetes, and certain cancers. A FAQ section addresses common questions about mitochondrial metabolism, and the article includes eight academic references.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Mitochondria are often referred to as the powerhouses of the cell since they produce most of the adenosine triphosphate (ATP) that serves as the primary energy source to support cellular function. However, the contribution of mitochondrial metabolism to cellular function is not limited to the production of ATP."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PubMed entry (PMID: 38030520) for a scientific research article published in Science Bulletin (Beijing) journal on January 15, 2024 (Epub November 16, 2023), DOI: 10.1016/j.scib.2023.11.029.

TITLE: "Mettl3-dependent m6A modification is essential for effector differentiation and memory formation of CD8+ T cells"

AUTHORS: Wenhui Guo, Zhao Wang, Yajiao Zhang, Yashu Li, Qian Du, Tiantian Zhang, Jin Hu, Yingpeng Yao, Jiarui Zhang, Yingdi Xu, Xiao Cui, Zhen Sun, Menghao You, Guotao Yu, Haojian Zhang, Xuguang Du, Jingyu Xu, and Shuyang Yu (corresponding author).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a news release from Science China Press (published via EurekAlert!) announcing a peer-reviewed study published in Science Bulletin on November 16, 2023 (DOI: 10.1016/j.scib.2023.11.029). The study, led by Dr. Shuyang Yu (College of Biological Sciences, China Agricultural University), Dr. Jingyu Xu (The Collaborative Innovation Center of Tissue Damage Repair and Regeneration Medicine of Zunyi Medical University), and Dr. Xuguang Du (College of Biological Sciences, China Agricultural University), investigated the role of Mettl3-dependent N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification in CD8+ T cell effector differentiation and memory formation.

--- SOURCE 8: Epigenetic control of CD8+ T cell tissue homing and tissue resident memory T cell precursors by the histone methyltransferase SUV39H1 ---
URL: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.05.13.593994v1.full-text

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a bioRxiv preprint (DOI: 10.1101/2024.05.13.593994) titled "Epigenetic control of CD8+ T cell tissue homing and tissue resident memory T cell precursors by the histone methyltransferase SUV39H1," authored by Guadalupe Suarez, Sandrine Heurtebise-Chrétien, Pierre-Emmanuel Bonté, Héloïse Beuchet, Jaime Fuentealba, Christel Goudot, Olivier Lantz, and Sebastian Amigorena (INSERM U932, PSL University, Institut Curie, Paris, France). The study investigates the role of SUV39H1, a histone 3-lysine 9 methyltransferase, in CD8+ T cell tissue homing and tissue resident memory T cell (T RM) differentiation.

Key findings: Deletion of SUV39H1 in CD8+ T cells increases homing to non-lymphoid tissues (liver, lungs, gut, skin) at steady state, during space-induced "homeostatic" expansion, and after flu infection. SUV39H1-deficient cells express CD49d and differentiate into CD69+/CD103- T RM cells after adoptive transfer or flu infection. SUV39H1-defective T cells that accumulate in lungs are fully functional in both Flu re-infection and lung tumor models.

Methodology: The authors used conditional SUV39H1 flox/flox CD4-Cre knockout mice, assessed steady-state tissue accumulation via flow cytometry and intravascular staining, performed adoptive transfer experiments of WT and SUV39H1-KO OT-I cells into lymphopenic RAG-KO mice, used a heterosubtypic flu infection model (X31 followed by PR8 challenge), and conducted CITE-seq (10x Genomics Chromium platform) single-cell analysis of lung-homing CD8+ T cells.

Key results: T CM (CD62L+CD44+) accumulated in lymphoid organs of SUV39H1-deficient mice. CD62L-CD44+ CD8+ T cells accumulated in non-lymphoid organs. SUV39H1 KO cells had higher expression of T RM marker CD69 and integrins CD49d/CD49a, with low expression of circulatory marker Ly6c and terminal effector marker CX3CR1. TCR-beta sequencing showed no increase in clonality among SUV39H1-deficient cells, indicating accumulation was not due to increased clonal size. Adoptive transfer experiments showed SUV39H1-KO cells accumulate up to 10 times more than WT cells in non-lymphoid organs. CITE-seq identified 9 clusters including T CM, effector, and T RM CD69 clusters, with trajectory analysis suggesting SUV39H1 regulates the developmental pathway of T RM cells.

Conclusion: SUV39H1 restrains CD8+ T cell tissue homing and T RM differentiation in WT mice. The authors recommend that SUV39H1 depletion or inhibition could enhance tissue homing in adoptive T cell therapies, optimizing target cell eradication and long-term protection against infection and cancer.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
We show here that at steady state, during space-induced "homeostatic" expansion, and after flu infection, deletion of the histone 3-lysine 9 methyltransferase SUV39H1 in CD8+ T cells, increases the homing to non-lymphoid tissues (including liver, lungs, gut and skin).
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: METTL3-mediated m6A RNA methylation promotes the anti-tumour immunity of natural killer cells | Nature Communications ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-25803-0

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Nature Communications (volume 12, article 5522, 2021) titled "METTL3-mediated m6A RNA methylation promotes the anti-tumour immunity of natural killer cells" by Hao Song, Jiaxi Song, Ming Cheng, and colleagues including Richard A. Flavell, Rui Sun, Hui Peng, Zhigang Tian, and others. The open-access article has 22k accesses and 202 citations.

**Background and Purpose:** Natural killer (NK) cells are central to anti-tumor immunity, but how their functions are regulated by epitranscriptional modification (N6-methyladenosine or m6A methylation) was previously unclear. METTL3 is the catalytically active subunit of the m6A methyltransferase complex (with METTL14 and WTAP).

**Key Findings:**
- **Reduced METTL3 in tumor-infiltrating NK cells:** METTL3 mRNA was decreased by ~75% and METTL14 by ~49% in tumor-infiltrating NK cells of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients; METTL3 was reduced ~34% in ovarian cancer ascites NK cells. In mouse models (B16/F10 melanoma pulmonary metastases and MC38 colorectal cancer liver metastases), METTL3 protein expression in tumor-associated NK cells decreased with tumor progression and correlated positively with NK cell numbers, NKG2D, T-bet, and IFN-γ expression, and negatively with the checkpoint receptor TIGIT.
- **TGF-β suppresses METTL3:** TGF-β treatment significantly decreased METTL3 protein expression in NK cells independently of SMAD3 (the TGF-βRI inhibitor GW788388, but not the SMAD3 inhibitor SIS3, counterbalanced the inhibition). TGF-β-treated NK cells showed ~22% reduction in m6A levels. IL-15 and IL-10 increased METTL3 expression.
- **METTL3 required for NK anti-tumor immunity:** Conditional knockout mice (Mettl3fl/fl-Ncr1Cre/+) showed accelerated tumor progression, more lung/liver metastases, and shortened survival across B16/F10 and MC38 tumor models. NK cell depletion experiments confirmed that METTL3 deficiency largely abrogated NK cell cancer immunosurveillance. METTL3-deficient NK cells showed lower cytotoxicity against RMA-S and YAC-1 target cells.
- **Homeostasis disturbance:** cKO mice had reduced NK cell percentages/numbers in spleen, liver, lung, and bone marrow; lower frequency of terminally mature stage 4 (CD11b+CD27−) NK cells in spleen and lung; downregulated KLRG1; and decreased expression of activating molecules (CD69, CD226, NKG2D, 2B4, Ly49H, Ly49D), FasL, and T-bet. Cell proliferation and apoptosis were unaltered.
- **Impaired IL-15 responsiveness:** METTL3-deficient NK cells failed to expand in response to IL-15 overexpression in vivo (a six-fold increase in WT vs. no more than two-fold in cKO) and showed inferior proliferation, survival, and cytokine production (GzmB, IFN-γ, TNF) in response to IL-15. IL-15 receptor expression (CD122, CD132) was unchanged, and STAT5 phosphorylation was preserved, but phosphorylation of AKT, MAPK, ERK, and mTOR was significantly decreased, leading to lower maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity.
- **Mechanism:** The gene encoding SHP-2 is m6A modified, and its protein expression is decreased in METTL3-deficient NK cells. Reduced SHP-2 activity renders NK cells hyporesponsive to IL-15 via suppressed AKT and MAPK signaling pathway activation.

**Conclusion:** m6A methylation (via METTL3) safeguards the homeostasis and tumor immunosurveillance function of NK cells by regulating SHP-2 expression and downstream IL-15 signaling (AKT-mTOR and MAPK-ERK pathways), a mechanism distinct from the SOCS3-dependent regulation observed in T cells.
</summary>

URL: https://acir.org/weekly-digests/2019/july/tox-is-so-exhausting

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This ACIR (Agency for Cancer Immunotherapy Research) weekly digest from July 3, 2019, is a special feature summarizing five recently published papers on the role of the transcription factor TOX in exhausted CD8+ T cells, which are common in cancer and chronic infections and are the major target of checkpoint blockade. Despite using different models (acute infection, chronic infection, tumors) and methods, the studies converged on several key findings: TOX preferentially plays a role in persistent antigen presentation settings (not acute infections), TOX is required for formation of exhausted CD8+ T cells via chromatin remodeling and RNA transcriptome alteration, TOX induces high expression of inhibitory receptors and decreases inflammatory cytokine production, and TOX expression is induced by the calcineurin/NFAT pathway. A positive correlation between TOX and TCF1 (a marker of progenitor-like CD8+ T cells) was mostly, but not universally, observed.

The five papers summarized include:
1. Khan et al. (Nature): Analyzed virus-specific CD8+ T cells in acute vs. chronic LCMV infection; found Tox was the most differentially expressed gene in exhausted T cells, expressed transiently/low in acute infection but persistently/high in chronic infection. TOX suppressed KLRG1+ effector differentiation via chromatin remodeling and regulated inhibitory receptors (PD-1, TIGIT, LAG3) and transcription factors (Eomes, TCF1). Initially induced by calcineurin via NFAT2, but sustained independently of calcineurin.
2. Seo et al. (PNAS): Used CD19-expressing B16-OVA melanoma with adoptively transferred CAR T cells; TOX/TOX2 double deficiency mediated tumor regression and improved survival. TOX, TOX2, and NR4A family members cooperated, induced by calcineurin via NFAT, and contributed to inhibitory receptor expression.
3. Scott et al. (Nature): Studied SV40-T antigen-driven liver cancer, B16F10 melanoma, and LCMV models using RNAseq and ATACseq. TOX was highly expressed in dysfunctional antigen-specific CD8+ T cells but not naive/effector/memory cells. Notably, high TOX correlated with low TCF1 (differing from Khan and Seo). TOX-knockout cells failed to persist in tumors. Suggested TOX-induced exhaustion serves as a negative feedback mechanism to prevent T cell overstimulation and activation-induced cell death.
4. Alfei et al. (Nature): In LCMV and human hepatitis C virus models, found TOX induction depended on antigen quantity but not affinity. Mutant-TOX T cells had decreased PD-1, increased cytokines, and elevated KLRG1 (more effector-like phenotype). TOX was required for T cell maintenance in dysfunction-promoting settings and promoted long-term maintenance of TCF1+ progenitor T cells.
5. Yao et al. (Nature Immunology): Used single-cell RNA sequencing in chronic LCMV; identified progenitor-like cells coexpressing Tox and Tcf7. Knockout of Tox shifted differentiation toward KLRG1+ short-lived effectors; TOX overexpression increased persistence of virus-specific CD8+ T cells. TOX activity was required for differentiation of progenitor-like TCF1hi CD8+ T cells and long-term immunity.

Conclusion: All five groups demonstrated TOX plays a crucial role in generating and maintaining exhausted CD8+ T cells (upregulated inhibitory receptors, decreased cytokines, epigenetic modulation) during persistent antigen presentation. TOX is highly expressed in human cancers including melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, breast cancer, and ovarian cancer, making TOX modulation a potential therapeutic target for reversing T cell exhaustion in human cancers.

The digest also includes brief summaries of related articles: a MUC16 bispecific T cell-engaging antibody (REGN4018) for ovarian cancer, cross-species single-cell analysis of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma revealing antigen-presenting cancer-associated fibroblasts, a review of CD8+CD28- immunosenescent T cells in cancer, and a study on the deubiquitinase Otub1 regulating IL-15-mediated priming of CD8+ T cells and NK cells.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"TOX preferentially plays a role in the setting of persistent antigen presentation, but not in acute infections; TOX was required for the formation of exhausted CD8+ T cells via chromatin remodeling and alteration of the RNA transcriptome; TOX induced high expression of inhibitory receptors and decreased the production of inflammatory cytokines; TOX expression was induced by the calcineurin/NFAT pathway."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: Epigenetic regulation of CD8+ T cell exhaustion - PMC - NIH ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12582961

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Epigenetic Regulation of CD8+ T Cell Exhaustion: Recent Advances and Update

**Source:** Frontiers in Immunology, Published Oct 21, 2025 (PMCID: PMC12582961, PMID: 41194917). Authors: Chunhong Li, Yixiao Yuan, Xiulin Jiang, Qiang Wang (corresponding author: wangqiang902497@126.com).

**Overview:** This mini-review synthesizes recent advances in the epigenetic mechanisms driving CD8+ T cell exhaustion in chronic infections and cancer, focusing on the integration of DNA methylation, histone modifications, transcription factors, RNA modifications, and non-coding RNAs.

### Key Findings:

**1. Exhaustion Fundamentals:**
- CD8+ T cells become "exhausted" under chronic antigen stimulation (persistent viral infections like HBV, HCV, HIV, or tumor microenvironment), characterized by loss of effector functions, sustained high expression of inhibitory receptors (PD-1, TIM-3, LAG-3, TIGIT, VISTA, CTLA-4), and reduced cytokine secretion (IL-2, TNF, IFN-γ).
- Exhaustion is distinct from anergy and senescence—it's driven by persistent antigen and exhibits graded functional deficits.
- Exhausted T cells show "epigenetic locking" (epigenetic lock-in): the phenotype is largely irreversible even after removal of inhibitory signals.
- Two subpopulations identified: progenitor-like exhausted cells (TCF1+/PD-1+) with partial self-renewal and terminal exhausted cells (PD-1hi/TOXhi) with closed chromatin and irreversible dysfunction.

**2. DNA Methylation:**
- Inhibitory receptor genes (PDCD1, TIM-3, LAG-3) are hypomethylated and transcriptionally active in exhausted T cells.
- Effector genes (IL-2, IFN-γ) are hypermethylated and repressed, creating an "epigenetic scar."
- DNMT3A reinforces terminal exhaustion; TET2 promotes demethylation of effector/stemness genes.
- Runx3 promoter demethylation promotes tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cell infiltration; decitabine (DAC) + anti-PD-1 therapy is ineffective without Runx3.
- GBP4 (GBP family member in PDAC) shows DNA hypomethylation in regulatory regions; high GBP4 expression enhances CD8+ T cell infiltration but upregulates immune checkpoints and promotes exhaustion, yet increases sensitivity to anti-PD-1 therapy.
- DNA methyltransferase inhibitors combined with ICIs (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) show promise for reversing exhaustion.

**3. Histone Modifications:**
- Repressive marks (H3K27me3) enriched at effector/memory gene promoters; activating marks (H3K4me3, H3K27ac) at exhaustion-associated cis-regulatory elements.
- EZH2 (PRC2) adds H3K27me3 to repress effector genes (IFNG, TBX21); PRC2 inhibition enhances naive/memory gene expression.
- Tex cells switch from acetate-dependent to citrate-dependent metabolism (downregulating ACSS2, maintaining ACLY), enhancing KAT2A–ACLY interactions for citrate-dependent histone acetylation at Tex-specific genes.
- Asxl1 regulates H2AK119 ubiquitination and PR-DUB pathways; Asxl1-deficient T cells synergize with anti-PD-L1 therapy.
- Histone lactylation (H3K9la) correlates with poor immunotherapy response in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma; IL-11 identified as downstream target activating immune checkpoint genes via JAK2/STAT3 pathway; cholesterol-modified siIL11 restores cytotoxic activity.
- Id2 binds via HLH domain to disrupt Tcf3–Tal1 complex, regulating chromatin accessibility at Slamf6 promoter; LSD1 inhibition (GSK2879552) rescues Id2-deficient phenotype.
- Distinct roles for SWI/SNF complexes: canonical BAF loss impairs initial responses; PBAF disruption enhances Tex proliferation and survival and improves tumor control with anti-PD-L1 therapy.

**4. Transcription Factors:**
- TOX is a central regulator, induced via calcineurin–NFAT2 pathway; recruits HDACs and DNMTs to exhaustion loci (PDCD1, LAG3, TIM3).
- Fli1 (ETS family) restricts effector differentiation; deletion enhances Teff responses.
- CD137 promotes Tex progenitor terminal differentiation via RelA/cRel NF-κB and TOX-mediated chromatin remodeling; MGP activates PD-L1 via NF-κB.
- NR4A family (NR4A1/2/3) regulates hyporesponsive states in CAR T cells and endogenous CD8+ T cells; triple NR4A-deficient CAR T cells promote tumor regression.
- ETV7 biases transcription toward terminal exhaustion; loss improves antitumor efficacy of CAR and endogenous T cells.
- Osr2 integrates biomechanical signals (via Piezo1/calcium/CREB axis) to promote terminal exhaustion, recruiting HDAC3 to reprogram epigenetic landscape.
- TCF-1 (TCF7) maintains progenitor-like Tex subset responsive to PD-1 blockade.

**5. RNA Epigenetics and Non-coding RNAs:**
- METTL3 catalyzes m6A methylation of Tcf7, Myc, and metabolic regulators; deficiency accelerates exhaustion.
- ALKBH5 (m6A demethylase) sustains effector functions and limits terminal exhaustion.
- miR-155/miR-31/miR-21 target Eomes, BATF, and cytokine signaling pathways.
- RNA modifications (m6A, m5C, Ac4C) and non-coding RNAs (miRNA, lncRNA, circRNA) modulate epigenetic and transcriptional machinery.

**6. Therapeutic Implications:**
- Novel therapeutic targets identified: DNA methyltransferases, HDACs, EZH2, BET family proteins.
- Combination strategies (epigenetic drugs + ICIs) aim for "partial unlocking" of exhaustion.
- Multi-omics biomarkers (ATAC-seq, methylome, histone modification profiling) can predict immunotherapy responsiveness.
- Epigenetic editing could enhance anti-exhaustion capacity in adoptive cell therapies (CAR-T).
- Early exhaustion precursors also emerge during acute infections with high-affinity ligand engagement; PD-1 signaling restricts their development.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Exhausted T cells exhibit chromatin landscapes markedly different from those of effector and memory T cells, displaying an 'epigenetic locking' that renders their phenotype largely irreversible."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 11: Stat5 battles Tox for epigenetic control of T cell exhaustion ---
URL: https://acir.org/weekly-digests/2023/december/stat5-battles-tox-for-epigenetic-control-of-t-cell-exhaustion

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Research digest article (December 20, 2023) from ACIR (Abramson Cancer Center's Cancer Immunology research site) reporting on a study by Beltra et al. published in Immunity (Dec 12, 2023) titled "Stat5 opposes the transcription factor Tox and rewires exhausted CD8+ T cells toward durable effector-like states during chronic antigen exposure."

Key findings: The study identified Stat5a as an antagonist to Tox-mediated T cell exhaustion programming. Using constitutively active Stat5a (STAT5CA) in chronic LCMV-infected mice, researchers found that STAT5CA drove more CD8+ T cells toward effector-like differentiation (Ly108-Tim3+) rather than Tex precursors (Ly108+Tim3-), reduced Tox expression per cell, and increased effector molecules. Genetic deletion of Stat5a-b produced the opposite effect, with more cells becoming Tex precursors and higher Tox levels. ATACseq revealed that STAT5CA cells had uniquely distinct chromatin profiles with reduced exhaustion marks and that the Tox locus itself contained high numbers of direct Stat5-binding sites.

Long-term studies showed STAT5CA cells outnumbered controls at day 27, differentiating into a distinct effector-NK-like state. In a therapeutic B16 tumor model, STAT5CA substantially decreased tumor burdens and enhanced survival. Endogenous Stat5-deficient cells remained stuck in Texprog state and failed to transition to Texint/Texterm, and this could not be rescued by PD-L1 blockade. An orthogonal IL-2:IL2Rb system selectively expanding Tex cells into Texprog2 and Texint states worked best when combined with anti-PD-L1 administered simultaneously (better than with constitutive Stat5a expression). While rewired cells showed reduced Tox and enhanced effector functions with Teff/Tmem-like chromatin patterns, epigenetic scars of exhaustion remained.

Author interview highlights: First author Jean-Christophe Beltra described the most surprising finding as demonstrating that Stat5 manipulation could not only confer durable resistance to exhaustion but also partially rescue already fully-committed exhausted cells, rewiring them toward a hybrid epigenetic state. He views this as proof-of-concept that the developmental trajectory of exhausted CD8+ T cells can be redirected, and notes that engineered/cytokine-based tools now enable cell-type-specific targeting to overcome prior off-target limitations, though more research is needed to identify optimal signal combinations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We were very thrilled to see that manipulating Stat5 not only triggered a durable resistance of antigen-specific CD8+ T cells to exhaustion (even in the most stringent conditions), but also partially rescued cells that were already fully committed to the exhaustion lineage." — Jean-Christophe Beltra, first author
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 12: Frontiers | Fundamentals to therapeutics: Epigenetic modulation of CD8+ T Cell exhaustion in the tumor microenvironment ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cell-and-developmental-biology/articles/10.3389/fcell.2022.1082195/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article, published in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology (January 4, 2023), examines the epigenetic mechanisms driving CD8+ T cell exhaustion in the tumor microenvironment (TME) and explores therapeutic strategies to reprogram exhausted T cells. The authors (Blake, O'Connell, and Aldhamen from Michigan State University) address why many patients fail to respond to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies like anti-PD-1, attributing this resistance largely to the fixed, irreversible epigenetic state of terminally exhausted CD8+ T cells (Texterm).

Key points covered:
- T cell differentiation: During chronic antigen exposure (cancer, chronic viral infections), CD8+ T cells lose effector function and differentiate into exhausted states rather than forming memory T cells. Progenitor exhausted cells (Texprog) express TCF1, have stem-like proliferative capacity and respond to ICB, while terminally exhausted cells (Texterm) express TOX, lose TCF1/T-bet, upregulate inhibitory receptors (PD-1, Tim-3, LAG3, CD38), and are resistant to ICB therapy.
- Key transcription factors: TOX is described as the "master regulator" of exhaustion, inducing epigenetic remodeling via histone acetylation and DNA methylation. T-bet antagonizes terminal exhaustion by competing with Eomes for T-box binding sites at the Pdcd1 promoter. Blimp-1 (prdm1) drives exhaustion through transcriptional repression and is antagonized by TCF1. EZH2, a histone methyltransferase, has pleiotropic effects dependent on its phosphorylation status. YY1 drives PD-1, LAG3, Tim3 expression and represses IL-2.
- Epigenetic regulation: Tex cells display unique genome-wide chromatin remodeling, with decreased accessibility at effector genes (IFNγ, TNF-α, IL-2, KLRG1) and increased accessibility at exhaustion genes (PD-1, Tim-3, LAG3, TOX, TCF7). Texterm chromatin state is fixed and irreversible - anti-PD-1 therapy only changed ~10% of the epigenetic landscape in Texterm cells. The SLAMF7 receptor was shown to promote exhaustion by upregulating inhibitory receptors and exhaustion-associated transcription factors.
- Technologies: ATAC-seq (assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing) profiles open chromatin; ChIP-seq and MNase-seq (CUT&RUN) identify protein-DNA binding and histone modifications; multiomic approaches (NOME-seq, EpiMethylTag) combine methods.
- Therapeutic approaches: Broad-spectrum epigenetic inhibitors include DNMT inhibitors (decitabine, azacytidine - approved for MDS/AML, shown to reprogram CAR-T cells), HDAC inhibitors (etinostat re-sensitizes tumors to ICB; HDAC6 inhibitors ACY-1215/ACY-241 enhance effector function and reduce exhaustion markers in melanoma), and BET inhibitors (JQ1 reversed T cell exhaustion in AML). Narrow-spectrum approaches include EZH2 inhibition - the first EZH2 inhibitor was FDA-approved in 2020 for relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma (69% vs 35% response rate with vs without EZH2 mutation). The authors conclude that combining epigenetic reprogramming with ICB therapy represents a promising avenue to re-sensitize exhausted T cells and overcome treatment resistance.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Despite exciting results with ICB therapies, many patients with solid tumors still fail to respond to such therapies and patients who initially respond can develop resistance." "once cells reach terminal exhaustion, it cannot be undone and likelihood of ICB resistance increases" "anti-PD-1 therapy was able to only change 10% of the epigenetic landscape to Texterm cells, implicating that the fixed chromatin state of Texterm cells is a major limitation for anti-PD-1 therapy" "the terminal epigenetic state of Texterm is fixed and irreversible, even after reactivation, curative therapy, or following ICB therapies" "the distinction between exhausted T cell subtypes is critical because although progenitor exhausted CD8+ T cells are responsive to ICBs, terminally exhausted cells are not"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: 2025-8359 ---
URL: https://www.excli.de/vol24/2025-8359/2025-8359.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in EXCLI Journal 2025 (EXCLI J 2025;24:Doc578) by Maqbool et al. examining the role of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modifications in epilepsy. 

**Background/Context:** Epilepsy is a widespread neurological disorder affecting roughly 100 million people who will experience at least one seizure in their lifetime. Lifetime prevalence is about 5.8 per 1,000 in developed regions and 10.3 per 1,000 in developing areas. Current treatments inadequately control the disease in many patients, especially those with drug-resistant epilepsy.

**m6A Modification Machinery:** m6A is the most prevalent internal mRNA modification in eukaryotic mRNAs, regulating splicing, export, translation, and stability. It is controlled by:
- **Writers** (methyltransferases): METTL3, METTL14, WTAP, ZC3H13, VIRMA/KIAA1429, RBM15, HAKAI/CBLL1, plus newly discovered METTL16, METTL5/TRMT112 (for rRNA), and PCIF1
- **Erasers** (demethylases): FTO (first discovered) and ALKBH5
- **Readers** (m6A recognition proteins): YTHDC1-2, YTHDF1-3, IGF2BP1-3, and hnRNPs (hnRNPA2B1, HNRNPC/G)

**m6A in Neuronal Function:** m6A regulates neurodevelopment, synaptic plasticity, autophagy, axonal outgrowth, neural stem cell behavior after ischemic injury, and neuronal stress responses. Synaptic genes undergo age-related m6A shifts (hypermethylated in young mice become hypomethylated in older animals). METTL3, YTHDF1, and FTO are key modulators of synaptic function.

**Dysregulation in Epilepsy:** m6A dysregulation affects neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, and disease development through mechanisms involving autophagy (TRPML1), oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Key findings include:
- YTHDC2 and xCT (glutamate-cystine antiporter) are key factors in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) with hippocampal sclerosis
- Increased m6A methylation of Nrf2 mRNA is associated with high seizure frequency and neuronal apoptosis
- SRF/METTL3 interplay regulates m6A modifications and oxidative stress in epileptic neurons
- Downregulation of FTO leads to increased Nrf2 m6A modifications and hippocampal cell damage in rat epilepsy models
- EGR1 can trigger METTL3-associated suppression of VIM to reduce neuronal damage

**Diagnostic Biomarker Potential:** Analysis of the GEO GSE143272 dataset identified seven differentially expressed m6A regulator genes in epilepsy patients: RBMX, HNRNPC, WTAP, RBM15, YTHDC1, YTHDC2, and CBLL1. A random forest model and nomogram were constructed to predict epilepsy risk, and qRT-PCR confirmed differential expression in blood samples. Epileptic patients were divided into two distinct m6A patterns (cluster A and B) showing different immune cell components and cell death patterns.

**Prognostic Significance:** m6A patterns correlate with autophagy, ferroptosis, and cuproptosis-related genes, suggesting m6A modifications influence cell death pathways in epilepsy. m6A regulators also strongly correlate with immune cell components, offering a basis for exploring autoimmune epilepsy connections (via LGI1 and GAD autoantibodies).

**Therapeutic Approaches:** Potential therapeutic strategies include:
- Targeting m6A methylation of miRNA-134 (which has neuroprotective and antiepileptic benefits)
- Compound 7d, a synthetic FTO inhibitor that improves m6A methylation levels and has anticonvulsant effects in mice
- Small molecules, RNA editing technologies, and precision medicine approaches
- Potential personalized therapeutic strategies for drug-resistant epilepsy

**Conclusion:** The review highlights m6A modulation as a transformational therapeutic avenue in epilepsy, offering new biomarkers for diagnosis and outcome prediction, with potential to revolutionize drug-resistant epilepsy treatment.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Dysregulation of m6A machinery promotes epilepsy by exacerbating oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuronal damage." "Recent findings highlight the critical role of m6A methylation in epilepsy, mainly in seizure susceptibility and disease development." "The glutamate-cystine antiporter (xCT), targeted by the m6A reader protein YTHDC2, has been recognized as a key factor in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) with hippocampal sclerosis." "Analysis of the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) GSE143272 dataset found differential expression of seven major m6A regulator genes in epilepsy patients: RBMX, HNRNPC, WTAP, RBM15, YTHDC1, YTHDC2, and CBLL1." "By synthesizing a chemical known as 7d, which functions as an inhibitor for the demethylase FTO... Compound 7d reduces FTO thereby improving m6A methylation levels in cells and has anticonvulsant effects in mice."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Intertwined regulation between RNA m6A modification and cancer metabolism - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10120304

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed review article published in Cell Insight (2022 Dec 5;2(1):100075, DOI: 10.1016/j.cellin.2022.100075) by Jiaxu Liu, Hao Huang, Minghao Zhang, Guoliang Qing, and Hudan Liu (corresponding author) from Wuhan University, China. The review examines the intertwined bidirectional regulation between RNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification and cancer metabolism.

KEY TOPICS COVERED:

1. **RNA m6A modification basics**: m6A is the most common, abundant, and conserved internal RNA modification in eukaryotic mRNAs. It is present in protein-coding mRNAs, lncRNAs, rRNAs, and snRNAs. Modification sites have a typical DRACH consensus sequence and are enriched in CDS and 3'UTR regions, particularly around the stop codon.

2. **Dynamic regulation by writers, erasers, and readers**:
   - Writers: METTL3 (catalytic core, SAM-binding), METTL14 (stabilizes METTL3), and WTAP (adaptor protein) form the canonical m6A methyltransferase complex.
   - Erasers: FTO (demethylates m6A, m6Am, and m1A) and ALKBH5 (m6A-specific, nuclear-localized) are α-KG-dependent dioxygenases requiring Fe2+ and α-KG.
   - Readers: YTH domain proteins (YTHDC1/2, YTHDF1/2/3), FMRP, and IGF2BP proteins that impact RNA stability, translation efficiency, and splicing.

3. **m6A regulation of glucose metabolism**: METTL3/WTAP complex modifies GLUT1, HK2, ENO1, PKM2 transcripts to promote mRNA stability or translation. YTHDF1 accelerates PKM2 translation; FTO promotes LDHB and PFKP stability in AML. METTL3 affects glycolysis indirectly via APC and HDGF transcripts. MYC and HIF1α master transcription factors are also modulated by m6A, with context-specific outcomes (stabilization or degradation depending on tumor type).

4. **m6A regulation of glutamine metabolism**: FTO targets SLC1A5 (glutamine transporter) in clear cell renal cell carcinoma. METTL3 promotes GLS2 expression in ESCC. YTHDF1 enhances GLS1 translation, conferring cisplatin resistance in colorectal cancer cells.

5. **m6A regulation of lipid metabolism**: m6A affects PPARα mRNA, including circadian regulation of lipid metabolism via Bmal1 deletion.

6. **Metabolites regulating m6A machinery**:
   - SAM/SAH: SAM is the universal methyl donor; SAH is an allosteric inhibitor of METTL3. GNMT regulates the SAM/SAH ratio and acts as a tumor suppressor in HCC.
   - α-KG and R-2HG: α-KG is required for FTO/ALKBH5 activity. Mutant IDH1/2 (present in ~80% of grade II-III gliomas and 10-20% of AML) converts α-KG to R-2HG, which competitively inhibits FTO and increases m6A levels, suppressing MYC/CEBPA pathways.
   - Citrate, succinate, and fumarate: These TCA cycle metabolites can occupy the α-KG-binding pocket of ALKBH5 and FTO, inhibiting demethylase activity (though validated mainly in cell-free systems).
   - NADP(H)/NADH: Potentiate FTO activity as strong binding partners and activators.

CONCLUSION: The review highlights that both methylases and demethylases can show pro-tumorigenic roles in metabolism, depending on tumor context. It proposes that simultaneous targeting of RNA m6A modifications and metabolic pathways may yield synergistic anti-tumor effects, representing a novel cancer treatment approach.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"RNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) has been identified as the most common, abundant and conserved internal modification in RNA transcripts, especially within eukaryotic messenger RNAs (mRNAs)." "Metabolic reprogramming has been widely recognized as a hallmark of cancer." "Recent emerging evidence reveals reciprocal regulation between the m6A modification and disordered metabolic events in cancer cells, adding more complexity in the cellular network of metabolic rewiring." "The SAM/SAH ratio is capable of regulating m6A modification by modulating the METTL3-mediated enzymatic reaction." "simultaneous targeting of RNA m6A modifications and metabolic pathways may yield synergistic anti-tumor effects, paving a new way for cancer treatment modality."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Frontiers | Interplay Between m6A RNA Methylation and Regulation of Metabolism in Cancer ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cell-and-developmental-biology/articles/10.3389/fcell.2022.813581/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology (03 February 2022) titled "Interplay Between m6A RNA Methylation and Regulation of Metabolism in Cancer." The review examines the link between N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modification and metabolic reprogramming in cancer, hypothesizing that m6A dysregulation of metabolism contributes to cancer proliferation, initiation, and metastasis.

**Key Topics Covered:**

**m6A Regulation Mechanisms:**
- Writers (methyltransferases): METTL3/METTL14 complex, WTAP, HAKAI, ZC3H13, VIRMA, ZCCHC4, METTL5, METTL16
- Erasers (demethylases): FTO and ALKBH5 (Fe2+/α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases), ALKBH3 (tRNA-specific)
- Readers (recognition proteins): YTHDF1/2/3, YTHDC1/2, IGF2BP1/2/3, hnRNPC/hnRNPA2B1, eIF3, HuR
- m6A affects mRNA processing, translation, decay, nuclear export, and miRNA maturation

**m6A Regulation of Cancer Metabolism:**

*Glucose metabolism:*
- Colorectal cancer (CRC): METTL3 stabilizes GLUT1 and HK2 mRNAs, promoting CRC via the GLUT1-mTORC1 signaling axis
- Cervical cancer: METTL3 regulates glycolysis via PDK4; YTHDF1 and IGF2BP3 binding regulates PDK4 mRNA stability and translation
- Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC): FTO demethylates PKM2 mRNA promoting tumorigenesis; METTL3 inhibition combined with 2-deoxyglucose suppresses HCC
- Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML): R-2HG inhibits FTO activity, suppressing aerobic glycolysis via the FTO/m6A/YTHDF2-LDHB axis
- Gastric cancer: METTL3 and WTAP promote glycolysis via HDGF, GLUT4, ENO2, and HK2
- Glioblastoma (GBM): lncRNA JPX enhances FTO-mediated PDK1 mRNA demethylation promoting aerobic glycolysis
- Lung cancer: YTHDF2 promotes G6PD mRNA translation; reduced FTO enhances MYC translation via YTHDF1
- Breast cancer: METTL3 overexpression enhances PDK4 expression

*Lipid metabolism:*
- METTL3 and YTHDF2 knockdown decreased lipid accumulation in HCC
- FTO modulates triglyceride deposition and regulates SCD, MOGAT1, and FAS
- YTHDF2 regulates cholesterol homeostasis in GBM and lipogenic genes (ACC1, FAS, SCD1)
- METTL3/YTHDF2 regulate DEGS2 sphingolipid metabolism in colorectal cancer

*Amino acid metabolism:*
- METTL14 regulates GOT2, CSAD, and SOCS2 in HCC
- YTHDF1 mediates glutamine metabolism and cisplatin resistance in colon cancer
- AMPKα2 inhibits CRC growth by altering FTO expression

*Other metabolic processes:*
- YTHDF1 regulates iron metabolism and TFRC expression in hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma

**Control of m6A by Metabolites:**
- NADP binds to FTO, decreasing m6A methylation and promoting adipogenesis
- Citrate binds to the α-KG/FTO complex inhibiting enzyme activity
- R-2HG (produced by mutant IDH) inhibits FTO, increasing m6A levels and reducing aerobic glycolysis in leukemia
- Succinate and isocitrate also regulate α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases

**Therapeutic Applications:**
- STM2457 (METTL3 small-molecule inhibitor) showed promise for treating myeloid leukemia in AML mouse models
- FB23 and FB23-2 (FTO inhibitors) offer therapeutic strategies for leukemia
- Entacapone (FDA-approved drug) identified as a selective FTO inhibitor
- METTL3 depletion sensitizes cells to doxorubicin, irradiation, and chemotherapy
- FTO inhibition with anti-PD-1 blockade may reduce immunotherapy resistance in melanoma
- Dac51 blocks FTO-mediated immune evasion
- YTHDF2 deficiency impairs NK cell antitumor activity
- METTL3 is a prognostic factor for poor outcomes in HCC, thyroid carcinoma, pancreatic cancer, CRC, and gastric cancer
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We hypothesize that m6A modification could dysregulate the expression of glucose, lipid, amino acid metabolism, and other metabolites or building blocks of cells by adaptation to the hypoxic tumor microenvironment, an increase in glycolysis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and abnormal expression of metabolic enzymes, metabolic receptors, transcription factors as well as oncogenic signaling pathways in both hematological malignancies and solid tumors."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: m6A RNA Methylation Mechanism | Encyclopedia MDPI ---
URL: https://encyclopedia.pub/entry/23782

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an encyclopedia article on "Video Upload Options" focusing on epitranscriptomic modifications and specifically N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA methylation. The article covers how epitranscriptomic modifications affect RNA biology, including stability, transport, splicing, and translation, and participate in global intracellular mRNA metabolism and gene expression regulation.
