It has been documented that γδ T cells have important roles in controlling mucocutaneous infections ([6](#r6), [7](#r7)). We next performed an *S. typhimurium* model of colonic infection to determine the functional consequences of the expanded γδ T cells in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice. Strikingly, *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice were better protected from infection than their WT littermates, manifested in significantly reduced weight loss and delayed fatality ([Fig. 1 *C* and *D*](#fig01)). Moreover, *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice had a lower bacterial burden in their feces, cecum, spleen, and liver than WT littermate mice ([Fig. 1 *E* and *F*](#fig01)). To exclude the possibility that the protective phenotype observed in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice during infection might be mediated by CD4+ T lymphocytes, we performed *S. typhimurium* infection with *Alkbh5f/f CD4-Cre* mice. We found that ALKBH5 deletion in αβ T cells did not contribute better protection to *Alkbh5f/f CD4-Cre* than their littermate controls ([*SI Appendix*, Fig. S5 *E–G*](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)). To further confirm that the protective phenotype observed in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice during infection was mediated by γδ T cells rather than other lymphocyte populations, we crossed *Alkbh5f/f* and *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice onto TCRδ-deficient (*TCR*δ*−/−*) mice for targeted deletion of γδ T cells. Of note, *Alkbh5f/f TCR*δ*−/− Lck+* mice showed similar pathological outcomes compared with *Alkbh5f/f TCR*δ*−/−* mice upon *S. typhimurium* infection, including comparable weight loss, survival rate, and fecal bacterial burden ([Fig. 1 *G–I*](#fig01)). Taken together, these results indicate that expanded γδ T cells in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice lead to a more efficient immune response against *S. typhimurium*.

### Loss of ALKBH5 Has No Impact on IFN-γ and IL-17 Production, Proliferation, and Apoptosis of Mature γδ T Cells.

Similar to αβ T cells, γδ T cells can exert their immune functions by secreting proinflammatory cytokines such as IFN-γ, IL-17A, and IL-4 ([3](#r3), [4](#r4), [17](#r17)–[19](#r19)). To further address the phenotype of *S. typhimurium* infection as to whether it was only attributable to an increased number of γδ T cells or also to their enhanced function, we next assayed the cytokine changes secreted by γδ T cells in WT and *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice. γδ T cell effector fate is largely dependent on TCR-γδ signaling strength in the thymus ([16](#r16), [17](#r17)). We confirm no big changes in the percentage of IFN-γ– or IL-17–producing γδ T cells between *Alkbh5f/f* and *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice in the thymus and peripheral immune tissues ([*SI Appendix*, Figs. S7 *A* and *B* and S8 *C* and *D*](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)), suggesting that the quality of γδ T cells and the strength of TCR-γδ signaling are not affected by ALKBH5 deficiency. Furthermore, we also found that loss of ALKBH5 did not alter the proportion of IFN-γ–, IL-17–, or IL-4–producing αβ T cells in both *Lck-Cre* and *CD4-Cre* mice compared with their littermate control WT mice ([*SI Appendix*, Figs. S5*D* and S8 *A* and *B*](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)). Thus, we conclude that the quality of γδ T cells and the strength of TCR-γδ signaling are not affected by ALKBH5 deficiency.

To better understand the quantitative increase of γδ T cells in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice, we tested whether proliferation and apoptosis of mature γδ T cells had changed in those mice. Surprisingly, we did not observe enhanced proliferation or impaired apoptosis in mature γδ T cells isolated from the thymus of *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice ([*SI Appendix*, Fig. S7 *C–F*](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)). Together, these findings imply that loss of ALKBH5 neither changes the cytokine profile nor alters proliferation or apoptosis of mature γδ T cells.

### Depletion of ALKBH5 in Thymocytes Promotes the Expansion of γδ T Cell Precursors.

To further explore mechanistically how ALKBH5 deficiency facilitates the expansion of γδ T cells, we next investigated whether loss of ALKBH5 affected the proportion and number of γδ T progenitors at early developmental stages. Since αβ T cells and γδ T cells are both derived from thymic DN cells, we first evaluated these cells isolated from *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice and WT littermates. Interestingly, *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice had significantly more DN lymphocytes than WT mice in the thymus ([Fig. 2 *A–C*](#fig02)). It is well-known that the DN population can be further subdivided into four subsets according to their expression of surface markers CD44 and CD25: CD44+CD25− (DN1) cells, CD44+CD25+ (DN2) cells, CD44–CD25+ (DN3) cells, and CD44–CD25− (DN4) cells ([45](#r45)). In *Lck-Cre* transgenic mice, the ALKBH5 deletion is initiated at the DN2 stage and completed by the DN3 stage ([42](#r42), [46](#r46)). In accordance with this, we observed that the frequency of DN3 cells and the numbers of DN2 and DN3 cells were markedly increased in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice ([Fig. 2 *D–F*](#fig02)), suggesting that ALKBH5 is involved in the development of early γδ T cell precursors. To exclude the effect of *Lck-Cre* toxicity, we used *Lck-Cre*–positive littermate controls to further detect positive data in γδ T cells, and we also found markedly increased numbers and frequencies of γδ T, DN, DN2, and DN3 cells in the *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* group compared with the *Lck+* WT group ([*SI Appendix*, Fig. S9](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)).

Until now, few surface markers have been identified on developing γδ T cells, and most studies have used CD73+ TCRγδ+ DN lymphocytes as γδ T progenitors that are committed to the γδ lineage ([18](#r18), [47](#r47)). Human γδ T cells are usually characterized based on the features of their TCRδ variable region (Vδ), while mouse γδ T cell subsets are distinguished by the Vγ chain they bear, most of which are either Vγ1.1 or Vγ2 ([48](#r48)–[50](#r50)). Therefore, we next analyzed whether loss of ALKBH5 affects CD73-expressing TCRδ+ Vγ1.1+ and TCRδ+ Vγ2+ progenitors ([Fig. 2*G*](#fig02)). We observed that ALKBH5 deletion slightly affected the frequency of TCRδ+ Vγ1.1+ and TCRδ+ Vγ2+ cells at the DN stage, as well as their progenitor subsets in thymus ([*SI Appendix*, Fig. S10](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)). Of note, compared with *Alkbh5f/f* mice, *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice had more immature TCRδ+ Vγ1.1+ cells, TCRδ+ Vγ1.1+ precursor cells, and γδNKT Vγ1.1+ progenitors at the DN stage ([Fig. 2*H*](#fig02)). Similarly, increased numbers of immature TCRδ+ Vγ2+ cells, TCRδ+ Vγ2+ precursor cells, and γδNKT Vγ2+ progenitors at the DN stage ([Fig. 2*I*](#fig02)) were found in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice. Finally, we further determined the number of mature γδ T cell subsets in the thymus, and found highly increased counts in all these subpopulations in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice compared with control *Alkbh5f/f* mice ([*SI Appendix*, Fig. S11](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)), indicating that the increased number of mature γδ T cells observed above is due to the expansion of γδ T cell precursors.

### Absence of ALKBH5 Promotes the Proliferation of γδ T Cell Precursors and Expands the γδ T Cell Repertoire during the Embryonic Stage.

These above findings prompted us to hypothesize that ALKBH5 deficiency might increase the proliferation rate of γδ T cell progenitors. Therefore, we labeled the cells in vivo with bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU), a thymidine analog used to identify proliferating cells. As expected, the frequency of BrdU-positive γδ T cell progenitors was significantly higher in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice compared with WT littermates ([Fig. 3 *A* and *B*](#fig03)). On the other hand, no obvious changes were observed regarding the apoptotic rate of these γδ T cell progenitors ([Fig. 3 *C* and *D*](#fig03)), suggesting that γδ T cell precursors in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice were expanded because of increased proliferation rather than reduced cell death.

From a developmental point of view, it has been shown that murine γδ T cells begin to appear during the middle and late period of embryonic development (embryonic day ∼13.5; ∼E13.5) ([17](#r17)). We then analyzed the quantity of γδ T cells in the thymus of *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice at different fetal stages. Surprisingly, the increased frequency of γδ T cells was observed in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice as early as day E14.5 ([Fig. 3 *E* and *F*](#fig03)), suggesting that ALKBH5 affected the γδ T cell population during midterm fetal development. Taken together, these data indicate that loss of ALKBH5 promotes the proliferation of γδ T cell precursors and leads to an expanded γδ T cell repertoire during embryonic development.

### Loss of ALKBH5 Results in an Altered Jagged1/Notch2 Signaling Pathway in γδ T Cell Precursors.

To explore the molecular mechanisms underlying the expanded γδ T cell progenitors in the absence of ALKBH5, we performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) on γδ T cell precursors isolated from the thymus in *Alkbh5f/f* and *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* cohoused independent littermates. Overall, about 698 genes (*P* < 0.05) were differentially expressed in ALKBH5-deficient γδ T cell progenitors, including 339 down-regulated genes and 359 up-regulated genes ([*SI Appendix*, Fig. S12*A*](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)). Since m6A RNA modification is mainly involved in mRNA decay, we reasoned that removing its eraser ALKBH5 likely would promote the degradation of certain mRNA transcripts with increased m6A levels. Among those differentially expressed genes identified from *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice, *Jagged1* was the most markedly down-regulated gene ([Fig. 4*A*](#fig04)). Jagged1 is a key ligand for Notch, a pathway which is both necessary and sufficient for T cell lineage commitment ([23](#r23)). Pathway analysis revealed that Notch signaling was one of the most substantially reduced signaling cascades in the γδ T cell progenitors isolated from *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice ([Fig. 4*B*](#fig04)). In-depth analysis further showed that Jagged/Notch signaling genes and their target genes, such as *Jagged1*, *Notch2*, *Hey1*, *Hes1*, *Fabp7*, and *Gzmb*, were indeed down-regulated, suggesting that the Jagged1/Notch2 signaling pathway was functionally suppressed in ALKBH5-deficient γδ T cell precursors ([Fig. 4 *A* and *C*](#fig04) and [*SI Appendix*, Table S1](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)). In addition, pathway analysis implied that most of the genes up-regulated in the absence of ALKBH5 are involved in regulating the cell cycle ([*SI Appendix*, Fig. S12*B* and Table S2](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)), which is also consistent with our flow cytometric analysis of γδ T cell progenitors mentioned above ([Fig. 3 *A* and *B*](#fig03)). Next, we validated by qPCR and flow analysis that the expression of Jagged1 and Notch2 was down-regulated at both mRNA and protein levels in the γδ T cell progenitors of *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice ([Fig. 4 *D* and *E*](#fig04)). Besides, downstream components of Notch signaling such as its effector genes *Hey1* and *Hes1* ([23](#r23), [51](#r51)) were also confirmed to be markedly decreased, while the cell-cycle factor *Cdkn1a* ([52](#r52)) was significantly increased in the absence of ALKBH5 ([Fig. 4 *C* and *F*](#fig04)). Taken together, this evidence suggests that ALKBH5 regulates the development of γδ T cells through Jagged1/Notch2 signaling, thereby regulating the proliferation of γδ T cell precursors.

We next sought to understand whether impaired Jagged1/Notch2 signaling in the absence of ALKBH5 occurs only in γδ T cell progenitors but not in mature γδ T cells. Therefore, we performed RNA-seq on mature γδ T cells isolated from three independent *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice as well as WT littermates. We found many fewer up- and down-regulated genes in ALKBH5 KO mature γδ T cells compared with precursor T cells. Surprisingly, the dysregulation of Jagged1/Notch2 signaling and related gene expression observed in γδ T cell progenitor cells was absent in γδ T mature cells in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice ([*SI Appendix*, Fig. S13 *B* and *D–F* and Table S3](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)). Of note, the level of *Jagged1* and *Notch2* mRNAs markedly decreased in WT mature γδ T cells compared with WT γδ T progenitors ([*SI Appendix*, Fig. S13*C* and Tables S1 and S3](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)), indicating that Jagged1 expression in γδ T cells may have temporospatial characteristics. Taken together, this evidence indicates that ALKBH5 regulates the development of γδ T cells by influencing the expression of Jagged1 and Notch2 mRNAs, and through these other Notch-related genes in γδ T cell progenitors.

### ALKBH5 Deficiency Enhances m6A RNA Modification on *Jagged1* and *Notch2* mRNAs to Decrease Their Stability and Expression.

To address mechanistically how ALKBH5 affects Jagged1 and Notch2 mRNA levels, we first confirmed by dot blot and mass spectrometry that the m6A levels in total mRNA of thymus lymphocytes increased in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice compared with *Alkbh5f/f* mice ([Fig. 5 *A* and *B*](#fig05)). Based on our previous m6A RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP)–seq data from T cells ([37](#r37), [53](#r53)), we found highly enriched and specific m6A peaks on *Jagged1* and *Notch2* mRNAs ([Fig. 5*C*](#fig05)). m6A RIP combined with qPCR revealed that *Jagged1* and *Notch2* m6A enrichment was markedly increased in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice compared with WT littermates ([Fig. 5*D*](#fig05)). RNA m6A methylation is understood to mainly affect RNA stability. To further prove that increased m6A led to more rapid degradation of *Jagged1* and *Notch2* mRNAs, we performed RNA decay analysis and identified that *Jagged1* transcription was more rapidly degraded in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice than in WT littermates ([Fig. 5*E*](#fig05)). Although the degradation of *Notch2* transcription was slightly accelerated in the absence of ALKBH5 ([Fig. 5*F*](#fig05)), it could be enough to reduce the expression level of *Notch2* mRNA over time compared with WT littermates. These data suggest that ALKBH5 deletion enhances m6A modification on *Jagged1* and *Notch2* mRNAs to decrease their stability and expression in γδ T cells.

#### Fig. 5.

[![Fig. 5.](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/8b2f/9388086/cea104103cc8/pnas.2203318119fig05.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=9388086_pnas.2203318119fig05.jpg)

Data represent one out of three independent experiments. (*B*) Liquid Chromatography/Mass Spectrometry (LC-MC) analysis of m6A RNA modification in the thymocytes isolated from *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* and *Alkbh5f/f* mice (*n* = 6 or 7 per group). Unpaired *t* test was used for statistical analysis. Data represent one out of three independent experiments (mean ± SD). (*D*) m6A RIP–qPCR analysis showing m6A enrichment of *Jagged1* and *Notch2* mRNAs in total thymic γδ T cells from *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* and *Alkbh5f/f* cohoused three independent littermates. (*E*) RNA decay analysis showing *Jagged1* mRNA degradation in total thymic γδ T cells treated with actinomycin D for 2 and 4 h from *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* and *Alkbh5f/f* cohoused three independent littermates. The residual RNAs (mRNA remaining) were normalized to 0 h. Paired *t* test was used for statistical analysis. *n* = 3 to 5 mice in each group for a one-time independent experiment. Data represent three independent experiments combined (mean ± SD). \**P* < 0.05, \*\**P* < 0.01; n.s., not significant.

To further confirm that defective Jagged1 signaling contributed to the observed specific γδ T cell expansion in *Alkbh5f/f Lck-Cre* mice, we crossed *Jagged1f/f* mice with *Lck-Cre* transgenic mice to assess the function of Jagged1 in developing T cell populations. Although *Jagged1* KO in T lymphocytes did not affect the early development of T cells ([*SI Appendix*, Fig. S14 *A* and *B*](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)), the frequency of γδ T cells was significantly increased in the thymus and spleen from *Jagged1f/f Lck+* mice compared with the control littermates ([*SI Appendix*, Fig. S14 *C* and *D*](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)), suggesting the inactivation of Jagged1 also contributes to the expansion of the γδ T cell pool which phenocopies *Alkbh5f/f Lck-Cre* mice. Collectively, loss of ALKBH5 promotes the development of γδ T cell progenitors through targeted suppression of Jagged1/Notch2 signaling.

## Discussion

In this study, we discovered that ALKBH5 in thymic lymphocytes plays a critical role in the cell-fate decision between αβ T and γδ T cell lineages by targeting the Jagged1/Notch2 signaling pathway. We observed that loss of ALKBH5 results in a marked expansion of γδ T cells, with a minor effect on αβ T cells in both the thymus and periphery. It is well-demonstrated that γδ T cells are required to combat invasive bacterial infection, and may have great promise for the development of novel immunotherapies ([6](#r6), [7](#r7)). Surprisingly, expanded γδ T cells led to a more efficient immune response against *S. typhimurium* infection, while the depletion of γδ T cells eliminated this protective role in *Alkbh5f/f Lck+* mice, together suggesting that loss of ALKBH5 specifically affects the expansion of γδ T cells. ALKBH5 deletion had no impact on cytokine profiles, and affected neither proliferation nor apoptosis of mature γδ T cells; it did, however, expand the pool of developing γδ T cell progenitors and enhanced their proliferative capacity during embryonic development. Previously, the Notch signaling pathway was shown to be necessary and sufficient for T cell lineage commitment ([23](#r23)). However, whether specific Notch receptor–ligand interactions influence the later cell-fate decision by early thymocyte progenitors to become γδ T cells in mice is still unknown ([54](#r54), [55](#r55)). Here, our data demonstrate that loss of ALKBH5-mediated RNA m6A levels promotes the proliferation and differentiation of γδ T precursors through targeting the Notch signaling genes, and show which specific Notch receptor–ligand interaction controls the development of murine γδ T cell progenitors in the thymus.

Our findings raise the intriguing question of how ALKBH5 affects the proportion and number of γδ T cells in the thymus. Although αβ and γδ T cells originate from a common thymic lymphocyte progenitor ([9](#r9)), γδ T cell precursors are believed to branch off from the αβ T cell development pathway before or at the time of TCR-α rearrangement at the DN2 stage ([42](#r42)). There is evidence that DN progenitors have the potential to change the timing of the divergence of αβ and γδ T cell lineages to the late DN2 to DN3 developmental stages ([56](#r56)). Our previous work shows that m6A writer METTL3 deletion has much greater impact and not opposite roles over T cell function compared with that of m6A eraser ALKBH5 deletion or FTO deletion ([37](#r37), [57](#r57)), possibly due to unknown m6A erasers and a much more complicated regulatory network of m6A function. In the present study, we observed that the frequency of DN3 cells and the number of DN2 and DN3 cells are significantly increased in the thymus in the absence of ALKBH5, suggesting that ALKBH5 deletion in thymic lymphocytes enhances the γδ T precursor pool at the DN2 to DN3 stages. Furthermore, our data also show that ALKBH5 deficiency results in a significant expansion of γδ T cell progenitors in the thymus, including TCRδ+ Vγ1.1+, TCRδ+ Vγ2+, and γδNKT subsets. However, the generation of γδ T cell subpopulations is developmentally regulated during ontogeny, such that Vγ5 cells develop during the fetal period, Vγ6 cells around birth, Vγ4 cells in the neonatal period, and Vγ1 and Vγ7 cells at the adult stage ([41](#r41), [58](#r58)). After their egress from the thymus, several γδ T cell subsets naturally establish residency in predetermined mucosal and epithelial locations, as exemplified by the restricted location of the murine Vγ5+ subset to the intestinal epithelium and epidermis, and loss of Vγ5+Vδ1+ cells due to a failure of thymic selection ([59](#r59)–[61](#r61)). Vγ5+Vδ1+ cells comprise 90% of mouse epidermal γδ T cells, and the intraepithelial lymphocyte network of TCRVγ5+ plays a critical role in the regulation of cutaneous inflammation ([60](#r60), [61](#r61)). Therefore, we do not rule out other subsets of γδ T cell precursors that may have changed during ontogeny in the absence of ALKBH5. Further studies will address which populations of other γδ T cell precursors are differentially induced by the loss of ALKBH5 during ontogeny.

Notch signaling is involved in the regulation of lymphocyte development and function ([23](#r23)). In mammals, this pathway is composed of four Notch receptors (Notch1 to Notch4) and five ligands: Jagged1, Jagged2, Delta1, Delta3, and Delta4. Recent evidence indicates that Notch receptor–ligand interactions have been implicated in governing cell-fate decisions during T lymphocyte differentiation ([24](#r24), [54](#r54), [62](#r62), [63](#r63)). By RNA-seq and m6A epigenomic analysis, we confirm that loss of ALKBH5-mediated m6A RNA modification directly suppresses Jagged1/Notch2 signaling in γδ T cell progenitors, which in turn promotes the development of immature γδ T cells. However, we readily admit that there might be other signaling pathways contributing to the observed γδ T cell progenitor defects upon ALKBH5 deletion. In humans, Jagged1 induces mainly αβ lineage differentiation, whereas Jagged2-mediated Notch3 activation primarily results in γδ T cell development and represses αβ lineage differentiation by inhibiting TCR-β formation ([54](#r54)). Interestingly, murine bone marrow–derived stem cells do not respond to Jagged1 signals, while Jagged1 signals can influence the differentiation of T cell progenitors along γδ T cell lineages during a brief window of their development between the DN1 and DN3 stages of thymic development ([55](#r55)). These results suggest the different mechanisms of γδ T cell development in mice and humans. Out of curiosity, we compared the expression of Jagged1 and Notch2 in mature and immature γδ T cells, and were surprised to find that the level of Jagged1 and Notch2 expression in mature γδ T cells is very low and significantly decreased compared with γδ T cell precursors ([*SI Appendix*, Fig. S13*C*](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.2203318119/-/DCSupplemental)), point

args.summary:
This is a scientific research article from the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) investigating the role of the RNA m6A demethylase ALKBH5 in regulating the development of γδ T cells. The study was conducted by researchers affiliated with institutions led by Hua-Bing Li, with correspondence to Richard A. Flavell (Yale University) and Weiguo Hu. The paper was received February 24, 2022, accepted July 2, 2022, and published August 16, 2022, under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Depletion of ALKBH5 in lymphocytes (using Alkbh5f/f Lck-Cre mice) causes a specific expansion of γδ T cells in the thymus and peripheral tissues (spleen, lymph nodes, intestinal epithelial lymphocytes, and lamina propria lymphocytes), with little impact on αβ T cells.
- This expanded γδ T cell population confers enhanced protection against gastrointestinal Salmonella typhimurium infection, evidenced by reduced weight loss, delayed fatality, and lower bacterial burden. The protective effect was confirmed to be γδ T cell-mediated through TCRδ knockout experiments.
- ALKBH5 deficiency does NOT alter cytokine production (IFN-γ, IL-17, IL-4), proliferation, or apoptosis of mature γδ T cells.
- Mechanistically, loss of ALKBH5 promotes the expansion and proliferation of γδ T cell precursors (including DN2/DN3 stage cells, TCRδ+ Vγ1.1+, TCRδ+ Vγ2+, and γδNKT subsets) starting during embryonic development (as early as E14.5).
- ALKBH5 deficiency increases m6A RNA modification levels on Jagged1 and Notch2 mRNAs, leading to their reduced stability and expression. This suppresses Jagged1/Notch2 signaling in γδ T cell precursors, which in turn enhances the proliferation and differentiation of γδ T cells.
- RNA-seq analysis revealed approximately 698 differentially expressed genes in ALKBH5-deficient γδ T cell progenitors (339 down-regulated, 359 up-regulated), with Jagged1 being the most markedly down-regulated gene. Notch signaling was among the most substantially reduced pathways.
- The Jagged1/Notch2 pathway dysregulation was specific to γδ T cell precursors, not mature γδ T cells.
- Validation with Jagged1f/f Lck-Cre mice confirmed that Jagged1 inactivation phenocopies the γδ T cell expansion observed in ALKBH5-deficient mice.

CONCLUSION: The study establishes that ALKBH5 and m6A RNA modification serve as a developmental checkpoint in the decision between αβ T and γδ T cell lineages, regulating γδ T cell early development through targeted suppression of Jagged1/Notch2 signaling.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504)Abstract

N 6-methyladenosine (m 6 A) is one of the most universal, abundant and conserved types of internal post-transcriptional modifications in eukaryotic RNA, and is involved in nuclear RNA export, RNA splicing, mRNA stability, gene expression, microRNA biogenesis and long non-coding RNA metabolism. AlkB homologue 5 (ALKBH5) acts as a m 6 A demethylase to regulate a wide variety of biological processes closely associated with tumour progression, tumour metastasis, tumour immunity and tumour drug resistance. ALKBH5 serves a crucial role in human digestive system tumours, mainly through post-transcriptional regulation of m 6 A modification. The present review discusses progress in the study of the m 6 A demethylase ALKBH5 in gastrointestinal tract cancer, summarizes the potential molecular mechanisms of ALKBH5 dysregulation in gastrointestinal tract cancer, and discusses the significance of ALKBH5-targeted therapy, which may provide novel ideas for future clinical prognosis prediction, biomarker identification and precise treatment.

**Key words:**m 6 A, ALKBH5, RNA demethylation, gastrointestinal tract cancer, therapeutic target

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504)Introduction

1.
In total, >100 RNA modifications (termed the epitranscriptome) are currently known in living organisms, and are involved in various biological processes that are associated with multiple functions, including adipogenesis, stem cell differentiation and the heat shock response ([1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b1-ijmm-55-02-05463),[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b2-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Methylation of the N 6 position of adenosine was first identified in eukaryotic mRNAs in the 1970s. This modified base is referred to as N 6-methyladenosine (m 6 A) ([3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b3-ijmm-55-02-05463),[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b4-ijmm-55-02-05463)). m 6 A has been found to be a prevalent and abundant internal modification of a wide range of RNAs, including but not restricted to mRNAs, transfer RNAs, ribosomal RNAs, microRNAs (miRNAs/miRs) and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) ([5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b5-ijmm-55-02-05463)).

m 6 A serves a role in physiological and pathological processes. m 6 A is involved in growth and development ([6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b6-ijmm-55-02-05463)), DNA damage repair ([7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b7-ijmm-55-02-05463)), and osteogenic differentiation ([8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b8-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The dysregulation of pathways controlled by m 6 A modification may be a key factor in diabetes ([9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b9-ijmm-55-02-05463)), autoimmune diseases ([10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b10-ijmm-55-02-05463)), tumours ([11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b11-ijmm-55-02-05463)) and other diseases. Changes in m 6 A levels are associated with various cellular processes ([12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b12-ijmm-55-02-05463)), removal and recognition of m 6 A modifications on transcripts can affect nuclear RNA export ([13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b13-ijmm-55-02-05463)), RNA splicing ([14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b14-ijmm-55-02-05463)), mRNA stability ([15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b15-ijmm-55-02-05463)), miRNA biogenesis ([16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b16-ijmm-55-02-05463)), lncRNA metabolism ([17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b17-ijmm-55-02-05463)) and circular RNA (circRNA/circ) stability ([18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b18-ijmm-55-02-05463)). m 6 A modification, a dynamic and reversible RNA modification, is regulated by three types of molecules, namely writers, readers and erasers. m 6 A methyltransferases (writers) are responsible for adding m 6 A modifications; m 6 A recognition proteins (readers) are responsible for recognizing and binding m 6 A-modified transcripts; and demethylases (erasers) are responsible for removing m 6 A modifications ([19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b19-ijmm-55-02-05463)) ([Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#f1-ijmm-55-02-05463)).

m 6 A writers consist of multiple components, including methyltransferase like (METTL)3, METTL14 and Wilms' tumour-associated protein (WTAP) ([20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b20-ijmm-55-02-05463)). METTL3 and METTL14 perform mammalian cellular m 6 A methylation-related functions by forming a stable METTL3/METTL14 heterodimer ([21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b21-ijmm-55-02-05463)). WTAP colocalizes with this complex and interacts with the complex to influence its m 6 A methylation activity, acting as a regulatory subunit ([20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b20-ijmm-55-02-05463),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b21-ijmm-55-02-05463)). These were the earliest known m 6 A methylases, and novel m 6 A writers have since been identified; these include METTL16 ([22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b22-ijmm-55-02-05463)), METTL4 ([23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b23-ijmm-55-02-05463)), METTL5 ([24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b24-ijmm-55-02-05463)), RNA-binding motif protein 15 ([25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b25-ijmm-55-02-05463)), zinc finger CCCH-type containing 13 ([26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b26-ijmm-55-02-05463)), zinc finger CCHC-type containing 4 ([27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b27-ijmm-55-02-05463)) and vir-like m 6 A methyltransferase-associated protein (also known as KIAA1429) ([28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b28-ijmm-55-02-05463)), which are jointly involved in the regulation of RNA methylation. The YT521-B homology (YTH) family of proteins were the first readers to be identified, and there are five proteins carrying the YTH structural domains in the human genome, which are divided into nuclear [YTH N6-methyladenosine RNA binding protein (YTHD)C1] and cytoplasmic m 6 A readers (YTHDF1, YTHDF2, YTHDF3 and YTHDC2) ([29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b29-ijmm-55-02-05463)). There are also other m 6 A-recognizing proteins, such as heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs) ([30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b30-ijmm-55-02-05463)), namely heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein A2/B1 (HNRNPA2B1), heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C (HNRNPC), heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein G and insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA binding protein 1/2/3 (IGF2BP1/2/3) ([31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b31-ijmm-55-02-05463)).

Fat mass and obesity-associated protein (FTO) was recognized as the first m 6 A mRNA demethylase, and the identification of FTO defined the concept of reversible RNA modification ([32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b32-ijmm-55-02-05463),[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b33-ijmm-55-02-05463)). A second m 6 A eraser, AlkB homologue 5 (ALKBH5), was subsequently identified ([34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b34-ijmm-55-02-05463)). FTO and ALKBH5 both belong to the AlkB family of non-heme Fe(II)/α-ketoglutaric acid (α-KG)-dependent dioxygenases ([35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b35-ijmm-55-02-05463)). They have a function opposite to that of writers; they catalyse the oxidative demethylation of m 6 A in RNA to remove the m 6 A modification from RNA ([32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b32-ijmm-55-02-05463),[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b34-ijmm-55-02-05463),[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b36-ijmm-55-02-05463)). m 6 A acts as a 'conformational marker' that induces major overall conformational changes in RNA, thereby regulating the substrate specificity of the m 6 A demethylases FTO and ALKBH5 ([37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b37-ijmm-55-02-05463)). In terms of substrate selection, FTO tends to catalyse the 3-methylthymine modification of single-stranded DNAs (ssDNAs), the 3-methyluracil modification of single-stranded RNAs (ssRNAs) and the m 6 A modification of ssRNAs ([32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b32-ijmm-55-02-05463),[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b38-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The unique loop in FTO (residues 210-223) and the short loop between β2 and β3 (residues 85-88) contribute to the recognition of the sequence and structure of the RNA substrate. Compared with FTO, ALKBH5 has a different structural conformation at this position when it binds to nucleic acids, and thus, has a more stringent substrate selection preference, catalysing only m 6 A ssDNA and m 6 A ssRNA modifications ([34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b34-ijmm-55-02-05463),[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b38-ijmm-55-02-05463)-[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b40-ijmm-55-02-05463)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504)ALKBH5

2.
Chen _et al_ ([41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b41-ijmm-55-02-05463)), Aik _et al_ ([35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b35-ijmm-55-02-05463)), Feng _et al_ ([40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b40-ijmm-55-02-05463)) and Xu _et al_ ([42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b42-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported the crystal structures of zebrafish ALKBH5 and human ALKBH5, which improved the understanding of the substrate selectivity and different demethylation mechanisms of AlkB family proteins. Zhou and Han ([36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b36-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported the cloning, protein expression and purification, crystallization, and X-ray data collection of ALKBH5 to provide insights into the potential mechanism of its specific substrate selection. Purslow _et al_ ([43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b43-ijmm-55-02-05463)) examined the conformational dynamics of ALKBH5 in solution, providing the first atomic-resolution model of the ALKBH5 protein in its disordered conformational state. The aforementioned study provides biochemical data support for the future analysis of the conformational dynamics of ALKBH5 in determining its activity and selectivity.

ALKBH5 belongs to the non-heme Fe(II)/α-KG-dependent dioxygenase AlkB family of proteins, and the human AlkB family has nine members, including ALKBH1-8 and FTO ([44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b44-ijmm-55-02-05463)). α-KG-dependent dioxygenases are an extended superfamily of enzymes that catalyse a wide range of oxidative reactions; these enzymes share the same double-stranded β-helical core fold (DSBH fold), although they act on different substrates and have conserved 2-oxoglutarate (2OG; also known as α-KG) and Fe 2+ binding sites ([45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b45-ijmm-55-02-05463),[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b46-ijmm-55-02-05463)). ALKBH5, similar to other AlkB family proteins, binds 2OG and a metal cofactor (Fe 2+) in a conserved manner ([35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b35-ijmm-55-02-05463),[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b42-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The core of the ALKBH5 catalytic structural domain consists of the typical conserved DSBH fold, which consists of a total of 11 β-strands and 7 α-helices ([42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b42-ijmm-55-02-05463)) ([Fig. 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#f2-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The different substrate specificities of different AlkB proteins are determined by the composition of the external secondary structural elements of the conserved DSBH fold, with the most notable structural difference being the so-called 'nucleotide recognition lid', which is unique to the AlkB protein subfamily ([47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b47-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The cap region is further classified into two sections, Flip1 (residues 117-129) and Flip2 (residues 136-165) ([48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b48-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Compared with those of ALKBH2 and FTO, the Flip1 region of ALKBH5 has an uncovered and relatively large space in the active site, and the Flip2 region is highly flexible ([42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b42-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The unique composition and conformation of these regions may confer unique substrate-selective features to ALKBH5 ([40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b40-ijmm-55-02-05463)). In addition, the unique disulfide bond structure (between residues Cys-230 and Cys-267) of ALKBH5 is highly conserved only among different species of ALKBH5 proteins, which prevents double-stranded DNA and double-stranded RNA from accessing the active site of ALKBH5 and determines the binding preference of ALKBH5 for single-stranded substrates ([40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b40-ijmm-55-02-05463),[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b42-ijmm-55-02-05463)).

Endogenous ALKBH5 is predominantly found in the nucleus, where it colocalizes with nuclear speckles, and is less abundant in the cytoplasm ([34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b34-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Nuclear speckles are integrally regulated nuclear bodies that promote gene expression, and >30 nuclear speckled proteins serve crucial roles in both transcription and splicing ([49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b49-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The demethylation activity of ALKBH5 affects mRNA export, RNA splicing, mRNA stability, gene expression and the assembly of mRNA processing factors in nuclear speckles ([34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b34-ijmm-55-02-05463),[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b50-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Under normal physiological conditions, ALKBH5 is highly expressed in the lungs, followed by the testis, pancreas, spleen and ovaries ([51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b51-ijmm-55-02-05463)). ALKBH5 serves a key role in meiosis, and has been found to participate in spermatogenesis ([34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b34-ijmm-55-02-05463)), skeletal muscle development ([52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b52-ijmm-55-02-05463)), learning and memory ([53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b53-ijmm-55-02-05463)), and other biological behaviours. ALKBH5 is involved in osteoarthritis ([54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b54-ijmm-55-02-05463)), pulmonary fibrosis ([55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b55-ijmm-55-02-05463)), stroke ([56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b56-ijmm-55-02-05463)), systemic lupus erythematosus ([57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b57-ijmm-55-02-05463)) and diabetes ([58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b58-ijmm-55-02-05463)) as an important biomolecule. In addition, ALKBH5 is closely associated with a variety of tumours.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504)Dual role of the ALKBH5 gene in digestive tract tumours

3.
ALKBH5 has been extensively studied in a variety of tumours, such as glioblastoma (GBM) ([59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b59-ijmm-55-02-05463)), head and neck squamous cell carcinoma ([60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b60-ijmm-55-02-05463)), colorectal cancer (CRC) ([61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b61-ijmm-55-02-05463)), ovarian carcinoma ([62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b62-ijmm-55-02-05463)), cervical cancer ([63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b63-ijmm-55-02-05463)), acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) ([64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b64-ijmm-55-02-05463)), breast cancer ([65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b65-ijmm-55-02-05463)), melanoma ([66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b66-ijmm-55-02-05463)), hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) ([67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b67-ijmm-55-02-05463)), and lung cancer ([68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b68-ijmm-55-02-05463)), and serves a role in tumour growth ([69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b69-ijmm-55-02-05463)), tumour metastasis ([70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b70-ijmm-55-02-05463)), tumour immunity ([71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b71-ijmm-55-02-05463)), tumour drug resistance ([62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b62-ijmm-55-02-05463)) and tumour metabolism ([72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b72-ijmm-55-02-05463)). ALKBH5 has been shown to act through several important pathways, including the PI3K/AKT ([73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b73-ijmm-55-02-05463)), Janus kinase 1 (JAK1)/STAT3 ([74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b74-ijmm-55-02-05463)), Wnt ([75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b75-ijmm-55-02-05463)), NF-κB ([76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b76-ijmm-55-02-05463)) and mTOR ([77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b77-ijmm-55-02-05463)) pathways. However, the potential mechanism of ALKBH5 in cancer has not been fully investigated and is controversial. ALKBH5 serves dual roles in different types of cancer as either a tumour promoter or a tumour suppressor ([78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b78-ijmm-55-02-05463),[79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b79-ijmm-55-02-05463)) and occasionally serves both pro- and antigenic roles in the same type of cancer ([67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b67-ijmm-55-02-05463),[80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b80-ijmm-55-02-05463)) ([Fig. 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#f3-ijmm-55-02-05463); [Table SI](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#SD1-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The molecular mechanism of ALKBH5 needs to be further investigated.

The present review focuses on the research progress regarding the role of ALKBH5 in digestive system tumours, paying attention to the regulatory roles of different targets of ALKBH5, as well as the current research status of small-molecule inhibitors targeting ALKBH5.

### Oesophageal cancer (OC)

OC is a highly malignant tumour of the digestive system, and most cases are diagnosed at advanced stages, resulting in a high recurrence rate and poor prognosis ([81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b81-ijmm-55-02-05463)). OC is the eighth most commonly diagnosed cancer and the sixth most common cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide ([82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b82-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The incidence and mortality rates of OC vary by sex, and it is more common in male patients than in female patients ([82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b82-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The major histologic subtypes of OC include oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and oesophageal adenocarcinoma, of which OSCC is the most common squamous-cell carcinoma ([83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b83-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Currently, the biological role and regulatory mechanism of ALKBH5 in OC have been less well studied than those in other digestive system cancers, and research progress is relatively limited ([73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b73-ijmm-55-02-05463),[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b84-ijmm-55-02-05463)-[90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b90-ijmm-55-02-05463)).

Reduced ALKBH5 expression, which is frequently detected in OC tissues, accelerates OC cell proliferation, migration and invasion ([91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b91-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Chen _et al_ ([92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b92-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported that ALKBH5 inhibited miR-194-2 through m 6 A demethylation, promoted RAI1 expression, activated the Hippo signalling pathway and inhibited Yes associated protein/tafazzin function to prevent the malignant behaviour of OC. Xue _et al_ ([93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b93-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported a positive feedback loop between miR-193a-3p and ALKBH5, which decreased the expression of ALKBH5 in OC, and promoted the growth and metastasis of OC. Qiao _et al_ ([94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b94-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported that serine hydroxymethyltransferase 2 regulated the stability of c-myc mRNA through METTL3/FTO/ALKBH5/IGF2BP2-mediated m 6 A modification, thereby promoting the malignant progression of OC with immune escape.

Some researchers have proposed the opposite, suggesting that ALKBH5 promotes the progression of OC and acts as a tumour-promoting factor ([95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b95-ijmm-55-02-05463),[96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b96-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Nagaki _et al_ ([95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b95-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported that ALKBH5 downregulated p21 expression and regulated the cell cycle to promote the proliferation of OC cells. At present, the mechanisms of m 6 A modification and regulation of lncRNAs in tumours are as follows: m 6 A can cause structural remodelling of lncRNAs, thus affecting the interaction of lncRNAs with proteins regulating RNA-protein interactions ([97](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b97-ijmm-55-02-05463)); m 6 A promotes transcriptional repression induced by lncRNAs ([25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b25-ijmm-55-02-05463)); lncRNAs act as competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs) under m 6 A modification regulation, regulating miRNA expression and biological functions ([98](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b98-ijmm-55-02-05463)); and m 6 A is involved in regulating the stability of lncRNA transcripts ([96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b96-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Wu _et al_ ([96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b96-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported that ALKBH5 stabilized the lncRNA CASC8 transcript and induced the upregulation of the lncRNA CASC8, which activated the Bcl2/caspase3 pathway by stabilizing the expression of heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein L, thus promoting the progression of OC and reducing the sensitivity of OC cells to cisplatin.

### Gastric cancer (GC)

GC is one of the most important malignant tumours globally and is characterized by high lethality ([99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b99-ijmm-55-02-05463)). GC ranks fifth in global incidence and fourth in mortality among all cancer types, with an incidence rate in men that is twice as high as that in women ([82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b82-ijmm-55-02-05463),[100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b100-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The World Health Organization histologic classification of GC includes stomach adenocarcinoma, gastric squamous cell carcinoma, gastric adenosquamous carcinoma, gastric undifferentiated carcinoma, gastroblastoma and gastric neuroendocrine neoplasms, with the vast majority of GCs being adenocarcinomas ([83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b83-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Emerging studies have reported the important role of m 6 A modifications in GC, and the molecular mechanisms of dysregulated m 6 A modifications and abnormalities in GC have received increasing attention; however, the function of ALKBH5 in GC remains controversial ([70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b70-ijmm-55-02-05463),[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b84-ijmm-55-02-05463),[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b85-ijmm-55-02-05463),[101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b101-ijmm-55-02-05463)).

ALKBH5 is commonly highly expressed in GC, and high ALKBH5 expression promotes the proliferation, invasion and migration of GC cells both _in vivo_ and _in vitro_ ([78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b78-ijmm-55-02-05463),[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b84-ijmm-55-02-05463),[102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b102-ijmm-55-02-05463)). High ALKBH5 expression is related to a poor prognosis in patients with GC ([74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b74-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Bioinformatics analysis revealed that ALKBH5 may be a key gene influencing the immune microenvironment of GC and regulating the progression of GC ([103](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b103-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Specifically, with respect to the molecular mechanism, the upregulation of ALKBH5 expression in GC is involved in the invasion and migration of GC cells through the regulation of the lncRNA NEAT1, which acts as a scaffold and affects the expression of downstream genes by regulating enhancer of zeste 2 polycomb repressive complex 2 subunit ([84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b84-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Wang _et al_ ([85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b85-ijmm-55-02-05463)) showed that the lncRNA NRON interacts with ALKBH5 to increase the mRNA stability and expression of Nanog, which serves an oncogenic role in GC. Fang _et al_ ([104](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b104-ijmm-55-02-05463)) found that ALKBH5 suppressed the m 6 A modification of the lncRNA TP53TG1, reduced lncRNA TP53TG1 stability, inhibited the binding of the lncRNA TP53TG1 to cellular inhibitor of PP2A and its ubiquitination-mediated degradation, and promoted the activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway, thereby promoting GC progression. ALKBH5, which is regulated by long-integrated non-coding (LINC)00659, upregulates JAK1 expression, activates the JAK1/STAT3 pathway, and promotes the proliferation and migration of GC cells ([74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b74-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Chen _et al_ ([78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b78-ijmm-55-02-05463)) found that ALKBH5 downregulated ChaC glutathione specific gamma-glutamylcyclotransferase 1 expression by erasing the m 6 A modification, disrupted reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis in GC, attenuated the chemosensitivity of GC cells, and promoted GC development and metastasis. Exposure to the environmental carcinogen N-nitroso compounds activates ALKBH5-zinc finger with KRAB and SCAN domains 3-YTHDF2-VEGFA signalling, promoting malignant progression of GC ([102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b102-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Upregulation of ALKBH5 expression enhances circFOXP1 expression by mediating the m 6 A modification level of circFOXP1 in GC, thereby regulating SOX4 expression and miR-338-3p to promote the progression of GC ([105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b105-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Suo _et al_ ([106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b106-ijmm-55-02-05463)) noted that the heat shock protein family A (Hsp70) member 4/ALKBH5/CD58 axis reduced cytotoxicity of CD8+T cell, inducing immune escape in GC cells.

However, it has also been reported that ALKBH5 expression is decreased in GC and that high ALKBH5 expression can predict a favourable prognosis, inhibit GC carcinogenesis and metastasis, and act as a tumour suppressor ([70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b70-ijmm-55-02-05463),[101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b101-ijmm-55-02-05463),[107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b107-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Bioinformatics analysis revealed that ALKBH5 serves an antitumour role in GC and is a potential prognostic marker and immunotherapy target for GC ([101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b101-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Hu _et al_ ([70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b70-ijmm-55-02-05463)) found that ALKBH5-IGF2BP3 upregulated the expression of PKMYT1 in an m 6 A-dependent manner, inhibiting the invasion and migration of GC cells. ALKBH5 negatively regulates YY1, thereby inhibiting the activation of the autophagy related 4B cysteine peptidase-dependent autophagy pathway and serving a protective role in GC development ([107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b107-ijmm-55-02-05463)).

### CRC

CRC is the third most prevalent cancer worldwide and the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths ([82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b82-ijmm-55-02-05463)). It is the second most common type of cancer diagnosed in women and the third most common type of cancer in men ([82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b82-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The onset of CRC is insidious, with symptoms often not presenting until it reaches an advanced stage, and effective cancer screening measures can reduce the incidence and mortality of CRC ([108](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b108-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Although research on CRC has made great progress, the specific molecular mechanisms that influence tumorigenesis and development remain elusive. Numerous studies have reported that ALKBH5-mediated m 6 A modification serves a role in CRC progression ([61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b61-ijmm-55-02-05463),[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b69-ijmm-55-02-05463),[109](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b109-ijmm-55-02-05463),[110](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b110-ijmm-55-02-05463)).

Histologic subtypes of CRC include colorectal adenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine tumours, with colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) being the most common type ([83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b83-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Bioinformatics analysis revealed that ALKBH5 expression is downregulated in CRC, downregulation of ALKBH5 is associated with distant metastasis and the clinicopathological features of CRC and high ALKBH5 expression enhances immune infiltration ([111](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b111-ijmm-55-02-05463)). ALKBH5, which acts as a tumour suppressor in CRC ([111](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b111-ijmm-55-02-05463),[112](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b112-ijmm-55-02-05463)), has been suggested to be independently associated with prognosis. ALKBH5 can suppress the growth and metastasis of CRC through various pathways and molecular mechanisms. For example, Zhang _et al_ ([109](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b109-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported that ALKBH5 targeted the PHD finger protein 20 (PHF20) m 6 A modification, downregulated PHF20 expression and inhibited CRC progression. Luo _et al_ ([110](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b110-ijmm-55-02-05463)) found that ALKBH5 removed the m 6 A modification of solute carrier family 7 member 11 mRNA and suppressed its transcription, and that upregulation of ALKBH5 expression promoted ROS release and ferroptosis in CRC. ALKBH5 can also promote CD8+ T-cell infiltration in the CRC tumour microenvironment via the NF-κB-C-C motif chemokine ligand 5 axis, attenuating the malignant behaviour of CRC ([113](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b113-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Furthermore, Wu _et al_ ([114](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b114-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported that ALKBH5 inhibited the proliferation and migration of CRC cells, and exerted antitumour effects by regulating the FOXO3-miR-21-sprouty RTK signaling antagonist 2 axis. Yan _et al_ ([115](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b115-ijmm-55-02-05463)) revealed that ALKBH5 and YTHDF1 might affect the immune architecture of COAD and that high ALKBH5 expression with low YTHDF expression might enhance the infiltration of immune cells and improve the immunotherapeutic efficacy of patients with colorectal adenocarcinoma. ALKBH5 can also serve a tumour suppressor role in CRC by regulating the tumour glycolysis pathway, downregulating the expression of jumonji domain containing 8 in an m 6 A-dependent manner, and inhibiting glycolysis by suppressing the enzymatic activity of pyruvate kinase M1/2 ([86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b86-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Ye _et al_ ([116](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b116-ijmm-55-02-05463)) demonstrated that in obese patients with CRC, the downregulation of ALKBH5 and FTO synergistically negatively regulated the expression of hexokinase 2 (HK2), a key enzyme in glycolysis, in an m 6 A-IGF2BP2-dependent manner, activating the FOXO signalling pathway and promoting glucose metabolism, which in turn increased the proliferative capacity of CRC cells. Ye _et al_ ([87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b87-ijmm-55-02-05463)) demonstrated that the ALKBH5-fatty acid binding protein 5 (FABP5)-fatty acid synthase-mTOR axis inhibited tumour progression by affecting lipid metabolism and autophagy in CRC. Shao _et al_ ([117](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b117-ijmm-55-02-05463)) revealed that ALKBH5 increased the sensitivity of CRC cells to radiotherapy and that the ALKBH5-circAFF2-YTHDF2-cullin associated and neddylation dissociated 1-Cullin1/NEDD8 axis was a potential chemotherapeutic target for CRC. ALKBH5 is downregulated in mutant p53-induced CRC and promotes CRC progression through the p53-ALKBH5-lncRNA CARMN-YTHDF2/YTHDF3-miR-5683-fibroblast growth factor 2-Akt/mTOR pathway ([118](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b118-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Feng _et al_ ([119](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b119-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported that ALKBH5 could affect the immunosuppressive function of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) in CRC by regulating arginase 1 expression, and could inhibit the progression of CRC.

However, Zhai _et al_ ([61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b61-ijmm-55-02-05463)) concluded that high ALKBH5 expression was related to a poor prognosis in CRC and that ALKBH5 acted as a proto-oncogene in CRC. The authors reported that ALKBH5 and IGF2BP1 decreased axin 2 expression in an m 6 A-dependent manner and facilitated the activation of the Wnt/β-catenin signalling pathway via the expression of dickkopf WNT signaling pathway inhibitor 1, which induced the accumulation of suppressive MDSCs in CRC, and decreased the antitumour activity of natural killer and CD8+ T cells. Furthermore, Shen _et al_ ([69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b69-ijmm-55-02-05463)) showed that ALKBH5 increased RAB5A expression in an m 6 A-YTHDF2-mediated manner, promoting the proliferation and invasion of CRC cells. Guo _et al_ ([120](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b120-ijmm-55-02-05463)) revealed that ALKBH5 upregulated lncRNA NEAT1 expression in colon cancer through methylation and promoted colon cancer progression. Fatty acid anabolism is considered to be related to prostate cancer ([121](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b121-ijmm-55-02-05463)), glioblastoma ([122](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b122-ijmm-55-02-05463)), ovarian cancer ([123](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b123-ijmm-55-02-05463)), lung cancer ([124](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b124-ijmm-55-02-05463)), breast cancer ([125](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b125-ijmm-55-02-05463)) and liver cancer ([126](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b126-ijmm-55-02-05463)) and is known as a novel therapeutic target. Sun _et al_ ([127](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b127-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported that ALKBH5 upregulated the expression of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A by removing its m 6 A modification, and promoted macrophage fatty acid metabolism with alternatively activated M2 macrophage polarization, accelerating the malignant progression of CRC. ALKBH5 increases the expression of Bet1 golgi vesicular membrane trafficking protein like (BET1L) in an m 6 A-mediated manner, and BET1L participates in the tumorigenesis and progression of CRC by regulating the steroid biosynthesis-related pathway ([128](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b128-ijmm-55-02-05463)).

### Liver cancer and gallbladder cancer (GBC)

Primary liver cancer is one of the most common malignancies of the digestive system, the sixth most common type of cancer and the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide ([82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b82-ijmm-55-02-05463)). The incidence of liver cancer differs between sexes. The incidence and mortality rates in men are 2 to 3-fold higher than those in women. In men, liver cancer ranks fifth in terms of incidence rate and second in terms of mortality rate among tumours ([82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b82-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Primary liver cancer includes HCC and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC), as well as other rare types. HCC is the most common primary malignancy of the liver, accounting for >80% of all liver cancer cases, and has a high mortality rate ([129](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b129-ijmm-55-02-05463)). An increasing number of studies have reported the dysregulation of the m 6 A modification in HCC and the regulatory mechanisms of m 6 A-related molecules, revealing the role of m 6 A in HCC ([67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b67-ijmm-55-02-05463),[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b73-ijmm-55-02-05463),[88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b88-ijmm-55-02-05463),[130](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b130-ijmm-55-02-05463)).

ALKBH5 has been identified as a tumour suppressor in HCC, suppresses tumour growth and metastasis in HCC, and is a prognostic factor in HCC, predicting favourable clinical outcomes ([67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b67-ijmm-55-02-05463),[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b73-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Chen _et al_ ([67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b67-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported that ALKBH5-IGF2BP1-mediated m 6 A modification led to post-transcriptional repression of LY6/PLAUR domain containing 1 (LYPD1) and that dysregulation of the ALKBH5/LYPD1 axis promoted the malignant behaviour of HCC cells. ALKBH5, together with IGF2BP1, downregulates the expression of progestin and AdipoQ Receptor family member 4 in an m 6 A-dependent manner and inhibits the activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway, thereby suppressing the malignant progression of HCC cells ([73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b73-ijmm-55-02-05463)). Zhang _et al_ ([131](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b131-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported that ALKBH5 in HCC regulated the decay of lncRNA LINC02551 mediated by IGF2BP1 recognition in an m 6 A-dependent manner, reduced the expression of the lncRNA LINC02551 and facilitated the degradation of DEAD-box helicase 24, thereby inhibiting epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in HCC. With the global increase in type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is becoming an increasingly significant risk factor for HCC ([132](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b132-ijmm-55-02-05463)). ALKBH5 promotes the expression of the lncRNA LINC01468, which mediates lipid metabolism, and promotes chemoresistance and tumour progression in NAFLD-associated HCC ([133](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b133-ijmm-55-02-05463)). ALKBH5, as a tumour suppressor, regulates ubiquitin protein ligase E3 component n-recognin 7 (UBR7) in an m 6 A-dependent manner, and UBR7 inhibits aerobic glycolysis in HCC cells by regulating the Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1-nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2-BTB domain and CNC homolog 1-HK2 axi ([134](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b134-ijmm-55-02-05463)).

However, some studies have reported an opposite role for ALKBH5. You _et al_ ([88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b88-ijmm-55-02-05463)) revealed that ALKBH5 promoted the proliferation, invasion and migration of HCC cells via the ALKBH5-MAP3K8 axis, and facilitated the activation of the ERK/JNK signalling pathway to regulate the recruitment of macrophages expressing programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1). Chang _et al_ ([130](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11637504#b130-ijmm-55-02-05463)) reported that ALKBH5 affected HCC progression by positively regulating TELO2 interacting protein 1. args.summary:
This is a scientific review article published in the International Journal of Molecular Medicine (2024 Nov 25;55(2):22, doi: 10.3892/ijmm.2024.5463) titled "Role of the m6A demethylase ALKBH5 in gastrointestinal tract cancer (Review)" by Lumiao Zhang, Mengjia Jing, Qianben Song, Yiming Ouyang, Yingzhi Pang, Xilin Ye, and Yu Fu and Wei Yan from the Department of Gastroenterology at Tongji Hospital and Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China.

The article reviews the role of ALKBH5 (AlkB homologue 5), a m6A (N6-methyladenosine) demethylase, in gastrointestinal tract cancers. Key background: m6A is a prevalent and conserved post-transcriptional RNA modification involved in nuclear RNA export, RNA splicing, mRNA stability, gene expression, microRNA biogenesis, and lncRNA metabolism. m6A modification is regulated by writers (methyltransferases such as METTL3, METTL14, WTAP and others), readers (YTH family proteins, hnRNPs, IGF2BP1/2/3), and erasers (demethylases FTO and ALKBH5). Both FTO and ALKBH5 belong to the AlkB family of non-heme Fe(II)/α-KG-dependent dioxygenases. ALKBH5 has a more stringent substrate selection than FTO, catalysing only m6A modifications on single-stranded nucleic acids. Structurally, ALKBH5 contains a conserved DSBH fold (11 β-strands, 7 α-helices), unique Flip1 (residues 117-129) and Flip2 (residues 136-165) nucleotide recognition regions, and a unique disulfide bond (Cys-230/Cys-267) that restricts access to double-stranded substrates. ALKBH5 is predominantly nuclear, colocalizing with nuclear speckles, and is highly expressed in the lungs, testis, pancreas, spleen, and ovaries.

A central theme is ALKBH5's DUAL role in digestive tract tumors—acting as either a tumor promoter or tumor suppressor, sometimes even both within the same cancer type. The review examines its role specifically in:

1. **Esophageal cancer (OC)**: Generally understudied. Reduced ALKBH5 accelerates OC cell proliferation/migration/invasion (tumor suppressor role). It inhibits miR-194-2, promotes RAI1/Hippo pathway, and prevents malignant behavior. However, some studies report ALKBH5 promotes OC progression—downregulating p21 to promote proliferation and stabilizing lncRNA CASC8 to activate Bcl2/caspase3 pathway and reduce cisplatin sensitivity.

2. **Gastric cancer (GC)**: ALKBH5 is commonly highly expressed and promotes proliferation/invasion/migration via multiple mechanisms (lncRNA NEAT1, NRON/Nanog, TP53TG1, JAK1/STAT3 pathway, circFOXP1, and immune escape via HSPA4/ALKBH5/CD58 axis reducing CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity). However, other reports show ALKBH5 can also act as a tumor suppressor predicting favorable prognosis, inhibiting invasion/migration (e.g., via IGF2BP3/PKMYT1 regulation and negative regulation of YY1 to inhibit autophagy).

3. **Colorectal cancer (CRC)**: ALKBH5 expression is typically downregulated and acts as a tumor suppressor—inhibiting growth/metastasis via targeting PHF20, promoting ferroptosis by removing m6A from SLC7A11, promoting CD8+ T-cell infiltration via NF-κB-CCL5 axis, regulating FOXO3-miR-21 axis, inhibiting glycolysis, and affecting lipid metabolism/autophagy. However, other studies report ALKBH5 as a proto-oncogene promoting poor prognosis, including via AXIN2/Wnt-β-catenin signaling, RAB5A enhancement, lncRNA NEAT1, and M2 macrophage polarization.

4. **Liver cancer/HCC**: ALKBH5 is generally identified as a tumor suppressor (regulating LYPD1, PAQR4, LINC02551, UBR7). However, other studies show it promotes proliferation/invasion/migration via the ALKBH5-MAP3K8 axis and ERK/JNK signaling, and promotes chemoresistance in NAFLD-associated HCC via LINC01468.

The review emphasizes that ALKBH5's potential molecular mechanisms in GI tract cancer are controversial and require further investigation, and discusses the significance of ALKBH5-targeted therapy, which may provide novel ideas for clinical prognosis prediction, biomarker identification, and precise treatment.

## Abstract

Pancreatic cancer has emerged as one of the most lethal malignancies, characterized by rising morbidity and mortality rates. Research has demonstrated that N6-methyladenosine (m 6 A) modification of RNA significantly influences RNA metabolism, and dysregulation of m 6 A is implicated in various human diseases. A clearer picture of how the divergent m 6 A methylation patterns affect immunological microenvironment in pancreatic cancer is still unknown. Based on an analysis of RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from the TCGA, GEO, and GTEx databases, we predicted and validated the expression of YTHDF2. Apoptosis and cell cycle analyses of YTHDF2 were conducted using flow cytometry, and a subcutaneous transplantation tumor model was established in BALB/c nude mice. The immune infiltration status and Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) were employed to evaluate cellular immunity and identify downstream target genes associated with the CD8+ T cell module. Additionally, machine learning-based integrative approaches were utilized to generate a predictive signature. The Western blot technique was employed to quantify YTHDF2 expression levels in PDAC cell lines and tissues. WGCNA and PPI unveiled TFG as the core gene regulation network conducting the function of the CD8+ T cell. Quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) assays were conducted to confirm the reduction in TFG expression subsequent to YTHDF2 knockdown. Integrative analyses using large-scale genomic data sets were conducted to reveal that YTHDF2 could affect pancreatic cancer cell apoptosis and the cell cycle, promote malignant biologic processes, and gene regulation in immune cells. YTHDF2 potentially modulates crucial molecular subgroups of immune checkpoint molecules in CD8+ T cells, thereby enhancing tumor immunogenicity and promoting anti-tumor immune responses.

**Keywords:** Immune microenvironment; Molecular oncology; Pancreatic cancer; m(6)A.

args.summary:
This is a PubMed article abstract (PMID: 39288628) published in International Immunopharmacology (2024 Dec 5;142(Pt B):113079, DOI: 10.1016/j.intimp.2024.113079, Epub 2024 Sep 16) titled "m6A reader YTHDF2 orchestrates CD8+ T cell infiltration to promote pancreatic cancer progression and predicts clinical outcome." Authors: Zhen Tan, Faxian Hei, Kai Ma, Ziqiang Lv, Haowen Zhang, Ning Sun, Weidong Guo, Mengqi Song, affiliated with the Department of Hepatobiliary Pancreatic Surgery at The Affiliated Hospital of Qingdao University, Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center, and Shanghai Pancreatic Cancer Institute.

The study investigates the role of the m6A reader YTHDF2 in pancreatic cancer, which is characterized by rising morbidity and mortality. Researchers analyzed RNA-sequencing data from TCGA, GEO, and GTEx databases to predict and validate YTHDF2 expression. Methods included flow cytometry for apoptosis and cell cycle analysis, a subcutaneous transplantation tumor model in BALB/c nude mice, immune infiltration status assessment, Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) to identify downstream target genes associated with the CD8+ T cell module, machine learning-based predictive signature generation, Western blot for YTHDF2 quantification in PDAC cell lines and tissues, and qRT-PCR validation.

Key findings: WGCNA and protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis identified TFG as the core gene in the regulatory network conducting CD8+ T cell function. YTHDF2 knockdown reduced TFG expression. Integrative analyses revealed that YTHDF2 affects pancreatic cancer cell apoptosis and cell cycle, promotes malignant biologic processes and gene regulation in immune cells. YTHDF2 potentially modulates crucial molecular subgroups of immune checkpoint molecules in CD8+ T cells, enhancing tumor immunogenicity and promoting anti-tumor immune responses. Keywords: Immune microenvironment, Molecular oncology, Pancreatic cancer, m(6)A. The authors declare no competing interests. The article was cited by a 2026 Theranostics review on RNA Modifications in T cell Immunity.
