Finally, to investigate whether Ythdf2 deficiency in HSCs had any impact on their short-term reconstitution potential upon pIpC administration, we competitively transplanted equal numbers of HSCs from pIpC-treated Ythdf2CKO and Ythdf2CTL mice into lethally irradiated recipients (Fig. 4 F). HSCs lacking Ythdf2 displayed decreased short-term myeloid and B-lymphoid reconstitution capacity, indicating that inflammation tempo-rarily weakened Ythdf2-deficient HSC activity (Fig. 4 H). Thus, our data indicate that YTHDF2 is induced by inflammation in HSCs and suggest that YTHDF2 may function to protect HSCs from excessive proinflammatory signals. The mechanisms through which YTHDF2 is induced by inflammation, and its precise in-volvement in protecting HSCs in this context, remain important open questions meriting further investigations.
Collectively, YTHDF2 expression is induced in HSCs by in-flammatory stimuli and its deletion results in constitutive acti-vation of proinflammatory pathways, consistent with myeloid bias. While YTHDF2 is not essential for long-term steady-state unperturbed hematopoiesis upon aging, Ythdf2 deletion causes progressive HSC expansion and failure of HSCs to reconstitute multilineage hematopoiesis. Because the activation of inflam-matory pathways in HSCs by infections or injury causes their proliferation and myeloid cell production, but in the longer term compromises HSC activity (Esplin et al., 2011; Essers et al., 2009; Pietras, 2017; Takizawa et al., 2017), HSCs must use mechanisms to counteract these signals and protect their long-term integrity.
While several studies indicated that proinflammatory signals are suppressed in HSCs at different levels of gene expression, in-cluding cell signaling, gene transcription, and RNA editing (Hartner et al., 2009; King et al., 2011; Sato et al., 2009), the functional significance of dynamic RNA modifications in this important aspect of HSC biology remains poorly understood. We suggest that the m6A-dependent mRNA decay pathway is a novel mechanism through which HSCs suppress inflammation and sustain HSC integrity. Interrogation of up-regulated proin-flammatory genes upon Ythdf2 deficiency in genetic rescue ap-proaches is warranted to further support this notion. Given our findings that YTHDF2 itself is induced by inflammation, we suggest that YTHDF2 may function in a negative feedback loop to prevent an excessive inflammatory response detrimental to HSC function. Thus, our work sets the stage for further investigations focusing on how YTHDF2 regulates HSC fates during inflammation upon acute and chronic infection. In closing, our data position YTHDF2 as an essential repressor of proinflammatory pathways in HSCs and highlight the key significance of m6A mRNA modifica-tion in long-term HSC maintenance upon aging.
Materials and methods Mice All mice were on the C57BL/6 background (backcrossed for ≥10 generations). Ythdf2fl/fl, Vav-iCre, and Mx1-Cre strains have been described previously (de Boer et al., 2003; Ivanova et al., 2017; Kühn et al., 1995). Congenic recipient mice were CD45.1+/CD45.2+.
All experiments involving mice were performed under Uni-versity of Edinburgh Veterinary oversight with UK Home Of-fice authorization. All control mice were littermates, and treatment groups were randomized among littermates.
Flow cytometry BM and splenic cells were prepared and analyzed as described previously (Guitart et al., 2017; Guitart et al., 2013; Kranc et al., 2009; Mortensen et al., 2011; Paris et al., 2019; Vukovic et al., 2016). Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell staining began with incubation with Fc block followed by biotin-conjugated anti-Lineage marker antibodies (anti-CD4, anti-CD5, anti-CD8a, anti-CD11b, anti-B220, anti-Gr-1, and anti-Ter119), APC-conjugated anti-c-Kit,APC-Cy7–conjugated anti-Sca-1,PE-conjugated anti-CD48,and PE-Cy7–conjugated anti-CD150 antibodies. Biotin-conjugated lineage markers were then stained with PerCP-conjugated streptavi-din. Staining of MPP1–4 populations was performed as above for hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells; however, BV711-instead of APC-conjugated anti-c-Kit was used and cells were also stained with APC-conjugated anti-Flt3– and BV421-conjugated anti-CD34 antibodies.
For PB and differentiated cell analysis, cells were stained with PerCP-conjugated anti-B220, APC-Cy7–conjugated anti-CD19, Pacific Blue–conjugated anti-CD11b, PE-Cy7–conjugated anti-Gr-1, APC-conjugated anti-CD8, and PE-conjugated anti-CD4 antibodies. To distinguish CD45.2 chimerism in transplan-tation experiments, BV711-conjugated anti-CD45.1 and Pacific Blue–conjugated anti-CD45.2 antibodies were used. For hemato-poietic stem and progenitor cell staining in transplanted mice, APC-conjugated anti-c-Kit and APC-Cy7-conjugated anti-Sca-1 were used; the remainder of the staining was as described above. For analyses of differentiated cells and PB in transplanted mice, cell suspensions were stained with BV711-conjugated anti-CD45.1, Pacific Blue–conjugated anti-CD45.2, APC-conjugated anti-CD11b, PE-Cy7–conjugated anti-Gr-1, PE-conjugated anti-CD4 and -CD8a, and APC-Cy7–conjugated anti-CD19. Flow cytometry analyses were performed using a LSRFortessa (BD Biosciences). Cell sort-ing was performed on a FACSAria Fusion (BD Biosciences).
Intracellular staining and flow cytometry analysis BM and splenic cells were prepared and analyzed as described previously (Guitart et al., 2017; Guitart et al., 2013; Kranc et al., 2009; Mortensen et al., 2011; Paris et al., 2019; Vukovic et al., 2016) followed by c-Kit enrichment (described below). Cells were incubated with Fc block and stained with biotin-conjugated anti-Lineage marker antibodies (anti-CD4, anti-CD5, anti-CD8a, anti-CD11b, anti-B220, anti-Gr-1, and anti-Ter119), APC-Cy7–conjugated anti-c-Kit, and Pacific Blue–conjugated anti-Sca-1. Biotin-conjugated Lineage markers were then stained with PerCP-conjugated Streptavi-din. Cells were then fixed and permeabilized using Phosflow Lyse/Fix, Phosflow Perm Buffer III, and stain buffer (all from BD Biosciences) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After processing, cells were stained with AF647-conjugated anti-pStat1 or anti-pStat3.

pIpC administration For gene deletion via activation of the Mx1-Cre promotor, mice were injected i.p. every other day with 300 µg pIpC (GE Healthcare) for a total of six doses over 11 d, as previously de-scribed (Guitart et al., 2017; Guitart et al., 2013; Kranc et al., 2009; Paris et al., 2019), and gene deletion was assayed by YTHDF2-GFP fusion protein fluorescence. To test the effect of innate immune activation, mice were injected i.p. with 300 µg pIpC (GE Healthcare) as described per experiment.
CD117 (c-Kit) enrichment Enrichment for cells expressing CD117 (c-Kit) was performed using CD117 MicroBeads and LS columns from Miltenyi Biotec, according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Histology Tibias and femurs were dissected and cleaned before fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h. Fixed bones were decalcified, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned. Sections were stained with H&E and mounted. Whole sections were imaged using a Vectra Polaris slide scanner, and representative images were taken at 10× and 20× magnification.
RNA-seq 100 HSCs per sample were sorted into 0.4% Triton X-100, RNase inhibitor, 10 mM dNTPs, and 10 µM Oligo dT before RNA-seq by SMART-Seq2 in the Single Cell Genomics Facility at the Medical Research Council Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine (University of Oxford). Alignments to the GRCm38 mouse ge-nome were performed using HISAT2 (Kim et al., 2015), and further analysis was performed in R. Counts were assigned to genes using the Rsubread package, and quality control analysis of the samples was performed with the SingleCellExperiment and scater packages. Differentially expressed genes were iden-tified using likelihood ratio tests computed by the edgeR pack-age. The RNA-seq dataset was deposited in GEO (accession no.
GSE142019).
m6A meRIP-seq m6A meRIP-seq library preparation was performed as previ-ously described (Lin et al., 2016) from Ythdf2CTL c-Kit–enriched cells. Reads from two biological replicates were aligned to the mouse GRCm38 genome using HISAT2 (Kim et al., 2015), and peaks were called using MACS2, version 2.1.1 with the nom-odel flag (Zhang et al., 2008). To analyze the distribution of m6A-associated reads along the transcripts, treat_pileup bed-graph file outputs from MACS2 were converted to bigWig format and used as input for the computeMatrix function of the deepTools package, version 2.5.5 (Ram´ ırez et al., 2014). Motif enrichment was done using Homer, version 4.10, selecting a motif length of six nucleotides. Background regions were generated by shuffling peaks along the transcriptome using the shuffleBed tool from the bedtools suite, version 2.28 (Quinlan and Hall, 2010). The GVIZ bioconductor package was used for peak visualization (Hahne and Ivanek, 2016). m6A meRIP-seq dataset was deposited in GEO (accession no. GSE142020).
GSEA and IPA GSEA was performed using GSEA software version 3.0 with 1,000 permutations and default parameters. Gene differential expression, computed by the edgeR package in R, was ranked by moderated t statistics, which takes into account variability be-tween genes in the ranking. Ranked genes were compared with gene lists in the Hallmark subset of the MSigDB database, ver-sion 7.0. IPA was performed using the Core Analysis Function offered by Qiagen’s Ingenuity Pathway Analysis software (Kr¨ amer et al., 2014). The interrogated RNA-seq and mass spectrometry datasets were filtered for adjusted P values of differential expression (FDR < 0.05), and the threshold for significant activation or inhibition was defined by an absolute Z-score value >2.
SLAM-seq analysis The SLAM-seq dataset (Paris et al., 2019) was analyzed using the SlamDunk pipeline (Herzog et al., 2017).
Mass spectroscopy analysis Immortalized Ythdf2CKO and Ythdf2CTL c-Kit–enriched cells (Paris et al., 2019) were pelleted, lysed, and processed according to (Wi´ sniewski and Rakus, 2014). Tryptic peptides were analyzed on a QExactive+ mass spectrometer connected to an Ultimate Ultra3000 chromatography system packed with 1.8 µm uChrom and separated by an acetonitrile gradient. Mass spectra were analyzed using MaxQuant against the Uniprot mouse database proteome, ID UP000000589.
Quantification and statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using Prism 6 software (GraphPad Software). P values were calculated using a two-tailed Mann–Whitney U test unless stated otherwise.

args.key_excerpts: "Our study positions YTHDF2 as a repressor of inflammatory pathways in HSCs and highlights the significance of m6A in long-term HSC maintenance."
args.summary:
This is a scientific research article published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (2020, Vol. 218, No. 3, e20200829) by Mapperley et al., investigating the role of the mRNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) reader YTHDF2 in hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) function and inflammatory pathway suppression.

**Background:** m6A is an abundant internal mRNA modification recognized by "readers" like YTHDF2, which promotes degradation of m6A-modified transcripts. Prior work showed YTHDF2 inactivation results in HSC expansion and compromises acute myeloid leukemia, but its role in long-term HSC maintenance was unknown.

**Key Findings:**
1. **Serial transplantation failure:** HSCs from 8-12-week-old Ythdf2 conditional knockout (Ythdf2CKO) mice failed to efficiently repopulate multilineage hematopoiesis upon secondary transplantation, showing myeloid bias.
2. **Proinflammatory signature:** Ythdf2-deficient HSCs showed upregulation of 81 transcripts and downregulation of 33, with significant activation of inflammation-related pathways (IFN-α, IFN-γ, inflammatory response, TNF-α signaling, IL6/JAK/STAT3). These HSCs displayed elevated Sca-1 protein and increased phospho-STAT1/STAT3 levels.
3. **m6A-modified inflammatory transcripts:** m6A-seq identified increased expression of m6A-modified transcripts involved in inflammation (Stat1, Il6ra, Gadd45g) in Ythdf2CKO HSCs, with corresponding increases in protein levels (STAT1, IFN-γ inducible protein 47, TNF receptor 2).
4. **Aging studies:** 60-65-week-old Ythdf2CKO mice displayed myeloid bias, HSC and progenitor expansion, and HSCs failed to reconstitute multilineage hematopoiesis upon transplantation.
5. **Inducible deletion:** Using Mx1-Cre mediated deletion (Ythdf2iCKO), researchers found progressive loss of lymphoid output, myeloid bias, and eventual failure of aged HSCs to reconstitute long-term multilineage hematopoiesis.
6. **Inflammation response:** YTHDF2 expression was induced in HSCs by both acute and chronic inflammation (pIpC-induced), and Ythdf2-deficient HSCs showed impaired reconstitution following inflammatory challenge.

**Conclusions:** YTHDF2 functions as a repressor of inflammatory pathways in HSCs, protecting them from excessive proinflammatory signals. The m6A-dependent mRNA decay pathway is proposed as a novel mechanism through which HSCs suppress inflammation and sustain integrity. YTHDF2 may function in a negative feedback loop during inflammation. The authors suggest that m6A mRNA modification is key to long-term HSC maintenance during aging.

**Methods:** The study used conditional knockout mice (Vav-iCre and Mx1-Cre), serial transplantation assays, RNA-seq, m6A meRIP-seq, SLAM-seq, and mass spectrometry-based proteomics. Data deposited in GEO (accession nos. GSE142019 and GSE142020).

--- SOURCE 1: m6A mRNA methylation controls T cell homeostasis by targeting IL-7/STAT5/SOCS pathway - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5729908

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article (published in Nature, 2017) investigates the in vivo biological role of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) mRNA methylation in T cell homeostasis and differentiation. The study, conducted by researchers at Yale University, Stanford University, and Jinan University, used conditional knockout mice for METTL3 (the m6A "writer" protein) and METTL14 in T cells.

**Key findings:**
- Deletion of METTL3 in mouse T cells disrupts T cell homeostasis and differentiation. In a lymphopenic mouse adoptive transfer model, Mettl3-deficient naïve T cells failed to undergo homeostatic expansion and remained in the naïve state for up to 12 weeks, preventing colitis.
- The mRNAs of SOCS family genes (Socs1, Socs3, and Cish) were marked by m6A and exhibited slower mRNA decay and increased expression in Mettl3-deficient naïve T cells.
- Increased SOCS family activity consequently inhibited IL-7-mediated STAT5 activation and T cell homeostatic proliferation and differentiation.
- m6A plays a role in the inducible degradation of Socs mRNAs in response to IL-7 signaling, reprogramming naïve T cells for proliferation and differentiation.
- METTL14 KO mice showed identical phenotypes to METTL3 KO mice, confirming the role of the m6A writer complex.
- Reintroducing wild-type METTL3 (but not catalytically dead METTL3) rescued the differentiation defects.
- siRNA-mediated Socs1 knockdown partially rescued the in vivo differentiation defects of Mettl3 KO naïve T cells.
- The study demonstrates that m6A targets a group of immediate-early inducible genes for rapid mRNA degradation upon IL-7 stimulation, allowing IL-7/JAK signaling to activate STAT5.

**Methodology:** The study employed CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing to generate conditional knockout mice, RNA-Seq, m6A-RIP-Seq, ribosome profiling, s4U-Seq, RNA degradation assays, and adoptive transfer colitis models.

**Conclusions:** This is the first demonstration of the in vivo biological role of m6A modification in T cell-mediated pathogenesis. The study reveals a mechanism where m6A controls T cell homeostasis by inducible degradation of Socs gene family mRNA, relieving the block on IL-7 signaling. The findings suggest that T cell-specific delivery of m6A-modifying agents might be effective therapeutics for autoimmune diseases.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Frontiers | Multiple Functions of RNA Methylation in T Cells: A Review ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2021.627455/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Multiple Functions of RNA Methylation in T Cells: A Review

**Publication details:** This mini review article was published in Frontiers in Immunology (Section: T Cell Biology) on April 12, 2021 (Volume 12, Article 627455). Authors: Yinong Chao, Hua-Bing Li, and Jing Zhou, from the Shanghai Institute of Immunology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, China. DOI: 10.3389/fimmu.2021.627455. It is part of the research topic "Post-Transcriptional Regulation in Tregs."

**Core purpose:** This review summarizes recent findings on how RNA methylation regulates T cell homeostasis and function, discusses open questions in the field of RNA modification, and explores potential therapeutic strategies targeting RNA methylation to orchestrate beneficial T cell immune responses.

**Background:** Over 170 types of RNA modifications have been identified, creating the field of "RNA epigenetics." RNA methylation is a key post-transcriptional regulation mechanism comprising diverse forms, including N6-methyladenosine (m6A), N6-2'-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am), N1-methyladenosine (m1A), and 5-methylcytosine (m5C).

**Key findings by modification type:**

1. **m6A (N6-methyladenosine):** The most frequent RNA modification, preferentially enriched in 3'UTRs, long internal exons, and near stop codons. The "writer" complex contains METTL3, METTL14, and WTAP, plus VIRMA, RBM15/15B, CBLL1, and ZC3H13. "Erasers" are FTO and ALKBH5. "Readers" include YTHDF1-3, YTHDC1-2, HNRNP family, and IGF2BPs. Key findings include:
   - METTL3 ablation in T cells disrupted T cell homeostasis; METTL3-deficient naïve CD4+ T cells differentiated into fewer Th1 and Th17 cells, more Th2 cells.
   - METTL3-mediated m6A modification targets the SOCS gene family, promoting mRNA degradation upon IL-7 stimulation, relieving block on the IL-7/STAT5 pathway.
   - Conditional METTL3 deletion in Tregs (Mettl3flox/floxFoxp3Cre) caused severe systemic autoimmune disease with mice dying at 8-9 weeks old, due to loss of Treg suppressive function via the IL2-STAT5 pathway.
   - METTL3 deletion in CD4+ T cells dampened Tfh differentiation after LCMV challenge; METTL3 stabilizes TCF7 mRNA to initiate Tfh differentiation.
   - YTHDF1-deficient mice showed enhanced antigen-specific CD8+ T cell antitumor responses via increased DC cross-presentation.
   - METTL3 deficiency in dendritic cells caused maturation defects and reduced CD4+ T cell stimulation.

2. **m6Am:** Terminal modification of the first nucleotide after the mRNA 5'cap. PCIF1 is the only conserved methyltransferase. FTO acts as demethylase. Its function remains controversial regarding effects on translation vs. mRNA stability.

3. **m1A:** Found at position 58 of tRNA T-loop, also in rRNA and mRNA. Writers include TRMT6/61A, TRMT61B, TRMT10C, and NML; erasers are FTO, ALKBH1, ALKBH3; readers are YTHDF1-3 and YTHDC1. m1A at tRNA position 58 remains constant during early CD4+ T cell activation, questioning its regulatory role in T cell activation.

4. **m5C:** Writers include NSUN1-7 and DNMT2; readers are ALYREF and YBX1; no erasers identified yet. A study found reduced mRNA m5C levels in CD4+ T cells from SLE patients; NSUN2 expression is dramatically reduced in SLE patients' CD4+ T cells, with m5C hypomethylated transcripts enriched in eukaryotic translation elongation and protein methylation pathways.

**Concluding remarks:** m6A acts as a "brake" to modulate transcription during T cell activation. Knowledge gaps remain regarding whether "writers" and "erasers" contribute equally to m6A sites, and whether other RNA methylations function as "gas pedals" or "pace keepers" in T cell clonal expansion, differentiation, and effector functions. Future research may reveal novel therapeutic targets for T cell-related inflammatory diseases, infections, and cancer immunotherapy.

**Funding:** Supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China, Shanghai Science and Technology Committee, and multiple postdoctoral programs.
</summary>

## METTL3 Gene Overview (GeneCards Database Entry)

This GeneCards page provides comprehensive annotation for the **METTL3** (Methyltransferase 3, N6-Adenosine-Methyltransferase Complex Catalytic Subunit) gene, a **protein-coding** gene with a knowledge score of 75/100.

### Core Function
- METTL3 encodes the **catalytic subunit** of the **m6A methyltransferase complex** and is the core enzyme that installs N6-methyladenosine on internal adenosine residues in eukaryotic mRNAs.
- Works with **METTL14** (forming a heterodimer) to target consensus RNA sequences and regulate **mRNA stability**, **splicing**, and **translation**.
- The METTL3-METTL14 heterodimer forms a N6-methyltransferase complex that methylates adenosine at N(6) positions of RNAs, regulating circadian clock, embryonic/hematopoietic stem cell differentiation, cortical neurogenesis, DNA damage response, T-cell differentiation, and primary miRNA processing.

### Disease Associations
- Associated disorders include: **cancer**, **acute myeloid leukemia**, **hepatocellular carcinoma**, **obesity**, and **Nail Patella Syndrome 5**.
- Additional disease links from MalaCards include **Lung Non-Small Cell Carcinoma** and **Colorectal Cancer**.
- 2 disorders listed from MalaCards; 10 structural variants; 3 pathways; 453 protein interactions and 5 DNA/RNA interactions; 5 drugs; 84 review publications and 1,552 total publications.

### Gene Identifiers
- **HGNC:** 17563; **NCBI Gene:** 56339; **Ensembl:** ENSG00000165819; **OMIM:** 612472; **UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot:** Q86U44
- Aliases include MT-A70, Spo8, M6A, IME4, MTA70, and several others.
- Gene families: 2.1.1.- Methyltransferases, 7BS N6-adenosine DNA/RNA methyltransferases, m6A methyltransferase complex, MT-A70-like family.

### Genomic Location
- **GRCh38/hg38:** chr14:21,498,128-21,511,362 (13,235 bp), minus strand
- **Cytogenic band:** 14q11.2
- 47 integrated GeneHancer regulatory regions

### Protein Details
- Canonical protein **Q86U44-MTA70_HUMAN**: 580 amino acids, 64,474 Da molecular mass
- Enzyme: EC 2.1.1.348 (mRNA m(6)A methyltransferase)
- 1 canonical form, 20 alternate forms, 2 computationally predicted forms, 67 resolved structures
- Subunit of WMM complex (MAC subcomplex: METTL3 + METTL14; MACOM subcomplex: WTAP, ZC3H13, CBLL1/HAKAI, VIRMA, and RBM15/RBM15B)
- Numerous post-translational modifications including phosphorylation, glycosylation, ubiquitination, and acetylation
- **Sumoylation inhibits N6-adenosine-methyltransferase activity**; desumoylated by SENP1
- Known crystal structures include the METTL3-METTL14 complex (PDB 5il0, 5tey) and various inhibitor-bound complexes.

### Key Functions (UniProt)
- m6A methylation occurs at 5'-[AG]GAC-3' consensus sites
- Regulates mRNA stability (methylation promotes mRNA destabilization/degradation)
- Essential for embryonic stem cell differentiation, male fertility/spermatogenesis, oogenesis, spermatogonial differentiation and meiosis
- Involved in DNA damage response (recruits POLK to damage sites after UV irradiation)
- Required for T-cell homeostasis (methylates SOCS family transcripts: SOCS1, SOCS3, CISH)
- Mediates methylation of Xist RNA for X-chromosome inactivation
- **Enhances translation initiation independently of methylation** (promotes translation via cytoplasmic translation initiation machinery)
- During SARS-CoV-2 infection, adds m6A modifications dampening innate immune response (decreases RIGI binding)
- **Overexpressed in cancer tissues** including lung adenocarcinoma and colon adenocarcinoma
- Methyltransferase activity regulated by miRNAs and inhibited by sumoylation

--- SOURCE 6: The Role of m6A Methylation in Tumor Immunity and ... ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/14/8/1042

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed open-access review article published in the MDPI journal Biomolecules (2024, Vol. 14, Issue 8, Article 1042; DOI: 10.3390/biom14081042), titled "The Role of m6A Methylation in Tumor Immunity and Immune-Associated Disorder." The article was authored by Siyu Mu, Kaiyue Zhao, Shanshan Zhong, and Yanli Wang (corresponding author), affiliated with the Department of Neurology and Department of Infectious Diseases at The First Affiliated Hospital of China Medical University (Shenyang) and the Department of Hepatology at Beijing Tsinghua Changgeng Hospital. It was submitted July 1, 2024, revised August 11, 2024, accepted August 14, 2024, and published August 22, 2024. The article has received 5997 views and 19 citations.

MAIN TOPIC: The review examines how N6-methyladenosine (m6A) — the most prevalent and significant internal mRNA modification in eukaryotic cells — functions as a post-transcriptional regulator of immune responses, influencing tumor immunity, immune-associated disorders, and immunotherapy outcomes across multiple cancer types and systemic diseases.

KEY CONTENT:

1. M6A MACHINERY (Writers, Readers, Erasers):
- Writers (methyltransferases): METTL3, METTL14, WTAP, RBM15/RBM15B, VIRMA (KIAA1429), ZC3H13. METTL3 is the central catalytic element; METTL3-METTL14 form the core heterodimer complex.
- Readers (signal converters): YTHDF1/2/3, YTHDC1/2, IGF2BP1/2/3, HNRNPA2B1, eIF3. Nuclear readers (YTHDC1, HNRNPC, HNRNPA2B1) mediate splicing and RNA processing; cytoplasmic readers (YTHDF1/2/3) regulate translation and decay.
- Erasers (demethylases): FTO and ALKBH5.
- m6A was discovered in 1974 by Desrosiers et al. and is concentrated near stop codons and 3' UTRs.

2. M6A IN IMMUNE CELLS:
- HSPCs: METTL3 disruption reduces m6A levels and alters cell proliferation; ALKBH5 regulates the metabolic switch from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation.
- Macrophages: m6A modification of STAT1 mRNA promotes M1 polarization; reduced METTL3 is associated with increased M2 polarization; METTL3 ablation in myeloid macrophages promotes tumor growth and metastasis; METTL14 loss in macrophages inhibits CD8+ T cell antitumor function.
- Dendritic cells: METTL3 enhances translational efficiency of CD40, CD80, and TIRAP, promoting DC maturation and T cell activation; YTHDF1 negatively modulates antitumor immune response by restricting neoantigen presentation.
- T cells: METTL3 inhibition affects Socs mRNA degradation and disrupts the IL-7/STAT5/SOCS signaling pathway, critical for T cell reprogramming and proliferation.
- B cells: METTL14 deletion severely hampers B cell development; YTHDF1 and YTHDF2 affect early B cell maturation.

3. CANCER-SPECIFIC FINDINGS BY SYSTEM:
- Esophageal Cancer: M1 macrophages negatively correlate with lymph node metastasis (good prognosis); M2 macrophages positively correlate with metastasis; PD-L1 expression negatively correlates with YTHDF2, METTL14, and KIAA1429; HNRNPA2B1 and HNRNPC mediate PD-L1 expression.
- Gastric Cancer: YTHDF1 loss enhances antitumor immunity via DC recruitment activating CD4+ and CD8+ T cells; ALKBH5 is a promising biomarker (downregulated ALKBH5 associated with SLC7A2 and CGB3 downregulation); HSPA4/ALKBH5/CD58 axis activates PD1/PDL1 pathways enabling immune evasion; YTHDF3 is a prognostic marker linked to unfavorable outcomes via PI3K/AKT pathway activation; low KIAA1429 expression associated with survival benefit in anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy.
- Liver Cancer: ALKBH5 has controversial roles (tumor suppressor vs. promoting proliferation/metastasis via JNK/ERK pathways and MAP3K8-IL-8-macrophage recruitment); YTHDF2 deletion in Tregs diminishes tumor growth; METTL5 positively correlates with infiltration of multiple immune cells and PD1/CTLA4 expression.
- Pancreatic Cancer: METTL3 influences PD-L1 expression via MALAT1 and DCLRE1B; METTL16 is a novel immunotherapy target in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, positively associated with B cell and CD8+ T cell infiltration.
- Colorectal Cancer: YTHDF1 is a biomarker for immunotherapy outcomes via the m6A-p65-CXCL1/CXCR2 axis; targeting YTHDF1 enhances anti-PD1 therapy in MSI-H CRC and overcomes resistance in MSS CRC; METTL3/METTL14 loss enhances IFN-γ-Stat1-Irf1 signaling; lactoacylated METTL3 promotes immunosuppression; ALKBH5 fosters CD8+ T cell infiltration via NF-κB-CCL5 axis; IGF2BP3 positively correlates with NK CD56dim cells and predicts better PD-1/CTLA-4 therapy responses.
- Gallbladder Cancer: YTHDF2 upregulation promotes proliferation/migration and gemcitabine resistance via the YTHDF2/DAPK3 axis; IGF2BP3 stabilizes CLDN4 mRNA promoting macrophage immunosuppressive polarization.
- Lung Adenocarcinoma: LRPPRC (m6A reader) upregulation negatively correlates with immune cell infiltration and predicts low PD-1 immunotherapy response; M2-TAMs attenuate CD8+ T cell antitumor responses via METTL3 upregulation (relevant to nivolumab resistance); LAG3 correlates with immune cell infiltration.
- Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma: LRPPRC negatively correlates with Th2 cells but positively with protective immune cells; ALKBH5 suppresses RIG-I-mediated IFNα secretion and reduces tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes.
- Thyroid Cancer: METTL3 negatively correlates with CD70 expression; CD70 blockade with cusatuzumab reverses anti-PD-1 therapy resistance; YTHDF3 positively correlates with CD4+ T cell and macrophage infiltration.
- Pituitary Adenomas: YTHDF2 high expression associated with increased M2 macrophages and PD-L1 expression.
- Gliomas/GBM: HSPA7 promotes macrophage infiltration via YAP1/LOX upregulation (silencing enhances anti-PD1 therapy); ALKBH5 upregulation associated with poorer prognosis; ALKBH5 knockout activates immune system, increases antitumor cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-2), reduces pro-tumor cytokines (IL-10, IL-13), and reduces PD-L1 levels.

CONCLUSIONS: The review emphasizes that m6A modification is an integral mechanism in tumor immune regulation, immune evasion, and various immune dysregulation disorders. Targeting m6A methylation as an immune checkpoint and for novel diagnostic/therapeutic approaches in cancers and aging-related diseases holds promise. The expression patterns of m6A regulators can influence disease susceptibility to immunotherapy, facilitating diagnostic/prognostic models and pioneering new therapeutic approaches.
</summary>

"This review emphasizes the challenges and prospective directions of m6A-related immune regulation in various systemic diseases throughout the body." "The potential for targeting m6A methylation as an immune checkpoint and novel diagnostic therapeutic avenue in cancers and aging-related diseases holds promise." "METTL3 in macrophages contributes to the regulation of tumor progression. Ablation of METTL3 in myeloid macrophages promotes tumor growth and metastasis." "Targeting YTHDF1 using CRISPR or VNPs-siYTHDF1 enhances the efficacy of anti-PD1 therapy in microsatellite instability—high (MSI-H) CRC and overcomes resistance in microsatellite-stable (MSS) CRC."

SUMMARY:

This is a review article published in Cell Death Discovery (Volume 10, Article 331, 2024) examining the role of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modification in the tumor microenvironment (TME). The paper has 7717 accesses and 38 citations.

The article covers three main sections:
1) m6A modification components: writers (methyltransferases including METTL3, METTL5, METTL14, METTL16, WTAP, RBM15/15B, VIRMA/KIAA1429, PCIF1, ZC3H4, ZC3H13), erasers (demethylases FTO, ALKBH5, and ALKBH3), and readers (YTHDF1/2/3, YTHDC1/2, IGF2BPs, and cytoplasmic METTL3).

3) Potential therapeutic strategies targeting m6A in the TME.

Key findings include:
- m6A is the most common epigenetic modification in eukaryotic mRNAs, occurring at the N6 position of adenosine, mostly in coding sequences, 3' ends of transcripts, and stop codons.
- TME is characterized by hypoxia (oxygen partial pressure below 10 mmHg), metabolic reprogramming, acid accumulation, and immunosuppression.

Open questions addressed include how m6A proteins function in each tumor type, the interplay between TME cells, m6A, and tumors regarding treatment efficacy, and whether m6A could be a therapeutic target by affecting metastatic niches.

--- SOURCE 1: tox-is-expressed-by-exhausted-and-polyfunctional-human- ... ---
URL: https://scispace.com/pdf/tox-is-expressed-by-exhausted-and-polyfunctional-human-10n3v5rxrt.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research paper published in Science Immunology (2020) titled "TOX is expressed by exhausted and polyfunctional human effector memory CD8+ T cells" by Sekine et al. The study investigated how two transcription factors, TOX and TCF-1, shape CD8+ T cell exhaustion and memory differentiation in humans.

Key findings: Under physiological conditions, effector memory (TEM) and effector memory RA (TEMRA) CD8+ T cells primarily expressed TOX, whereas naive and central memory cells primarily expressed TCF-1. TOX expression defined cytolytic gene/protein signatures. In the context of chronic HIV infection, exhausted HIV-specific CD8+ T cells commonly expressed TOX (often clustering with activation markers and inhibitory receptors like PD-1, TIGIT, 2B4, and CD39) and rarely expressed TCF-1. However, functionally competent CD8+ T cells specific for CMV or EBV also expressed TOX, either with or without TCF-1. A similar pattern was observed in HIV-specific CD8+ T cells from elite controllers (individuals who control viral replication without ART). The study identified three distinct memory CD8+ T cell populations: early-differentiated TOX−TCF-1+ cells, progenitor-like TOX+TCF-1+ cells, and effector-like TOX+TCF-1− cells.

Methods included RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, 28-color flow cytometry with UMAP/Phenograph clustering, Western blots, MHC class I tetramers, and functional assays from peripheral blood samples of HIV− donors (n=30), HIV+ viremic (n=23), HIV+ aviremic on ART (n=17), and elite controllers (n=10) recruited at Karolinska University Hospital, Lima Peru, University of Alabama at Birmingham, and Massachusetts General Hospital.

The authors concluded that TOX identifies both exhausted and functionally replete human effector memory CD8+ T cells specific for chronic viruses (CMV, EBV, HIV), and that exhaustion is not necessarily defined solely by TOX expression. The study proposes TOX as a universal regulator of human memory CD8+ T cells specific for chronic viruses, and defines a functional spectrum of HIV-specific CD8+ T cells based on TOX/TCF-1 expression where IL-2 production was associated with increased TCF-1 and decreased TOX, while cytolytic cells displayed a TOX+TCF-1− phenotype.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Collectively, these data suggest that TOX identifies exhausted and functionally replete human effector memory CD8+ T cells specific for chronic viruses, such as CMV, EBV, and HIV."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: TOX is so exhausting! - Accelerating Cancer Immunotherapy Research ---
URL: https://acir.org/weekly-digests/2019/july/tox-is-so-exhausting

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This ACIR (Agency for Cancer Immunotherapy Research) weekly digest from July 3, 2019, is a special feature summarizing five recently published papers on the role of the transcription factor TOX in exhausted CD8+ T cells, which are common in cancer and chronic infections and are the major target of checkpoint blockade. Despite using different models (acute infection, chronic infection, tumors) and methods, the studies converged on several key findings: TOX preferentially plays a role in persistent antigen presentation settings (not acute infections), TOX is required for formation of exhausted CD8+ T cells via chromatin remodeling and RNA transcriptome alteration, TOX induces high expression of inhibitory receptors and decreases inflammatory cytokine production, and TOX expression is induced by the calcineurin/NFAT pathway. A positive correlation between TOX and TCF1 (a marker of progenitor-like CD8+ T cells) was mostly, but not universally, observed.

The five papers summarized include:

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This eLife-reviewed preprint presents a multidisciplinary study of the catalytic mechanism of METTL3, the catalytic component of the METTL3-14 complex, which is the major enzyme depositing N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications on human mRNA. Using a combination of crystal structures with bisubstrate analogues (BAs), mutational analysis, classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) free energy calculations, the authors elucidate the complete mechanism of substrate binding, methyl transfer, and product release.

Key findings:
- **Bisubstrate analogues (BAs)**: Four BAs (BA1, BA2, BA4, BA6) were crystallized in METTL3-14. BA2 and BA4 showed SAM-like moieties that bind like the natural SAM cofactor, while BA1 and BA6 showed divergent interactions.
- **Two distinct adenosine binding conformations**: The BA2 structure shows adenosine buried in the active site (representing the transition state), while BA4 shows adenosine in a solvent-exposed encounter complex conformation. Adenosine swaps between these conformations during catalysis.
- **Key active site residues**: D395, P396, E481, K513, and Y406 are critical for adenosine binding and catalysis. Alanine mutation of D395, Y406, E481, and K513 almost completely abolishes METTL3 catalytic activity. These residues are highly conserved.
- **SAM priming**: SAM binding to the apo enzyme causes conformational changes in K513 and H512 side chains that prime the active site for adenosine recognition by making space for the substrate.
- **Y406 as gatekeeper**: The flexible Y406 side chain acts as a gatekeeper, recruiting adenosine through π-π interactions and stabilizing the active site loop 1 (ASL1) before flipping out to allow adenosine to enter the catalytic site.
- **Direct methyl transfer without deprotonation**: QM/MM (DFTB3/MM) free energy simulations show methyl transfer occurs via an SN2 mechanism directly to the N6 position without prior deprotonation of adenosine-N6 (which has a high pKa of ~17). The reaction is exoergic by ~4 kcal/mol with a barrier of 15-16 kcal/mol.
- **Rate-limiting step**: Since the methyl transfer barrier (15-16 kcal/mol) is lower than the experimentally measured catalytic turnover barrier (~20 kcal/mol, from turnover of 0.2-0.6 min⁻¹), the dissociation of SAH and product RNA is suggested to be the rate-limiting step.
- **Electrostatic contributions**: E481 and K513 contribute to catalysis through electrostatic stabilization. After methyl transfer, deprotonation of m6NH2+ occurs readily through water wires connecting the N6 position to the protein-solvent interface.
- **BA2 as transition state analogue**: The BA2 structure shows the adenosine-N6 positioned 1.9 Å from the SAM Cε carbon with an angle of 160.9°, close to the optimal 180° for SN2 methyl transfer, confirming it as a transition state mimic.
- **Broader implications**: The proposed mechanism likely applies to METTL4 and other MT-A70 family members of MTases. The atomistic information is useful for understanding other RNA MTases and designing transition state analogues as inhibitors, which is relevant for treating cancers like acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

The work was assessed by eLife as "important" in significance with "compelling" strength of evidence.
</summary>

3. **Readers** (RNA-binding proteins): YTHDF1 (promotes translation), YTHDF2 (promotes degradation), YTHDF3 (cooperates with YTHDF1/2), YTHDC1 (promotes splicing), YTHDC2 (increases translation), IGF2BP1/2/3 (promote stability and translation), HNRNPC, HNRNPA2B1, eIF3 (promotes cap-independent translation).

**Mitochondrial Dysfunction Manifestations (Section 2):**
- **Structure/Function:** Mitochondria have a double-membrane structure (outer membrane, inner membrane, intermembrane space, matrix); inner membrane folds form cristae where oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) occurs. About 99% of mitochondrial proteins are encoded by nuclear genes; mtDNA encodes 13 core OXPHOS proteins (7 in complex I, 1 in complex III, 3 in complex IV, 2 in complex V), plus 22 mt-tRNAs and 2 mt-rRNAs.
- **Energy metabolism/biogenesis:** Mitochondrial diseases feature OXPHOS deficiency. PGC-1α is the main regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, acting through NRF1/NRF2 and TFAM. AMPK, cAMP-PKA-CREB, CaMK/p38 MAPK, and Sirt1 pathways regulate PGC-1α.
- **Mitochondrial dynamics:** Fission is mediated by DRP1 (recruited by MID49, MID51, MFF). Fusion involves MFN1/MFN2 (OMM) and OPA1 (IMM). Defects cause mitochondrial dysfunction and disease.
- **Mitophagy:** Ub-dependent pathway (PINK1-Parkin pathway) and Ub-independent pathways (NIX/BNIP3L, BNIP3, FUNDC1 receptors that bind LC3). Both insufficient and excessive mitophagy are harmful.
- **ROS:** Complex I and III are main ROS production sites. Antioxidant systems include GSH (glutathione peroxidase), thioredoxin-2 (TRX2/peroxiredoxin), and catalase. Low ROS are necessary for normal function; high ROS damage DNA, proteins, and lipids.
- **Calcium homeostasis:** Ca2+ enters mitochondria via VDAC and MCU complex; extrusion via NCLX. Calcium overload inhibits OXPHOS, disrupts cristae, and can trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and cell death.
- **Cell death:** Includes apoptosis (BCL-2 family, Bak/Bax, Cyt c release), necroptosis (RIPK1/RIPK3), ferroptosis (dependent on ETC/ROS-driven lipid peroxidation), and pyroptosis (NLRP3 inflammasome).
- **Mitochondria-targeted therapy:** Emerging strategies include mitochondriotropic particulate carriers, triphenylphosphonium (TPP) derivatives, amphipathic peptoids, mitochondria-targeted RNAi nanoparticles, magnetic-field-driven mitochondria-targeted ceria nanosystems, and platinum-based terminal-sensitive projectiles for cancer therapy.
</summary>

"Mitochondrial dysfunction directly disrupts core cellular processes, such as energy metabolism, redox balance, and apoptosis regulation, serving as a central driver of diverse pathologies."

--- SOURCE 11: METTL3-dependent m6A modification programs T follicular helper cell differentiation ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7910450

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Nature Communications (Feb 26, 2021; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-21594-6) investigating the role of METTL3-dependent N6-methyladenosine (m6A) mRNA modification in T follicular helper (TFH) cell differentiation. The study was conducted by researchers from China Agricultural University, the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and the Third Military Medical University, led by corresponding author Shuyang Yu.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers used conditional knockout mice (Mettl3 fl/fl Cd4-Cre mice) to delete METTL3 in CD4+ T cells, then subjected mice to LCMV-Armstrong viral infection and KLH immunization. They employed flow cytometry, RNA-seq, m6A-miCLIP-seq, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), bone marrow chimeric mice, adoptive transfer models, cell-trace violet (CTV) labeling, and retrovirus transduction with wild-type or catalytically dead METTL3 constructs.

KEY RESULTS:
1. Conditional deletion of METTL3 in CD4+ T cells impaired TFH differentiation and germinal center (GC) responses in a cell-intrinsic manner in mice, with TFH cells more severely affected (21.4-fold change) than TH1 cells (1.9-fold change).

2. METTL3 deficiency caused reduced GC B cells, plasma cells, and LCMV-specific IgG antibody concentration (at both day 8 and day 56 post-infection).

3. METTL3 was essential for early TFH commitment, with METTL3-deficient cells showing delayed proliferation (stalled at 3rd-4th divisions vs. 5th-6th for controls), reduced Bcl-6+CXCR5+ TFH cells, elevated apoptosis, and reduced TCF-1 expression.

4. RNA-seq revealed 515 upregulated and 252 downregulated genes in METTL3-deficient TFH cells. Key TFH signature genes including Tcf7, Bcl6, Cxcr5, Icos, and Pdcd1 were decreased, while Prdm1, Id2, and pro-apoptotic genes (Bcl2l11, Bax) were elevated.

5. METTL3's effects required its m6A methyltransferase catalytic activity—wild-type but not catalytically dead METTL3 (D395A/W398A mutations) rescued TFH differentiation defects.

6. m6A-miCLIP-seq showed that m6A modification of the Tcf7 mRNA 3' UTR stabilizes the transcript. Loss of METTL3 or mutation of the Tcf7 3' UTR m6A site resulted in accelerated Tcf7 mRNA decay.

7. Ectopic expression of TCF-1 (encoded by Tcf7) rectified TFH defects caused by METTL3 deficiency.

CONCLUSION: METTL3 stabilizes Tcf7 transcripts via m6A modification to ensure activation of the TFH transcriptional program, demonstrating that post-transcriptional regulation plays a pivotal function in promoting TFH cell differentiation. Notably, METTL3 deficiency also reduced TH17 cell differentiation upon protein immunization, while TH2 and Treg differentiation were unaffected. The article notes that METTL3-dependent m6A effects on mRNA stability are cell-context dependent, as YTHDF2 promotes m6A-modified mRNA decay while IGF2BPs stabilize methylated transcripts.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Immunology (22 January 2024, Volume 15) titled "The RNA m6A writer METTL3 in tumor microenvironment: emerging roles and therapeutic implications" by Weiqi Su, Lin Che, Wenting Liao, and Huilin Huang from Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, Guangzhou, China.

The article systematically reviews the roles of METTL3 (Methyltransferase-like 3), the core catalytic component of the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methyltransferase complex, in the tumor microenvironment (TME) and its implications for cancer immunotherapy.

**Key Content:**

1. **METTL3 Structure & Function**: METTL3 consists of a methyltransferase domain (MTD) that binds S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) and a zinc finger domain (ZFD) that recognizes RNA GGACU consensus. It plays an oncogenic role in most cancers but has tumor-suppressive functions in renal cell carcinoma and endometrial tumors.

2. **Roles in Innate Immunity**:
   - **TAMs**: METTL3 facilitates M1 macrophage polarization via STAT regulation. Loss of METTL3 promotes immunosuppressive TME and tumor growth. It contributes to M2-TAM-mediated therapeutic resistance (oxaliplatin in CRC, immuno-resistance in LUAD).
   - **MDSCs**: METTL3 promotes MDSC migration/accumulation through CXCL1 via BHLHE41 in CRC and G-CSF regulation in bladder cancer.
   - **NK/iNKT cells**: METTL3-mediated m6A on SHP-2 activates AKT-mTOR and MAPK-ERK pathways essential for NK cell homeostasis and tumor immunosurveillance. Depletion impairs iNKT cell proliferation/differentiation via Creb1.
   - **Neutrophils & DCs**: METTL3 suppresses tumor-associated neutrophil recruitment in papillary thyroid cancer via c-Rel/RelA, and promotes DC cytokine production and T cell activation via CD40, CD80, and TIRAP.

3. **Roles in Adaptive Immunity**:
   - METTL3 is required for T cell homeostasis and differentiation (regulating Socs1/3, Cish mRNAs, Tfh signature genes).
   - METTL3 regulates PD-L1 expression - upregulating it via IGF2BP3 in bladder/breast cancer, but destabilizing it via circIGF2BP3/PKP3 axis in NSCLC.
   - Regulates Treg suppression function and circQSOX1-mediated immune evasion in CRC.
   - Modulates chemokine production (CXCL1, CXCL5, CCL20) and metabolic regulation (lactylation-driven METTL3 upregulation in tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells via JAK1-STAT3).

4. **Stromal Cells**: METTL3 promotes cancer-associated fibroblast-mediated tumor growth (COL10A1 in LUSC) and angiogenesis through VEC regulation (LRP6, DVL1, HDGF, TEK, VEGFA targets).

5. **METTL3 Inhibitors & Immunotherapy**:
   - METTL3 correlates negatively with anti-PD-1/PD-L1/anti-CTLA4 therapy efficacy across multiple cancers.
   - Discovered inhibitors include: Eltrombopag (allosteric inhibitor), UZH1a and UZH2 (non-nucleoside inhibitors), STC-15 (orally bioavailable, Phase 1 clinical trial, synergistic with anti-PD1), STM2457 and STM3006 (second-generation inhibitors, activate dsRNA-mediated interferon signaling, synergistic with anti-PD-1 in mice).

6. **Discussion**: METTL3 may also exert m6A-independent functions. Research on METTL3 inhibitors is still in infancy with clinical evidence urgently needed. Future directions include AI-based inhibitor design and targeted protein degradation strategies.

--- SOURCE 1: Progression of m6A in the tumor microenvironment ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-024-02092-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Cell Death Discovery (Volume 10, Article 331, 2024) examining the role of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modification in the tumor microenvironment (TME). The paper has 7717 accesses and 38 citations.

The article covers three main sections:
1) m6A modification components: writers (methyltransferases including METTL3, METTL5, METTL14, METTL16, WTAP, RBM15/15B, VIRMA/KIAA1429, PCIF1, ZC3H4, ZC3H13), erasers (demethylases FTO, ALKBH5, and ALKBH3), and readers (YTHDF1/2/3, YTHDC1/2, IGF2BPs, and cytoplasmic METTL3).
2) The relationship between m6A methylation and TME characteristics including hypoxia, metabolic reprogramming (glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism), and immunosuppression.
3) Potential therapeutic strategies targeting m6A in the TME.

Key findings include:
- m6A is the most common epigenetic modification in eukaryotic mRNAs, occurring at the N6 position of adenosine, mostly in coding sequences, 3' ends of transcripts, and stop codons.
- TME is characterized by hypoxia (oxygen partial pressure below 10 mmHg), metabolic reprogramming, acid accumulation, and immunosuppression.
- Under hypoxia, HIF-1α promotes YTHDF1/2 expression in HCC and lung squamous cell carcinoma; low FTO expression accelerates CRC malignant progression while high ALKBH5 promotes female malignant tumors.
- m6A regulates the Warburg effect (glycolysis) through YTHDF1/2/3, YTHDC1/2, WTAP, METTL3, and FTO, affecting T cell immune function and immune evasion.
- In lipid metabolism, METTL3 reduces CES2 levels to promote lipid deposition in HCC; YTHDF2 regulates cholesterol metabolism in gliomas.
- In amino acid metabolism, YTHDF1 promotes glutaminase expression affecting tumor metabolism.
- m6A-mediated metabolic dysregulation generates an acidic environment; both hypoxia and acidity promote immunosuppressive TME by inhibiting T cells, B cells, and NK cells while supporting immunosuppressive cells (TA-MSCs, CAFs).

Open questions addressed include how m6A proteins function in each tumor type, the interplay between TME cells, m6A, and tumors regarding treatment efficacy, and whether m6A could be a therapeutic target by affecting metastatic niches.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"m6A is the most common epigenetic modification in eukaryotic mRNAs."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Mettl3-catalyzed m6A methylation determines CD8+ T cell ... ---
URL: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.01.06.697843v1.full-text

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a bioRxiv preprint (DOI: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.01.06.697843) titled "Mettl3-catalyzed m6A methylation determines CD8+ T cell differentiation fate in tumor." It is a new results preprint that has not been peer-reviewed.

**Authors and Affiliations:** Puspendu Ghosh, Debashree Basak, Shaun Mahanti, Soham Chowdhury, Ishita Sarkar, Anwesha Mandal, Anwesha Kar, Snehanshu Chowdhury, and Shilpak Chatterjee (Division of Cancer Biology and Inflammatory Disorder, IICB-Translational Research Unit of Excellence; CSIR-Indian Institute of Chemical Biology, Kolkata, India; Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR), Ghaziabad, India); Anupam Gautam (University of Tübingen and Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen, Germany); Sandip Paul (JIS Institute of Advanced Studies and Research, JIS University, Kolkata, India). Corresponding author: Shilpak Chatterjee (schatterjee@iicb.res.in).

**Summary of Key Findings:**

**Background/Problem:** Heterogeneity in patient responses to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) is dictated by the relative abundance of exhausted CD8+ T cell (Tex) subsets. Progenitor exhausted (pTex) cells remain sensitive to ICB, while terminally exhausted (tTex) cells are refractory. The molecular cues determining these divergent fates were poorly defined.

**Main Finding:** The RNA methyltransferase Mettl3 is identified as a central regulator of Tex fate. Across murine tumor models, human T cells, and adoptive transfer systems, Mettl3 expression is selectively enriched in tTex cells and inversely correlated with TCF1+ pTex populations.

**Mechanism:** Mettl3 drives terminal exhaustion by stabilizing DNMT3B transcripts via m6A modification, which enforces CpG methylation and chromatin compaction at memory-associated loci. This establishes the Mettl3-m6A-Dnmt3b axis as a molecular rheostat coupling epitranscriptomic regulation to epigenetic remodeling.

**Therapeutic Implications:** Inhibition of the Mettl3-Dnmt3b axis reprograms chromatin accessibility toward memory-like states, preserving progenitor potential and effector function. T cells lacking Mettl3-Dnmt3b activity persist longer, mount robust recall responses, and achieve superior tumor control with enhanced responsiveness to PD-1 blockade — revealing a tractable pathway to improve the durability of cancer immunotherapy.

**Key Experimental Results:**

**Result 1 — Mettl3 expression positively correlates with CD8+ T cell exhaustion:** Using MC38 and YUMM1.7 murine tumor models, YUMM1.7 tumors were found to harbor more tTex cells (PD1+Tim3+) and were less responsive to ICB. Mettl3 expression was elevated in YUMM1.7 intratumoral CD8+ T cells and increased with tumor progression, correlating positively with exhaustion markers (PD1, Tim3, CD39, TOX) and inversely with TCF1. scRNA-seq analysis of 9,056 murine CD8+ T cells revealed Mettl3 enriched in exhausted clusters (Tex1, Tex2) and largely absent from the pTex/memory cluster. Analysis of human scRNA-seq data from 4,588 intratumoral CD8+ T cells across five malignancies (breast cancer x2, colorectal cancer, endocervical adenocarcinoma, skin melanoma) confirmed METTL3 was significantly higher in Tex cells than in pTex clusters. Chronically stimulated human CD8+ T cells exhibited markedly higher Mettl3 expression than acutely stimulated cells.

**Result 2 — Mettl3 inhibition alleviates exhaustion while promoting T Mem generation in vitro:** In vitro differentiation experiments with human CD8+ T cells showed Mettl3 expression progressively increased under chronic TCR stimulation (Tex conditions) but declined under IL-15/IL-7 memory-inducing conditions. Mettl3 knockdown (shRNA) impaired Tex differentiation (reduced PD1+Tim3+, PD1+CD39+, PD1+CTLA4+ frequencies, increased TCF1) and improved cytokine production (IFN-γ, TNF-α), while Mettl3 overexpression enhanced exhaustion. Under memory conditions, Mettl3 knockdown promoted stem cell memory (SCM)-like cell formation (CD45RA+CD62L+), elevated memory markers (TCF1, FOXO1, CCR7), and enhanced recall responses. A rescue experiment confirmed that reintroducing Mettl3 into knockdown cells restored the exhausted phenotype.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here, we identify the RNA methyltransferase Mettl3 as a central regulator of Tex fate. Across murine tumor models, human T cells, and adoptive transfer systems, Mettl3 expression is selectively enriched in tTex cells and inversely correlated with TCF1+ pTex populations."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Targeting the RNA m6A modification for cancer immunotherapy ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12943-022-01558-0

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published on March 16, 2022, in Molecular Cancer (Volume 21, article number 76), titled "Targeting the RNA m6A modification for cancer immunotherapy." It is an open-access article by Xinxin Li, Shoubao Ma, Youcai Deng, Ping Yi, Jianhua Yu, and colleagues.

The article provides a comprehensive overview of how N6-methyladenosine (m6A), the most abundant epigenetic modification of RNA, influences cancer immunotherapy. It covers:

1. **Regulation of m6A modification**: m6A is dynamically regulated by three types of enzymes—writers (methyltransferases like METTL3, METTL14, WTAP, RBM15, VIRMA, ZC3H13), erasers (demethylases FTO and ALKBH5), and readers (binding proteins like YTHDC1/2, YTHDF1/2/3, HNRNP family, IGF2BPs, PRRC2A).

2. **Role in immune cells**:
   - **NK cells**: YTHDF2 and METTL3 positively regulate NK cell anti-tumor immunity.
   - **Macrophages**: METTL3 promotes proinflammatory cytokine production and anti-tumor function; METTL14 boosts CD8+ T cell activation; YTHDF2 negatively regulates inflammatory responses.
   - **Dendritic cells**: METTL3 promotes DC activation and maturation; YTHDF1 negatively regulates anti-tumor immune responses by enhancing lysosomal protease translation.
   - **T cells**: METTL3 regulates CD4+ T cell homeostasis, Treg cell function, and Tfh cell differentiation; ALKBH5 positively regulates IFN-γ expression.

3. **Role in remodeling the tumor microenvironment (TME)**: m6A regulators in tumor cells affect immune cell infiltration and ICB efficacy. METTL3 and METTL14 expression levels correlate with immune cell infiltration in various cancers (CRC, HCC, BC, CC, HNSCC, TGCT, ccRCC).

4. **Therapeutic strategies proposed**: Combining m6A regulator inhibitors with immune checkpoint blockers; developing programmable m6A gene-editing systems; enhancing anti-tumor immune responses in T cells/NK cells via m6A modification; using nanoparticles targeting tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) to deliver m6A-related molecules.

The review aims to help understand how m6A modifications intrinsically and extrinsically shape immune responses in the TME to improve cancer immunotherapy design.

TOX suppressed KLRG1+ effector differentiation via chromatin remodeling and regulated inhibitory receptors (PD-1, TIGIT, LAG3) and transcription factors (Eomes, TCF1). Initially induced by calcineurin via NFAT2, but sustained independently of calcineurin.
2. Seo et al. (PNAS): Used CD19-expressing B16-OVA melanoma with adoptively transferred CAR T cells; TOX/TOX2 double deficiency mediated tumor regression and improved survival. TOX, TOX2, and NR4A family members cooperated, induced by calcineurin via NFAT, and contributed to inhibitory receptor expression.
3. Scott et al. (Nature): Studied SV40-T antigen-driven liver cancer, B16F10 melanoma, and LCMV models using RNAseq and ATACseq. TOX was highly expressed in dysfunctional antigen-specific CD8+ T cells but not naive/effector/memory cells. Notably, high TOX correlated with low TCF1 (differing from Khan and Seo). TOX-knockout cells failed to persist in tumors. Suggested TOX-induced exhaustion serves as a negative feedback mechanism to prevent T cell overstimulation and activation-induced cell death.
4. Alfei et al. (Nature): In LCMV and human hepatitis C virus models, found TOX induction depended on antigen quantity but not affinity. Mutant-TOX T cells had decreased PD-1, increased cytokines, and elevated KLRG1 (more effector-like phenotype). TOX was required for T cell maintenance in dysfunction-promoting settings and promoted long-term maintenance of TCF1+ progenitor T cells.
5. Yao et al. (Nature Immunology): Used single-cell RNA sequencing in chronic LCMV; identified progenitor-like cells coexpressing Tox and Tcf7. Knockout of Tox shifted differentiation toward KLRG1+ short-lived effectors; TOX overexpression increased persistence of virus-specific CD8+ T cells. TOX activity was required for differentiation of progenitor-like TCF1hi CD8+ T cells and long-term immunity.

Conclusion: All five groups demonstrated TOX plays a crucial role in generating and maintaining exhausted CD8+ T cells (upregulated inhibitory receptors, decreased cytokines, epigenetic modulation) during persistent antigen presentation. TOX is highly expressed in human cancers including melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, breast cancer, and ovarian cancer, making TOX modulation a potential therapeutic target for reversing T cell exhaustion in human cancers.

The digest also includes brief summaries of related articles: a MUC16 bispecific T cell-engaging antibody (REGN4018) for ovarian cancer, cross-species single-cell analysis of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma revealing antigen-presenting cancer-associated fibroblasts, a review of CD8+CD28- immunosenescent T cells in cancer, and a study on the deubiquitinase Otub1 regulating IL-15-mediated priming of CD8+ T cells and NK cells.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"TOX preferentially plays a role in the setting of persistent antigen presentation, but not in acute infections; TOX was required for the formation of exhausted CD8+ T cells via chromatin remodeling and alteration of the RNA transcriptome; TOX induced high expression of inhibitory receptors and decreased the production of inflammatory cytokines; TOX expression was induced by the calcineurin/NFAT pathway."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 12: The transcription factor TOX controls differentiation and ... ---
URL: https://mediatum.ub.tum.de/doc/1452066/1452066.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a doctoral dissertation (PhD thesis) by Francesca Alfei at the Technical University of Munich (Technische Universität München, TUM), submitted November 14, 2018 and accepted July 31, 2019, examining the role of the transcription factor TOX in controlling the differentiation and maintenance of CD8+ T-cells during chronic viral infections. The thesis was supervised by Prof. Dietmar Zehn, with examiners Prof. Percy A. Knolle and Prof. Robert Thimme.

BACKGROUND: The immune system is divided into innate and adaptive immunity. CD8+ T-cells are the cytotoxic arm of adaptive immunity that recognize peptide:MHC class I complexes and kill infected cells via perforin and granzymes, while producing IFNγ, TNF and other cytokines. The LCMV (lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus) mouse model was used. LCMV Armstrong causes an acute, cleared infection, while LCMV Clone 13 (which differs by only three amino acids) causes a persistent chronic infection. Zinkernagel and Doherty used this model to discover MHC restriction (Nobel Prize 1996). LCMV has dominant epitopes (Db/NP396, Db/GP33, Kb/GP34) and a subdominant one (Db/GP276). TCR-transgenic P14 cells specific for the gp33 epitope were used.

KEY CONCEPTS: Upon acute infection, CD8+ T-cells differentiate into short-lived effector cells (SLECs: KLRG1high, CD127low) and memory precursor effector cells (MPECs: KLRG1low, CD127high) that form long-lived memory (Tcm and Tem). In chronic infections, persistent antigen stimulation drives CD8+ T-cells into a state of "exhaustion" – dysfunctional cells with impaired cytokine production (IL-2, TNF, IFNγ) and high expression of inhibitory receptors such as PD-1, LAG-3, CD244, CD160, Tim-3, and CTLA-4. Exhaustion is driven by cell-intrinsic factors (inhibitory receptors), cell-extrinsic factors (IL-10, TGF-β negatively; IL-2, IL-7, IL-21 positively), and CD4+ T-cell help. Treg cells suppress virus-specific T-cell responses. Key transcription factors controlling exhaustion include Irf4, T-bet, Blimp-1, Eomes, VHL, and Foxo1.

METHODOLOGY & KEY FINDINGS: The researchers developed an experimental system using recombinant LCMV Clone 13 strains – a low-affinity variant (C6) and a gp33-deficient variant (A3) mixed with wild-type virus – to independently vary TCR affinity and antigen quantity. Findings showed antigen amount is a more critical determinant of exhaustion than TCR affinity. Transcriptional profiling revealed TOX (Thymocyte selection-associated high mobility group box protein) as one of the most upregulated genes in chronically stimulated T-cells. TOX expression correlates with the chronic phenotype, is induced by high antigen levels, and is maintained after antigen withdrawal. TOX was also found to be expressed in human HCV-specific CD8+ T-cells, correlating with high PD-1 levels (and persisting even after antiviral treatment).

In the absence of TOX, dysfunctional T-cells are forced toward an effector phenotype with decreased PD-1, increased KLRG-1, and greater cytokine production, leading to better viral clearance but increased immunopathology. TOX absence also caused a substantial loss of the critical Tcf-1+ progenitor population, impairing long-term survival of dysfunctional CD8+ T-cells. TOX was dispensable for memory CD8+ T-cell generation in acute infection. The Tcf-1+ memory-like progenitor population (identified in both mouse and human chronic infections) maintains the immune response and responds to PD-1 blockade.

CONCLUSION: TOX is a key regulator of the differentiation program that drives chronically stimulated T-cells toward a dysfunctional/exhausted phenotype. TOX both induces exhaustion and ensures T-cell fitness for long-term maintenance, preventing acquisition of effector phenotype and protecting the host from overwhelming immunopathology. This makes TOX a major target for future immunotherapeutic approaches, including in cancer and chronic viral infections (HIV, HCV).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"TOX expression correlates with the chronic phenotype and it is maintained after antigen withdrawal in chronically stimulated mice. TOX is induced by high antigen levels and its absence strongly affects dysfunctional T-cells, which are forced to acquire an effector phenotype, with decreased PD-1 but increased KLRG-1 expression and cytokines production.", "The transcriptional profile analysis revealed the transcription factor TOX as one of the most upregulated genes in chronically stimulated T-cells.", "TOX promotes the dysfunctional phenotype in CD8+ T-cells, nonetheless ensures their fitness for long-term maintenance during chronic infections. Importantly, TOX prevents the acquisition of the effector phenotype and triggers a response in T-cells that protects the host form overwhelming immunopathology.", "T-cells, developed in chronic infection, with high levels of PD-1 and low levels of cytokines could undergo re-expansion in a secondary host mouse and protect it from acute viral infection, while retaining the exhausted phenotype.", "A recent study showed that a form of NFATc1 that is both constitutively active and unable to interact with AP-1 promotes the exhaustion program and upregulates TOX expression, linking for the first time TOX to the exhaustion program."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Metabolic Control of m6A RNA Modification - eScholarship.org ---
URL: https://escholarship.org/content/qt8z134484/qt8z134484.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article by Joohwan Kim and Gina Lee (University of California Irvine) published in Metabolites (2021, Vol. 11, Issue 2) examining how metabolites, nutrients, and cellular metabolic pathways regulate N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modification. m6A is the most prevalent and evolutionarily conserved internal mRNA modification, controlling RNA metabolism including stability and translation, and plays roles in development and disease states such as cancer and diabetes.

The review describes the key m6A enzymes (writers, erasers, and readers): The main writer complex consists of METTL3/METTL14 and adaptor proteins (WTAP, VIRMA, ZC3H13, RBM15), which methylates adenosine at the RRA*CH consensus motif. Other methyltransferases include METTL16 (targets UACA*GAGAA motif in snRNA/mRNAs, functions as homodimer), METTL5-TRMT112 (18S rRNA), and ZCCHC4 (28S rRNA, which has an autoinhibitory loop that opens upon substrate binding). Readers (YTHDF, YTHDC, HNRNP, IGF2BP) control RNA fate including splicing, stability, export, and translation. Erasers are ALKBH5 and FTO (ALKB family dioxygenases), making m6A a reversible process.

Regulation of m6A by metabolites: S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) is the universal methyl donor produced by one-carbon metabolism (folate and methionine cycles, with serine providing one-carbon units). The product SAH acts as a strong allosteric inhibitor of METTL3. Notably, the Km of SAM for METTL3 (~100 nM) is much lower than cellular SAM levels (>10 µM), while SAH levels (~5 µM) exceed the IC50 (~1 µM), suggesting complex regulatory dynamics. METTL16 provides SAM-dependent feedback regulation: high SAM leads to MAT2A mRNA methylation and degradation, while low SAM causes METTL16 to tightly bind MAT2A mRNA and promote its splicing/translation to synthesize more SAM.

Eraser regulation: FTO and ALKBH5 are αKG (α-ketoglutarate)-Fe(II)-O2-dependent dioxygenases. TCA cycle metabolites succinate and fumarate act as competitive inhibitors of αKG (IC50 ~30 µM for ALKBH5, ~150 µM for FTO; citrate also inhibits with IC50 ~300 µM). The oncometabolite R-2-hydroxyglutarate (R-2HG), produced by mutant IDH enzymes, competitively inhibits FTO (IC50 ~130 µM). Surprisingly, R-2HG exhibited anti-tumor activity by increasing m6A on cMyc and CEBPA mRNAs, destabilizing these growth-promoting transcripts. Iron (Fe(II), Km ~1 µM for ALKBH5) is essential for demethylation, with iron delivery via transferrin complexes released in lysosomes. NADPH and NADH were identified as FTO activators (NADPH strongest, ~90% induction in FTO vs ~30% in ALKBH5); the pentose phosphate pathway is the main NADPH source, and NADK/G6PD knockdown increased cellular m6A levels. FTO-mediated m6A demethylation is linked to adipogenesis, and FTO knockout mice resist high-fat diet-induced obesity.

The review concludes by highlighting future directions: studying whether low methionine diets (which extend lifespan) work via m6A methyltransferase inhibition, tissue-specific m6A differences potentially driven by metabolic activities, connections between nutrient-signaling pathways (mTORC1, PI3K-Akt, AMPK) and m6A regulation, metabolic regulation of m6A readers, and the potential for combined targeting of cancer metabolism and m6A enzymes for therapeutics. The work was funded with no external funding.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The N6-adenosine methylation (m6A or N6-methyladenosine) is the most abundant mRNA internal modification." "As this is a reversible enzymatic process, metabolites can directly influence the flux of this reaction by serving as substrates and/or allosteric regulators." "R-2HG suppressed the growth of tumors expressing high FTO levels. Specifically, the R-2HG-induced m6A modification of cMyc and CEBPA mRNAs destabilized these transcripts. Therefore, by decreasing the growth-promoting cMyc and CEBP signaling activities, R-2HG suppresses tumor progression." "From the screen, NADH and NADPH were identified, along with vitamin C (ascorbate), a previously known cofactor of dioxygenases... NADPH was the strongest binding partner and activator of FTO, followed by NADH." "Fto knockout mice are resistant to high-fat diet-induced obesity, while the overexpression of Fto results in obesity."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: M6A Demethylase ALKBH5 in Human Diseases: From Structure to Mechanisms ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/2/157

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Biomolecules (2025, Vol. 15, Issue 2, Article 157; DOI: 10.3390/biom15020157) by Miaochun Fang, Liwen Ye, Yue Zhu, Linying Huang, and Shun Xu from Guangdong Medical University, China. The review comprehensively examines the m6A demethylase ALKBH5 in human diseases, from structure to mechanisms.

The article covers:
1. **Background**: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant, dynamically reversible internal modification in eukaryotic RNA, enriched in long internal exons, stop codons, or 3' UTRs of mRNA and lncRNAs, occurring in the RRACH consensus motif. It regulates gene expression post-transcriptionally. ALKBH5 is one of two major endogenous m6A demethylases (along with FTO).

2. **Structure**: ALKBH5 belongs to the AlkB subfamily of Fe(II)/αKG dioxygenases (9 members: ALKBH 1-8 and FTO). The human ALKBH5 gene is localized at 17p11.2 and encodes a 395-amino-acid protein (~43 kD). Its core structure consists of a double-stranded β-helix (DSBH) domain containing eight antiparallel β-strands and two nucleotide recognition loops (NRL1 and NRL2). The DSBH scaffolds three Fe(II)-binding residues (His204, Asp206, His266) forming a conserved HXDXnH module. NRL2 contains Lys147 and Arg148 that interact with RNA phosphate backbones for substrate recognition.

3. **Catalytic mechanism**: Demethylation involves dioxygen activation and substrate oxidation. Fe(II) and 2OG activate dioxygen, forming a Fe(IV)-oxo intermediate that oxidizes inert C-H bonds. ALKBH5 demethylates m6A by oxidizing N6-methyl, forming a transient N6-hydroxymethyladenosine (hm6A) intermediate that spontaneously decomposes into adenosine within a few hours, releasing formaldehyde and producing succinate.

4. **Biological functions**: ALKBH5 localizes to Golgi apparatus, cytosol, and nuclear speckles. It regulates RNA metabolism (splicing, translation, mRNA stability - though with both stabilizing and destabilizing effects on different mRNAs), cell proliferation (G0/G1 cell cycle arrest when silenced), apoptosis, development (essential for spermatogenesis, oocyte meiosis, neuronal development), oxidative stress response, mental stress response (hyperactivated in major depressive disorder), and cancer (acts as both oncogene in some cancers and tumor suppressor in others, including lung, glioblastoma, hepatocellular, colorectal, gastric, endometrial, and breast cancers).

5. **Human diseases**:
   - **Metabolic disorders**: Regulates glucose metabolism (glycolysis, aerobic oxidation, pentose phosphate pathway, glycogen synthesis, gluconeogenesis) and lipid metabolism (adipogenesis regulation); role in T2DM remains controversial.
   - **Immune system disorders**: Involved in neutrophil mobilization, bacterial infection defense, viral infection immunity (PEDV, rotavirus, HIV-1), rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, tumor immune microenvironment shaping, and autoimmune diseases (EAE, thyroid disease, primary Sjögren's syndrome).
   - **Reproductive system disorders**: Promotes reproductive system cancers (ovarian, cervical, endometrial), essential for germ cell (sperm and oocyte) development, and impacts miscarriage (both increasing and reducing risk depending on context).

6. **Inhibitors**: The review highlights development of ALKBH5 inhibitors, though the concluding sections on inhibitor development were not fully captured in the available text.

The article has 25 citations, 6,717 article views, and belongs to the Molecular Medicine section of Biomolecules. The review emphasizes that ALKBH5 shows bidirectional roles in multiple diseases and represents a potential therapeutic target but requires further investigation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant, dynamically reversible, and evolutionarily conserved internal chemical modification in eukaryotic RNA."
</key_excerpts>
